title: Payouts soar as use of force by Burlington police on Black residents hits record high
description:
“The fact that the data show record-high disparities in use-of-force on Black subjects demands our immediate attention and a meaningful response,” Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Payouts soar as use of force by Burlington police on Black residents hits record high.
text:
The Burlington Police Department on North Avenue in Burlington on Thursday, August 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
When a call for police to help discipline a child over stealing escalated into a hospital visit, Burlington mother Cathy Austrian filed a complaint with the city’s police oversight body hoping to spur change. 
The body, the Police Commission, found the incident — in which officers restrained Austrian’s son, who is Black and has emotional and intellectual disabilities, and called in paramedics to inject him with ketamine  — to be a troubling violation of the department’s own use-of-force policy. But the department disagreed, with then Police Chief Jon Murad backing the officers’ actions as an appropriate use-of-force. 
So Austrian turned to the courts, suing the city in 2024 over excessive use-of-force and racial discrimination. This summer that case was settled for $150,000. 
The lawsuit was the latest in a string of five cases Burlington has settled over police use-of-force since 2019, amounting to nearly $1.5 million in payouts to aggrieved parties, and costing the city an additional $747,500 in legal fees, according to records obtained by VTDigger through a public records request. Like Austrian’s case, all five involve people who are Black or have mental health challenges. 
“The case is over, but the family’s hope is that the consequences from this case actually continue to drive change forward,” Austrian’s lawyer, Hillary Rich, an attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont, said. 
As the cost of use-of-force has risen for Burlington taxpayers in recent years, the department’s use-of-force against Black people has too, reaching an all-time high of 99 in 2025, according to the department’s latest data, recorded since 2012. Black residents are overrepresented among these use-of-force incidents, at six times the rate of their population share, a VTDigger analysis of the department’s data found.  
The city and department began working years ago, amid a national reckoning over policing, to address use-of-force. But the numbers show a persistent racial gap, and advocates and Black leaders say not enough has been done to close it.
“The fact that the data show record-high disparities in use-of-force on Black subjects demands our immediate attention and a meaningful response,” Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak wrote in a statement to VTDigger, in response to the disparities. “These trends are not simply a data point to monitor — they are a serious equity concern that requires us to examine how policing practices, policies, and broader community conditions contribute to these outcomes.”
‘What do we do about it as a city?’
Following a 2020 executive order from Gov. Phil Scott, in the wake of the death of George Floyd, the Burlington police department adopted a statewide policy on use-of-force, encouraging deescalation tactics to reduce the need for force during encounters. 
In 2025, use-of-force rose to the highest number since recorded data in 2012. 
As overall incidents rose, so did the number of both Black and white people involved. But incidents involving Black people hit a record 99 in 2025, compared with an annual average of 56 in prior years. In 2025, 230 white people were involved in use-of-force incidents, compared with an average of 177 in previous years.
The raw numbers, however, point to a racial disparity: Black people’s share of use-of-force incidents outpaces both their share of the population and their share of arrests. 
The rate at which Black people experience use-of-force in Burlington is roughly six times greater than their share of the population. Black people represented 28% of total use-of-force incidents in 2025 but only around 4.7% of the Burlington population, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. White people represented 65% of use-of-force incidents in 2025 and 85% of the city’s population.    
Black people have made up 16% of all arrests in Burlington since 2012, but 24% of use-of-force incidents since 2012 — a 50% higher representation in use-of-force incidents relative to arrests. White people have made up 70% of arrests since 2012, and represent 70% of use-of-force subjects. 
Relative to their share of interactions with the police, Black people were represented in use-of-force incidents at nearly three times the rate of white people in 2025. Black people were disproportionately injured during use-of-force incidents with Burlington police in 2025. 
Stephanie Seguino, a University of Vermont economist who studies racial disparities in Vermont traffic stops, said there tend to be two explanations for these disparities: Black behavior is more criminal or Black people are perceived to be more criminal. Police departments often use the former explanation, she said, while research points to the latter to be true. 
Seguino, a former member of the city’s Police Commission, sought to target implicit bias when she was on the Commission in 2021, which recommended further training for such bias when responding to Austrian’s complaint. 
Interim Police Chief Shawn Burke said the department follows guidance from the Vermont Criminal Justice Council for implicit bias training under Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing policy. 
“The rates reported by BPD on their internal reviews of their data, is for their review to look for disparities in how they police their community. The data suggest a disparity exists, but does not establish the basis of the disparity or that biased policing occurred,” Christopher Brickell, executive director of the Vermont Criminal Justice Council, wrote in a statement to VTDigger. 
When presenting the 2025 use-of-force data during a Police Commission meeting in May, Burke said the department needs to “interrogate the data” and “keep asking questions about it,” regarding the apparent racial disparities. He contextualized the rise in use-of-force incidents by a rise in gunfire incidents since 2022. 
Stephanie Seguino in her office in Burlington on Thursday, August 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Seguino said she historically has not seen meaningful analysis of the data occur. 
“What do we do about it as a city, especially given these lawsuits that have cost taxpayers a lot of money, and that’s the problem that I see. There’s no inquisitiveness, there’s no desire to dig deeper or even to identify it as a problem,” she said. 
In a statement to VTDigger, a spokesperson for the Mayor’s Office said the city has been examining the data in recent months and is now “at a point where we need to do a qualitative dive on specific incidents to better understand any trends.” 
In that review, the city has identified two areas where they see the greatest racial disparity: 3.5% of Black trespass incidents resulted in use-of-force in 2025, compared to 1.6% for white trespass incidents. And 18.2% of Black disorderly conduct incidents resulted in use-of-force compared to 10.3% of white disorderly conduct incidents. 
‘How much it has cost the city’ 
While Austrian’s case was the most recent to be settled with the city, the largest was an excessive use-of-force case involving three Black brothers — Albin, Charlie and Jeremie Meli — who settled with the city in 2023 for $750,000. It was filed the same year as another lawsuit that alleged excessive use-of-force against Mabior Jok, who is also Black, which settled for $215,000. 
Former Burlington City Councilor Ali Dieng remembers approving those settlements during his time on the council. He worried that the payouts, paid for in part by the city’s insurer and the city’s liability insurance reserve fund, would cause the city’s insurance premiums to rise. 
“Unnecessary use-of-force for those two cases, it was not right and do you see how much it has cost the city,” Dieng said.
The city’s liability insurance premiums have risen over the past five years but it has done so on par with inflation rates, according to information provided by the Mayor’s Office. 
Cities often pay millions each year to settle police misconduct cases. New York City, for example, averages $170 million in police settlement spending per year, while a smaller city like Cambridge, Massachusetts, averages at $11,400 per year, according to an analysis by The Marshall Project. Cambridge has a population of 122,588 people, while Burlington’s population is only 44,019. 
Seguino expressed concern that on top of the near $1.5 million the city has paid in settlements, taxpayers fronted additional legal fees to represent these cases. The city spent $747,500 in legal fees to defend the five cases, according to information provided by the Mayor’s Office. 
Ali Deng on North Avenue in Burlington on Thursday, August 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
For Dieng and Seguino, this amount creates an accountability concern because an officer can repeatedly use excessive force but face little consequence while the cost is shifted to the public. 
In one of the five cases, an officer punched Douglas Kilburn, a man in poor mental health who was later found dead, according to court filings. The officer faced no discipline, and instead received a letter of reprimand for swearing during the altercation, then-Police Chief Jon Murad announced in 2020 after an investigation. 
The officer is now tied to another excessive use-of-force lawsuit currently pending in U.S. District Court that alleges that he used excessive force against another individual and that the department has “intentionally failed” to train, discipline or supervise city police officers. Murad, the police chief during the incident, declined to comment, and the city’s lawyers could not be reached for comment in time for publication. 
In the Kilburn case, which the city settled for $45,000, as well as the Austrian case, the department has deemed the officers’ use-of-force as appropriate. But Rich and Seguino see them as an example of officers not following the department’s commitment to deescalation. 
The department’s use-of-force policy has a strong emphasis on deescalation. In 2025, the department facilitated a refresher training for officers in its primary deescalation program, called Integrating Communications, Assessment, and Tactics, a spokesperson for the Mayor’s Office told VTDigger. 
“In those instances, we’re very methodical about seizing opportunities in which to create distance, contain people within a dwelling or a physical area, where then we can begin a communication strategy, either using crisis negotiators or in concert with our social workers that we have on team or the street outreach team,” Burke said in an interview with VTDigger, describing its mental health response
One of those mental health response teams, CARES mental health response program, which was created in the wake of the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, was terminated by the city late last year. City council members warned that gaps in crisis response could remain despite the Howard Center taking on some of the work.
The Rev. Mark Hughes, executive director of the Vermont Racial Justice Alliance, also expressed concern that the city has been backtracking on its commitments made during 2020, referencing a landmark resolution passed by the City Council in 2020, which outlined steps to systematically address racial disparities.
“This question was asked and answered five years ago,” Hughes said, referring to how to address racial disparities in the city’s policing. For him, the solution goes beyond more implicit bias training for police officers, and instead requires systematically addressing racial disparities throughout various city departments by utilizing the city’s Racial Equity, Inclusion and Belonging office. That office has been used to examine use-of-force disparities, according to the Mayor’s Office. 
“This process included engagement with REIB (Racial Equity, Inclusion and Belonging) Director Dr. Kelli Perkins, who was very helpful in developing new questions of the data,” the mayor’s spokesperson wrote in its statement to VTDigger. 
But for Hughes, addressing the racial disparities goes beyond examining the data and means accountability for the police department.  
“The city has got to make some tough decision because there is no reason why we should have to live in a city that is normative — that our law enforcement officers are just going to be more aggressive,” Hughes said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Payouts soar as use of force by Burlington police on Black residents hits record high.

title: Missouri child abuse investigators are overwhelmed again as backlogs return
description: JOPLIN — Ashley Allen had worked almost four years as a child abuse and neglect investigator for the Missouri Children’s Division when she quit in April.  Some days it seemed like the printer in her Jasper County office never stopped churning out reports from the state’s child abuse and neglect hotline, Allen told The Independent. text:
Ashley Allen, of Joplin, quit her job as an investigator for the Missouri Children's Division in April due to an overwhelming caseload. Now she works as a case manager for First Steps, which provides services for families with young children with disabilities. Allen also founded a nonprofit, Community Closet of Joplin, that distributes donated clothing and goods to people in need. (Steph Quinn / Missouri Independent).JOPLIN — Ashley Allen had worked almost four years as a child abuse and neglect investigator for the Missouri Children’s Division when she quit in April. 
Some days it seemed like the printer in her Jasper County office never stopped churning out reports from the state’s child abuse and neglect hotline, Allen told The Independent. She’d get two or three reports each day — more, if colleagues called out. 
Usually, she had 24 hours to verify a child’s safety. For emergencies, she had three. Often, she found herself driving across the county with little information to guide her search.
“I have a list of people to call and things to type, but I just got a three-hour emergency,” Allen said. “I have to run to Reeds to go find a family with no address and no name.”
The thing was, she loved the work. She loved advocating for families, and she “tried to go above and beyond” to work with them to keep kids in their homes when it was safe.
A punishing caseload and intensifying pressure to complete checklists and clear cases made the work overwhelming, Allen said. 
The day she quit, Allen said she felt so anxious she “wanted to throw up.”
“It’s those emails, like, ‘Hey, why haven’t you done this yet?’” Allen said. “I’m doing 10 other things, and I don’t feel that case is ready to close yet.”
The division measures its child abuse and neglect caseloads against a goal of no more than 15 open cases per worker at any given time — the same standard used by national organizations like the Child Welfare League of America to accredit state agencies. Allen had more than 30 open cases when she left.
Allen’s caseload is no longer unusual, and in parts of the state it would now count as light.
‘This job is impossible’: High turnover, low morale plague Missouri child welfare agency

For most of 2025, data from the Missouri Department of Social Services showed fewer than 10 of the state’s 46 judicial circuits averaged more than 15 open cases per worker at the end of the month. At the end of June this year, workers in 21 of Missouri’s 46 circuits averaged more than 15 open cases, though that number decreased to 13 in July, the most recent month of available data.
Workers in St. Louis County have had the highest average caseloads in the state each month this year. They averaged 89 open cases at the end of June, while St. Louis City workers averaged 55. At the end of July, the county figure had climbed to 97 and the city’s to 58.
As workers juggle more reports, it’s taking them longer to clear cases, prolonging the division’s intervention before a case is closed or referred to the court system. 
The number of circuits where the average time to close a report over the past six months exceeded 45 days more than quintupled, from four to 23, between January and July. In St. Louis County, the average case as of the end of July took 144 days, or four and a half months. 
State law requires the division to finish investigations within 45 days, and allows more time only when staff document a specific reason — a pending forensic test, a prosecutor’s written certification, a witness who can’t be reached. Even then, the law sets a hard limit: 90 days, or 120 for reports involving sexual abuse. In St. Louis County, the average investigation took 144 days. 
Allen said that when workers are spread too thin, it directly impacts children and families.
“You’ve got kids to see that may or may not be unsafe, but you don’t get around to seeing them because of all the other things that you have to do, and it puts some families on the backburner,” Allen said. “And there are kids that are safe where we’re pestering their families.”  
Children’s Division Director Sara Smith declined an interview request from The Independent. She also declined to comment on submitted questions about current staff turnover rates, caseloads and efforts to move children in foster care toward reunification or permanent placements, citing a legislative hearing scheduled for Aug. 26 that will cover related topics.
The division has struggled with staffing shortages and high turnover for years. But current and former employees interviewed by The Independent say the latest surge in caseloads is being compounded by something else: new rules and increasingly prescriptive policies that require more steps to move cases forward.
Workers and supervisors said changes introduced over the past year and a half have added layers of consultation, checklists and supervisory review while limiting their discretion in working with families. The result, they said, is that cases take longer to close even as workers are being asked to handle more of them.
 Workers ‘do not know which way is up’

In 2020, citing diminished state revenue due to the COVID-19 pandemic, then-Gov. Mike Parson cut 300 state jobs. Of those, 200 were in the Social Services Department. Almost 100 were in the Children’s Division. Former Department of Social Services Acting Director Jennifer Tidball turned down a funding offer from the state Senate to help with staffing.
With fewer investigators, turnover of frontline division staff — including investigators, foster care case managers and hotline workers — reached 55% in fiscal year 2022, and staff in September 2022 told The Independent, “this job is impossible.” The number of backlogged cases statewide surpassed 10,000 by September 2023, with more than 6,000 overdue cases in St. Louis alone. 
Lawmakers that year approved funding to add back 100 positions, after former division director Darrell Missey pitched a plan to tamp down caseloads and shift the division’s focus toward preventing kids from going into foster care. By September 2024 the division had cleared 80% of the backlog. At the end of fiscal year 2025, turnover among frontline division staff was 40%.
The backlogs climbed back anyway — and not because the state stopped filling jobs. As of the end of November last year, only 79 positions across the division were vacant. The current state budget this year funds 1,781 field positions, which is the same as last year. 
Frontline staff interviewed by The Independent point to policy changes enacted over the last year and a half as a major reason cases are taking longer to move through the system. 
With caseloads and backlogs again mounting, the division is poised to restructure its abuse and neglect response team on Sept. 1 to place workers under more centralized state supervision and create specialized career pathways. The changes will not add staff and, according to a January email from the division to The Independent, are intended to help retain workers and create “a more tenured, experienced workforce.”
Ahead of the restructuring, workers said, the division has rushed to tackle investigation backlogs by assigning experienced staff from other teams, including foster care case managers, to help with overdue cases, leaving those teams overextended.
Daniel Johnston, a supervisor with the division, told The Independent that staff from his office who agreed to temporarily help with investigations earlier this year were asked to stay on as workers quit due to the workload and rapid policy changes. Johnston said he was speaking in an individual capacity because he did not have permission to speak on behalf of the division.
“As more staff left and the state office did not allow us to replace them, they were asked to do more,” Johnston said. 
The time workers spent on investigations, Johnston said, “took them away from working with children and families to get permanency” through reunification, adoption or legal guardianship. Normally, those workers meet with children and their biological and foster families, providing services, helping families navigate legal processes and making sure kids’ needs are met while in state custody.

“I feel this delayed cases by at least a few months,” Johnston said.
There were 12,633 Missouri children in foster care at the end of June, according to state data. That’s 11.4% less than September 2021, when the number of kids in foster care peaked at 14,265. But it’s 14.4% more than a five-year low of 11,041 in February 2025. 
The increase began roughly around the same time the division was rewriting the policies that staff say were designed to keep children out of state custody.

One current division employee said workers in their office have so many open cases that they “do not know which way is up.” The employee spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation.
“I think that creates a more dangerous environment for children when you have investigators with 50 cases open and they can’t remember what they’ve done from one case to the next,” they said.
A statement from the department said the restructuring was based on staff feedback and is intended to “better balance workloads, provide more focused training and support to team members, and create greater consistency in how we respond to children and families across Missouri.”
Parents who have experienced assessments or investigations by the division described frequent caseworker turnover and mixed messages due to miscommunication or changing policies.
Angel Ornelas, of Oakville in south St. Louis County, whose son was placed in foster care in August 2025 because the state determined his medical needs weren’t being met, told The Independent her son’s caseworker confided to her that she was planning to quit. Ornelas’ son, who is still in foster care, has had several caseworkers.
“She told us she was going to quit because of how many cases were coming in,” Ornelas said. “She first went from 10 cases as a new person, and so many people were coming in. So now she had 50 cases at her desk.”
“She said, ‘I can’t do this,’” Ornelas said.
  Restructuring 

The restructuring is part of ongoing efforts by the Children’s Division to address longstanding problems of staff turnover and high caseloads without increasing funding.
In a January email to The Independent, the department described the creation of specialized teams as a way to maximize “efficiency within currently allocated funding levels.”
That has included the expansion of a team focusing on older foster youth and the launch in January of a critical investigations unit, which zeros in on child fatalities and near-fatalities due to alleged abuse or neglect.
Right now, workers can be assigned any hotline report within their circuit, from an assessment to see if a family needs services to address safety concerns to an investigation involving criminal allegations and close cooperation with law enforcement. Starting in September, they’ll start off focusing on family assessments and, with experience, join teams with specialties such as newborn assessments or sexual abuse investigations. And instead of reporting to supervisors in local offices, they’ll answer to regional managers leading specialized teams.
While staff said they hope the reorganization will lighten their workload, some said that without additional staff hires, they don’t see how it could. 
A November 2025 policy required workers to meet with a supervisor within 72 hours of a potential case of abuse or neglect being assigned, even when they determined children to be safe. The same memorandum introduced three “consult guides” to structure the meetings and four checklists for supervisors to use when reviewing and submitting workers’ reports to close cases.
Three current division employees who spoke to The Independent on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retaliation pointed to changes last year to “team decision-making” meetings. The meetings brought together parents, division workers, the juvenile office and guardians ad litem at major turning points in families’ cases — prior to removals, after kids were moved into temporary placements with relatives or when foster parents were struggling.
The workers said the meetings, which included a neutral facilitator unfamiliar with the case, helped engage parents in safety planning and create stability in foster care.
Children’s Division Director Sara Smith (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
An August 2025 message alerted division staff that they should no longer conduct the meetings prior to removing children from their homes. It indicated they should continue to conduct the meetings within 10 days of a child being placed with a relative through a Temporary Alternative Placement Agreement, which is part of a 2020 state law.
An April 2026 policy instructed workers to meet with a circuit manager — their boss’s boss — whenever families scored at “high” or “very high” risk of future child abuse or neglect according to a required risk assessment form and they did not recommend either services or a child’s removal from the home. 
Allen said the form can put families under unwarranted scrutiny.
“There’s a lot of things held against families that put some families at high risk that really shouldn’t be,” Allen said. 
A point gets added to a family’s risk score if a parent was abused or neglected as a child, or if the primary caretaker “has a historic or current alcohol or drug problem.” Families who have had previous encounters with the division are also scored at higher risk, even if past reports of abuse or neglect were not substantiated. 
“They might be 20 years sober and clean now,” Allen said, “but for something that happened 20 years ago.” 
Not everyone who tracks the division thinks more workers is the answer.
Richard Wexler, executive director of the National Coalition for Child Protection Reform, an advocacy group that argues child welfare systems remove too many children, told The Independent that while he doesn’t doubt that workers are overwhelmed, he doesn’t think the division needs more staff.
Wexler, who disagreed with Missey’s approach of hiring workers to reduce backlogs, said the state should invest in concrete assistance to alleviate poverty and services for families faced with substance use disorders or mental health conditions.
And Wexler said that type of assistance should come from a separate state agency, leaving division workers to focus on families where those services weren’t enough.
“That begins to ease your caseloads,” Wexler said, adding: “Give most workers the chance to do the job, and they’re more likely to stick around, because they will not burn out the same way.” 
Johnston, the supervisor with the division, said policies are making it harder to help children and families.
“Leadership needs to give us the tools and staff to do quality work, trust our work, preserve the relationships local circuits have and get rid of unnecessary barriers that inhibit our progress,” Johnston said. “I feel like they are doing the opposite of all that.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri campaigns draw $75M in big donations, much of it from undisclosed donors
description: Roughly $75 million in large-dollar donations poured into Missouri politics this year. That’s a lot of cash for an election year with no governor or U.S. Senate race. text:
Missouri voters are increasingly being asked to settle some of the state’s biggest policy questions themselves. They just may never know who spent millions trying to persuade them (Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector).Roughly $75 million in large-dollar donations poured into Missouri politics this year.
That’s a lot of cash for an election year with no governor or U.S. Senate race.
Where did all that money go? More than $42 million flowed to committees fighting over constitutional amendments, referendums and other ballot measures. Amendments 4 and 5, the Republican-backed proposals that 80% of voters rejected earlier this month, consumed tens of millions before a vote was cast.
And there’s still more to come, with the November abortion fight already pulling in millions in donations and campaigns over congressional redistricting and the initiative process still fighting for a spot on the ballot.
Missouri requires contributions over $5,000 to be separately reported to the state ethics commission within 48 hours, creating a running record of the biggest checks. And no one has cut more big checks this year than the Missouri REALTORS.
The trade association has put $7.3 million into Missouri campaigns this year, all but $25,000 of it aimed at ballot fights. That is more than twice the total from this year’s biggest individual donor and nearly four times what retired investor Rex Sinquefield has contributed.
For years, Sinquefield was the name most closely associated with big political checks in Missouri. He has given $1.98 million this year.
But he is no longer No. 1 among individuals. Mike Rayner, a retired businessman from Town and Country, has given $3.1 million this year, making him Missouri’s largest individual political donor so far.
There is another difference between Rayner and Sinquefield and many of the biggest players on the list: We know who they are.
Roughly $23 million in large donations came through advocacy nonprofits that do not publicly disclose their donors.
Missouri Action gave $6.5 million. Secure Missouri gave $2.95 million. Missouri Promise Inc. gave just over $2 million. American Policy Coalition gave $2.05 million. The Fairness Project gave $1.75 million.
Millions already pouring into Missouri ballot fights over taxes and majority rule

There are plenty more farther down the list.
Most of that anonymous money was concentrated in support of Amendment 5, the GOP-backed plan to overhaul Missouri’s tax code. But the dark money pendulum swings in the other ideological direction if you include donations late last year to the campaign seeking to overturn Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map. Well over $4 million came from groups that don’t disclose their donors.
Federal tax law generally allows these nonprofits to keep their contributors private. So a Missourian who gives $100 to a candidate can have their name and address show up on a campaign finance report. But when a nonprofit drops $1 million into a campaign, the trail may stop at the name of an organization and a mailing address.
That doesn’t necessarily mean the source of every dollar is unknowable. Sometimes you can piece together funding through tax records, grant disclosures or other public filings. Health Forward Foundation, for example, wasn’t counted here as dark money because the origin of its wealth, a legacy healthcare endowment, is a matter of public record.
But for much of the money, the public has no right to know who supplied it. In some cases, we may never know.
About one-quarter of the large contributions came from addresses outside Missouri. But even that number can be misleading. Missouri Action and Secure Missouri use Missouri addresses. That tells you where the check was mailed from. It doesn’t tell you where the money actually came from.
Missouri voters are increasingly being asked to settle some of the state’s biggest policy questions themselves. They just may never know who spent millions trying to persuade them.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lincoln petition fraud investigation becomes political
description: Lincoln City Council and Nebraska’s leading Republican consulting firm clash in the court of public opinion.
text:
Lincoln City Councilman Brody Weber durring a press conference in Lincoln on Aug. 13, 2026 (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The fallout from alleged fraud involving three conservative-backed petitions seeking to reshape Lincoln local elections continues as the Democratic-led Lincoln City Council and Nebraska’s most influential Republican political consulting firm clash in the court of public opinion. 
City Councilman Brody Weber hosted a press conference last week calling into question the ongoing investigation by Lancaster County law enforcement of fraudulent petition signatures for three Lincoln-focused petitions. He criticized the Good Government Lincoln petition leadership for restarting the signature gathering while the investigation continues. 
A Democratic challenger to the county attorney is asking for a special prosecutor because Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon, a Republican, has ties to Republican consultants with Axiom Strategies who are involved in the petition effort. Condon has not paid Axiom for any consulting services, according to state campaign financial disclosure forms. Condon paid Red Rider Strategies for campaign consulting.
Weber, after his press conference, said there should be “independent individuals involved in the investigation.”
Before the announcement of the arrests of five out-of-state individuals who helped circulate petitions, the petition group had accused city officials of undermining their efforts. 
Weber called for a “full investigation” of the Good Government Lincoln leadership to explore whether they were involved in the fraud. He also has issues with the group blaming city officials before the investigation was public. 
“I think that some individuals need to look at themselves in the mirror before they point fingers at city officials next time,” Weber said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Chief Deputy Ben Houchin said the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office had found no evidence of a political motive for the alleged fraud in their ongoing investigation. 
Jessica Flanagain, a consultant to the Good Government Lincoln ballot campaign, said it’s “not a mystery why career politicians don’t want to see an initiative for term limits get on the ballot — it will pass overwhelmingly.” 
Flanagain, a partner at Axiom Strategies, said “criminal actors” defrauded the group and Good Government Lincoln will “fully cooperate with law enforcement.” She added that it has “stringent protocols” for its signature gathering, but the “criminals worked around it.”
A Nebraskan signs a petition for a ballot initiative. (Courtesy of Rebecca S. Gratz)
Axiom Strategies — more specifically Flanagain — runs most high-profile GOP campaigns in Nebraska. Flanagain had worked for Gov. Jim Pillen as a consultant before leaving the campaign in March. Axiom Strategies is working on the campaigns of Nebraska Rep. Mike Flood and Sen. Pete Ricketts. 
Attorney General Mike Hilgers, whose office may become involved with the petition investigation, is a client of Axiom Strategies. 
Hilgers has been criticized by the Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana group and the Nebraska Democratic Party for not taking a more public approach in the investigation. Hilgers was highly involved in legal investigations of the medical cannabis petition campaigns, which voters overwhelmingly approved. 
His investigation is waiting for a Nebraska Supreme Court ruling as he is looking to appeal a Lancaster County District Court judge’s ruling that the petition had enough valid signatures.
Before the criminal investigation, Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird’s campaign said the proposed Republican-led ballot measures come straight out of the “Donald Trump playbook,” claiming “they can’t beat Mayor Leirion, so they are trying to change the rules and misrepresent their proposals.” 
There have been ripple effects from the fraud investigation. 
Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s office announced late last week that former Omaha state Sen. Brett Lindstrom lacked enough signatures to run for Nebraska governor as a nonpartisan because a significant number of signatures “were found to be fraudulent.” 
Advocates for All Nebraskans has paused its local petition effort to establish a minimum staffing level for sworn police officers in the capital city. The group said in a press release that it was because they had seen “hostility” from Lincoln city officials and that “the local petition landscape is tainted” by a “concerning pattern of destructive political efforts run purely for profit.”
“This pause is necessary to protect our front-line officers and preserve the integrity of the ballot initiative process itself from two major destructive forces,” the press release said. 
There have been calls from Pillen and Evnen, whose term will end in January, for the state Legislature to reverse a 2015 decision that allowed paying per signature. 
Jordan Brownstein, chief executive officer of On the Ballot, a subcontractor for Good Government Lincoln, said in a statement that the organization is working with law enforcement “to ensure every bad actor involved is brought to justice and that whoever directed this sabotage is identified and exposed.”
“The fraud that was discovered is outrageous and the worst kind of dirty political tricks. It victimizes voters, the democratic process and the petition sponsors,” Brownstein said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: A truce to end the redistricting wars
authors: Special to the New Jersey Monitor
description: Requiring congressional district boundaries to hew closely to county lines could help end the redistricting wars, writes Brad Van Arnum. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
text:
Requiring congressional district boundaries to hew closely to county lines could help end the redistricting wars, writes Brad Van Arnum.By Brad Van Arnum
Ever since Texas redrew its Congressional map last summer, redistricting and gerrymandering have become part of a national debate. Texas’ decision to redraw its House map in the middle of the decade, which was legal but not the norm, spurred Missouri, California, and Florida (among other states) to redraw their own maps, with both parties hoping to gain more House seats in the process.
Unfortunately, these new House maps have come at the expense of voters in these states, who might now find themselves in a House district that makes little geographical sense. In Texas, for instance, the new Congressional map was designed to elect more Republicans by drawing long, tendril-shaped districts that combine the state’s cities with distant rural areas. The redistricting wars over the last year have produced contorted maps that violate the basic idea of representation in the House: that districts should be drawn to represent distinct areas of a state with common legislative interests.
The recent Supreme Court decision Louisiana v. Callais has compounded the problem by taking away a crucial guardrail that had restrained some of the worst excesses of gerrymandering. By weakening Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, the Supreme Court has allowed states to weaken the political power of voters of color. Already, in the brief time since the decision, multiple states in the South have passed new House maps that deliberately divide minority communities, making it much harder for voters in these communities to have a voice in Congress.
Democratic-led states have already responded to the Supreme Court’s decision by threatening to redraw their own House maps with additional districts that would elect Democrats. However, this would require large cities to be divided across more House districts, meaning that blue states would be following the same playbook of vote dilution in order to offset the maps that southern states have drawn. In doing so, they would be reducing the opportunity for those districts to elect racial minorities.
As hard as it might be to envision a truce in the redistricting wars, I think the moment calls for imagining a new guardrail that both parties could live with. One potential solution would be a national rule limiting how many times a state’s House map could split a county.
Specifically, Congress could write legislation stating that counties could only be split one time beyond what is mathematically needed. Compared to other potential remedies, this one would be straightforward, difficult for states to circumvent, and unlikely to be struck down by courts.
House districts generally contain about 750,000 people, so this rule would mean that any county with a population under that threshold (the exact figure varies from state by state, and can be found by dividing a state’s total population by its number of House districts) could only be split once. As one example, under a national county rule such as the one I am proposing, Mercer County in New Jersey, which is home to roughly 400,000 people, could only be split once, meaning that it could contain two House districts at most.
A national law limiting county splits would prevent both Democrats and Republicans from engaging in the worst forms of gerrymandering. Because counties are fixed geographical units that almost never change boundaries (and the law could stipulate that 2020 county boundaries be used, to discourage states from changing them), both parties would find drawing maps to their political advantage much more difficult. Fortuitously, several major cities in America, such as Baltimore, Jacksonville, Indianapolis, and Philadelphia, coincide with county boundaries, meaning that a national rule against excessive county splitting would protect these and other cities from being needlessly divided in Congressional maps.
New Jersey offers an especially interesting example of how a national law could help protect counties from being unduly split. We only have 21 counties, with just three (Bergen, Essex, and Middlesex) that are populous enough to be split twice. Every other county in the state could only be split once, which would make gerrymandering the Garden State much more difficult.
In the hypothetical House map below, which I drew using a program known as Dave’s Redistricting, I have divided New Jersey into 12 districts that I think represent distinct areas of the state, while meeting the requirements of my proposed national rule against excessive county splits. I used our present congressional map as a starting point, though I had to make major changes in certain places, such as in Monmouth and Union counties (both of which are currently split more than would be permissible under my proposal).

Even though a national rule limiting county splits might be tough to apply in a state with as few counties as New Jersey, it would still allow for a reasonable House map to be drawn. The map I drew demonstrates that increasing minority representation is still possible even with constraints on county splitting. Not only would my 8th, 9th, and 10th districts likely elect members of color to Congress, but in my map, I’ve made the 3rd a majority-minority district (which it is not currently), and I’ve also redrawn the 12th district so as to avoid dividing the Asian-American community of central New Jersey, as the current map does.
With the midterms approaching this fall, and the possibility of both the House and Senate switching party control, it is imperative to find a way to prevent any further escalation of the redistricting wars. Much damage has already been done to representative democracy in just the last year, but it is not impossible to devise a new guardrail that both parties could tolerate. The status quo of free-for-all gerrymandering simply cannot become the new norm.
Brad Van Arnum is a resident of West Windsor who closely follows redistricting. He has a bachelor’s degree in economics from The College of New Jersey and a master’s degree in political science from Rutgers University.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: The national focus on politicians’ health is making its way into the Oklahoma GOP race for governor
description: Mike Mazzei’s performance in recent debates has created a conundrum for him and our state’s pool of undecided Republican voters who are still trying to suss out their best nominee for governor. Most charitably, some of Mazzei’s public appearances have just felt awkward and uncomfortable when watching from afar.  At times, he’s managed to come […]
text:
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, during Maze’s watch party in Bixby, Okla. Supporters gathered to watch results in the Republican primary election. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)
Mike Mazzei’s performance in recent debates has created a conundrum for him and our state’s pool of undecided Republican voters who are still trying to suss out their best nominee for governor.
Most charitably, some of Mazzei’s public appearances have just felt awkward and uncomfortable when watching from afar. 
At times, he’s managed to come across as plain mean, reminiscent of behaviors exemplified by President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Mazzei.
During a Republican primary debate, the 61-year-old babbled some weird gibberish in an attempt to mock a debate moderator who got tongue-tied, and then he appeared to silently laugh at a joke only he viewed as funny. His three GOP opponents sharing the stage with him didn’t even crack a grin.
He has struggled to answer direct questions, smiled at odd times, argued with a different debate moderator and even held up a finger indicating that she should wait on him to finish when she was trying to get him back on topic and enforce time limits.
At that same debate, Mazzei and his GOP runoff opponent Gentner Drummond were asked the unusual question of whether they would make their health records and tax returns available to the public. (Both said they would, though Mazzei qualified that by noting the great thing about the primary process is Oklahomans already get to see if a candidate has the endurance and stamina to go all the way.)
Both men are competing to win a pivotal nomination on Aug. 25. For the past four gubernatorial elections, the winner of the GOP primary election has gone on to win in November.
While it’s common for U.S. presidential candidates to release their tax returns and for the sitting president to release the results of his annual physical, that’s not typically an expectation of Oklahoma’s governor.
In response to the debate question, Drummond last week released his health screening results, which shows he suffers from hypertension and high cholesterol that’s controlled with medication. However, as of writing this, he had yet to release his tax returns.
But Drummond also went a step further: He took a drug test.
And he challenged Mazzei to do the same.
Drummond, 62, insisted to Oklahoma Voice that he wasn’t “suggesting one way or the other” that Mazzei is unable to perform the job (although NonDoc reported Drummond’s campaign manager, Matt Parker, said last month that voters are “realizing there is something not quite right about Mike Mazzei”).
And that appears to be exactly what Drummond is doing by suddenly releasing his health records and the results of a drug test that, by the way, came back negative.
Rather than put all this speculation to rest, Mazzei told Oklahoma Voice earlier this month that he would not discuss releasing his health or financial records.
Mazzei went a step further by acknowledging the elephant in the room and said that his opponent’s campaign is suggesting he’s unfit for office and “probably on some unhelpful medication.”
He said he’s not been on any medication since a 2008 car accident, in which he suffered nerve damage to his back and missed many votes while serving as a state senator. And Mazzei also insisted that he’s not on “any pain medication now.”
In prior elections, Oklahomans might have taken him at his word and moved on.
But those days are gone.
If Mazzei’s campaign doesn’t believe that, it need only look at the growing focus on health that federal officials have faced. 
Surely Mazzei has not forgotten the fervor over deciding whether former U.S. President Joe Biden underwent a cognitive decline while in office, and the rampant speculation that his allies covered it up. Questions about the Democrat’s mental acuity and physical endurance grew more pointed after a disastrous debate performance against then Republican nominee Donald Trump.
Trump, who recently turned 80, has faced continuing scrutiny about his health and age. 
But even more recently, Americans were left to speculate over the wellbeing of Kentucky’s Republican U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, who abruptly vanished without explanation from public sight. After weeks of speculation and mounting pressure, McConnell, who at one time served as the president of the Senate, released a statement saying that he had fallen and been hospitalized since. He said he had received “excellent care” while also dealing with a case of mild pneumonia.
Oklahomans deserve proof and peace of mind that they’re electing someone with the stamina and acuity to represent them on a statewide and national stage. 
And voters deserve to know if Mazzei is just a bad public speaker and debater or if that’s being exacerbated by some other underlying health condition.
This should not be a guessing game.
Mazzei makes his living crunching numbers, not public speaking. Drummond is an experienced orator who makes his living as an attorney arguing. So maybe it’s simply a matter of being outperformed.
I’m glad that Mazzei says he’s not using pain medicines. 
But if he’s not, why isn’t he willing to prove it by releasing a copy of his most recent physical and a drug test?
That way he can put all this speculation to bed, and voters can focus on issues that affect them most.

name: WyoFile
title: Early voting in Wyoming’s primary election trails historic 2022 contest, clerks say
authors: Rebecca Huntington, CJ Baker, Powell Tribune, Jonathan Gallardo, Gillette News Record, Jasmine Hall, Jackson Hole News&Guide, and Hannah Romero, Green River Star
description:
Some officials reported voters frustrated by election rule changes. Monday marks the last day for early voting before Wyoming’s primary, when voters will decide on a slew of high-profile open seats.
The post Early voting in Wyoming’s primary election trails historic 2022 contest, clerks say appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming’s primary election features a number of high-profile races, including open contests for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House. But even with that attention, fewer Wyomingites are casting early ballots compared to the last time they decided on a similar slate of prominent races.
Heading into the final weekend before Tuesday’s primary, officials in a handful of Wyoming counties reported lower turnout this year than in 2022.  Some election officials chalked that up to that election’s heated race between Republicans Liz Cheney and Harriet Hageman, which drove turnout to historic levels. 
A 2023 election law change that shortened early and absentee voting to 28 days beginning in 2024, down from 45 days in 2022, might have also played a role. Wyoming has changed several election laws in recent years, and some of those changes are still catching voters by surprise, local officials say. 
In Campbell County, where Republicans made up 96% to 97% of all ballots cast in the last two primaries, more than 3,300 people had voted as of Friday afternoon. More than 2,800 people voted at the elections office, and 488 ballots had been mailed in or dropped off. 
Those figures slightly trailed 2022, which was the busiest primary election in Campbell County history, with more than 12,000 ballots cast. That year, 40% of all ballots — 4,990 — were cast before Election Day. That included 3,941 people who voted at the elections office, and 1,049 who dropped off or mailed in their ballots.
Michelle Leiker, Campbell County’s elections coordinator, has seen a steady stream of voters, but her office hasn’t experienced long lines. They’ve made some changes to streamline the process, such as having voters fill out the application for an absentee ballot before they step into the office. 
Leiker has fielded questions from voters frustrated about not being able to change their party, the result of a 2023 law intended to curb crossover voting. The law requires voters wanting to change their party to do so before candidates for partisan positions begin filing for office. A 30-day residency requirement has also raised questions, Leiker said.
But for the most part, it’s been business as usual, at least in Campbell County.
Hard to match 2022 primary
On the other side of the state, Teton County Clerk Maureen Murphy anticipated more early voters would arrive Monday, but she wasn’t sure Teton County would beat its 2022 stats, when all of the county and statewide executive offices were last on the ballot.
“I do think that the Liz Cheney and Harriet Hageman representative race that year really brought people out,” Murphy said. “Just because it was such a national news story.” 
The contest between Cheney and Hageman was arguably the most closely watched congressional race in the state’s history. Cheney angered many of the state’s Republicans for her vocal criticism of President Donald Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, and Trump himself visited the state to support Hageman, his pick to unseat one of his biggest political rivals at the time. Pundits viewed the election as a referendum on Trump, and the race drew international attention.
Donald Trump embraces Wyoming’s then congressional candidate Harriet Hageman at a “Save America” rally in Casper on, May 28, 2022. Hageman, who was endorsed by Trump ran against Liz Cheney. (Natalie Behring)
Ultimately, voters cast more than 182,000 ballots across Wyoming, which was the highest raw count in a midterm primary election on record and the highest turnout rate since 1994, according to WyoFile reporting from the time. About 40% of Wyoming’s voting-age population participated.
Voting picks up 
At lunchtime Friday, a line of voters wound up the stairs as people waited to cast ballots at the election office in the basement of the Teton County Administration Building.
“It started upticking on Wednesday,” Murphy said. 
By Friday, Teton County had beat its early voting turnout for the 2024 primary. Two years ago, 1,045 residents voted in-person early and 403 turned in absentee ballots. 
In comparison, 1,748 people had voted early as of Friday afternoon. But absentee ballots were down, with just 179 delivered. During the fiery congressional race four years ago, 3,274 Teton County residents voted early, nearly double this year’s figure so far, while 808 mailed or dropped off absentee ballots, more than four times as many as this year’s tally to date. 
The 2022 election cycle brought about a significant change to Wyoming elections. Before 2024, Wyoming voters could change their party affiliation up to Election Day and at the polls. Lawmakers passed House Bill 103 during the 2023 session, which created a deadline to change or declare party affiliations.
A voter trades a registration ticket for a ballot in Teton County on Nov. 3, 2020. (Angus M. Thuermer, Jr/WyoFile)
The law was spurred by a 2022 mass exodus of Democrats who registered as Republicans in the primary to vote for Cheney. Teton County led the charge, and 75% of the county’s nearly 6,000 registered Republicans voted for the then-congresswoman. Meanwhile, Hageman won 66.3% of the entire state.
Even though an election cycle has already passed with the party affiliation change in place, Murphy and other Teton County election officials have said voters are still taken by surprise. 
A new residency rule passed in 2025 has also caught Wyoming newcomers unaware, Murphy said. House Bill 146 dictates that Wyoming residents can’t register to vote unless they’ve lived in the state for at least 30 days. The clerk’s office has had to ask prospective voters who have driver’s licenses or identification from other states to come back with proof of 30-day residency. 
“That’s been the biggest confusing one,” Murphy said.
Early voting up, absentee ballots down
After a slow start to early and absentee voting in Park County, Elections Deputy Katie Johnson said things picked up late last week, putting the northwestern Wyoming county on track for what she expects to be a “very typical turnout for us.”
As of 2 p.m. Friday, more than 3,200 Park County voters — or roughly 19% of all the registered voters — had cast their ballots. Of those, more than 93% cast Republican ballots. 
The figure includes 2,193 people who voted early at the courthouse in Cody, and that number was steadily rising as Johnson spoke. 
Early voting had been tepid through early last week, but starting on Wednesday, “it has just ballooned,” Johnson said. Nearly 250 early voters cast ballots at the courthouse on Thursday, with Friday on pace for even higher participation.
“Hopefully, the enthusiasm continues,” Johnson said.
Park County should easily break its previous primary record of 2,350 early votes, set in 2022, but it’s a different story with absentee voting. As of Friday, roughly 1,040 absentee ballots had been submitted to the clerk’s office, representing a steep drop from the 2,300 absentees cast in the 2022 primary.
It is possible that the county could approach the 1,525 absentee votes cast in the 2024 primary, as there were another 600 of the ballots yet to be returned as of Friday. For whatever reason, “people have just been slow to return those,” Johnson said.
It was a similar story in Natrona County, where absentee ballots lagged behind both 2024 and 2022. 
“We have had 1,987 requests and have received 1,401 as of 10:30 this morning,” Clerk Tracy Good said in a Friday email. That’s down from 2,472 mail-in ballots submitted two years ago and 2,613 in 2022. 
Voters cast early ballots on Friday, April 14, 2026, at the Natrona County Courthouse in Casper, Wyoming. (Joshua Wolfson/WyoFile)
But those voting early and in person had cast 2,945 ballots through Thursday, surging past 2024 when 2,097 people had cast ballots with two days left to vote. So far, Natrona County’s early voting still trails 2022 when a total of 4,200 people voted early. 
When asked about the impact of new election laws, Good reported “no major effects.”
Park County has a slew of contested local races, almost entirely on the Republican side, but Johnson said there isn’t any particular contest pulling in voters. That’s unlike the 2022 primary featuring Cheney and Hageman, when some early voters came in and openly shared their thoughts on the candidates (Park County Republicans went for Hageman by a 3:1 margin).
This time around, “we just get people coming in saying, ‘Well, it’s time to vote,’ or ‘doing my civic duty,’” Johnson said. “There’s not anybody that’s, like, fired up.”
The deputy clerk said the Legislature’s new 30-day residency requirement has not caused any significant issues. Johnson said she’s only had to turn away one couple — as the former Georgians had moved to Park County just four days before they sought to vote — while another man had to go home and retrieve a utility bill to prove how long he’d lived in Cody.
“I really anticipated that we would run into an issue at some point, but we haven’t,” Johnson said, “and everybody has been very understanding of the law change and, if they need extra documentation, bringing that with them.”
She noted that much of the county’s turnout will hinge on how many people show up on Election Day itself.
Sweetwater County has also experienced a jump in early voting and drop in absentee ballots. 
As of Friday, 929 residents voted early, while 757 delivered absentee ballots via the mail, dropbox or hand delivery to the election office. In previous elections absentee ballots were more popular, with 1,550 cast in 2022 and 1,134 in 2024. In contrast, fewer people tended to vote early, with 880 early voters in 2022 and 506 in 2024. 
A voter casts her ballot in the Sweetwater County primary election on Aug. 20, 2024. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
County Clerk Cindy Swenson said Sweetwater County has not been largely impacted by new election laws. 
“Most registered voters have a Wyoming Driver’s License or Wyoming ID, therefore, not too many people have had to provide proof of residency so far,” Swenson said in an email. “The party change deadline has been the most challenging for our voters and brings in the most complaints.”
Swenson also noted that some voters had expressed concern about not being able to vote if they are married since the name on their driver’s license does not match the last name on their birth certificate. However, she said, “this has not stopped anyone from voting in Sweetwater County.” 
As well as leading the Teton County Clerk’s Office, Murphy is president of the County Clerks’ Association of Wyoming. Clerks are keeping their heads down while running their own elections right now, and she wasn’t aware of any statewide turnout trends for early voting, she said. But she noted that many counties don’t have in-person early voting, and even fewer have dropboxes for absentee ballots. Three people need to man a polling center and some smaller counties don’t have the staff, she said. Many Wyomingites mail in their absentee ballots. 
But Laramie County also noted an increase in early in-person voting but a decrease in absentee ballots compared to 2024. This year both types of voting are still below 2022, when there was a 45-day voting period and barn-burner of a House race. 
When it comes to the 2026 primary, Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee said in a Friday email that there was one thing that was firing up voters in her county.
“Numerous voters have expressed irritation at being bombarded by political mailers, calls, and text messages,” Lee said.
The post Early voting in Wyoming’s primary election trails historic 2022 contest, clerks say appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: Closing the trust gap
description:
Wyomingites understand our state’s potential. They just need decision-makers to really listen, writes guest columnist Josh Dorrell.
The post Closing the trust gap appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
At the 3rd Thursday Street Festival in downtown Sheridan last month, someone told me something I haven’t stopped thinking about.

Opinion

She asked about the challenges the Wyoming Business Council and other institutions faced during this year’s legislative session. She suggested low voter turnout in the 2024 primary election might explain it. I asked whether apathy caused the 27% turnout. She said, “I think it was trust.” She must have seen the quizzical look on my face, because she continued, “We used to trust that the people running for office had our best interests in mind, and we used to trust that they would listen to what really mattered.” I saw disappointment on her face, but also resolve.
We’ve heard this same theme in listening sessions, ice cream socials, pancake breakfasts and happy hours across the state this summer. I keep thinking about it because it isn’t cynical. It isn’t angry.
It’s a recognition that Wyomingites expect more. They want leaders who listen to what is happening in their communities, understand the consequences and then act. 
In that serious 3rd Thursday conversation, juxtaposed by a festive community, I could sense the woman’s frustration that she couldn’t connect with the people making decisions shaping her city. Where the gap between what she knew and what got decided was widening. 
This summer, the Business Council is doing our part to understand and ultimately close that gap. We’ve held conversations in over 32 locations, and we’re still going — not to present a plan, but to build one together. We’re asking people what Wyoming’s economy looks like from where they stand, what’s getting in the way and what we should be doing about it. Thousands of Wyomingites have weighed in, both in person and online.
I expected to hear frustration, and I did. When we asked them to describe our economy in a single word, two words came up more than any others: “stagnant” and “potential.” 
Read those together, and you have the whole story. Wyoming is full of people who can see what is possible but are frustrated that we are not getting there fast enough. That’s not apathy. Apathy doesn’t show up to be heard. Apathy doesn’t drive an hour to a listening session or spend a lunch break telling a state agency what’s broken. What we found instead was a state full of people paying close attention, waiting to see if attention runs both ways.
What struck me most about these conversations — and it’s a little humbling — is that over and over, people thanked us for listening without getting defensive. For asking a question and then being quiet long enough to hear the answer.
That’s the real issue. Too many of us stopped believing the conversations happening around kitchen tables, in coffee shops and throughout our communities ever make their way into the rooms where decisions are made. Younger Wyomingites said it most directly. They are trying to build careers and lives in their home state while quietly concluding their voices are not being taken seriously. That’s a warning.
On Aug. 13, we asked nearly 600 Wyomingites how much they believed that what they say shapes what gets decided. The top two responses were “some” (39%) and “very little” (29%). Those aren’t accusations. They are a measurement of exactly how much distance we have left to close.
For Wyomingites who have concluded that showing up doesn’t change anything, I would ask you to test that assumption. Speak up. Attend the meeting. Send the email. Ask the hard question. Vote. Then keep paying attention after Election Day.
There is a difference between not being heard and choosing not to speak.
But the government has an obligation, too.
Listening cannot become another exercise where we collect comments, thank everyone for participating and then move on. If we ask Wyomingites to give us their time, experiences and ideas, we owe them something in return: action, accountability and an explanation of what happens next.
In the coming weeks, everything we’ve heard this summer will go where it belongs: into the rooms where decisions are made and in front of people with the authority to act.
So here’s where I’ve landed. Wyoming doesn’t have a trust problem, not really. Wyomingites still love this place fiercely, and you can hear it in every hard thing they tell us. What Wyoming has is an action gap: a distance between what people say and whether it changes anything. That gap is the most fixable problem we found all summer, and closing it is the most important work in front of us.
Whether those we elect to listen take action remains to be seen, but what I know for sure is we’ll be carrying the message of the “Team of Thousands,” and those in office will have a hard time ignoring it.

name: WyoFile
title: Scientists link the West’s extreme snow drought to climate change
description:
New study finds snow droughts could be more than four times as frequent than before the industrial revolution.
The post Scientists link the West’s extreme snow drought to climate change appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Bare ground flanked the edges of ski runs. It rained in December. Flower beds never went dormant. Snow plows sat gathering rust. As these conditions took hold across Greater Yellowstone and the West last winter, Marianne Cowherd, a snow scientist at Montana State University, was hit with question after question. 
“People around me would ask if the snow was so bad because of climate change, and I would find myself having to answer, ‘Probably?’” Cowherd said. “But I don’t really know for sure. And I said that a lot of times over the course of the winter.” 
She wasn’t alone. Researchers in Colorado and Wyoming faced similar queries. So they teamed up to find answers. “By the time March and April rolled around, we decided that really we should try to do the formal steps that you need to take to understand whether or not it was caused or attributable to climate change,” Cowherd said.
They found that, yes, human-caused climate change is to blame for this year’s snow drought. According to their research, recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, a lack of snow this severe across the West is more than 4 times more likely to occur because of human-caused warming.
The burning of fossil fuels, like coal or oil, for power releases greenhouse gases that trap heat and cause the Earth to warm. While there are many types of planet-warming emissions, the main contributors to warming are carbon dioxide and methane. Scientists have monitored atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1958, and it has increased every year since. 
This warming increases drought events, decreasing annual snowfall and prompting spring runoff earlier each year. Higher temperatures and lower precipitation also elongates the wildfire season and a warmer climate drives more intense, large-scale fires on the landscape. In ecosystems like Greater Yellowstone, warming impacts wildlife like wolverines dependent on robust snowpacks to build dens, or the timing of the spring green-up that ungulates such as elk and pronghorn rely on to sustain migration. Climate change also disrupts agriculture and harms human health with extreme heat, and increases natural disasters. 
“It’s not something that we would expect to happen in the way that it did if there were no climate change occurring,” Cowherd added.
That likelihood is even higher in areas that were especially hard hit, like the Upper Colorado River Basin, where climate change made this winter’s extreme snow drought 14 times more likely.  
The south end of Fremont Lake — Wyoming’s second largest natural water body — was totally free of ice on February 1, 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
The research stemmed from a high-resolution dataset compiled by the U.S. National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research supercomputer, housed in Cheyenne that tracks how watersheds change across a landscape, going all the way back to 1850. Cowherd and her co-authors were able to compare this winter to winters before the industrial revolution, when humanity’s large-scale planet-warming emissions hadn’t yet begun. 
“We’re not just looking at the average temperature for this year and saying, OK, it was really warm, therefore this is a climate-attributed drought,” Cowherd explained. “We’re actually building a good guess of what the world would have been like if there were no climate change, and that’s how we do the actual attribution.”
The researchers’ models predict that in the current climate, snow drought would occur every 6.8 years, compared to just once every 30 years during preindustrial times. Cowherd says it’s important to understand events like this snow drought, because of how vital snow is for replenishing water resources in the mostly arid Mountain West. She hopes land managers can use findings like these to proactively plan for the warming that has already occurred. But she also sees a thread of hope in the research. 
“This is a negative impact of anthropogenic climate change, and that is difficult to hear, difficult to learn, but it also means that it’s within our control to a certain degree,” she said. “If we pursue these lower emission scenarios … we would expect years like this to happen less frequently.”

text:
Blue Cross of Idaho held Idaho's contract for government employee health insurance since 2004. (Photo courtesy of Blue Cross of Idaho)Months after one of Idaho’s largest health insurers asked the state for help with unusual billing practices by a North Idaho hospital, the insurer is still waiting for assistance. 
Blue Cross argues that Post Falls ER & Hospital is out-of-network for health insurers and instead relies heavily on a new arbitration process created by Congress. And the insurer argues the hospital’s methods are driving up the cost of health care — with the hospital being paid more than usual for services — that will trickle back to patients through premium hikes. 
Insurer asks Idaho Department of Insurance to investigate hospital billing practice

In November, Blue Cross asked the Idaho Department of Insurance to investigate the hospital’s use of the tool. Since then, the regulatory state agency hasn’t released information about the status of its investigation.
By the spring, the Idaho Legislature was considering a bill to try to prevent freestanding emergency rooms, such as the Post Falls facility, from billing for high charges. But the bill failed, after one powerful lawmaker hoped the two businesses could resolve their dispute without legislative intervention. 
Now, Blue Cross is getting the word out to patients.
“You have in-network options,” a new billboard in North Idaho says. “Post Falls ER & Hospital isn’t one of them.”
A Blue Cross website calls the facility the only hospital in Idaho that isn’t in-network for the insurer.
In a July Facebook post, the hospital seemed to push back.
“We accept all commercial insurance regardless of network status!” Post Falls ER & Hospital posted. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How does the arbitration process work?

The Post Falls ER & Hospital opened in 2024. The facility was Nutex Health’s first micro-hospital in Idaho. The firm recently filed an application to add a micro-hospital in Meridian, the Idaho Statesman reported. 
In arbitration, which Blue Cross says it often loses, the hospital is often receiving payouts that are four to five times as much as the insurer typically pays other providers for the same services, the insurer recently told state officials.
In one case, the hospital charged more than $14,000 for a diagnosis code meant for treating a migraine, the insurer said.
“Post Falls ER and Hospital is not a victim of unfair reimbursement rates; rather, the numbers clearly show they are a statistical outlier using the (arbitration) process as a primary revenue strategy, not a last resort to obtain a fair and reasonable payment,” Blue Cross of Idaho’s Chief Strategy Officer Drew Hobby wrote in a May letter to the Idaho Department of Insurance, which the Idaho Capital Sun obtained from Blue Cross. 
After contract dispute with East Idaho hospital, Legislature’s task force to study health insurers

Nutex Health Chief Operating Officer Wesley Bamburg denied the company’s strategy was to rely heavily on the arbitration process, saying the company’s hope in every market it serves “is to be in network under fair, market-based contracts.” But he said its North Idaho micro-hospital is not in network for any health insurers. 
“We have several active and productive conversations underway with multiple health plans, at various stages, and we are encouraged by the progress being made,” he said by email. “Our goal is long-term agreements that support patient access while ensuring the services we provide to this community remain sustainable.
In Blue Cross’s letter to the state in May, the insurer described its difficulty negotiating with Nutex. The two companies only negotiated by email until March, when the Legislature considered its bill to force a deal, Hobby wrote. 
After a back and forth over several reimbursement rates — which are redacted in the letter — Blue Cross officials agreed to a rate proposed by Nutex on Sept. 4, according to the letter. Then almost a week later, Blue Cross says that Nutex “turned down their own offer.” One offer that the hospital previously rejected would’ve been “the highest rate in the state of Idaho,” the letter said. 
Since then, Blue Cross of Idaho Vice President for Provider Partnerships Todd York said the insurer has run into delays or non-responses. He said he’s had to hire two temporary workers and pull two other full-time staff off other work to handle the high load of arbitrations. 
Bamburg, with Nutex, said he wouldn’t comment on contract negotiations. Asked why the company turned down its own offer in negotiations with Blue Cross, he said, “What we can say generally is that a contract negotiation is never about a single number in isolation.”
“As discussions progress, it is normal for both parties to refine their positions and evaluate alternatives as additional information becomes available. That is how negotiations are supposed to work, and it is how durable agreements are reached,” Bamburg said. 
 When Congress created the arbitration process, officials didn’t expect many claims. Then they ballooned.

Blue Cross’ issues with the hospital seem to be part of a bigger problem.
In 2021, when Congress first created the arbitration process — formally called Independent Dispute Resolution — through the federal No Surprises Act, federal officials only predicted it would be used 22,000 times each year. In the years since, 3.4 million disputes came through, according to the Congressional Budget Office. 
National news outlets have highlighted how the process is being used — including New York Times coverage about a surgeon earning up to $440,000 for breast reductions, and a STAT investigation into how Nutex Health’s finances have changed under the new arbitration process. 
Under the federal law, arbiters can only pick what the health insurers and providers claim is fair payment, not to meet their offers in between.
Idaho’s U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, who chairs the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement that he’d be open to revising the process.
“Allegations of misuse and abuse of the independent dispute resolution process are deeply concerning and risk undermining patient protections Congress intended with enactment of the No Surprises Act,” Crapo said in a written statement. “Congress and the Administration should work together to identify and close loopholes, hold bad actors accountable and ensure the law works for patients as intended.”
