CONTACT US



In an Idaho legislative hearing on a bill to attempt to rein in the practice, Senate Bill 1319, the state senator sponsoring the bill, Sen. Treg Bernt, R-Meridian, turned over much of his presentation time to Blue Cross.
“What we’ve seen is this business model is replacing one surprise bill with another surprise bill,” Mike Reynoldson, Blue Cross’s senior vice president of government affairs and public relations, told state lawmakers in a February committee hearing.
Under the federal law that created the arbitration, patients are protected from unexpected bills at hospitals. But, he said, insurers will likely need to pass on high costs from arbitrated health expenses to consumers. 
“Because when the price of emergency care goes up, the next year, when Idaho insurers set their insurance premiums and their insurance rates, we have to take into consideration those excessive amounts that were paid to these entities,” Reynoldson said. “This is a bill about controlling the cost of health care.”
 Idaho lawmaker halts bill to intervene in Blue Cross’s dispute with Post Falls ER & Hospital

Rep. Jordan Redman, R-Coeur d’Alene, speaks from the Idaho House floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
After the Idaho bill passed the Senate widely on a 24-11 vote, it never advanced out of the House Business Committee. The committee’s chairman, Rep. Jordan Redman, R-Coeur d’Alene, said in an interview that he’d met with the hospital and the insurer and hoped the two could reach a deal without the Legislature stepping in.
“You guys should be able to figure out how to work together and come to an agreement, right?” Redman said in an interview. “Where you hear one side of the story, you hear the other side of the story — it’s probably somewhere in the middle (of) where, actually, you guys need to meet.”
Redman saw the bill as forcing the hospital to enter an agreement for set pay rates. 
“If that doesn’t work for their business model, … the last thing we want is for hospitals to be closing around the state and not have services for the constituency,” Redman said. 
If the two parties can’t land on common ground, he anticipated the Legislature would revisit the issue next year. 
“And we’ll probably be having the same conversation,” Redman said. 
The status of an investigation by the Idaho Department of Insurance is unclear. The agency declined an interview but confirmed it is still looking into the issue.
“The Department can confirm that we are reviewing concerns related to Post Falls Emergency Room and Hospital and Nutex,” Department of Insurance spokesperson Julie Robinson said. “Once our review is complete, we will be able to provide a more detailed response.”
The Department of Insurance denied two public records requests for communications between agency staff and the hospital and insurer, citing an exception to the state’s public records law for documents related to reports by public agencies responsible for regulation of “financial institutions” as well as a state law related to the agency that exempts working papers from public release.

title: Rural, impoverished areas of Alabama lack access to attorneys
description: Large swaths of Alabama lack a sufficient number of attorneys to help residents with legal issues, according to Harvesters of Hope, a legal nonprofit that is recruiting attorneys to underserved areas. Based on figures obtained from the organization, almost two-thirds of the counties in the state can be classified as legal deserts, places with less […]
text:
A courtroom in the Scott M. Matheson Courthouse in Salt Lake City is pictured on Wednesday, June 10, 2026. Rural areas in Alabama, particularly impoverished ones, have a shortage of attorneys. (Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) 


Key points

According to a nonprofit, almost two-thirds of counties in Alabama are legal deserts, defined as having less than one attorney per 1,000 people.
The shortages are particularly acute in impoverished areas and minority communities, limiting access to legal representation in proceedings like evictions.
Suggested remedies include loan forgiveness for working in rural areas and improved technology access.




Large swaths of Alabama lack a sufficient number of attorneys to help residents with legal issues, according to Harvesters of Hope, a legal nonprofit that is recruiting attorneys to underserved areas.
Based on figures obtained from the organization, almost two-thirds of the counties in the state can be classified as legal deserts, places with less than one attorney per 1,000 people.
“That means some of those people are not getting legal services, or not as well because that is just the economics of it, time and effort,” said Tom Heflin, one of the founders of Harvesters of Hope.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The dearth of attorneys is particularly large in impoverished areas and minority communities. In theory, Alabama has enough attorneys listed in the Alabama Bar Association for the population, which is a ratio of roughly 340 people for every attorney. But the figure overstates the practical number who can serve the legal needs of the residents living in the state.
According to Harvesters of Hope, about 78% of attorneys in Alabama are based in seven counties.
Tom Perry, a co-founder of Harvesters of Hope and a former president of the Alabama Bar Association, said that the number is smaller after considering the people on the Alabama Bar Association website based outside the state or retired.
A subset of those serves as judges, prosecutors and counsel for governments who may not be able to provide legal services for the community.

“You can see that leaves us with a very low number in counties,” Perry said. “We had some counties with one lawyer or no lawyers.”
The national average for the U.S. is about four attorneys for every 1,000 residents, according to the American Bar Association.

Aging attorneys

According to Harvesters of Hope, Coosa County is in the worst shape with one licensed attorney per 3,397 people, with Lamar close behind at one attorney for  3,393 people. Hale County has a ratio of 2,462:1; Randolph County has a ratio of 2,344:1 and Pickens County has a ratio of  2,063:1.
Attorneys in affected areas are also getting older. Coosa County, for example, currently has three attorneys who can serve slightly more than 10,000 residents. However, by 2030, only one of them will be younger than 70 years old. In Lamar County, another legal desert, four attorneys are available to provide legal services to the 13,500 people living in the area, but by 2030, three will be less than 70 years old.
A report published last fall by the Legal Services Corporation, a federally funded nonprofit that provides funding for civil legal aid for people with lower incomes, estimated that about 41% of counties in the United States qualify as legal deserts.
A study published by Iowa State University in 2025 found that most rural counties in the contiguous U.S. qualify as legal deserts. Ronald Flagg, president of Legal Services Corporation, said in an interview on Friday that while about 20% of the population lives in rural areas, only 2% of attorneys practice there.
“Almost every state, at a minimum, has pockets of rural areas which are underserved, and are deserts, versus you go out west to Alaska and other places where they are even more prevalent,” he said.
Legal deserts have a particular impact on vulnerable populations because many of the people living in such places are people of color or with those who earn lower incomes.
Hale County, located in the Black Belt, has a poverty rate of almost 24% and a Black population of 55%. Greene County, also a legal desert, has a Black population of 80%, with more than a third of residents living in poverty.
“We have seen over time  that people with professional opportunities, experiences, skills and education, are often moving out of the communities in which they were raised and going to urban areas where the jobs and economic opportunities are greater,” Flagg said.
Law school grads could earn license through work rather than bar exam in some states

A lack of earning power in rural areas can contribute to shortages, said Daniel Pasciuti, an associate professor in sociology at Georgia State University who studies access to justice.
“When you get done, you kind of have done all this work for school for years to get your law degree,” he said. “You are looking for an income, even if you are not looking to have some lavish lifestyle, you are looking to be able to survive and be able to pay off your student loans.”
That is not often possible in places that are considered legal deserts, where there are few residents to sustain a legal practice and many people unable to afford the services of an attorney.
The pull of urban areas
Even if those issues are fixed, Pasciuti said there is the issue of geography. Most law schools, and by extension law firms, are based in urban areas.
“Even as you get older, even having paid off your student loans and you don’t necessarily need the lifestyle anymore, you are now, probably, rooted in that space,” Pasciuti said. “You are not going to upend your life and move to the middle of nowhere, or the middle of some rural area, after you have been living in Atlanta for 10 years and you have your house, possibly a significant other, have kids, whatever it is.”
Alabama commission finds wide disparities in courts costs in different counties

Absent private law firms, nonprofits may step in.  Guy Lescault, executive director for Legal Services Alabama, which provides assistance on civil cases for those who qualify,  said that there are one million people who are eligible for services, many of them living in rural areas.
“We have 120,000 calls in our call center a year,” he said. “Those are people who are in rural areas that we cannot serve. Just do the numbers, if there are a million eligible clients, and we have limited offices, limited services, then it is a big problem in terms of access to justice.”
Lescault said that the primary issue that people seek help from Legal Services Alabama is affordable housing, including legal representation during eviction procedures. With limited resources, many face legal proceedings without the assistance of an attorney. That often leads to less-than-ideal outcomes for tenants.
It also creates a logistical problem for clients. If a county has only one attorney who is representing one party in a divorce, then the other party needs to find a lawyer from outside the area to serve as counsel.
People can secure an attorney who can travel, but that can also be problematic.
“If I go and advise you on an expungement, and I practice law in Birmingham and I come over to a county in the Black Belt, Marengo County or Perry County, I come to you and you might like me, we may have a rapport, but I am probably I am not going to be back to answer your questions on future matters,” Heflin said.
Harvesters of Hope is trying to address the problem by recruiting attorneys to underserved areas directly. According to the website, the nonprofit provides financial assistance, mentoring and management tools to sustain a law office in a rural area.
The organization, launched last August, placed 10 attorneys in rural counties throughout the state. An additional eight attorneys may be placed in the coming months, Heflin said.
“We are well ahead of where we set our goals,” he said.
Flagg said addressing the shortages would require incentives like loan forgiveness to encourage attorneys to work in rural areas. Allowing people without a law degree to provide select legal services may also help.
States such as Alaska and Montana, with sparsely populated areas have developed such programs.
“They developed, in the last several years, a community justice worker program where trained people who were already in the community, they may be social workers or might be healthcare workers, can be trained to help people get food stamps or help with a denial of food stamps,” Flagg said.
Using technology like video conferencing may also help.
Flagg also mentioned establishing a booth in a location to allow people to speak with an attorney.
“There is a kiosk in the library or community center where you can easily connect to a lawyer either online, or otherwise to a lawyer in a city that is some distance away in terms of driving,” he said.

description: A dozen small, rural Tennessee hospitals are at “immediate risk” for closure, potentially exacerbating a longstanding problem in a state with one of the highest hospital closure rates in the nation.  The calculation, by The Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, is drawn from examining multi-year hospital losses in institutions with limited assets[...]
text:
A new report finds 12 rural Tennessee hospitals for immediate closure (Credit: Getty images)A dozen small, rural Tennessee hospitals are at “immediate risk” for closure, potentially exacerbating a longstanding problem in a state with one of the highest hospital closure rates in the nation. 
The calculation, by The Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, is drawn from examining multi-year hospital losses in institutions with limited assets. The center also reported that 19 rural hospitals in Tennessee are “at risk” of closing.
Tennessee ranks 6th in the number of its rural small hospitals at imminent risk, according to the report. 
Rural Tennessee needs family doctors. Can $200,000 lure them to the state’s small towns?

The report does not identify the hospitals. Harold Miller, president and CEO for the center, said Friday that is intentional.
“Since things can get much better or much we wouldn’t want to label and individual hospital as being at risk of closing if it has already taken (or is taking) actions that will significantly improve its circumstances, nor would we want to label a hospital as ‘not at risk’ at the same time it is trying to solve a new financial crisis,” he said. 
Miller said it was important to understand that even hospitals that remain open may eliminate key services.
Two rural hospitals in the state have closed their inpatient services, the report noted. 
He also stressed it is the smallest hospitals that face the greatest risk of closure.
Rural hospitals are at risk for closing in nearly every state, but Tennessee ranks high among closures.
The state lost 10 rural hospitals since 2015. Only Texas has seen a greater number of hospital closures in that time period: 14. 
The biggest driver of closures are losses incurred for caring for private insurance payments, the report finds. Private insurers are paying less than the real cost of services. In Tennessee, hospitals may also be impacted by future Medicaid cuts and the decision not to expand the Medicaid program to include more low-income patients.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Issue Spotlight: Gubernatorial candidates on future of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion
description: Arkansas’ next governor will likely help shape the state’s Medicaid expansion, which faces an uncertain future. The state requested permission to continue the program through the end of 2028 after the Trump administration denied its request to renew the program, which provides health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income Arkansans.  When Medicaid was crea[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas’ next governor will likely help shape the state’s Medicaid expansion, which faces an uncertain future.
The state requested permission to continue the program through the end of 2028 after the Trump administration denied its request to renew the program, which provides health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income Arkansans. 
When Medicaid was created in 1965, it was only for parents of young children and people with disabilities. The Affordable Care Act allowed states to expand coverage, and in 2013, Arkansas became the first state to use a hybrid expansion model that purchases private health insurance for low-income people with federal funds. 
The federal waiver for Arkansas’ program, originally known as the Private Option and now called Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME, expires on Dec. 31. 
The state has asked the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to keep Arkansas’ expansion valid for two more years to give the state time to develop a new program.  
Here’s what Arkansas’ three gubernatorial candidates said about how they would tackle this issue if they win November’s election:
Libertarian Colt Shelby 
Colt Shelby said the governor should take a lead role in ensuring Arkansas’ version of Medicaid expansion is extended indefinitely. The program is critical to providing more than 200,000 Arkansans healthcare, and that coverage is “a crucial lifeline” for rural hospitals, he said.
Shelby said every Medicaid program needs to be evaluated, and as governor, he would create a team to reform Arkansas Medicaid.
Issue Spotlight: What Arkansas gubernatorial candidates say about legalizing recreational marijuana

Shelby said in an email that the federal government “has to give flexibility with Medicaid to better address our specific health care needs.”
“We have to stop trying to copy and paste things that are not working,” he wrote.
BlueCross BlueShield provides three of ARHOME’s six plans. Centene Corporation, who provides the other three plans, has announced it will stop participating in the program next year. 
Supporting Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion includes bringing additional carriers into the marketplace, Shelby said. 
“Our Governor should work to help expand healthcare coverage and to support our rural healthcare providers and not be a consistent roadblock,” he said. “I will not tolerate the current cronies and the current political profiteers to determine health care.”
Shelby said he would ask big corporations to hire full-time employees instead of having people work less than 40 hours “so they can avoid insurance.” Additionally, Shelby said he would focus on a one-on-one program to identify the workforce and connect them to good-paying jobs that provide healthcare, which would avoid the need for Medicaid coverage.
“I would root out any abuse in the system and build more accountability to make sure those billing Medicaid are playing by the rules,” he said. 
Democratic Sen. Fred Love
State Sen. Fred Love said cutting Arkansans off Medicaid is the quickest way to close more maternity wards and rural hospitals, an issue the state is already struggling with. Hospitals depend on Medicaid funding to stay open, especially in communities where there isn’t another payer source available, he said.
“We’ve been down this road before,” Love said in an email. “That’s exactly why Arkansas adopted the Private Option in 2013 and 2014, to reduce uncompensated care and prevent hospitals from collapsing under the weight of unpaid medical bills.”
Love vows order halting school vouchers if elected Arkansas governor 

The Trump and Sanders administrations have offered “no serious alternative” to Medicaid expansion, Love said. Their response to Arkansas mothers and families amounts to saying “You’re on your own. Figure it out,” he said. 
“This isn’t a healthcare plan. It’s an abandonment of responsibility,” Love said. “The quality of life as we know it will decline, when mothers who are in labor have to drive 50-100 miles to the nearest hospital to deliver their baby.”
Less than a third of Arkansas counties have hospitals with labor and delivery units, which sometimes results in women giving birth in ambulances during the long drive to the nearest facility.
As governor, Love said would prioritize keeping all Arkansans safe and with the best quality of life possible.
“The first thing we must do is, elect officials who actually care about Arkansans, not just by saying they do, but show it with actions,” he said. “Having a state surplus isn’t doing us any good, if lives are at risk.”
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders
In response to questions about how she would address Medicaid expansion, Sanders’ campaign manager referred the Advocate to a letter Department of Human Services Secretary Janet Mann sent to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services earlier this month. 
In the letter, Mann notes the program’s rejection was due to a 2025 federal law imposing budget neutrality, which requires ARHOME to not cost the federal government more than would be projected without the program. 
Mann requests a two-year extension of Arkansas’ current program waiver to provide sufficient time to wind down the existing program while developing and implementing a new system. Mann said she believed the extension is a “prudent step” that will allow officials to work with state lawmakers to develop a solution. 
“Helping capable individuals transition off the sidelines so we can focus resources on those truly in need remains a top priority,” Mann wrote. “Shifting to a new program on the same day we initiate the new work requirement policy could distract from those efforts.”
When Sanders took office in 2023, the state sought federal approval for requiring able-bodied Medicaid recipients to work, volunteer, attend school or have dependent children in order to remain eligible. Officials said Medicaid expansion enrollees who didn’t meet the requirement would not lose coverage. The state sought another work requirement waiver in 2025.
Arkansas was the first state to impose work requirements on Medicaid expansion, and more than 18,000 Arkansans lost coverage before a federal judge blocked the policy in 2019. 
Arkansas is preparing to implement work requirements for Medicaid expansion mandated by the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump last year.

title: Health coordinator, school board head running in GOP primary for Arkansas Senate seat
description: Voters in southeast Arkansas are choosing the Republican nominee Tuesday to succeed a lawmaker who stepped down to work in the attorney general’s office.  Republicans Missy Wardlaw of Hermitage and Harrell Wilson of Rison are both looking to fill the Senate District 1 seat vacated by former state Sen. Ben Gilmore. The district in southeast […]
text:
Cleveland County School Board President Harrell Wilson (left) and veterans healthcare coordinator Missy Wardlaw (right) are both vying for the Republican nomination in Senate District 1. (Photos courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State's office).Voters in southeast Arkansas are choosing the Republican nominee Tuesday to succeed a lawmaker who stepped down to work in the attorney general’s office. 
Republicans Missy Wardlaw of Hermitage and Harrell Wilson of Rison are both looking to fill the Senate District 1 seat vacated by former state Sen. Ben Gilmore. The district in southeast Arkansas is composed of Ashley, Bradley, Chicot and Cleveland counties, as well as parts of Drew, Grant, Jefferson and Lincoln counties.
Polls will open at 7:30 a.m. Tuesday and close at 7:30 p.m. Early voting for the primary began Aug. 11. Registered Democrats are unable to vote in the GOP primary, under a party rule adopted in 2025. 
The winner of the special primary will face Democratic nominee Tomeka Butler, mayor of Eudora, in Nov. 3’s general election. The winner will serve until the end of Gilmore’s term in 2029.
With the seat vacant, Republicans hold a 28-6 supermajority in the Senate. Gilmore won his 2024 reelection bid with more than 77% of the vote, beating Libertarian Asher Williams.
The longtime president of Cleveland County’s school board, Wilson entered the race with endorsements from Gilmore and the state’s top elected Republicans, including Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. He said working at his family’s sawmill business and his engagement in the community prepared him for public office.
“It gives me a different point of view than most people because of running that business,” he said. “I have always participated in community activities throughout Cleveland County to try to build up the local community, make it stronger.”
When asked what his specific policy priorities would be, Wilson noted that his general priorities were faith, family and farming, as well as cutting taxes. He also pledged to continue “defending the life of the unborn,” and fighting for farmers. 
Wardlaw, a veterans healthcare coordinator, is the wife of term-limited Republican Rep. Jeff Wardlaw. She ran for her husband’s House District 94 earlier this year but was defeated in the primary.
She counted the listening skills she said she cultivated through her work as one of her qualifications for the Senate seat.
“I’ve worked in healthcare for 20-plus years, and I get to sit down and visit with a lot of people. There’s just a lot of places where people could benefit from having help or having someone to call, and I want to be that help,” Wardlaw said.
Wardlaw said she didn’t have a single top policy priority. But she cited economic development and rural healthcare as two areas she was passionate about, and said she supported Medicaid expansion with work requirements. 
She said the Legislature should create new incentives for the forestry industry.
“Researching and learning different ways to utilize pulp, and letting our state set up incentives to try and attract those businesses to come here, so we can build jobs back in that industry,” Wardlaw said.
Both Republicans also favored cutting taxes if it was possible to do so responsibly, and allowing local governments to regulate or prohibit data centers. 
The candidates appeared to diverge on whether changes were needed to the LEARNS Act of 2023, which overhauled parts of Arkansas’ public education system and established a universal school voucher program.
Wilson, who has been on Cleveland County’s school board since 2012, said he’s seen the benefits of LEARNS in his own school district through high test scores.
“LEARNS is what we have in place, and we see the benefits of some of that right now,” Wilson said. “One of our school districts within this (Senate) district, Crossett, has made great strides in their scores and in their reading.”
To support any changes to LEARNS, he said, it would need to “benefit the kids.”
Wardlaw said she was fine with school choice and that she doesn’t see the voucher program, also known as Education Freedom Accounts, going away any time soon. At the same time, she said, the program needs more accountability — something she said would be her primary focus where the LEARNS Act is concerned if she is elected.
“I just feel that if you’re going to use tax dollars and accept them, then you should have one standardized test that everybody takes, so you can actually judge where the strengths and weaknesses are in all the (educational) settings,” Wardlaw said. 
She doesn’t think the voucher program is a bad idea, but its universal eligibility doesn’t help public education, Wardlaw added, nor was it “a smart thing” financially. When eligibility for the program was limited to students who attended poorly-performing public schools, she said, “the spending of (the voucher program) was a little more controlled.”
“I don’t think it should be a free for all for any kid to go to any school they want, and there would be no restrictions,” Wardlaw said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV DEP says Fundamental Data controls site of proposed Tucker County data center, power plant
description: The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection determined this week that Fundamental Data, the company proposing to build a massive data center and power plant complex in Tucker County, did have legal site control when it was approved for an air quality permit last year. The determination from the DEP came after the Department of […]
text:
An anti-data center yard sign sits on the side of the road outside of the Billy Motel & Bar outside of Davis in Tucker County, West Virginia, on Saturday, Nov. 1, 2025. (Photo by Caity Coyne/West Virginia Watch)The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection determined this week that Fundamental Data, the company proposing to build a massive data center and power plant complex in Tucker County, did have legal site control when it was approved for an air quality permit last year.
The determination from the DEP came after the Department of Commerce, which oversees the state’s high impact data center certification process, questioned who actually owned the land in correspondence last month.
The DEP previously gave Fundamental Data until Aug. 7 to provide evidence showing it controlled the proposed site of the development. 
Fundamental Data missed that deadline, but did provide the agency with an almost entirely redacted copy of its sale and purchase agreement for a 291-acre tract of land in Tucker County on Monday. The sale was between Western Pocahontas Properties and Fundamental Data, and occurred on July 19, 2024.
Laura Crowder, director of the Division of Air Quality, in a letter to Fundamental Data on Wednesday, said that the redactions in that agreement were appropriate as they constituted “confidential business information.” She said the redacted details were “not necessary” for the Division of Air Quality to determine legal site control. As such, she continued, the redacted land sale was “sufficient” to meet the standards under which Fundamental Data was issued an air quality permit last year.
A spokesperson for Fundamental Data said in a news release Thursday that the redacted information includes “financial terms and other negotiated commercial provisions” between the company and Western Pocahontas Properties. It does not include, per the press release, “information regarding the facility’s permitted environmental obligations, emissions limits, monitoring requirements, testing requirements or reporting obligations.”
Casey Chapman, a representative for Fundamental Data, defended the company’s choice to heavily redact information provided to the state. Since filing for an air quality permit last year, the company has faced scrutiny for its lack of transparency with the public, including residents who live near the proposed project site and who are worried about the potential consequences of the development.
“Private is not the same thing as secret,” Chapman said. “The economics and negotiated terms of a private land transaction have nothing to do with what comes out of a stack. The public has every right to know what this facility is permitted to emit and what environmental standards it must meet. Those requirements are public.”
While that information is public, other details regarding Fundamental Data’s proposed activities — including the size of the proposed structures and detailed information on emissions outside of estimates — have not been made available. Experts called to testify about the company’s proposals and who were able to see other redacted information have questioned how the company will keep emissions below required levels.
Fundamental Data said in a separate news release Friday that the determination from the DEP “provides a clear resolution” to questions over who has control of the land in Tucker County. Now, Chapman said, the company intends to ”continue advancing the Ridgeline Facility through the applicable regulatory process.”
“We said we would provide straight answers and work through the regulatory process,” Chapman said. “We did exactly that. The State reviewed the documentation, verified the property against the permitted site, and confirmed that the requirement was satisfied. We appreciate the Division’s thorough review and look forward to continuing to move the project forward.”

title: Regulate AI companies, not AI in schools, North Dakota state superintendent says
description: The leader of North Dakota’s public schools last week advised lawmakers to focus artificial intelligence regulations on companies providing AI and chatbots, but leave AI use in the classroom up to school boards and educators. Levi Bachmeier, the state superintendent of schools, testifying in front of the Legislature’s artificial intelligence and data center[...]
text:
Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier speaks about a statewide education survey on student technology use during a press conference on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The leader of North Dakota’s public schools last week advised lawmakers to focus artificial intelligence regulations on companies providing AI and chatbots, but leave AI use in the classroom up to school boards and educators.
Levi Bachmeier, the state superintendent of schools, testifying in front of the Legislature’s artificial intelligence and data center committee, expressed concern about young students and their exposure to AI, especially chatbots, but recognized AI can be a valuable tool. 
His main concern stems from chatbots that act as companions and advisors to age groups that can be easily influenced. 
“If I had to pick a villain, it would be companion chatbots,” Bachmeier said Thursday during a meeting held at Minot State University. 
North Dakota lawmakers explore options for limited regulation of AI

In his presentation, he said legislators should focus on requiring companies to make it clear that users are interacting with an AI-driven chatbot rather than a human being and put age limits on access to chatbots. 
Bachmeier said some states have banned using artificial intelligence in public schools, but he said that is an overreaction. 
He said North Dakota needs to have student safety as the top priority, including protecting their personal information, but said families and educators need to be on board when finding a balance on the use of AI. 
He said companies need to be held liable for chatbots that promote self-harm or other dangerous behavior. 
“Doing nothing to me feels potentially dangerous,” Bachmeier said. 
Later in the meeting Michael Marinaccio, executive director of the Center for Responsible Technology, said parents and educators need to make clear to students the dangers of chatbots. 
“Students need to be informed that this is distorting their brains,” Marinaccio said. 
He also called for legislation with strong age verification for access to chatbots. 
Bachmeier said an outright ban on AI in schools may deny students important educational tools. 
He said schools are not likely to have dedicated classes on how to use AI responsibly, but are more likely to incorporate it into traditional courses.
Bachmeier also advocated for technology that can set time limits on use and provide parents with information on how devices are being used. He said that monitoring could be especially helpful with school-district owned devices. 
Bachmeier also said that while school-issued devices such as iPads and laptop computers help make sure all students had access to comparable technology, schools could consider keeping those devices at school to limit screen time. 
“We may be making parenting harder,” Bachmeier said. 
The committee also heard AI can be used to produce child sexual abuse material and the long-term effects on victims.  Members also learned from experts about how chatbots and AI works, recent cases of AI platforms going rogue and AI as needed for national security. 
The meeting did not address data center development. Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, chair of the committee, said the group’s next meeting and potentially a subsequent meeting could be focused entirely around data center management and physical infrastructure. 
The committee’s next meeting is Sept. 1 at the Capitol. Written testimony can be submitted to edohm@ndlegis.gov.

description: The National Weather Service expects a dangerous heat wave to continue through Aug. 20 in West Tennessee. text:
Parts of Tennessee are expected to see extreme heat through Aug. 20, according to the National Weather Service. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The National Weather Service expects a dangerous heat wave to continue through Aug. 20 in West Tennessee.
In Memphis, the maximum heat index — what the temperature feels like to the human body — is expected to remain at or above 107 degrees through Thursday. Heat indices in more rural areas of the state are also forecast to exceed 100 degrees for most of the week.
The agency issued an extreme heat warning for the entire mid-south region through 8 p.m. Sunday. Southwest and Southern Middle Tennessee are expected to remain at slight risk for extreme heat from Aug. 22 through Aug. 27, according to NWS.
Heat indices in West Tennessee cities are expected to top 100 degrees from Aug. 15 through Aug. 20, 2026, according to the National Weather Service. (Courtesy of the National Weather Service)
“Many areas are forecast to see their hottest temperatures so far this year or even in the past few years,” NWS stated Friday. “There will be little nighttime relief from the heat and urban areas may not cool below 80 degrees Fahrenheit.”
The number of “unusually warm” summer nights has risen since 1970 in 95% of 243 major cities across the United States, according to an analysis of data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration by Climate Central, a nonprofit that tracks climate change and its impact.
The nonprofit states that human-caused climate change made extreme overnight temperatures around three times more likely across the majority of the contiguous United States, particularly in the South, Southeast and West.
Census data model: Nearly 50K Tennessee households may not have access to air conditioning

From 1970 to 2025, Memphis saw an increase of 12 nights of above-normal temperatures from June through August, according to Climate Central’s analysis. Nashville saw 28 more hot summer nights compared to 1970, and Chattanooga saw a 42-night increase.
NWS recommends limiting outdoor activity during the hottest hours of the afternoon, staying hydrated and accessing air conditioning or cooling centers if possible. 
But according to a U.S. Census data model released in May, 49,722 Tennessee households may not have access to any kind of air conditioning. An estimated 3,200 of those households are in Shelby County. 
The model is experimental, and Christopher Uejio, a Florida State University professor who modeled his own estimate of residential air conditioning across the United States in 2025, said the Census model may overestimate air conditioning access in rural areas and underestimate it in cities.
The Census model uses information from American Housing Surveys and data from the American Community Survey from 2019 through 2023. Its margin of error for Tennessee’s 49,772 households without air conditioning is plus or minus 3,972 households.

title: Heat-related illnesses spike in Colorado as climate change fuels record temperatures
description: As temperatures reached 97 degrees Fahrenheit in Colorado Springs on Aug. 8, breaking a 57-year-old daily record, attendees at a music festival held at Blocktickets Park felt the heat. More than 70 people in attendance at the Tacos and Tequila Festival were treated for heat-related illnesses, including at least seven who were hospitalized after “experiencing[...]
text:
Crowds gathered in downtown Denver for Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)As temperatures reached 97 degrees Fahrenheit in Colorado Springs on Aug. 8, breaking a 57-year-old daily record, attendees at a music festival held at Blocktickets Park felt the heat.
More than 70 people in attendance at the Tacos and Tequila Festival were treated for heat-related illnesses, including at least seven who were hospitalized after “experiencing serious symptoms of dehydration and/or intoxication,” according to the Colorado Springs Fire Department, which declared the festival a “mass casualty” event.
The festival-goers were among a record number of Coloradans who sought medical treatment for heat-related illnesses this summer, amid unprecedented extreme heat fueled by climate change — a trend that’s projected to continue to intensify for years to come, as governments around the world struggle to curb the greenhouse gas emissions pushing global temperatures higher and higher.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Between May 3 and Aug. 8, a total of 1,124 patients in 18 of Colorado’s most populous counties were hospitalized or visited an emergency department or urgent care because of heat stroke, heat exhaustion or another heat-related illness, according to data from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment’s Syndromic Surveillance Program. Data for the state’s other 46 counties is not collected as part of the program.
Those figures put Colorado on track for a heat-related illness rate of 13.6 per 10,000 medical visits in summer 2026 — surpassing the previous record of 8.9, set in 2024, and more than double the rate observed when CDPHE began tracking HRI data in 2019.
Last month was Colorado’s second-hottest July in 132 years of record-keeping, and a heat wave lasting from July 25 to 28 was the state’s hottest four-day period on record, according to a report from the Colorado Climate Center last week.
More frequent, more intense heat waves are the most direct and unambiguous result of human-caused climate change to be felt in Colorado, state climatologists found in a 2024 report. Rising levels of greenhouse gases in the Earth’s atmosphere, mostly the result of burning oil, gas and coal, caused average global temperatures to rise by more than 2.3 degrees Fahrenheit over pre-industrial levels as of 2024, according to federal data — and parts of Colorado, including much of the Western Slope, are among the areas in the U.S. where average temperature increases have been most severe.
What may sound like small upticks in monthly or yearly average temperatures can in fact mean big swings in the likelihood of extreme heat events. In the half-century before 1930, Denver recorded a high of 100 degrees or more less than once every seven years on average, according to the National Weather Service; since 2020, those days have occurred on average four times a year.
Globally, extreme heat kills more people each year than floods, hurricanes, wildfires and other weather-related disasters combined. But despite being one of the most straightforward impacts of a warming climate, this increasingly dangerous heat can be “invisible” to the public and to policymakers, said Sara Meerow, an associate professor of geography at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies planning and governance in an era of extreme heat.
“You don’t get the same dramatic photos that you do, say, from a wildfire or a hurricane, of devastation and destruction,” Meerow said in an interview. “People who are suffering from heat are often suffering alone. It doesn’t lend itself to the same sort of visible imagery, and also doesn’t always have really visible infrastructure damage.”



Quotation







Communities that haven't historically thought a lot about about heat now really have to ... When it starts to become a chronic issue for a community, then you really have to figure out how to live with this.


– Sara Meerow, associate professor of geography at the University of Colorado Boulder


That may be especially true in Colorado, where the impacts of drought and wildfire often take center stage — and where residents are less accustomed to dealing with extreme heat, even as they quickly become more frequent. One 2017 city of Denver study estimated that if global greenhouse gas emissions continued to rise, the average number of 100-degree days could reach 34 per year by 2080.
“Communities that haven’t historically thought a lot about about heat now really have to,” said Meerow. “If it’s just a couple of days, people can change their routines. They can maybe escape to the mountains, go to the pool — you can adapt quite easily to that. When it starts to become a chronic issue for a community, then you really have to figure out how to live with this.”
Worker safety
Colorado’s hazardously hot summer comes as state lawmakers have struggled to pass a law requiring employers to take concrete steps to mitigate risks from extreme temperatures in the workplace. A bill introduced in 2025 would have required employers to provide shade or shelter in extreme conditions, implement temperature-related safety plans for job sites and make water available for workers. Amid opposition from business groups, it failed to advance out of committee.
A scaled-back version of the bill, introduced earlier this year, aimed to provide employers more “flexibility” in developing their own plans to be submitted to the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment for approval. But lawmakers eventually stripped out that provision, too, passing an even narrower version requiring CDLE to collect data on temperature-related injuries and publish a “model” injury prevention plan on its website.
Injury risks for workers begin to rise at a daily heat index of 85 degrees Fahrenheit, and increase sharply above 90 degrees, according to a 2025 study that analyzed Occupational Safety and Health Administration data.
At the federal level, OSHA under President Donald Trump is moving to rescind Biden-era rules requiring employers to take steps like mandatory breaks and providing access to water and shade, The New York Times reported earlier this month.
Milton Jones, president of the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union, last week accused the Trump administration of “bowing to special interests and leaving workers at risk.” The UFCW represents tens of thousands of Colorado workers employed at meatpacking plants and grocery stores.
“Whether a UFCW member works in harvesting at a meatpacking plant in the summertime or fulfilling grocery orders outside in the sun, heat poses a potentially fatal risk to every worker,” Jones said in a statement. “Despite the progress made to establish a federal standard, the Trump administration has made it clear that it intends to side with big businesses fighting these protections rather than workers in danger of heat-related illness and death.”
Older people and people experiencing homelessness are also among those at significantly higher risk of injury, illness or death from extreme heat. Denver joined a growing number of U.S. cities when it began operating free cooling centers in 2021; all city recreation centers now open their doors as daytime cooling centers when the NWS issues a heat advisory for the region, though some advocates say the hours are too limited.
Cities like Denver — through its Office of Climate Action, Sustainability and Resiliency — are taking more proactive approaches to mitigating and managing extreme heat in the future, including through the hiring of “chief heat officers” and the development of heat action plans.
“I think all communities are going to have to do that — not just the larger, better-resourced cities in the state,” Meerow said. “The climate and the heat that we have experienced in the past is just no longer a good precedent. It’s no longer what we can expect in the future.”

title: Tough questions for North Dakota’s congressional delegation
description: The U.S. Congress recently wrapped up its work. North Dakota’s delegation is back in the state to convince constituents that the House and the Senate are not hamstrung by partisanship and, in the case of majority Republicans, are not mired in foolish fealty to an increasingly feckless president. North Dakota Sens. John Hoeven and Kevin […]
text:
North Dakota Sen. John Hoeven, left, speaks during a press conference next to Sen. Kevin Cramer and U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak at the North Dakota Petroleum Council in Bismarck on July 7, 2025. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The U.S. Congress recently wrapped up its work. North Dakota’s delegation is back in the state to convince constituents that the House and the Senate are not hamstrung by partisanship and, in the case of majority Republicans, are not mired in foolish fealty to an increasingly feckless president.
North Dakota Sens. John Hoeven and Kevin Cramer and Rep. Julie Fedorchak, Republicans all, will be doing their dog-and-pony shows across the state for the next few weeks. They will be spinning the Trumpist boilerplate which, if recent history is any guide, will be exercises in ducking tough questions while trying to explain away the president’s failing domestic and foreign policies. This will come as no surprise. It has been their modus operandi since they boarded the Trump bandwagon to drink his swill, defend his lies, pardon his boorish and revenge-driven conduct, and ignore his use of the national treasury as his personal piggybank. 
Nonetheless, North Dakotans should seek out the representative and the senators ask them questions. Suggestions from friends, colleagues and others about what to ask helped generate my list of questions. Here they are, some based on casual conversations or sometimes heated exchanges with people from every point on the political spectrum, and a few with no particular political bent at all. All are North Dakotans who understand that what happens in Washington, D.C., affects lives in their state and communities. 

Do you support the Trump tariffs, which have cost North Dakotans millions of dollars in lost Canadian tourism, increased the cost of home building, are costing farmers incalculable dollars in higher fertilizer and fuel prices, and have soured relations with one of our strongest allies and largest trading partner?
The president said he would reduce gasoline prices to $2 a gallon or lower as soon as he took office. In North Dakota, the price at the pump is near $4 a gallon and over $5 for diesel fuel. State-based trucking companies and one-truck entrepreneurs who own their own rigs are being hurt badly. The costs for food and other basics have been rising more than 3% a month, which, in effect, is a cumulative tax of thousands of dollars on American families. In light of those impacts on your constituents, do you support the administration’s economic policy?
Do you agree with the administration’s story about the Reflecting Pool liner damage, and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum’s doubling down with the vandalism story in light of evidence the pool’s problem was caused by an incompetent contractor? What is your view of the former two-term North Dakota governor’s performance at Interior?
Given that North Dakota’s elections are conducted without fraud or error, and there is no credible evidence of extensive voter fraud anywhere in the nation, why do you support Trump’s “Save America Act” that calls for so-called election reform? Furthermore, the presidency, Senate, House and majority of state governments, including North Dakota, are in Republican control? Does that mean elections where Republicans won were fraudulent?
Do you support Trump’s pardon of people convicted of crimes related to the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, which included some with North Dakota ties?

Don’t expect straight answers. North Dakota’s three Trumpelstitskins have mastered the dance, the shuck-and-jive, the duck-and-cover, the deflection and the muddle. Rep. Fedorchak will conduct her staged virtual meetings which will be filtered to favor her fans. Sen. Hoeven will appear before friendly groups to announce more federal dollars for defense contractors and big industrial agribusiness. Sen. Cramer will hit the talk radio circuit, take all questions, and grin through shallow and meaningless non-answers. Not one of them will summon the courage to criticize their president’s grifting, economic debacle, divisive meanness or failing war.
History will not be kind to these three.

title: Michigan’s cyclosporiasis cases near 14,000 as outbreak continues
description: Michigan has documented 13,909 cases of cyclosporiasis, according to the state’s Department of Health and Human Services, up from the 12,485 cases reported last Thursday. The department is issuing weekly updates on the number of documented cases with weekly updates on hospitalizations, as well as cases recorded in each of Michigan’s 83 counties. A total […]
text:
The Department of Health and Human Services, Lansing | Susan J. DemasMichigan has documented 13,909 cases of cyclosporiasis, according to the state’s Department of Health and Human Services, up from the 12,485 cases reported last Thursday.
The department is issuing weekly updates on the number of documented cases with weekly updates on hospitalizations, as well as cases recorded in each of Michigan’s 83 counties.
A total of 314 people have been hospitalized with cyclosporiasis, up from 279 reported last Thursday. There have also been two deaths, which were reported earlier this month.
Cyclosporiasis has been detected in 73 counties. Wayne, Oakland, Washtenaw, Ingham and Genesee counties have the highest number of reported cases.
The state health department announced on July 1 that it was investigating the outbreak, which is caused by the microscopic Cyclospora parasite and spreads through contaminated food or water. Symptoms can emerge two days to two weeks after exposure and include watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, cramping, bloating, increased gas, nausea and fatigue.
On Aug. 6, the state dropped its recommendations for residents to purchase whole heads of lettuce rather than bagged salad greens, and to remove their outer layers, wash the inner leaves and cook them when possible. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As new case reports slow and emergency department visits decline, the state recommends residents observe basic food safety practices such as handwashing, separating foods that could contain harmful germs like raw meat or unwashed fruits and vegetables during preparation, and cooking food to the proper temperature to kill germs.
On July 17, Taylor Farms de Mexico issued a voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico. On July 24, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said it is continuing its investigation into infections linked to iceberg lettuce from the region along with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state and local health departments.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services says its data suggests that the majority of contaminated produce is likely no longer available for consumption, though it advises residents to continue to avoid recalled lettuce.
The CDC is issuing weekly updates on cyclosporiasis cases, documenting 13,895 cases as of Aug. 11, with 10,455 cases – including many from Michigan – yet to be confirmed through laboratory testing.
The federal agency notes its reports do not include probable cases, which may result in lower case counts than those reported by state health departments. 
The CDC is investigating multiple clusters of Cyclospora cases including a multistate outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce affecting 15 states: Arkansas,  Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
Michigan remains the hardest hit state, with the CDC recording up to 6,999 cases.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: From headlines to campaign ads: how the Memphis Safe Task Force narrative went unchallenged
description: In January, I published an open letter to the Memphis media. It was not an attack on journalists. It was an appeal to journalism. My argument was straightforward: if Memphis was going to have an informed public conversation about crime, policing and public safety, local media would have to do more than repeat official statements. […]
text:
Claims about the success of the Memphis Safe Task Force have been repeated and amplified into campaign ads. Pictured: task force agents conduct a traffic stop in January. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht/Tennessee Lookout)In January, I published an open letter to the Memphis media. It was not an attack on journalists. It was an appeal to journalism.
My argument was straightforward: if Memphis was going to have an informed public conversation about crime, policing and public safety, local media would have to do more than repeat official statements. It would have to interrogate them. It would have to examine the assumptions beneath the headlines, test public claims against available evidence and ask whether the narratives presented to the public matched the realities on the ground.
Unfortunately, that did not happen.
Recently, Memphis residents have seen  campaign advertisements from state Sen. Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee for the 9th Congressional District  and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Republican nominee for governor, celebrating the Memphis (un)Safe Task Force as an unquestionable success. They confidently claim the Task Force helped reduce crime by roughly 40% and portray it as the decisive reason Memphis has become safer.
Nah.
Those commercials reveal precisely why journalism matters.
Before the Safe Task Force ever arrived in Memphis, violent crime was already declining. In fact, by many measures, the city had already reached its lowest violent crime levels in roughly 25years. That reality alone should have prompted the most obvious journalistic question:
How much of the continued decline can actually be attributed to the Task Force?



				Across the country, public safety has become one of the most powerful political brands in American politics. Fear mobilizes voters. Crime statistics become campaign slogans. a			


Instead, public officials largely controlled the narrative while the public received relatively little independent scrutiny of the underlying claims. There were notable exceptions: MLK50 and the Institute for Public Service Reporting consistently provided some of the most rigorous and critical coverage of the Task Force, interrogating official claims rather than simply amplifying them. But they were exceptions in a media ecosystem that too often allowed the official narrative to set the terms of the public conversation.
Crime trends rarely have a single cause. They are shaped by countless variables: long-term policing strategies, demographic changes, prosecutorial decisions, economic conditions, community intervention efforts, seasonal fluctuations, neighborhood investments and broader social patterns. To simply announce that a new task force arrived and crime declined is not analysis. It is chronology.
Journalism is supposed to ask whether the evidence supports the conclusion.
That scrutiny becomes even more important because the task force has never simply been about crime statistics. It has always been about political messaging.
Traffic citations outnumber federal task force’s arrests in Memphis; sparse data leaves impact murky

Throughout the past year, public officials repeatedly held press conferences celebrating the initiative. Statistics were presented as proof of effectiveness. Talking points were repeated across interviews and news stories. Over time, those official narratives migrated almost seamlessly into campaign advertisements.
That progression should concern all of us.
Because once political messaging becomes accepted public fact without sustained examination, campaign consultants no longer have to persuade voters. They simply inherit narratives that have already been normalized.
The media’s responsibility was never to oppose the Task Force, nor was it to endorse it.
Its responsibility was to verify.
To ask whether crime reductions could legitimately be credited to the initiative. To examine what measures were being used. To investigate not only what was counted, but what remained invisible.
Public safety cannot be evaluated simply by broad percentage claims. It requires asking harder questions about sustainability, constitutional policing, community trust, racial disparities, long-term outcomes, and whether enforcement strategies actually make neighborhoods healthier after the cameras leave.
Those are not partisan questions. They are journalistic ones. Unfortunately, they were too often overshadowed by official narratives that went largely unchallenged. That failure matters because narratives shape elections.
Today, candidates confidently campaign on the Task Force because the underlying story has already been accepted by much of the public. The campaign commercials are not creating a new narrative. They are capitalizing on one that was insufficiently examined when it mattered most.
This extends far beyond one election or one task force.
Across the country, public safety has become one of the most powerful political brands in American politics. Fear mobilizes voters. Crime statistics become campaign slogans. Success is declared before the evidence has been fully evaluated.
When journalists fail to distinguish between measurable outcomes and political marketing, democracy suffers.
Memphis deserves better. We all deserve better.
Residents understand that public safety cannot be measured solely by press conferences or campaign commercials. They know the difference between being heavily policed and being genuinely safe. They know that neighborhoods become safer through stable housing, quality schools, economic opportunity, accountable institutions and trust between communities and government — not simply because another law enforcement initiative has been given a memorable name.
None of this is an argument against law enforcement. It is an argument for accountability. And accountability begins with asking difficult questions before political advertisements answer them for us.
I warned that our media environment was becoming increasingly vulnerable to narrative management rather than narrative examination.
The campaign commercials that recently filled our television screens are not evidence that warning was misplaced. They are evidence that it was ignored.
The next time elected officials announce dramatic successes or unveil impressive statistics, I hope Memphis journalism does what journalism exists to do: ask not only whether the numbers are accurate, but what they actually prove.
Because the public deserves more than a compelling narrative.
It deserves evidence.
And it deserves a press willing to distinguish the two.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: When a principled stand gets in the way of effective campaigning
description: People who claim to hate politics should love how Jeff McLaughlin has pursued elected office. In his near-decade in the Alabama House of Representatives, the Democrat from Guntersville shunned political donations and self-financed his campaigns while becoming a leading voice for campaign finance reform. He led the effort to stop PAC-to-PAC transfers, which a[...]
text:
A line of voters wrapped around a polling location in Huntsville at midmorning on Nov. 5, 2024. Jeff MCLaughlin, the Democrats' nominee for attorney general, had not raised any money through the end of July.  (Anna Claire Vollers/Stateline)People who claim to hate politics should love how Jeff McLaughlin has pursued elected office.
In his near-decade in the Alabama House of Representatives, the Democrat from Guntersville shunned political donations and self-financed his campaigns while becoming a leading voice for campaign finance reform. He led the effort to stop PAC-to-PAC transfers, which allowed politicians to shuffle donations through multiple political action committees and obscure the real source of their funding.
“This will not cure every problem we have with our campaigns,” McLaughlin said during one debate in 2007. “It will address what I think is the most single egregious problem we have with our campaigns.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
His efforts often put him at odds with members of his own party. But McLaughlin was sincere. In the face of a difficult re-election campaign in 2010, he stuck to his self-financing standards, telling the Press-Register that October that accepting “tens of thousands of dollars” meant “there are always strings attached.”
The problem with not accepting that money, as McLaughlin noted at the time, was not having money for TV spots. He ended up spending a little under $15,000 on that race. His challenger, Republican Wes Long, spent over $139,000. And McLaughlin lost.
That December, the new GOP majority in the Legislature enacted the PAC-to-PAC ban. They named the law after McLaughlin, less a personal tribute to McLaughlin than a way of rubbing the Republican victory in the faces of Democrats. And their version of the measure has some large holes in it.
It’s hard not to respect someone who makes the hard climb up the high road, particularly in a state where the powerful work hard to trip up the righteous. Money corrodes democracy, and like other toxic substances, it needs to be carefully regulated.
But you can’t create those protections without being in power. You can’t get into power without communicating your message. And you can’t do that without money.
McLaughlin tried to reclaim his House seat in 2014. He self-financed his campaign again, to the tune of about $40,000. His Republican opponent, Will Ainsworth, spent more than $334,000. And McLaughlin’s six-point loss in 2010 became a 20-point rout.
Reclaiming that Guntersville seat was always going to be difficult. North Alabama shifted red after 2010, and 2014 went even worse for Alabama Democrats than 2010 did. But getting outspent by a factor of 8-to-1 would suggest rethinking the strategy.
For better or worse, McLaughlin stuck with the approach in a nonpartisan campaign for mayor of Guntersville in 2025. He managed to tie incumbent Leigh Dollar in the general election but lost a subsequent runoff by 18 percentage points.
The sad truth is that what’s admirable in politics is not necessarily what’s practical. McLaughlin’s self-financing approach proved ineffective in a race to represent 40,000 people in the Alabama House and a mayoral contest for a city with a population of about 9,000.
Now McLaughlin is the Democrats’ nominee for Alabama attorney general in a statewide race with up to 3.8 million voters. Self-financing won’t work.
Just look at all the money that flowed into the fight for the Republican nomination for attorney general earlier this year. Katherine Robertson, Jay Mitchell and Pam Casey spent nearly $10 million trying to prevail, and flooded the airwaves with commercials reminding you there was an election.
Many of those spots were despicable. Robertson (the eventual winner) and Mitchell ran a gutter campaign of attacks on transgender children and Muslim Americans while toadying to Donald Trump, seemingly disconnected from the state they claim to represent. It was very good evidence of the need for campaign finance reform.
But McLaughlin isn’t making that argument. As far as I can tell, he’s not making any public case for his candidacy.
That’s not hyperbole. McLaughlin doesn’t have a campaign website. As of last week, he hadn’t given any interviews. (Our own Ralph Chapoco made several efforts — through McLaughlin’s office and the state Democratic Party — to reach the candidate last month, and got nothing.) As of July 31, he reported $100 in his campaign account.
McLaughlin is free to campaign how he chooses. He is making some appearances this week, and perhaps he’ll become more public in the fall. 
But his aversion to fundraising, however understandable, means McLaughlin is ghosting the electorate. How do his positions compare to Robertson, who accepts and spends PAC money with no hesitation? What does he want to do as Alabama attorney general? How would he use the office to protect consumers and promote public safety? We don’t know.
It’s not enough to say that McLaughlin is a long shot. So is every other statewide Democratic candidate. McLaughlin will draw hundreds of thousands of votes simply for being the party’s nominee. He owes it to those supporters to let them know how he would serve as attorney general.
And if he sees opportunities to control money in politics, he may get more people behind him. But he can’t expect voters to flock to him like a beacon in the night. He’s got to spend money to stop money.
That’s an unfortunate paradox for a candidate like McLaughlin. He has an admirable public record. And in Alabama, being admirable isn’t enough.
