name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Philadelphia stands out for its approach for revisiting felony murder in Pa.
description: In the three weeks since the deadline for a legislative felony murder fix passed, district attorneys around the state have started grappling with how to proceed with resentencing.
text:
SCI Somerset on Wednesday, June 2, 2021. (Photo by Commonwealth Media Services)In two GOP-led meetings last week, county district attorneys across the state repeatedly spoke about the oncoming “chaos” created by the state legislature’s failure to create a sentencing structure for felony murder. The discussions took place in the wake of a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling that mandatory life sentences were unconstitutional.
“People are going to be treated disparately in every county across the commonwealth, and that’s very dangerous because there will be no uniformity. We will still have no idea what’s going on,” said Westmoreland County District Attorney Nicole Ziccarelli on Thursday. “It will create chaos and violations in our communities … that scares me a great deal. That’s something that keeps me up at night.”
Data from the state Department of Corrections indicate that Westmoreland County has nine felony murder cases that could now be revisited. That number pales in comparison to the caseload Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner will oversee, which accounts for almost half of the state’s 1,100-plus cases. 
Westmoreland County District Attorney Nicole Ziccarelli speaks to Republican lawmakers about felony murder on Aug. 13, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
Krasner and other district attorneys pointed to another decade-old resentencing effort for juveniles automatically sentenced to life. The U.S. Supreme Court ruling reversing automatic life sentences for juveniles impacted less than 500 people in Pennsylvania prisons.
“I think we have a clear example with the way juvenile lifer cases were handled. That individualized resentencing was carefully done with as much record and as much expert testimony as it necessary,” Krasner told the Capital-Star. “It worked. And I think the parole board also worked.”
One of them was Robert Saleem Holbrook. Krasner held up Holbrook, now the executive director of the Abolitionist Law Center, as an example of someone who returned to everyday life after decades in prison and became a part of the community.
“We want justice done. And that justice has to be done in a way that resources are devoted to everyone that’s going to be involved in these resentencing hearings,” said Holbrook.
The state’s highest court gave the General Assembly 120 days to draft a solution, but the Democratic-controlled House and the Republican-controlled Senate didn’t come to a consensus before the July 24 deadline. Also known as second-degree murder, the charge is brought when someone is killed during the commission of another felony, even if the defendant did not intend to cause the person’s death. 
In more than 80% of cases, the underlying crime is a robbery or burglary. Kidnapping, arson and sexual assault make up between 2-5% of cases each, though certain crimes involved multiple elements.
 Using juvenile resentencing as a template

Hundreds of other “juvenile lifers” also returned to Philadelphia over the years after decades in prison. A 2025 report found that just 4% went on to commit another crime. 
“That is very important, and should be very important to any legislator who’s thinking about a legislative solution. It should be very important to any judge who may be doing an individualized resentencing,” added Krasner, noting that Philadelphia’s homicide and violent crime rate is at a record low. 

Who’s serving felony murder sentences in Pennsylvania prisons?


He said that a Philadelphia group will collaboratively determine the best way to prioritize old felony murder cases using that experience as a guide. Starting with the oldest cases, they’ll identify those who used their time in prison to mentor others or develop skills and have a record of good behavior, thus making them good candidates for reintegrating into society.
“One of the good things about these resentencings is we’re not guessing,” said Holbrook. “We know what they’ve been doing in jail for quite some time, and I think that brings clarity to their capacity for reform.”
But other district attorneys don’t remember juvenile resentencing being so smooth. 
The office of Allegheny County Deputy District Attorney Ronald M. Wabby Jr. handled the case that prompted the Supreme Court to overturn mandatory life sentences. Derek Lee was convicted in 2016 for a 2014 home-invasion robbery in Pittsburgh. 
He said one judge tried to levy a seven-and-a-half to 15-year murder sentence for a juvenile.
Allegheny County Deputy District Attorney Ronald M. Wabby Jr. speaks to lawmakers about felony murder on Aug. 13, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
“A similar situation will occur now because there’s no framework to accomplish anything,” he warned. “(Judges) could do anything they want. It’s a frightening concept … they could over sentence, they could get probation for murder. There’s no floor. There’s no ceiling.”
Citing that experience with juvenile cases, Wabby said the simplest solution for old second-degree murder cases would make everyone eligible for parole after a set number of years rather than resentencing every case. 
“The lesson we’ve learned from resentencing all of those people is the idea that all you’re doing is hurting the victims, and that’s what we’re trying to avoid,” he continued. “The parole board is better geared to be ‘flooded’ than the court system. The court system already is overburdened with the idea that we have to deal with the crime that happens each and every day across the commonwealth … the parole board, they’re already geared to do this.”
One proposal would cap that at 35 years — the preferred bill for most Republicans — while the Democratic-led effort picked 30 years. 
Krasner and Holbrook rebuffed both, pointing to Pennsylvania’s neighboring states. Four — including blue states like New York and red states like West Virginia — have minimum sentences of 15 years.
“Pennsylvania is an outlier already now when it comes to the number of people serving life without parole sentences,” said Holbrook. “The parole board is in a position to make determinations of who should be paroled and who should not be paroled.”
 Preserving life without parole as an option

A big concern for district attorneys has been protecting the option to seek life sentences, even for those who weren’t the principal cause of violence. 
If there’s no option for life with parole, Adams County District Attorney Brian Sinnett said he doesn’t know if he’ll ever offer second-degree murder again. 
A specter of justice in Pennsylvania

“There was no reason under the present climate to pursue first-degree murder versus second-degree murder while life without parole was the same sentence for both,” Sinnett told the Capital-Star. “None of these were jury verdicts of second-degree murder … when there was no practical difference, it made more sense if you could get a case resolved.”
Like many counties — with the notable exception of Philadelphia — all of the seven Adams County cases were accepted as part of a plea bargain. 
“This was a plea agreement where the person agreed to life without parole, and that’s why I think it’s different than a trial,” he continued. 
Sinnett described the two second-degree murder cases he oversaw in his role, saying that he consulted with victim families before finalizing agreements. Plea bargains allow prosecutors to resolve cases without going to trial, even if the case has the “intentional” aspect that could make it a first-degree murder case. 
To protest a Democratic proposal expanding medical release, several Republicans have posted photos and videos of some heinous crimes, including Sinnett’s prosecution of Kristopher Gartrell, who murdered, tortured and sexually assaulted an 87-year-old woman.
“I’ve been doing this long enough to know that you never know for sure what a jury is going to do. One juror could hold up the whole process and you have to try it again,” he said, noting that trials can be particularly traumatic for victim families. “The ordeal of having to testify, of having to have your loved one’s life ripped apart … is all very troubling for people.”
Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner takes questions from reporters after a press conference in Harrisburg on Friday, Oct. 21, 2022 (Capital-Star photo).
Some Republicans have claimed that most second-degree murderers aren’t so-called getaway drivers or lookouts.
Krasner called that a “lie,” saying he just prosecuted a case where several men were stealing cars. One, who played the role of a getaway driver, didn’t even know his accomplices had firearms.
“Any prosecutor who is telling you there are no getaway drivers should be ashamed of him- or herself,” he added. “But it is true that there’s a very, very wide range of culpability.”
Historically, Philadelphia has approached cases differently than the rest of the state.
A 2021 state-commissioned report from the Philadelphia Lawyers for Society Equity found that Pennsylvanians living outside of Philadelphia and Allegheny County were more than twice as likely to plead guilty — rather than going to a trial — when compared to the rest of the state.
“There’s not a defendant in the world who is pleading guilty to second-degree murder or first-degree murder unless they’re facing the death penalty,” asserted Krasner. “Even though there have been no executions (for decades), there are jurisdictions … where they threaten the death penalty in order to coerce a plea to life without parole.”
Pennsylvania hasn’t executed anyone since 1999.
 Beyond county borders

Decisions in one county wouldn’t just impact those residents because their homes might be elsewhere, added Indiana County District Attorney Robert Manzi Jr., naming judges in progressive Philadelphia as a concern.
The 500-plus cases originating in Philadelphia County are “not something that’s going to stay there, right? That’s very concerning,” he continued. “The train comes right from Philadelphia into Cambria County and disperses all over western Pennsylvania … it is something truly for people throughout the state to be worried about.”
He wasn’t alone in his claim.
“You want to talk about people being treated disparately? You want to talk about danger on the streets? Worry about Philadelphia,” said Ziccarelli. 

What happens when the clock runs out on felony murder legislation?


She’s part of the board of the Pennsylvania District Attorneys Association, which supports a Republican proposal for a 35-year minimum sentence. That organization represents every county district attorney in the state, with the exception of Krasner.
“The biggest reason they’re talking like this is because many of these counties are financially dependent on prisons, and on those prisons being full of Philadelphians,” said Krasner. “They’d rather have Philadelphians, many of them Black and brown, locked up because those aren’t their voters.”
Holbrook was more blunt in his response. 
“That’s unfortunately a continuing narrative that Harrisburg has of Philadelphia, and as someone that was up in those areas and around those types of people, I can assure you that it’s rooted in racism,” he said. “They’re always using ‘Philadelphia’ as a talking point to advance racist narratives in Pennsylvania.”
He said conservative politicos made the same arguments about juvenile lifers’ resentencing after the U.S. Supreme Court decisions. 
On a call with Krasner, a victims rights advocate and himself, Holbrook said it embodied Philadelphia’s approach to resentencing. 
“We’re demonstrating that this is a community problem. You would not expect all of us to be on a call trying to figure out how to handle the situation in a way that prioritizes not our individual offices’ needs, but the communities’ needs,” he continued. “We wish that Harrisburg would take that same approach.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio attorney general candidate calls for investigation of ties between JobsOhio and Intel
description: One candidate for Ohio attorney general is calling for the state inspector general to investigate new revelations about ties between the head of the state’s quasi-public economic development agency JobsOhio, the governor’s office, and Intel, a company that has received millions. The other candidate hasn’t responded to questions about the matter. John Kulewic[...]
text:
Then-Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger and Gov. Mike DeWine joined by politicians and business leaders break ground ceremony for Intel’s new semiconductor manufacturing site, September 9, 2022, in Licking County, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for the Ohio Capital Journal / Republish photo only with original story)One candidate for Ohio attorney general is calling for the state inspector general to investigate new revelations about ties between the head of the state’s quasi-public economic development agency JobsOhio, the governor’s office, and Intel, a company that has received millions.
The other candidate hasn’t responded to questions about the matter.
John Kulewicz, the Democratic nominee for AG, last week amended his complaint to Ohio Inspector General Randall J. Meyer with details of other possible conflicts of interest on the part of Josh Rubin, a lobbyist who chairs the board of JobsOhio, that were reported last week by the Capital Journal. 
The latter calls itself a private corporation. But it was created by the General Assembly and Gov. Mike DeWine appoints its board. 
JobsOhio chairman lobbies for Intel, a company that got millions from JobsOhio

JobsOhio was allowed to lease the state liquor franchise for far less than it was worth. It has since disbursed more than $2 billion in what at least used to be public money to businesses in the form of incentives.
Kulewicz’s complaint says that Rubin’s dual roles raise questions about whether he’s using JobsOhio funds to benefit his lobbying clients.
The Capital Journal’s new reporting showed that “Mr. Rubin continues to lobby for Intel even during his tenure as chairman of the board,” the amended complaint said. “Mr. Rubin was actively lobbying the governor on Intel’s behalf as recently as April 2026.”
It added, “This conduct continues to raise ethical questions about Rubin’s ability to serve the interests of the People of Ohio versus the interests of his clients and his own pecuniary interests as CEO of the CJR Group.”
A spokesman for Keith Faber, Kulewicz’s Republican opponent in the attorney general’s race, didn’t respond to questions for this story.
Last week’s analysis of lobbying disclosures and other records showed that Rubin was registered to lobby both JobsOhio and the governor on behalf of Intel from the time Gov. DeWine appointed him to the JobsOhio Board in September 2023 until the beginning of this year. 
They also show that Rubin actively lobbied DeWine for Intel through that period and into 2026. 
The state has awarded Intel more than $600 million for construction of what is now a long delayed chip-making plant northeast of Columbus. JobsOhio has awarded at least $27 million for the project.
With the project delayed by at least five years and its future uncertain, Rubin is in a position likely to have some authority over whether to try and claw back some portion of the money JobsOhio has awarded. The agency won’t answer questions about the matter.
A spokesman for DeWine said Rubin’s multiple roles didn’t amount to a conflict. Despite being registered to lobby JobsOhio for Intel, his “activity and expense” filings show he actively lobbied the governor’s office on the Intel project, while he made no such filings regarding JobsOhio, DeWine Press Secretary Dan Tierney said.
In emailed responses to written questions, Kulewicz disagreed, saying, “This is an apparent conflict of interest. And at a time when we urgently need to restore public confidence in government, this also creates a clear appearance of impropriety. When you take on a job like this and answer the call to public service, you do so knowing that you can only serve the People of Ohio. You can’t serve both the public and the powerful.”
Faber’s spokesman was sent the same questions as the Kulewicz campaign. He didn’t respond.
With narrow exceptions, JobsOhio was exempted from the state’s ethics laws when it was created in 2011. 
Paul Nick, executive director of the Ohio Ethics Commission, said that his office for the most part doesn’t have jurisdiction over Rubin, the rest of the JobsOhio board, or its staff. However, he said, Rubin’s roles as a board member and an Intel lobbyist appear to contradict his pledge to the governor to “cease services for any clients on matters in front of JobsOhio…”
Nick said that when JobsOhio was created, the Ethics Commission advocated that it be subject to the same ethics laws that state agencies are. Kulewicz said that should happen now.
“JobsOhio replaced several functions of the Ohio Department of Development,” he said. “It serves a public purpose doing work on behalf of the People of Ohio. It would function better if it were subject to the same ethics rules and laws as everyone else who works on behalf of the People of Ohio.”
DeWine’s office and JobsOhio say JobsOhio’s ethics policy requires board members to declare possible conflicts and for the board to vote whether to recuse them. Both said it’s a strong policy.
A review of the few board records that are public apparently held no instances in which Rubin, a lobbyist with dozens of clients, declared a potential conflict. Asked multiple times to share documents showing that Rubin had ever declared a potential conflict, JobsOhio didn’t respond.
Kulewicz said that shows JobsOhio’s dealings need to be investigated by a third party. That’s why he filed his initial complaint regarding another Rubin client, utility giant AEP.
Kulewicz added that subjecting JobsOhio to open-meetings and records laws would allay suspicion and prevent the need for outside investigation.
“None of this would be necessary if the legislature were to remove this veil of secrecy,” he said. “That is my preferred method to correct this. We already have sufficient protections for trade secrets and certain business information in Ohio — JobsOhio does not require near-complete exemption from our public records laws. I would advocate for that change.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Supreme Court to stop hearing most murder cases by 2028
description: Starting next summer, Georgia’s highest court will no longer routinely hear appeals in murder cases. The decision was announced Thursday as part of a concurring opinion from Chief Justice Nels Peterson that was tied to a murder case out of Fulton County, Coleman v. The State, though it was not clear why Peterson’s opinion was […]
text:
The Nathan Deal Judicial Center is home to the state Supreme Court and Court of Appeals. John McCosh/Georgia RecorderStarting next summer, Georgia’s highest court will no longer routinely hear appeals in murder cases.
The decision was announced Thursday as part of a concurring opinion from Chief Justice Nels Peterson that was tied to a murder case out of Fulton County, Coleman v. The State, though it was not clear why Peterson’s opinion was attached to that case. Murder conviction appeals, which account for more than half of the Georgia Supreme Court’s published cases, will be heard in the Georgia Court of Appeals starting July 2027.
Legislative panel to confront Georgia’s ‘broken’ post-conviction system

Under Georgia law, the state’s high court has jurisdiction over all capital cases — that is, cases where the death penalty has been imposed. But the question of which court has jurisdiction over cases where the death penalty has not been sought has been a matter of judicial interpretation rather than law dating back to 1983, when the state’s current constitution was adopted.
Though numerous opinions since then have questioned the high court’s role in deciding these cases — including one from last year — the justices have continued to hear and issue rulings in murder cases not involving the death penalty. But in his concurring opinion, ​​Peterson called for an end to the longstanding practice, which he said takes up too much of the court’s workload and results in too many binding precedents.
“Focusing our limited judicial resources on resolving murder appeals ultimately detracts from the time to devote to the core tasks assigned to this Court by the Constitution and the General Assembly,” he wrote. 
The notice, he said, gives the Court of Appeals a “long lead time” to adjust to the change. But lawmakers, who allocate funding to the state’s court system, will have only one legislative session to allocate funding for the transfer, which lawmakers and legal experts say could involve adding a new panel of judges — or possibly more — to accommodate the influx of murder cases.
During a July meeting of the House Judiciary Committee, Court of Appeals Chief Judge Trenton Brown warned lawmakers that a change in jurisdiction of that magnitude would require millions of dollars in extra resources to accommodate the increased workload.
“Moving that volume of work would create an unfunded mandate on this court, already working at or above its present capacity,” Brown said.
Rep. Scott Holcomb, an Atlanta Democrat. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Rep. Scott Holcomb, a lawyer and Atlanta Democrat who sits on the committee, said it’s too early to know exactly how much the change will cost. But he said lawmakers will need to begin reallocating funding next year when they reconvene for the 2027 legislative session, and that the full process could take several years.
“My prediction is likely it will take three to five years for us to have a really good understanding of precisely what the resource allocations need to be,” he said.
But Holcomb said he approves of the change, which will allow the Supreme Court to focus on their main responsibilities, such as constitutional and emergency cases. As Peterson pointed out in his opinion, Georgia’s status as a battleground state means emergency election cases will likely become more frequent.
“While there will be some short-term disruption with the shift, in the long term, I think our state will be better for it,” he said.
Lauren Shubow, an Atlanta-based criminal defense attorney who represents Georgians facing murder convictions, said she worries about the shift and what it would mean for her clients.
“It is well known that the workload of the Georgia Court of Appeals is outrageously high in comparison to other state appellate courts,” she said. “We don’t have enough judges as it is, and then to assign them these additional murders, which are some of the most complicated cases that exist, that would just be an additional burden on them.”
A decades-old law promised Georgians a second chance. A new law hopes to deliver on that promise.

For cases that go before the Supreme Court, all nine justices will hear and weigh in on a case, but cases in the Court of Appeals are decided by a panel of three judges. Leigh Ann Webster, a criminal appeals attorney and adjunct professor at the Emory University School of Law, said the change could leave Georgians who are appealing their murder convictions with less attention and fewer options for their cases to be thoroughly reviewed.
“It’s sort of inherent that you’re getting more consideration and review when you have nine people looking at it as opposed to three,” she said.
Additionally, Webster said, opinions issued by the Georgia Court of Appeals aren’t always as accessible as those from the Georgia Supreme Court. 
But Holcomb said while the change may be uncomfortable in the short term, the Supreme Court will still be able to weigh in on murder cases that require additional review.
“The benefit of the structure that’s been proposed by Chief Justice Peterson is that the Supreme Court can still take up any cases where the Court of Appeals makes a mistake, or where there needs to be guidance from the top court,” he said.
“I understand people having concerns, and since we’re talking about justice and liberty issues, those concerns are of course appreciated and valued,” he added. “But I do agree with the shift and think it’s in the best interest of the state to move in this direction.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: State corrections officers altered prisoner’s ID with racial caricature, lawsuit claims
description: A correctional officer at Newberry Correctional Facility in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula digitally altered a Native American prisoner’s ID to depict him wearing a feathered headdress, stereotypical Native American attire and facial paint, a lawsuit filed in Michigan state court in early August alleges. Dylan Leenheer, who is Native American and a member of the[...]
text:
Department of Corrections | Susan J. DemasA correctional officer at Newberry Correctional Facility in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula digitally altered a Native American prisoner’s ID to depict him wearing a feathered headdress, stereotypical Native American attire and facial paint, a lawsuit filed in Michigan state court in early August alleges.
Dylan Leenheer, who is Native American and a member of the Gun Lake Tribe, is suing the Michigan Department of Corrections, as well as three individual corrections employees involved in the incident, for violating the state’s Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act. 
The lawsuit claims that Leenheer faced “racial humiliation” from two corrections officers, Jay Stevens and Robert Marsh, and a library technician, JoLynn Cebula. It further alleges that the Michigan Department of Corrections had “institutional knowledge of, and failure to prevent or remedy, a broader pattern of similar misconduct” within the unit. 
“That is very telling about the environment and about how people who are Native American, who are non-white are being treated,” Maura Battersby, a senior attorney for Flood Law, who is representing Leenheer, said in an interview.
Specifically, the lawsuit alleges that Stevens, a correctional officer at the Newberry facility, created the ID with the racial caricature, and an image of the ID in the lawsuit identifies him as the issuer. Marsh, another correctional officer, was allegedly present in the room and at the computer when Stevens issued and altered the identification card. 
A scan of the temporary ID with a digitally altered image of Dylan Leenheer that is the subject of a civil rights lawsuit against the Michigan Department of Corrections. Screenshot.
Battersby noted that to the best of her knowledge, the correctional officers have faced no internal disciplinary action or repercussions for their actions. Leenheer is no longer incarcerated and has been released from MDOC custody as of the time of the lawsuit’s filing.
“That’s an approval on some level of the behavior, and truly the brazenness of posting the photo. It wasn’t just on his individual ID. They posted it various places with CO Stevens taking credit for it. Just so proud of his work,” she said. “The brazenness of it, that tells me that this is a systemic problem that is at least getting distant approval from higher up.”
That image was also posted on the window of Leenheer’s unit, the lawsuit states, “where it was visible to other prisoners and staff, subjecting Plaintiff to public humiliation on the basis of his race and ethnicity,” in violation of MDOC policies that prevent discrimination based on race, religion or ethnicity and prohibit staff from engaging in derogatory or humiliating behavior .
Battersby explained that posting the image made the incident not just a question of humiliation, but also of Leenheer’s safety — especially as there were only three Native American prisoners in the unit. 
“It’s the COs expressing to everyone that it’s okay to treat these people poorly, and now my client has to sit back and wonder what that treatment might be, and know that on some level or certainly fear that the COs wouldn’t intervene if someone were to attack them or something like that,” she said. “Having the people who are in charge of keeping you safe while you’re in there single you out as somebody who it’s okay to mess with is dangerous.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The suit also alleges that when Leenheer attempted to make photocopies of the altered identification card for use in court and in an internal grievance about the ID, Cebula, a library technician, refused to make the copies and laughed at the identification card while calling it “funny.”
“All allegations of discriminatory harassment are investigated by the department,” a spokesperson from the Michigan Department of Corrections, wrote to the Michigan Advance when asked to comment on the lawsuit, declining to provide further comment due to the ongoing litigation.
Leenheer filed a grievance on May 22, 2026, which was not formally received by MDOC until 33 days later on June 24, according to the lawsuit. In that time, he filed at least six urgent mental health care requests, all of which went unanswered. Also in that time, he was placed on a “loss-of-privileges sanction,” despite his own security classification sheet under MDOC that listed him as “misconduct free,” which meant he was denied sunlight and access to telephone contact with his family. 
The lawsuit further alleges that the problem of racial and ethnic harassment from correctional officers is a broader issue at the Newberry Correctional Facility, including sworn declarations from other prisoners that also say that Stevens had made other derogatory statements about Native American prisoners in the past. 
“MDOC knew or should have known of a pattern of racially and ethnically motivated misconduct at Newberry Correctional Facility,” the lawsuit states. 
The lawsuit also identifies two other alleged incidents in which Stevens and Marsh altered ID photos of two prisoners, one Black and one of “Indian-national-origin,” with other racial connotations.
“It’s not an isolated incident,” Battersby said.
She also raised concerns that this incident — as well as a string of misconduct citations, after Leenheer had never received one prior — came just after he became friends with Colby Skippergosh, one of the few other Native prisoners at Newberry, who had also filed a discrimination action against the MDOC with the Michigan Department of Civil Rights.
“If you’re going to discriminate against Native Americans, you sure wouldn’t want them to be comparing their stories and bolstering each other and supporting each other to, you know, push back on that. My gut tells me that you would want to discourage that,” she explained.
Leenheer’s complaint comes as MDOC has been under scrutiny for concerns about standards of medical care, especially at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility — where Battersby and her colleagues are also representing a number of clients. She said that this incident shows a broader pattern of the culture within the state’s prison system. 
“I think that they’ve created a system and an environment where this type of behavior thrives,” she said, referring to the MDOC. “The common theme is this notion that they can treat people any way they feel like while they’re in their custody, and this is just another iteration of that. And so I think that that’s a top-down systemic issue.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio domestic violence resources centers have faced rising requests for services
description: Ohio domestic violence shelters have been facing an increase in the need for their services long before the controversy surrounding Congressman Max Miller, but it has brought the spotlight back on the issue and advocates are sharing how Ohioans can get help they need. Miller requested an ethics probe from the U.S. House after he […]
text:
A domestic violence awareness ribbon. (Stock photo from Getty Images.)Ohio domestic violence shelters have been facing an increase in the need for their services long before the controversy surrounding Congressman Max Miller, but it has brought the spotlight back on the issue and advocates are sharing how Ohioans can get help they need.
Miller requested an ethics probe from the U.S. House after he was accused of domestic violence by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of Ohio GOP U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno.
Two other women have leveled allegations against Miller. The congressman has repeatedly denied wrongdoing, and said he believes the ethics investigation will end in his favor.
Even as fellow Ohio politicians on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about Miller staying in the reelection race for his seat representing Ohio’s 7th district in Congress, Miller has vowed to remain in the fight. The deadline for him to withdraw from the race and allow Ohio Republicans to replace him was Aug. 10.
In a 20-minute live stream on his X account earlier this month, he pushed back against the claims and public opinion of them.
At one point during the live stream, Miller said “if I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?”
“Would she have invited me to spend an afternoon at the playground with her and our daughter,” he went on. “Would she have written that we were in a friendlier place? No, she wouldn’t have, ladies and gentlemen.”
Domestic violence resource providers in the state say complexities about the issue can often be oversimplified in public conversations. Abuse can come from many sources, including physical violence, but also financial control, isolation from friends and family, and emotional manipulation.
“Survivors often continue to care for or stay with a partner between incidents out of fear, love, hope for change, or to protect their children, but that is not evidence that abuse didn’t happen,” the Ohio Domestic Violence Network said in a statement after Miller’s comments. “It’s one of the most common ways survivors are discredited when they come forward.”
  In Miller’s district 
Resource centers in Miller’s 7th Congressional District are providing services to a diverse and ever-increasing population.
In the first half of 2026, the Hope and Healing Survivor Resource Center that serves Summit and Medina counties saw a 27% increase in responses to hospitals for reports of intimate partner violence.
The center, which provides services at no cost, has seen an increase in clients served, and 23% more participants in their domestic violence prevention and outreach programs.
Already since January, the 24/7 support and crisis intervention hotline hosted by the center has received more than 3,500 calls.
“So, across the board, we’re just seeing an increase in demand,” said Teresa Stafford-Wright, chief executive officer at the center. “We have constantly seen an increase year after year for our services.”
 
 If you or someone you know is experiencing abuse:
National Domestic Violence Hotline: 800-799-7233, or text BEGIN to 88788
Ohio Domestic Violence Network 

The Ohio Domestic Violence Network’s 76 local programs provided services to nearly 75,000 survivors in 2025, with more than 120,000 call, texts, and chats answered, according to the network.
State shelters housed nearly 9,500 individuals, with half of those being children. But shelters are reaching capacity levels and lack  staffing to serve all those asking for help.
According to the network, more than 50% of all Ohio survivors seeking shelter were turned away last year.
Stafford-Wright said the survivors coming into shelters in Summit and Medina counties are dealing with more complicated needs on top of the trauma of domestic violence.
“There’s a lack of affordable housing that we’re seeing, which keeps survivors from being able to get away, there’s a lack of income, and on top of that you can have substance abuse issues as well,” Stafford-Wright said.
The impact of domestic violence is felt among all cultures and populations, creating a need for resources to help with language barriers, navigation of immigration issues and other legal hurdles amid domestic violence issues.
“A lot of the community members, if they’re dealing with domestic violence or human trafficking, they may need family law, they may also need victims of crime law, they may need assistance with immigration law,” said Anna Chen, manager of communications and civic engagement for Asian Services in Action.
“A lot of these survivors are, unfortunately, heavily taken advantage of by their abusers.”
Asian Services in Action is a social health and legal services agency that has a strong immigrant and refugee population. It’s also located in Miller’s district.
The organization staffs a federally qualified health center, provides civic engagement, and voter education as well.
Also included in their services is Ahimsa, a confidential service for survivors of domestic violence, human trafficking, and sexual assault. Ahimsa is a Sanskrit word for the concept of avoiding harm and violence.
“We were seeing that there were a lot of survivors in the immigrant-refugee population, and they are barred out of a lot of the resources in Northeast Ohio, just because they don’t have the language accessibility that we do,” said Emily Henthorn, manager of government affairs for Asian Services in Action.
Helping survivors may even mean the identification of cultural norms that might cause hesitation in reporting intimate partner violence, from patriarchal beliefs and downplay of abuse, to a religious aversion to divorce.
“So there’s a lot of coaching these women to believe that the abuse is happening, and it is real, because they tend to downplay, and … also we have to be very careful with confidentiality,” Henthorn said.
  Looking ahead 
Many centers rely on federal grant funding for the vast majority of their revenue, and some receive state funding, along with individual donations.
The Hope and Healing Survivor Resource Center’s funding is made up of about 75% grant funding, and without that funding, the center would have a lot of trouble continuing to provide the services, especially at no cost to the individuals.
“We’re hoping that in this new climate that we remain an organization that is seen as competent and is able to maneuver through the changing times,” Stafford-Wright said.
Henthorn said even more of their funding comes from grants, and they receive some from the Violence Against Women Act. But because of the population they serve, they’ve also seen a decrease in federal funds specifically going to their immigrant and refugee services.
“If we’re going to make it through the next few years of the Trump administration, we’re going to have to have more donations,” Henthorn said.
Advocates see the increase in public attention as a way to perhaps show those dealing with violence – or who may know someone that might be experiencing it – a way forward.
While headlines can bring attention to one particular case, Stafford-Wright said it’s important to remember that the person next door may be dealing with the same thing, and having someone that can help when the time is right will be vital.
“Try not to tell the person what they need to do in this moment, because sometimes you may alienate them,” Stafford-Wright said. “Definitely know the resources, be a listening ear, and stay close to that person.”
High-profile accusations can result in more people coming forward with their own experiences, and Henthorn warns against narratives that experiences are fictional or used for attention. Many times, it’s as simple as a lack of recognition of the problem, or the resources available.
“On average, it takes seven attempts to leave an abusive situation before a survivor gets out,” Henthorn said. “And a lot of times in those seven times, they’re seeing health care providers for injuries, they’re filing police reports, but people just aren’t seeing the signs.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. lawmakers propose guardrails on automatic license plate cameras as backlash grows
description: Flock’s ALPRs, otherwise known as Flock cameras, automatically capture images of passing vehicles and upload them to a database police can search. Law enforcement uses the data to help locate vehicles that may be linked to crimes, missing people or other police matters.
text:
A police officer uses the Flock Safety license plate reader system. Many left-leaning states and cities are trying to protect their residents’ personal information amid the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, but a growing number of conservative lawmakers also want to curb the use of surveillance technologies. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)As Pennsylvania lawmakers proposed measures to better regulate the use of automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and the data they gather, a major purveyor of the technology announced last Thursday it would tighten the optional controls on how police use its system.
Flock Safety said it would shorten the default period its system stores information about vehicles and their whereabouts from 30 days to seven days, although police departments that use it  could opt to keep the longer data retention period. 
The announcement came amid mounting public pushback against the tech’s broad deployment across the country following reports of law enforcement officers misusing it.
Earlier this month, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers nationwide have been charged or accused of misusing Flock and similar systems to spy on their spouses or intimate partners, exes and their exes’ new partners, the Post reported.
The Post story included an account of a mother from Leechburg, Armstrong County, who said she repeatedly warned police and the district attorney’s office that her police officer husband had used a competitor to Flock to stalk and threaten her. The officer, Michael McSherry, ultimately pleaded guilty to official oppression and served about 11 months in jail, according to the article.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“There is a clear misuse of this technology from some of the people who should be the guardians of it,” said Rep. Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia), who published a memorandum Tuesday seeking cosponsors on legislation he plans to introduce to create penalties for misusing ALPR data.
Flock’s ALPRs, otherwise known as Flock cameras, automatically capture images of passing vehicles and upload them to a database police can search. Law enforcement uses the data to help locate vehicles that may be linked to crimes, missing people or other police matters. 
Among other changes aimed at protecting privacy, improving accountability and keeping data secure, the Atlanta-based company also highlighted software features introduced earlier this year that it said automatically detects abnormal activity and flags it for review. Users will be required to use this feature going forward, it said.
It also noted new functionality in its software that allows departments to filter what kinds of reasons are permissible for other agencies to access cameras. A department could allow other departments to search its cameras for stolen vehicles but not for immigration enforcement, for example.
In a news release, the nine-year-old company said it believed its prior default data storage settings “struck a careful balance between safety and privacy.” It added  the changes would allow cities to keep their “current, democratically approved” retention period that fits its public safety strategy. 
“Abuse of Flock technology, at any level, is unacceptable,” CEO Garrett Langley said in the news release, which said the company will now require users to enter a criminal case number for every search. Flock did not respond to questions from the Capital-Star.
A Flock Safety license plate-reading camera is seen at Colfax Avenue and Franklin Street in Denver on Aug. 5, 2025. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)
Langley told the Washington Post that the company had not tightened controls itself because executives believed local officials would implement them.
“I had this hope that local lawmakers at the state and local level would move very quickly and they’d look at the things that we’re recommending as optional and say, ‘Great, we’re going to force it.’ And they haven’t,” he told the post. “Instead of waiting, we said, ‘Look, we should just move faster.’”
Chad Marlow, a privacy expert at the American Civil Liberties Union, said Flock has a history of responding to privacy concerns as what he calls “public relations nuisances.” 
“It’s more window dressing than anything else,” Marlow said, noting that unless a jurisdiction has a law mandating Flock data be deleted after a certain time, police departments can keep it as long as they want. And other features the company touted, such as the system to detect misuse, have never been evaluated independently.
“So saying they’re rolling it out everywhere when we don’t even know how well it works. To me, that’s not much of a privacy win,” Marlow said.
The devices, which Flock provides under contract to police agencies and businesses, have become the targets of a national effort to dissuade local officials from adopting them. Critics say the indiscriminate collection of data on peoples’ movements violates the constitution and is tantamount to mass surveillance.
In some cases, the cameras have also been vandalized or removed.
Proposals to set limits in Pennsylvania
A bipartisan group of Pennsylvania state representatives announced this week they would soon introduce legislation that would, among other things, create civil causes of actions for individuals or prosecutors to sue over misuse of the information.
Seventeen other states have laws that regulate the use of the cameras, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. They range from limits on how long police can keep data, such as California’s law requiring it to be deleted after 60 days unless it is evidence in a felony case, to Vermont’s, which requires officers to be certified to use an ALPR system.
Khan’s proposal, which already has bipartisan support, would give private individuals the right to sue and authorize the state attorney general and county district attorneys to investigate violations and bring civil enforcement actions. Among seven co-sponsors is Rep. Robert Leadbeter (R-Columbia).
It would also require clear rules for who may access such information, documented reasons for searches, audit trails, data retention standards and transparency measures, the memo says.

Flock Safety tightens safeguards as states, cities question surveillance network


Rep. Nathan Davidson (D-Dauphin) is a co-sponsor of Khan’s bill and introduced legislation that would prohibit law enforcement from sharing ALPR information with federal agencies or police in other states for purposes of tracking people who may travel to other states to obtain abortion care or other health care.
It stems, Davidson said, from a report in May 2025 that authorities in Texas had used a network of ALPRs to search for a woman who had a self-administered abortion, which is banned in Texas.
“I crafted a bill to prohibit the sharing of that data in the health care space, and it’s not just abortion care. It could also be vaccines,” he said. “I would not want them to be requesting license plate reader data that we have been using in law enforcement in Pennsylvania for those purposes in other states.”
A constituent’s concern about ALPR cameras in Rep. Jen O’Mara’s (D-Delaware) district prompted her to learn more about the issues involved with Flock and similar systems, she said. She has proposed a bill that would limit how government agencies can use ALPRs, what the data can be used for and require that the data be erased in a timely manner.
Flock Automated License Plate Reader as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)
“What we’re saying is that they can be used for legitimate law enforcement purposes, conducting criminal investigations, ensuring compliance with federal, state, and local laws enforcing state and local parking laws and controlling access to secured areas, and it’s only allowed to be used by government and law enforcement,” O’Mara said.
The legislation would also prevent ALPR camera and software providers from selling the data their systems collect.
“One of the components of my bill is that the manufacturer doesn’t own the data, so they can’t take the license plate information and use it on their own,” O’Mara said. 
Davidson’s bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January and awaits consideration. With the legislative session winding down at the end of this year, Davidson said his and Khan’s bills are unlikely to get to Gov. Josh Shapiro’s desk to become law.
“I think it’s about teeing up the ball and the conversation for next session,” he said.
O’Mara said lawmakers can still prepare to advance the bills quickly next session by gathering feedback from constituents and stakeholders, planning hearings and lining up committee votes.
“This may be the kind of thing that if we do all the legwork now … that we’re ready to go come January when we’re in a new session,” she said.
How do police departments in Pa. use the system?
The Capital-Star filed Right-to-Know requests for Flock system data from six Pennsylvania police departments earlier this year. Only one, the New Castle Police Department in Lawrence County, granted the requests for audit logs, while others are still pending or were denied. 
Allentown and Bethlehem each denied the requests, citing an exception in the state Right to Know Law for records related to criminal investigations. Allentown also cited the Criminal History Records and Information Act (CHIRA), which limits access to records created as part of a criminal investigation.
Marlow, of the ACLU, said license plate reader data and the audit logs are not investigative materials.
“They capture data on every single car that goes by without any suspicion that any of those cars are involved in a crime,” he said. “So maybe you could say that it’s pre-crime investigation, which isn’t really even a thing except in that ‘Minority Report’ movie, right?” 
Flock’s software automatically creates logs of internal and external searches for each police department’s ALPR database. Those records show the date, time, user, reason for the search, associated criminal case numbers and license plate numbers searched, among other pieces of information.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Departments may opt to share information with other agencies across the country. New Castle’s external search logs for 36 months from January 2024 through June 2026 contained more than 11 million records of searches of its database from other departments around the country. New Castle police users, in comparison, ran just over 10,000 searches in the same period.
An analysis of the data using an artificial intelligence agent showed a majority of searches, more than four out of five, did not list a case number. Nearly one out of five had vague or non-descriptive reasons such as “sus”, “atl”, or “cj.” It also showed nearly 36,000 searches labeled “test” run on Flock’s live national database.
The data also showed other police departments and agencies had listed “immigration” or “ICE” as the reason for thousands of searches of New Castle’s database. Flock doesn’t have a business relationship with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or other federal agencies, and sharing with federal agencies is disabled by default, Flock says on its website. Individual police departments may opt to share with federal agencies.
New Castle police Chief David Cumo did not respond to an email with questions about his department’s use of Flock cameras, of which the city has two. The city’s internal audit log showed some officers ran dozens of searches for the same license plate numbers over periods of hours, but listed consistent and specific reasons.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Why does Florida spend so much money on treatment for children with autism and special needs?
description: Florida in the past two years has spent more money than any other state in the nation providing a therapy called applied behavior analysis (ABA) to children with special needs including autism — $6.57 billion between 2023 and 2025. That’s the number Shena Grantham, Florida’s deputy secretary for Medicaid policy and quality, gave to members […]
text:
A blue ribbon task force is being asked to review Florida's Medicaid program and delivery of applied behavioral analysis services to autistic youth, and to submit a report to the governor and Legislature by Dec. 31. (Photo via the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)Florida in the past two years has spent more money than any other state in the nation providing a therapy called applied behavior analysis (ABA) to children with special needs including autism — $6.57 billion between 2023 and 2025.
That’s the number Shena Grantham, Florida’s deputy secretary for Medicaid policy and quality, gave to members of a blue-ribbon panel in Tallahassee this week reviewing ABA services in the Medicaid program that covers about 55,000 children aged 20 and younger.
Indiana ranked a distant second to Florida, spending $1.65 billion over the same two years. North Carolina ran a distant third, at $1.53 billion.
“There’s something unusual happening … that deserves a closer look,” Grantham told members of the Applied Behavior Analysis Task Force, which held its inaugural meeting last week.
The legislatively mandated “closer look” comes as a number of other issues come to a head.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released the State Medicaid and CHIP Applied Behavior Analysis Toolkit, a 173-page document meant to “support state Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) agencies in making decisions regarding ABA service provision for Medicaid and CHIP.”
The DeSantis administration announced in June that it was cracking down on fraud, waste, and abuse in Florida’s $38 billion healthcare safety net program. It was launched after the CMS sent a letter to Florida, as well as California, Maine, and New York, seeking information about Medicaid integrity and oversight and after CMS Director Mehmet Oz said on social media that “Florida has been a hotspot for health care fraud for years.”
Florida has switched its ABA delivery model to require managed care plans to cover services for children. Previously, patients, once authorized, saw the Medicaid ABA provider of their choice and the state paid for the services. Since 2025, the care must be provided by the state-contracted plans and the ABA providers who want to continue working with their clients are having to negotiate contracts with the plans in their regions.
Some providers are being dropped. Others have stopped treating Medicaid clients.
 ‘Agonizingly long waitlists’

Nicole Grabner is a disabled veteran and mother of two children with autism who drove four-plus hours from her home in Brevard County to Tallahassee to tell the task force she’s worried the cumulative changes are hurting Florida families who, she says, already are facing “agonizingly long waitlists” just to be approved for ABA.
Now, she said, the changes are interupting medically necessary care.
She told task force members that during her drive to Tallahassee she learned her youngest son had lost access to his ABA provider.
“These disruptions are kind of concerning, especially now that we are getting into the new school year, when consistency is most critical,” Grabner said. “Aggressive enforcement or administrative delays must never compound these delays for a child receiving early intervention services when a short pause in therapy causes devastating developmental regression.”
Applied behavior analysis uses structured interventions to decrease maladaptive behaviors and reinforce appropriate ones. ABA is common in the treatment of children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.
The Legislature established the 10-member task force as part of fiscal year 2026-27 budget negotiations. The task force is reviewing revisions of the state’s healthcare delivery model to “improve care experience and service continuity for enrollees and families receiving ABA services, while safeguarding long term program sustainability.”
Specifically, the legislation directs the task force to submit a report to the Legislature and governor by the end of the year examining at least six ideas:

Clinical care models that lead to best practices for provision of therapy at the appropriate ages.
Appropriate transitions for enrollees receiving ABA services across developmental, educational, and community settings.
Quality metrics for ABA therapy services.
Limits and use controls related to the length of time applied behavioral analysis services may be authorized.
Potential caps on the number of months an enrollee may receive ABA services.
Ways to enhance Medicaid provider enrollment and billing standards for ABA services, to promote program integrity and fiscal accountability.

The task force must submit its recommendations — along with the pros and cons of each proposal — to the governor and Legislature by Dec. 31.
‘Not set in stone’
Agency for Health Care Administration Secretary Shevaun Harris, chair of the panel as well as a non-voting member, suggested the group complete the bulk of its recommendations by the end of October, but added that the schedule was “not set in stone.”
Before a child can receive ABA services through Florida Medicaid, he or she must be referred by a doctor or child psychologist. The child also must undergo a comprehensive evaluation to formally diagnose or rule out autism and determine medically necessary therapies.
About 25% of children receiving Medicaid-covered ABA services — roughly 13,698 children — have not been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.
Despite cost-savings efforts in the past (which have included pilot programs and a moratorium on ABA provider enrollments) costs have continued to increase.
About 60,000 poor and low-income children in Florida receive applied behavioral analysis at a cost of about $2.3 billion, Grantham said, although she didn’t cite the year.
That’s more than Medicaid spent reimbursing hospitals caring for 966,900 children, covering prescription drugs for 1.4 million children, or paying for about 1.75 million doctor visits, she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Florida the outlier
Delivery of ABA services in Florida doesn’t track national trends.
AHCA’s data show that Medicaid doesn’t emphasize ABA services to children in Florida until they are older, compared to peers in other states.
While it doesn’t provide exact percentages, a chart prepared for the task force indicates fewer than 5% of children receiving ABA services in Florida were aged 2 or younger compared to more than 5% nationally. Likewise, fewer than 25% of the ABA services were provided to Florida children aged 3 to 5, compared to about 40% nationally.
About 45% of the Medicaid-covered ABA services are provided to children aged 6 through 10 in Florida compared to fewer than 40% nationally. And about 20% of the children receiving ABA services in Florida are between the ages of 11 and 15 compared to fewer than 15% nationally.
More than 5% of the children receiving ABA services in Florida were between the ages of 16 and 20 compared to fewer than 5% nationally.
According to Grantham, 99% of  Medicaid-covered ABA services for children are provided through managed care plans. The plans provide additional safeguards because they are in charge of ensuring a proper network of care providers are available for children, she said, and also are charged with ensuring authorization requirements are followed.
Florida Medicaid in February 2025 adjusted the rates it pays the managed care plans to include costs of ABA services. In June, Pediatric Associates  filed a challenge in state administrative court alleging Medicaid reduced payments paid to pediatricians by nearly $300 million over the past 20 months to increase reimbursements to managed care plans for providing the ABA services.
Largest Medicaid pediatric provider sues DeSantis administration over pay rates

The healthcare provider asserted the agency adopted the rates in violation of state and federal statutes and is asking a state administrative judge to issue a final order banning the state from applying them. It also is asking the judge to require the agency to recalculate rates going forward.
A final hearing in the challenge has been scheduled for Oct. 1-2.
Before filing the suit, Pediatric Associates maintains, it met with AHCA “at least five times” between January and May to discuss the new Medicaid payments and errors it alleges the agency made in determining the rates.
AHCA acknowledged in an April 17 correspondence to Medicaid managed care plans that inclusion of ABA services in value-based contracts that the managed health plans sign with providers “has the potential to result in access issues.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A letter to Luke Bronin
description: I hope these tips might help with the transition to becoming Congressman Bronin and a critical member of Connecticut’s delegation.
text:
Luke,
First of all, congratulations.
I write to you as a former four-term House member and long-time friend of Congressman John Larson.
I have an idea of the pain that Larson and his supporters are feeling. Having political power and losing it rather abruptly is something I, too, have experienced.

Toby Moffett

You are about to join the greatest deliberative democratic body in the world, one in which relatively few Americans have been members.
I had never been in that incredible House chamber before I was sworn in at age 29. A half century plus later, I still remember the goosebumps.
Like you, I ran against the Democratic Party establishment. I was one of 75 new Democrats elected to the U.S. House. We were called the “Watergate Babies” as the first freshmen class following the Nixon scandals. Most of us knew we had a lot to do and a lot to learn.
Twenty years ago, when Chris Murphy won that seat that I had once represented in the northwest part of the state and Joe Courtney did the same in the opposite corner, I wrote a piece for the Washington Post with some advice for their freshmen class.
So here I go again. I hope these tips might help with your transition to becoming Congressman Bronin and a critical member of Connecticut’s delegation.
(I realize you still have a general election to win, but it’s a pretty safe bet that you will. If the Republican candidate beats you, these tips could help her, too.)
My tips:
Term-limit yourself
You spent a lot of time and money selling the idea that people stay too long in Congress, so term-limit yourself. I did that a very long time ago, when first running for Congress.
It was something of an accident. But I think it turned out to be a good thing. I was speaking at Newtown High School and some student asked me “You say people stay in Congress too long. So how long will you stay?
I immediately answered, “If you see me there after five terms (ten years), tap me on the shoulder and remind me that I said I wouldn’t serve longer than that.”
My off-handed comment made headlines. And I was stuck with it. So I left after four terms, ran for the U.S. Senate and got beat. I don’t regret it.
But do it. Try five terms. Maybe six. Commit to leaving before somebody makes you leave.
Make Congressman Larson a mentor
I know this will not be easy. It may take a bit of time and some convincing, but John is a team player. He wants his current constituents, your future ones, to continue to have quality representation.
There are several reasons why this makes sense. First of all, John is immensely popular in the House Democratic Caucus. As you know, he was its chairman for some time. And quite frankly, there are going to be some mixed feelings from other members, old and young, over your beating him. A lot of them think you beat him simply by talking about his age. I assume even you would admit that there wasn’t much to criticize in his record as a progressive champion.
So, his mentoring you, for everyone to see, could quickly boost your image with fellow House Democrats. To say nothing of the fact that you could learn a lot from him. About how the place works. About how to get things done. About how to be a fierce progressive advocate while still being able to attract support from more conservative members – and even some Republicans.
Take him to breakfast one day soon at one of his favorite East Hartford diners.
Make surprise visits to other members’ offices
Shortly after the “Watergate Babies” class was sworn in, I got some advice from one of the older long-serving members.
 “Go visit other members’ offices, unannounced. Just walk in and introduce yourself. Meet the staff and talk to the member. It’ll be the start of some very good relationships.”
I took that advice. This sort of thing is not common in Congress. But it allows you to show some initiative and, yes, humility, from a member that is viewed something of a renegade. It helped me make friends I wouldn’t have otherwise had.
Become an advocate for Connecticut’s cities
Some years ago, you and I had a conversation about how our state’s cities are basically islands, sometimes even islands of despair, surrounded by affluent suburbs.
Many decades ago, someone had the not-so-bright idea of abolishing county, regional government here. It released the more affluent suburbanites from any real collective responsibility for our cities. Make this an issue.
This is something of a no-brainer for you. There are several other former mayors in the House —from Phoenix and Houston, for example.  One of them, Rep. Richie Neal, the former mayor of Springfield, is likely to be the chairman of the powerful Ways and Means Committee, the one on which Larson serves.
Neal will surely miss his long-time pal, But he’s a grown-up and knows you won fair and square. Get to know him. Do some work with him to help cities across the country.
Become a leader for changing how money controls our politics
You just ran in a system that is awash with money from the wealthiest and vested interests. The system is broken. It’s not something that’s easy to fix, but, at the very least, show your constituents that you see it as a big problem.
You’re also in a good position to talk about how Connecticut’s public finance system for state offices has diminished the role of money considerably.
Become a House gym rat
From your school days you know how sports enhances friendships and bonding. 
There is a gym several floors under the Rayburn Building. I spent a lot of time there, playing full court basketball — too much time in the eyes of my staff.
There were no party lines on that court. One of your first, unofficial acts, should be to show up down there.
Join a members’ prayer group
I don’t know if you’re religious or not, but this is a great place to build friendships and bridges.  
Like the gym, the prayer groups have no party lines.  Members let their guards down and become something like “regular” people.  I formed important partnerships with friends across the aisle on issues like human rights by just showing up at these early morning meetings.
Make sure the goosebumps haven’t disappeared
As I wrote to Murphy and Courtney and the other freshmen two decades ago, when you leave the Capitol late one night after a very long day and you look up at that lighted dome, if the goosebumps aren’t there, send in your resignation letter.
Best of luck, Luke.
Toby Moffett of Branford is a former four-term member of Congress from Connecticut, 1975-`983.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What trans youth need from CT leaders now
description: CT trans youth and families continue to reel from the year-old disruptions to their healthcare.
text:
One year ago, Connecticut experienced heart-wrenching seismic shifts to its transgender care landscape. 
One of its largest providers shuttered its doors entirely, and the other was forced to stop providing gender-affirming medical care services to its patients. An extension of the federal war waged against transgender people, these institutions were threatened with persecution and a potential loss of funding through proposed changes in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ (CMS) reimbursement rules.
To comply in advance, these institutions ended or limited their services, leaving trans youth and their families in a lurch. Forced to scramble for places to access necessary care, families weighed difficult decisions; healthcare costs grew as some families paid out of pocket for care, and others contemplated whether and how they might leave Connecticut for greener, often international, pastures where they might re-establish care.
The remaining Connecticut institutions were ill-equipped to deal with the deluge: their waitlists grew exponentially and still grow today—a sign there isn’t enough care to meet the demand. And, with clinics closing around the country and some insurance companies dropping coverage for gender-affirming health services, some families have little to no recourse for accessible and affordable care.
One year later, the threatened CMS rules still have not been passed. 
I spent the last year documenting the impact of these changes in care on youth and their families. The largest lesson: Our leadership was not showing up for these trans kids. Their lives had been disrupted, their care had been abruptly withdrawn, and our leaders looked the other way as our healthcare facilities discriminated against transgender children by ending their very necessary care. And they are still absent now as families sift through the rubble to find anything that can help them rebuild their lives.
Now, as with most disasters, after the immediate outpouring of sympathy, people have started looking the other way. Our organizations remain inactive, and Connecticut’s leadership’s absence fuels frustration and a sense of abandonment among trans youth and their families.
Our trans youth deserve better.
As one parent of a trans youth put it, “I really was hoping that our politicians here in Connecticut would have spoken up in our defense, also like having our back, somebody having our back.” They lament that support and defense never came from our leaders: “That didn’t really happen, somebody having our back in an institutional way, people with power having our back.”
Sadly, this isn’t new, though. Transgender communities have had to show up for themselves for decades, often unable to count on sustainable support from society and its leaders. In the trans experience, leadership is often comprised of fair-weather friends in high-powered places, who come to pride events and who court transgender voters. But when the bonds of their allegiance are tested against the real, systemic hardships faced by trans people, these bonds are frequently easily broken, and transgender people are left standing alone.
So, one year later, trans youth and families continue to reel from the disruptions to their healthcare. Connecticut leaders supportive, on paper, of protecting transgender youth, have not (yet) concretized this support in meaningful ways that support the needs of transgender youth and their families for care and for protection against further federal assaults.
On this grim anniversary, we have this opportunity to reflect on our leaders’ actions and inactions and consider how the next year might be different and how those in power can help rebuild trans care in Connecticut. It begins with enforcing extant laws and holding Connecticut institutions accountable for providing the care to the populations they have supported for years.
Work with them to reinstate care.
Support them by extending shield laws so they can operate fearlessly and stand up for our transgender youth and their families.
Connecticut enjoys the laudable status of being one of the first states to enact shield laws in 2022 to protect the delivery of gender-affirming healthcare.  In the current sociopolitical climate, Connecticut leadership is positioned to lead the charge in protecting trans youth in Connecticut and create a model of care and protection that can inspire other states and territories to do the same. Leadership must continue standing for trans youth by creating alternative sources of funding to rebuild and sustain transgender care so that any threat of the CMS rule is made innocuous.
Finally, private healthcare organizations remain more vulnerable to federal anti-trans attacks. Recognizing this, Connecticut leadership must create state-sponsored and/or state-directed avenues for transgender care that, as public entities and agencies, can wield the might of the Connecticut legislature and can be fully protected by our shield laws. 
Connecticut, our trans youth are looking to you to have their back now more than ever. Will you show up for them?
SJ Job is a psychologist at Yale University. The opinions expressed here are their own.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland’s primary results prove it’s time for ranked choice voting
description: In all but two counties in this year's primaries, there were races decided by a plurality vote, sending winners to the general with less than majority support and leaving a majority of voters disappointed. It's time for ranked choice voting, writes Mike Pellittierre.
text:
A sign points to a voting precinct in Frederick for the June primary elections. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)This primary season, I, like many independents, affiliated with the Democratic Party just so I could vote in the primary – the election that picks the vast majority of winners in Maryland since most voting districts, from local to federal, are not competitive. While I support opening the primaries, this is not about that.
I live in Maryland’s 5th Congressional District where an overwhelming 24 candidates were on the ballot. Unfortunately, I know that my preferred candidate didn’t have a realistic shot at winning. So, I, like many others, voted strategically: I looked at who I thought would be the top two and cast my vote for the one I liked better (or disliked least).
I live in Anne Arundel County: four candidates were on the ballot for county executive, but one had dropped out. So, it was effectively a three-way race. Again, I had to vote strategically. Do I risk voting for my preferred candidate, or do I compromise just to block someone else?
The results of our current voting rules speak for themselves. In the crowded primary to fill Rep. Steny Hoyer’s seat, state Del. Adrian Boafo won the Democratic nomination with roughly 32% of the vote. This means that in a fragmented field of more than 20 candidates, more than two out of every three voters cast ballots for other choices.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Here in Anne Arundel County, Councilmember Allison Pickard won the nomination for county executive in a hard-fought, multicandidate primary with 42.5% of the vote. Because our current system splits the field, over half the voters cast ballots for other choices, including 2.5% for a candidate who had already withdrawn. This isn’t a reflection on Ms. Pickard’s leadership, but rather a critique of an outdated system that forces strong candidates to advance with split pluralities instead of built-in majority support.
The same situation happened for our Republican neighbors, in the crowded, nine candidate primary for governor. While Dan Cox secured the nomination with roughly 45% of the vote, the highly competitive race split the remaining 55% of voters across the other choices. Just like in the Democratic contests, our current system forces a nominee to advance to the general election without the mathematically proven support of a broad party majority.
In fact, a look at the broader statewide data reveals that only two counties in all of Maryland managed to escape having a plurality winner this primary season.
Our current voting system drives us to nominate and elect leaders who lack the support of the majority. Instead of just voting for who we believe in, we, the voters, are forced to play political strategist. We have to figure out how to dodge spoiler candidates and vote—not for the person we actually want—but for the one who has the best shot at blocking the candidate we don’t want.
We can fix this: There is a better way. Ranked choice voting lets voters rank their candidates in order of preference, so we can be heard and factored into the final decision. It frees voters to vote for the candidate who they truly want without fear of wasting their ballot on someone that doesn’t have a chance. We can finally vote for a candidate, instead of against another.
This helps candidates and the parties, too. Winners walk away with a clearer mandate, because they have to earn a broad majority to win. Plus, parties can see voters’ true preferences, giving them a clear picture of what the electorate actually cares about. Best of all, campaign rhetoric tones down as candidates have to reach out to opponents’ supporters for backup votes, instead of pushing people away.
Ranked choice voting is simple, we rank our preferences every day. As a kid, my mom would send me into the store to buy milk: “Get 1%. If they are out of 1%, get skim.” It is just as intuitive at the ballot box. In places across the country already using it, exit polls consistently show that over 90% of voters find their RCV ballots easy to understand.
Cities across Maryland are already proving this works. Takoma Park has successfully used ranked choice voting since 2007. Greenbelt voters overwhelmingly approved it last fall, and Berwyn Heights voters just passed a ballot measure to explore it with 76% support. Other municipalities around the state are pursuing it because they know our local elections deserve better outcomes.
It’s time to vote better. It’s time for ranked choice voting.
