name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky Democrats look to midterm elections, governor’s race during annual statewide dinner
description: LEXINGTON — There was one elephant in the room during the Kentucky Democrats’ dinner Saturday evening — the upcoming primary for governor.  U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey noted to the sold-out room that he had to speak between the two Democratic candidates — Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear.  “Awkward!” McGarvey[...]
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, left, and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, right, talk to reporters ahead of the Kentucky Democrats' Forward Together Dinner. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)LEXINGTON — There was one elephant in the room during the Kentucky Democrats’ dinner Saturday evening — the upcoming primary for governor. 
U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey noted to the sold-out room that he had to speak between the two Democratic candidates — Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear. 
“Awkward!” McGarvey said to laughs in the room. “Hi, Mom. Hi, Dad. We love you both.” 
Beshear, who was the last speaker of the night, also addressed the primary. Both Coleman and Adkins have served in his administration since his first term starting in 2019. 
“I know it’s starting to ramp up. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins are both good friends of mine,” Beshear said. “They are both qualified to be governor. We’ve got to make sure we elect one of them to be the next governor.” 
Both Coleman and Adkins spoke at the Forward Together Dinner in Lexington, which had sold 550 tickets, beating last year’s sales number which had been the largest Kentucky Democratic Party dinner since 2012. While the May 18 primary is months away, the campaigns are still starting to take shape. 
“We had a conversation early on that no matter what happens next May, we’re going to help each other, and I want our supporters to know that too,” Coleman told reporters after the dinner. “I don’t want us to get too far down the road where you can’t back up and help support a Democrat win in November, because that’s ultimately the most important thing.”
Nevertheless, they are both competitors. Coleman said she has an advantage over Adkins with “energy and momentum.” However, Adkins says he does have that and pointed to his fundraising numbers, as his campaign recently said it raised more than $1 million in three weeks. 
Adkins told reporters that Beshear had told him he wouldn’t make a primary endorsement as he’s the head of the Kentucky Democratic Party and currently serves as the chair of the Democratic Governors Association, a group that backs candidates around the country. 
“He said, ‘I’m not going to make an endorsement in the race. Both of you have been valuable parts of this administration,’” Adkins said before adding that he respects the decision. 
Before the dinner, Beshear said that he thinks a contested primary is “going to help us.” Republicans are seemingly lining up behind U.S. Rep. James Comer, who hasn’t formally announced he is running for governor. Beshear noted he had a contested primary in 2019 before facing former Republican Gov. Matt Bevin and said he “was better for it.” 
“I think you see time after time that a strong primary with two qualified candidates makes those candidates better and builds energy,” Beshear said. 
Looking to November
Kentucky Democrats are also thinking about midterm elections. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who is the DGA vice chair this election cycle, said states like Kentucky and Michigan have leaders “doing exactly what we’re supposed to be doing: working together, thinking together, celebrating and mourning together, doing whatever we can to deliver for the people we serve and yes, even working across the aisle to GSD.” Whitmer censored her motto from “Get Shit Done” to “Get Stuff Done” for the night because “Andy doesn’t swear at the microphone.” 
“This November, we get to show who we are and what kind of politics we think we deserve,” Whitmer said.  
Charles Booker, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, talks to reporters after the Kentucky Democrats’ Forward Together Dinner. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Throughout the speeches, Democrats largely critiqued Republicans under President Donald Trump and focused on issues like rising cost of living, gas prices, the war in Iran and more. Charles Booker, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, criticized outgoing U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell for building “corruption” and the Republican nominee in the race, U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, particularly for running an ad during the primary election saying it’s “not a sin to be white.”
“If you want leaders that sow hate and division, that’s your choice,” Booker said. “I know you’re not making that choice.” 
Zach Dembo, the Democrat running for Barr’s open congressional seat in central Kentucky, also chided Republicans under Trump and reminded the crowd that his opponent, Republican Ralph Alvarado, was the 2019 running mate of Bevin. A recent Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee poll found that likely voters supported Alvarado and Dembo at 47% each and 6% were left undecided. 
“We are going to win, but it’s going to be by a tight margin y’all. We cannot afford anyone on the sidelines,” Dembo said before asking the Democrats in the room to support his campaign. 
Beshear, seen as a possible candidate for president in 2028, focused on a message for Democrats in Kentucky and beyond. He said he was proof “that Democrats can and should win everywhere in the United States of America.” Beshear pointed to his own wins in 2019 and 2023 and over-performing in elections in counties that Trump had won by wide margins. 
Beshear said early in his remarks that five people were shot about 1.5 miles from the dinner venue in Lexington and that one person had likely died. He added that the crowd was safe and it was not an active situation at the time. 
“Let’s think about the families of those that are involved, but having lost one of my closest friends in a shooting — let’s not live in fear. Let’s not let it take our energy from tonight. Because we know if we want to reduce or stop mass shootings in this country, we have got to elect Democrats that will actually do something about it,” Beshear said to cheers in the crowd. 
The governor said that Democrats “have to be the party that is seen as addressing Americans’ concerns,” such particularly on jobs, economic issues and healthcare access. 
“While we are dialed in on that next election, most Americans aren’t as political as the pundits think they are,” Beshear said. “When they wake up in the morning, they’re not thinking about the next race. They’re thinking about their job and whether they make enough to support their family. They’re thinking about the next doctor’s appointment for themselves or their parents or their kids. They’re thinking about the roads and bridges they drive to school — the public school (where) they drop their kids off — and whether they feel safe in their communities.”

name: VTDigger
title: Federal change to Endangered Species Act could affect Vermont’s vulnerable wildlife
description:
As the Trump administration rescinds the definition of “harm,” environmental experts explain what the change could mean for Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Federal change to Endangered Species Act could affect Vermont’s vulnerable wildlife.
text:
Jesup’s milk-vetch. Photo by Levi Smith/Wikimedia Commons

Via Community News Service, a University of Vermont journalism internship
President Donald Trump’s administration finalized a rule change last month that alters the definition of “harm” in the Endangered Species Act, loosening protections for endangered species and making them more vulnerable to habitat loss and extinction. 
Passed in 1973, the act previously defined “harm” broadly to include any actions that injure or kill a protected organism, including “significant habitat modification or degradation.” The Trump administration, however, argued that the definition amounted to regulatory overreach and interfered with private property rights.
That definition is now being rescinded, which would allow oil drilling, mining and logging to operate in wildlife habitats, as long as the animals that live there aren’t injured or killed, according to the Associated Press. 
Environmental law experts and conservationists are now evaluating what the change could mean for Vermont’s endangered species, conservation laws and development plans. They agree that while Vermont still has its own legal protections for listed species, the rollback of federal regulations could have a national impact that affects the state’s plants and animals.
“(These species are) listed because of loss of habitat, and that’s really difficult to restore and recover from,” said Patrick Parenteau, a professor of law emeritus and senior fellow for climate policy at Vermont Law and Graduate School. “They’re never going to recover if you start repealing the rules that are designed to protect that habitat.” 
Vermont has seven animal and three plant species listed as federally endangered or threatened, including the Canadian lynx and Jesup’s milk-vetch, a rare plant only found in Vermont and New Hampshire. 
The state also maintains its own list, which includes endangered species — 71 plants and 39 animals — and threatened ones, including 93 plants and 17 animals. Decisions about what species are listed are made by the state’s Endangered Species Committee. 

The Canadian lynx is an endangered species in Vermont that could be further threatened by habitat loss. Photo by kdee64 (Keith Williams), CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The committee, which includes three state officials and six ecology experts appointed by the governor, advises the Secretary of Natural Resources on issues relating to endangered and threatened species, including whether to alter the state’s lists of species, how to protect them and where to designate critical habitat.
The committee also weighs in on whether developers should receive permits when their plans could harm the state’s protected species.
Bryan Pfeiffer, a field naturalist who serves on the committee, said the state does not allow the presence of an endangered species to halt all development, but in his opinion, the federal rule change goes beyond what is considered sensible environmental policy.
“Most of the time we accommodate development,” he said, referring to Vermont. But at the national level, “This sort of reinterpretation of the notion of ‘harm’ really takes away (the country’s) ability to have reasonable threatened and endangered species protections.”
Pfeiffer explained that a species doesn’t need to be present in a habitat to be threatened by its destruction. For example, long-ranging species like the Canadian lynx rely on connected habitats across multiple states, meaning the federal change could shrink their range in states with looser laws.
“Imagine you’re on an airplane. You’ve taken a vacation, and you’re on your return flight home, only to find that the airport where you expect to land is now gone,” he said. “In many ways, that’s what this is like: You can damage habitat while a species is not there and still imperil the species.”

The Indiana bat is one of five bat species listed as endangered or threatened in Vermont. Photo by Adam Mann for the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons

Christophe Courchesne, the director of the Environmental Law Center at Vermont Law and Graduate School, said Vermont’s endangered species may fare better than those in states that defer to federal guidance. But he said there could still be areas of the law that were previously overlooked that the state may need to revisit.
“We could see gaps where the state needs to impose more restrictions in future cases without help from federal agencies. Going forward, the state will need to be vigilant to enforce state law,” he said.
The rule change is set to take effect on September 14, but environmental organizations have already sued to stop it. Both Courchesne and Parenteau said they believe the rule change has no legal basis and may not hold up in court.
“The Endangered Species Act itself does not permit this kind of wholesale rollback of the act’s science-based protections of species habitat that are inherent in allowing species to recover from the brink of extinction,” Courchesne said.
Parenteau said opponents may try to get a lower court to issue a preliminary injunction, which would prevent the change from taking effect while the case is argued.
“The strategy that the challengers are pursuing is to tie up the rule in court long enough so that the Trump administration is out of power, and a new administration could come in in time to reverse what they have done, reinstate the harm rule, and avoid a showdown in the U.S. Supreme Court,” Parenteau said.
Tara Miller, forest and wildlife program director at the Vermont Natural Resource Council, said that despite the federal changes, the organization will concentrate on improving state-level environmental protections. Currently, the group is focusing on programs that prevent forest division to increase the amount of connected habitat for species.
Miller acknowledged that debates over land use can be tough for municipalities trying to implement conservation initiatives while addressing the needs of their residents. Miller said, however, that they see enforcing these environmental policies as a force for good.
“If we look decades back to when we didn’t have these kinds of environmental regulations, there were so many negative impacts,” Miller said. “Things are always a balance, but it’s really important to have these regulations as an opportunity both to review projects and make sure that they’re what we want, for our needs, for our values and our communities.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Bridge demolition means long detours, downtown challenges for Lansing
description: LANSING — The demolition and rebuilding of a landmark bridge in this idyllic town along America’s greatest river has prompted convoluted detours for commuters and hurt businesses in the city’s historic Main Street district. The Black Hawk Bridge once spanned the Mississippi River to connect Iowa and Wisconsin, acting as a lifeline for Lansing for […]
text:
The new bridge being built across the Mississippi River at Lansing, Iowa, captures the classic look of the old Black Hawk Bridge while making marked improvements on all fronts. (Photo by Alex Burdzy)LANSING — The demolition and rebuilding of a landmark bridge in this idyllic town along America’s greatest river has prompted convoluted detours for commuters and hurt businesses in the city’s historic Main Street district.
The Black Hawk Bridge once spanned the Mississippi River to connect Iowa and Wisconsin, acting as a lifeline for Lansing for almost a century. It became regionally iconic, featured in a pivotal scene of the 1999 David Lynch film “The Straight Story.” Now, it is being replaced with a modernized lookalike.
The bridge’s era came to an end with its closure in October 2025 and its demolition — with thousands in attendance — two months later.
Shutting down the Black Hawk Bridge cut off Lansing from a crucial river crossing. The other nearest crossings are in Marquette, Iowa (more than 27 miles south), and La Crescent, Minnesota (about 35 miles north).
Lansing Mayor Mike Verdon said residents have felt the loss of the old bridge.
“Most of the residents of Lansing are either lifelong residents, or have a family history with the town, so they’re well acquainted with the history of the old bridge,” he said. “It’s hard to say goodbye to an old friend, but everyone is anticipating the opening of the new one.”
Many older residents of Lansing lament the loss of the old bridge’s iconic design and its “singing” — a reference to the hum produced by the steel grate road surface.
Workers on the new Lansing bridge in July 2026. (Photo by Alex Burdzy)
“I know people that work on both sides of the river that use that bridge to commute to work,” said Clayton Burke, the Iowa Department of Transportation’s project manager for the Black Hawk Bridge. “There are people that use it to get to medical services like dental services or the clinic, and there’s the grocery store in Lansing … and people use it to get to their loved ones.”
Those hardships will continue until the new bridge is completed, expected by spring 2027.
Why the Black Hawk Bridge was demolished
DOT employees started looking into a reconstruction project in 2003, Burke said.
At the time, they considered several possibilities. The bridge could be renovated in its current state to last a couple of years more, left alone until it became functionally unusable, or demolished and rebuilt entirely.
Demolition proved to be the best option due to the litany of issues with the old bridge.
For one, according to the DOT, the old bridge was just 21 feet wide with no shoulder, and its surface was made of a steel grate instead of concrete. Its replacement will be 40 feet wide with a concrete surface and a proper shoulder.
“If you break down, you can pull over and get out of the way, or if a very wide farm implement comes through, they will have space to get through without running into other vehicles,” Burke said.
The old bridge also pushed up abruptly against the Iowa side with a tight intersection near the edge of a bluff. The new bridge significantly expands the T-intersection.
“It’ll be easier for commercial vehicles to get through and turn and safely make that passage through,” Burke said.
View of the new Lansing, Iowa, bridge from the Driftless Area Education & Visitor’s Center in July 2026. (Photo by Alex Burdzy)
Additionally, the navigation channel underneath the bridge has been widened by 100 feet, making it easier for barges to negotiate the Mississippi’s main branch.
The original estimate for demolishing the old bridge and building its replacement was $140 million. The federal government was to shoulder 80%, and Iowa and Wisconsin were to split the rest. However, the La Crosse, Wisconsin, Tribune reports the cost has risen to $160 million.
Building a replacement bridge has not come without other challenges.
Naturalist Erin Cubbon at the Driftless Area Education & Visitors’ Center, an environmental museum and organization, has witnessed the decline in the town’s commerce and visitor traffic.
“We have noticed that our numbers are a little bit lower this year, but again we’re very lucky not to be affected as (much as) many of the businesses downtown,” she said.
Mayor Verdon gave this problem a more statistical framing.
“There are about 8,200 people living within a 30-mile radius of the bridge who use it regularly in both their personal and professional capacities,” he said. “It was clear from the onset that there would be a severe impact on the daily lives of each of us.”
To alleviate some of this isolation, the Iowa DOT set up a ferry service to connect Lansing to the other side of the Mississippi.
A ferry from Cassville, Wisconsin, initially served the crossing during the winter months of 2025-26. In the meantime, the contractors worked out a deal with Newt Marine Services out of Dubuque for a more permanent solution.
Newt Marine “actually built a brand-new ferry barge while Cassville was operating,” Burke said.
He applauded the team for its determination to finish an urgent project for the people of Lansing.
“They worked night shifts to get it done in time, overtime,” he said. “They put in a lot of effort and recognized that this is a critical service that we need to provide.”
The ferry can accommodate 675 to 700 vehicles per day.
When building the ferry dock, the construction firm had to consult the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to measure the impact of construction on the floodplains along the river. Modifying these landscapes too much can lead to increased risk of flooding, a major concern in a town like Lansing, where many residents live next to the Mississippi.
“Anytime you build a structure in a floodplain, the Corps gets very interested in the size of that structure and any impact it may have on future flooding in the area,” Burke said. “We don’t want to build something that will flood somebody’s house out.”
Iowa DOT project manager Clayton Burke in front of the new Lansing bridge’s T-intersection. (Photo by Alex Burdzy)
Burke said he and his team had an easy time working with the Corps and getting their necessary permits.
“We got this permit in record time so we could start building right away,” he said.
Officials also needed to address the new bridge’s effect on a local population of endangered mussels.
“There’s protected species like the Higgins eye pearly mussel,” Burke explained. “A big part of our mitigation was hiring a service to come remove those mussels and relocate them so that we weren’t taking them or destroying those mussels.”
Higgins eye pearly mussels are native to the stretch of the Mississippi between La Crosse, Wisconsin, and Muscatine, Iowa, and are federally listed as an endangered species.
Conservation also comes in the design of the bridge. The Black Hawk Bridge was a local landmark and a symbol of the area.
“Maintaining that iconic image of the bridge for the communities in the area was very important, and it is also more cost-effective than maintaining the old bridge in perpetuity,” Burke said.
Through the old bridge’s eligibility for the Historic Preservation Act, the new bridge is being built to closely resemble the old one. One part of this preservation is using older construction techniques, Burke said.
“We don’t typically build trusses on the National Highway System anymore, but in this case, we’re able to do it to mitigate the loss of that historic structure,” he said.
Truss bridges have fallen out of favor for modern bridge construction due to changes in styles, high maintenance levels and a labor-intensive construction process, among other reasons.
More construction headaches lie ahead
The new bridge’s completion will not be the end of Lansing’s reconstruction. The town’s 1.32-mile Main Street is expected to be rehabilitated in 2028.
According to documents from the Regional Planning Commission, reconstructing the road will address concerns such as traffic safety, walkability, accessibility, environmental impacts, historic preservation, lighting and streetscape amenities.
Small businesses in Lansing, Iowa, will be affected by the closure of Main Street in 2028. (Photo by Alex Burdzy)
Local Realtor Jack Sweeney was apprehensive about the timing of this second project for such a small town.
“If the DOT is going to come in and tear the street out, it’s too bad they couldn’t have done that at the same time and then the hurt would have been all at once,” he said about the bridge closure’s timing. “I feel sorry for those people down there in Lansing that are in business.”
Jackie Cooper is the executive director of Main Street Lansing, an organization whose mission is to enhance and support the historic district of Main Street.
As a result of the bridge’s closure, Main Street Lansing has stepped in to provide more community events to encourage people to stay in town. New events include the monthly “Cocktails & Connections” social and the inaugural Lansing Liberty Motorcycle Rally, which brought over 150 riders to town.
Additionally, many local businesses have hosted more events themselves, including live music and themed nights. These serve the important function of community continuity.
“While the bridge closure has presented real economic challenges, it has also highlighted just how committed Lansing is to supporting one another and adapting through difficult circumstances,” Cooper said.
This mission will become all the more important when the main avenue to get to the various businesses on Main Street will be shut off.
“Our focus will be on helping keep business owners, residents, and visitors informed with timely and accurate communication,” Cooper said. “This could include guidance on customer communication, business continuity planning, marketing strategies, signage, and ‘We’re Still Open’ campaigns to encourage people to continue shopping and dining downtown during construction.”
“Ultimately, we see this as an investment in Lansing’s future,” she said. “While construction will undoubtedly bring challenges, it’s also an opportunity to create a stronger, more vibrant downtown that will serve our businesses, residents and visitors for generations to come.”

title: ‘There it was’: Mike Baker jumps into lakes and digs through poison ivy for lost wedding rings and other precious things
description:
The “ring finder” has been at it for years. He routes part of the reward money for his finds to a local animal rescue organization.   
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘There it was’: Mike Baker jumps into lakes and digs through poison ivy for lost wedding rings and other precious things.
text:
On a sunny July Fourth weekend at Lake Dunmore, with his family running around “pretending to be sharks,” David Miles noticed an odd sensation — his wedding ring was no longer on his finger. 
Miles, a Montpelier resident, was about to celebrate his 46th wedding anniversary, and he rarely, if ever, removed his ring. He didn’t think it had been very long since it had slipped off his finger. Yet the prospect of finding it in the lake, which was full of swimmers, was daunting.  
After hours of digging around, Miles called off the search. As they were leaving, his daughter started a Google search. 
Enter Mike Baker, a professional ring finder. 
A family member called him immediately, and Baker assured Miles he would find the ring for him. He was right: They met the next morning, and two hours later Baker fished the ring from 3 feet of water and an inch of silt and pebbles. 
He’s done it hundreds of times over 15 years, venturing up mountains, into deep rapids and across state lines to turn up lost rings, jewelry, keys and other types of the most financially and emotionally valuable things humans own. 
Baker, a Barre resident, isn’t in it for the money. Half the reward money that people give him goes to his charity of choice, the Central Vermont Humane Society. He chose the local rescue organization because he has friends who work there and has adopted a few dogs from them over the years. He now has two dogs, Minnie and Brody. 
But he’s never set a specific rate for his efforts, because he wants to help everyone, regardless of their financial circumstances. 
“Even if they’re looking for a tractor part, something that’s not very expensive, but it’s very important, and they don’t have much money, it’s all part of it,” he said. 
“Like a journalist or a detective”
Baker demonstrated his search technique to VTDigger on a July morning in Hubbard Park, in his former hometown of Montpelier. He swung his metal detector in smooth, methodical passes back and forth, keeping an eye on the detector’s readings to distinguish precious metals from scrap metal and trash. 
Baker first bought a metal detector secondhand 15 years ago. At first he used it for nothing more than exploring his own property and the local forest. 

Metal detectorist and finder of lost rings (among other items) Mike Baker discusses his work at Hubbard Park in Montpelier on Thursday, July 16, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Once he’d “really been bitten by the bug,” he began watching YouTube videos from fellow metal detectorists. One of those YouTubers was Chris Turner, the founder of The Ring Finder, where hundreds of finder specialists around the world advertise their services. 
Baker is now one of three ring finders in the directory, including a recent addition, Amos Martin, who now covers most Champlain Valley calls. Baker has worked with him on a find before. 
“You got to ask a lot of questions, like a journalist or a detective,” Baker said.  
One of Baker’s proudest finds was for a widow who kept her husband’s ring on her thumb. When she lost it, she believed she’d flushed it down the toilet, prompting her children to comb through the septic system. It wasn’t there. 
By the time they called in Baker, the widow was in danger of losing her house to a tax sale, putting a looming deadline on the hunt. 
He spent five or six hours on a Saturday searching all around the area where the septic tank had gone to nature, finding sheet metal, toys and other old items, but no ring. He returned again the following Saturday and had spent another four hours searching when he thought to check near a clothesline where the woman might have chosen to hang her clothes. 
Buried 4 inches into the dirt was a thin, bent piece of metal, he said. 
“When I went into her kitchen, she turned, I held out my hand and I said, ‘Is that your husband’s ring?’ And she said, ‘Yeah, it is.’ And she turned white as a sheet,” he said. “It was just like her husband was part of that ring.”
“There it was”
Along with hours of labor, Baker’s efforts often require him to brave less-than-ideal conditions out in nature, from searching through the rapids of the Hudson River to digging around in poison ivy. 
And then there’s snow. He once received a call from a woman who had lost a rare vintage watch, worth tens of thousands of dollars, at the Okemo ski area in Ludlow. Okemo had received a foot of fresh snow the day she lost it, he said. 

David Miles and his wife Deb Dwyer show off their wedding rings, including the one Miles lost in Lake Dunmore. Contributed by David Miles

“As soon as the spring started melting the snow, I went back down,” he said. On his third trip, he was in the parking lot which still had 8 or 9 inches of snow that had been plowed in the parking lot. 
Bingo. “There it was,” he said, bringing a reward that made it his “best year ever” for donations to the humane society.  
After the Lake Dunmore episode, Miles brought Baker a rhubarb coffee cake alongside the reward money when he went to see him the following week. The two ended up chatting about their overlapping friends and places they’ve been. 
“Just a great guy, and really a happy ending to a ring that just spent an overnight in Lake Dunmore,” Miles said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont proposes changes to primitive camping in the state for the first time in 33 years
description:
Campers would be required to adhere to stricter policies surrounding campfires, where camps are set up in relation to bodies of water and following carry-in, carry-out practices.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont proposes changes to primitive camping in the state for the first time in 33 years.
text:
A pair of hikers head up the Monroe Trail in Camel’s Hump State Park in Duxbury on Thursday, August 6, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
After three decades, Vermont is looking to change its primitive camping rules to help take more preventive measures against wildfires and land pollution, according to the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation.
Vermonters who participate in primitive camping typically stay in a remote area without any modern amenities, such as running water, electricity, trash cans or bathroom facilities, forcing them to use the natural resources around them.  
Under the proposed new amendment to the rule, campers will no longer be allowed to cut or burn any live wood for campfires. They will also be required to set up their campsites 200 feet from rivers, streams, lakes and wetlands, instead of 100 feet, to better protect water quality and shoreline habitats. 
“I think a lot of Vermonters and our visitors really cherish the amazing forest ecosystems and other camping areas that we have here, and we want to protect them,” said Oliver Pierson, the director of forestry at the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation.
The rule was last updated in 1993 and is now being revised to make the expectations for campers who are going primitive camping even clearer, Pierson said. 
The proposed changes also establish stronger enforcement for compliance, allowing Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department wardens, along with other law enforcement, to issue trespass notices to campers that do not adhere to the policy. 
The proposed changes are set to only apply to lands managed by the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation, with lands governed by Fish and Wildlife to be under a separate rule.
Scott Ellis, a camper from Norwich who has been an avid camper his whole life, said he liked the changes to the rule and was surprised that campers were not already doing some of the practices, such as the “leave no trace” policy. 
While certain primitive camp sites in Vermont already had strict rules on picking up all their belongings and trash before leaving the campgrounds, the new amendment makes it obligatory.  
“This update is in line with how we’re going to respect our land in a better way,” Ellis said. “I think they’re doing it all the right way, and I’m on board with their new policy.” 
He added that he was also relieved to know the state would still allow for campfires, even if there were stronger restrictions regarding the kind of firewood that’s allowed. 
Pierson explained that a big reason for restricting the use of live wood for campfires was to help prevent wildfires from starting and spreading, while also reinforcing campers to make certain their fires are completely put out before they leave. 
“In most situations, we’re not prohibiting campfires because that’s obviously a big part of being out in the woods,” Pierson said. “But we are saying, ‘Hey, if you’re going to build a fire, please do it this way. Please extinguish.’” 
However, Mike McDonagh and Karsten Kurvenko, who are also avid campers across New England, seemed hesitant about the potential new rule. 
Originally from Massachusetts, the couple had been camping in Vermont for almost a decade when their daughter moved to Montpelier. 
After learning about the proposed changes, McDonagh and Kurvenko said they had already been following most of the practices already proposed “out of respect,” adding that all primitive campers should be following them, too. 
“You should definitely carry in, carry out,” McDonagh said. “I mean that’s kind of a no-brainer.” 
Similar to Ellis, however, a major concern for McDonagh and Kurvenko was the restrictions on using live wood, allowing for the use of only fallen wood. 
Kurvenko emphasized the importance of campers making sure they weren’t in drought season when making fires, but suggested that maybe the state should make the rules apply only to certain times of the year instead of all year round. 
“During drought season, fires could catch so fast even for a responsible person,” she said. “Maybe just sending out an alert is good enough.”   
The parks and recreation department is allowing the public to give feedback on the proposed changes before Oct. 9 through an online comment form or the two public hearings held on September 22 at the Manchester Community Library and on September 24 at the Waterbury Town Offices.
“We’re happy that people are getting out there and enjoying those lands,” Pierson, from the natural resources agency, said. “But you know, as use has increased, better information about how to protect sensitive forest ecosystems has come to light.” 
McDonagh and Kurvenko worry that the change could lead to stricter regulations that one day get rid of campfires altogether.
“Maybe you’re gonna get, out of 10 people, one knucklehead that doesn’t think about it,” McDonagh said. “So I guess there’s a risk there. But then, do you ruin it for the nine other people that are responsible?”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Thune says year-round higher ethanol blend will require compromising with small oil refiners
description: SIOUX FALLS — The year-round sale of higher ethanol-blended gasoline, called E15, does not have enough votes in the U.S. Senate unless it comes with compromises for small oil refineries, said Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota. Ethanol is a gasoline additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available year-round. […]
text:
From left, moderator Kimberly Reed, former president and chair of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, asks questions of U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, and U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, at the Midwest Agricultural Export Summit in Sioux Falls on August 12, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — The year-round sale of higher ethanol-blended gasoline, called E15, does not have enough votes in the U.S. Senate unless it comes with compromises for small oil refineries, said Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota.
Ethanol is a gasoline additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available year-round. Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent. Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver.
Opponents point to research showing emissions from higher ethanol blends could worsen summer smog — although the biofuels industry disputes that — while encouraging the conversion of grasslands for corn farming. Some lawmakers from oil-producing and refining states also oppose the expansion. 
Year-round ethanol blend bill passed by US House faces uncertain Senate path

The U.S. House approved a bill in May authorizing year-round E15 sales, and year-round E15 language is in the Senate version of the farm bill under consideration by that chamber’s Ag Committee.
Walter Wendland, president of the South Dakota Ethanol Producers Association, asked Thune during Wednesday’s Midwest Agricultural Export Summit in Sioux Falls whether Congress could approve year-round E15 without making concessions to small oil refiners regarding the exemptions they receive from the Renewable Fuel Standard.
“Probably not,” Thune said.
Thune said E15 supporters need senators on board from states with small oil refiners. He listed Montana, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Tennessee lawmakers as those who might be inclined to support E15, but won’t without addressing small refineries’ concerns.
“At some point, we’ve got to get this done,” Thune said. “And I think at some point it becomes a decision of what can you get the votes to do.” 
The dispute centers on the Renewable Fuel Standard, overseen by the Environmental Protection Agency. It requires oil refiners to blend a minimum amount of renewable fuels, such as ethanol, into their fuel supply, or pay for compliance credits. 
Refineries processing 75,000 or fewer barrels per day can obtain a small refinery exemption if they can show that complying with the standard would cause them “disproportionate economic hardship.” 
Whether the Renewable Fuel Standard is actually met depends partly on whether larger refiners make up for the exemptions granted to small refiners.
Current law allows no automatic exemptions. Small refiners must prove a hardship and can receive full or half exemptions. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The House bill would allow small refiners to receive automatic 75% exemptions, but the bill would require companies to aggregate their facilities rather than applying exemptions to individual plants. Seventeen of the 33 facilities that applied last year would be ineligible under that scenario. The House bill would not require exempted amounts to be reallocated to other refiners.
The Senate version would grant automatic full exemptions to small refiners without changing rules regarding aggregate versus individual facilities. The Senate version would require some reallocation of exempted amounts to other refiners.
Thune told the Sioux Falls audience that, “try as we did on the House-passed version of it, we weren’t going to get there, and it was the small refineries issue.” The Senate bill is a work in progress. 
Sioux Falls-based POET ethanol’s Senior Vice President of Corporate Affairs Joshua Shields said year-round E15 would be a positive development for biofuels, regardless of the changes to small refinery exemptions. 
“This is about expanding market access for homegrown biofuels,” he said in a statement. “When motorists are given the freedom to fuel with E15, a cleaner, more affordable option, that relies less on volatile petroleum spikes, we are confident that’s what they will choose.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo’s big sloppy crush on data centers finally attracts Ford’s attention
description: After the Current published the story by Jeniffer Solis Friday on the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada hoping to bury its collective head in the sand on data centers, Aaron Ford issued a statement reacting to the story and using the phrase “Lombardo’s taxpayer-funded data centers.”  Uttered by any number of other Democrats — Rep. […]
text:
Aaron Ford, left, and Joe Lombardo. (Photos: Michael Lyle; Richard Bednarski)After the Current published the story by Jeniffer Solis Friday on the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada hoping to bury its collective head in the sand on data centers, Aaron Ford issued a statement reacting to the story and using the phrase “Lombardo’s taxpayer-funded data centers.” 
Uttered by any number of other Democrats — Rep. Dina Titus, for instance — or their allied organizations, the slam against the governor might not be noteworthy. But in Ford’s case, it is, because asked more than once this summer by the Current’s senior reporter Dana Gentry if and why the state should continue bestowing hundreds of millions of dollars in tax breaks to data centers, Ford has punted, most recently deflecting the question by saying “I will continue to look at this.”
When he was a state senator, Ford was one of the primary sponsors of the 2015 legislation that created state tax breaks specifically for data centers in the first place. The legislation passed unanimously; in 2015, Anthropic and Open AI weren’t household words. 
In fiscal years 2021 and 2022, the state’s tax breaks to data centers totaled $97 million, according to the state Department of Taxation’s appropriately named Tax Expenditure Report.
The size of the state’s giveaway to data centers had well more than doubled to nearly $240 million in fiscal years 2023-24, the most recent period reported.
By the time the FY 25-26 report is released (no later than Nov. 10 of this year under state statute), the cost of data center tax breaks may have more than doubled again. Or more than tripled.
For decades, state officials of both parties have justified those tax breaks,  like all economic development “incentives” provided to Tesla, the NFL,  MrBeast, etc., by contending without the tax breaks the business activity wouldn’t come to Nevada.
Neither Nevada nor any other state can prove that contention, and in fact evidence abounds that government giveaways make little to no difference at all in companies’ location and relocation decisions. Given the hundreds of billions of dollars the AI/data center industrial complex is spending on data centers and its assertsion that the world simply must create as many data centers as it can as quickly as possible, it’s ludicrous to assume the decision to build a data center in Nevada hinges on tax breaks. The hundreds of millions in tax revenue the state has spent on data centers matters of a lot more to the people and perennially underfunded public services of Nevada than it does to Google, Microsoft, and Apple.
Ford, like the vast majority of Nevada politicians in both parties, has long been a champion of government assistance to private industries in the name of economic development. Last year both Ford and Lombardo backed giving public subsidies to California film corporations, including one now owned by the Trump-worshiping billionaires Larry and David Ellison, whose Oracle firm has been a substantial player in the AI-driven data center infestation.
While that massive expansion of the film tax credit, which would have been the largest public subsidy of private industry in the state’s history, did not pass, Nevada still has an older and smaller program that gives tax breaks to the film and video industries. 
That program was spearheaded by Ford in 2013.
Ford’s opponent in this year’s Democratic primary, Alexis Hill, campaigned against government giveaways generally and data centers specifically. But Hill was overwhelmingly outspent by Ford, and her campaign didn’t get traction.
Now Ford is being overwhelmingly outspent by Lombardo.
As of the last campaign finance filing, Benjamin Horowitz, who along with his tech venture capital partner Mark Andreesen has contributed at least $75 million to the nation’s largest AI industry political action committee, has also contributed at least $1 million to the main PAC supporting Lombardo.
In addition to being an ardent defender of billionaires, Lombardo is also among the most enthusiastic data center apologists with their name on a U.S. ballot this year.
Nevada Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo poses for a picture with Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Jan. 24, 2023. (Photo: Governor’s office)
In a not unrelated note, Lombardo spent most of his first month as governor in 2023 publicly bowing and scraping before the global poster child for publicly abhorred tech bros, Elon Musk. And over the last year or so Lombardo has found himself rationalizing, explaining away, and defending the atrocious working conditions in scofflaw Musk’s preposterous Las Vegas tunnels.
Meanwhile, public fear and loathing of AI and its data centers has only intensified over the summer.
Lombardo’s wildly unpopular stance as a data center cheerleader presents Ford with an opportunity to sharply distinguish himself on what has emerged as one of the most high-profile public policy issues in Nevada and the nation. 
So far, Ford has failed to grasp that opportunity, instead allowing his campaign to slip into the usual stuff of Nevada gubernatorial campaigns: largely policy-free tit-for-tat sniping between the contenders over campaign-generated micro-scandals
Ford’s reference Friday to “Lombardo’s taxpayer-funded data centers” signals his position on data centers may be evolving.
To which a lot of Nevadans would say: It’s about time.
Portions of this column were first published in the Daily Current newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Why polling is so prone to prediction problems in primary races
description: As races from other places and times have shown us, when it comes to primaries, anything can happen.
text:
IT’S PRIMARY SEASON across the country, bringing a close to months of intraparty wrangling – and uncorking the predictable seasonal scolding directed at pollsters who released surveys in the run-up to the elections that widely missed the mark.  
In the last two weeks, Democratic primaries in Michigan and Wisconsin featured outcomes that were very different from the margins shown in late primary polling. In the primary for US Senate in Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed eked out a 1-point win over the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens after the final two polls in the race showed him with a double-digit lead. Meanwhile, on Tuesday, in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin, Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist member of the state legislature, was narrowly defeated by the Milwaukee County executive, David Crowley. While there was little polling in the final stretch, what there was seemed to show a comfortable victory for Hong.  
Here in Massachusetts, so far there is relatively little in the way of public polling or even leaked internal poll results in the run-up to the September 1 primary, Just one public poll has been released in the Democratic Senate primary between incumbent Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton over the last three months, same as the GOP gubernatorial contest. There were a few earlier in the cycle but nothing recent, even as primary day rolls closer. Polling in the US House districts with competitive primaries is even more sparse. But as we enter the final weeks, we may see a bit more, which makes it worth pausing to reflect on what they actually tell us.  
First and foremost, primary polls are very imprecise, missing the final margin by an average of 13 points according to a recent analysis by Strength in Numbers. Primary polling challenges stem from a fairly durable set of reasons that have little to do with the newer methodological challenges of election polling. 
There are no partisan or ideology cues for voters (or pollsters). In general elections, an enormous amount of the potential variation in outcomes is accounted for simply by the fact that some people prefer voting for Democrats and some prefer voting for Republicans. They will vote that way in the vast majority of cases. These preferences are fairly easy to address in poll results, through the process of weighting the final poll results by party. In primaries where all or most voters are members of one party and clustered in one part of the political spectrum, sorting voters into the correct ideological distribution is much less precise.  
In primaries, there are more candidates in voters’ preferred ideological space. With two or more candidates in a given party primary, many voters will be comfortable with any of them. This can be mysterious to close political observers who see stark differences between the candidates and can’t imagine drifting from one to another. But the fact is that voters can and do move from one candidate to another in very large numbers, since they may see several as potentially appealing. Think about any recent presidential primary and you’ll see examples of this, with candidates growing and fading in succession as the primary continues.  
There is more likely to be last-minute upheaval, which can also have bigger impacts. In general elections, there are relatively few huge shifts in the field at the last possible minute. Even replacing Joe Biden as the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 happened months before Election Day. Primaries, however, are notoriously volatile. In the Wisconsin primary, former lieutenant governor Mandela Barnes, who was polling in second place, dropped out of the race with less than two weeks to go. Meanwhile, David Crowley’s victory was remarkable not only because of the huge polling lead Francesca Hong enjoyed just weeks earlier, but because Crowley had actually dropped out of the race and only reentered it on July 18. When it comes to primary upheaval, perhaps the biggest national example in recent years is Joe Biden’s primary consolidation in 2020 after his New Hampshire debacle in 2020, when support shifted to him at lightning speed. 
Voters tune in late and change their minds late. Even as political junkies are riveted by primaries for months ahead of time, primary polls often show huge swaths of voters undecided even days before voting. In both of the Wisconsin polls conducted after Barnes dropped out, Crowley showed a huge jump in support, which was still growing even in the final days. In one of the late polls, a full 34 percent of likely primary voters were still undecided or did not select a major candidate. That was an internal poll from the Crowley campaign, likely distributed to emphasize Crowley’s huge jump in support and potential path to victory if the undecided vote broke his way.  
Overall turnout varies enormously in primaries. Even in a stable environment without last-minute surprises, we often see huge swings in turnout in party primaries. A good example of turnout affecting margins is the 2014 Massachusetts gubernatorial primary. Nearly every poll, including ours, vastly overstated Martha Coakley’s margin of victory. In our case, it was due to greatly overestimating turnout. High-engagement voters who reliably cast ballots no matter what were more likely to support her main opponent, Steve Grossman, leading to his stronger-than-predicted performance in what proved to be a low turnout affair. Because Coakley nevertheless won, the pillorying we suffered was less severe than what takes place when polls peg the wrong winner, though the polling error was just as large.  
Estimating turnout demographics in an atypical primary is very imprecise. In the 2018 Democratic primary in Massachusetts for the US House between 10-term incumbent Michael Capuano and Ayanna Pressley, Pressley drew support from a flood of younger, atypical primary voters in her insurgent victory. These voters only became likely voters over the summer, in the weeks before the primary, hearing about an exciting new candidate and deciding to cast a ballot. The one public poll done in Wisconsin after Barnes dropped out suffered from the opposite problem: too many young people and would-be Hong supporters ended up in the final sample compared with the demographic profile of the Democratic electorate that actually voted last week. If vote choice is closely linked to one of the demographics the poll gets wrong, it can have a very significant impact on the poll’s accuracy.  
Here in Massachusetts, the Democratic primary for Senate, the Republican matchup for governor, and a handful of US House primaries are the major races coming in just over two weeks. With little or no recent polling and a very unsettled electorate, there are few tea leaves to even try to read. The best thing to do is just go vote and then watch election returns rather than look to prediction markets, since nobody actually knows anything.  
As races from other places and times have shown us, when it comes to primaries, anything can happen. 
Steve Koczela is president of the MassINC Polling Group.

name: VTDigger
title: For emergency department staff, violence at work is a dangerous and demoralizing reality
description:
When patients with extreme psychological distress turn violent, providers are left with very few options.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For emergency department staff, violence at work is a dangerous and demoralizing reality.
text:
Sam Demers, a nurse in the Emergency Department at the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington, on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
On the afternoon of Aug. 29, 2025, 24-year-old Destiny Hubbell was in a Morrisville emergency room for a mental health emergency examination, when she grew angry and agitated. She started spitting at healthcare workers, on their faces and in their eyes, court documents show. 
“Now you’re infected!” she repeated as she spit.
Hubbell threatened to strangle Elizabeth Couto, a registered nurse at the hospital, who knew Hubbell from repeat visits to the ED, according to court documents. 
The incident led Hubbell to be charged with four counts of assault with bodily fluids on a protected professional — a category healthcare workers, who cannot refuse to engage with a patient, fall into. She also had one charge of threatening a healthcare worker. 
Nearly a year later, in June, a Lamoille County judge found her guilty on all five counts and sentenced her to 3.5-10 years.
The sentencing is rare, but the issue of repeat violence against healthcare workers is not. Verbal and physical attacks on healthcare workers have become so prevalent that they’ve become the “daily reality of emergency care,” one emergency nurse told VTDigger. It’s a reality that’s become so normalized that it often goes underreported and unaddressed. Many nurses told VTDigger that the lack of any real consequences has acted as a deterrent for hospital workers to report violent incidents.
Now, the recent Lamoille County sentencing has opened up a broader concern about how to help individuals with extreme mental health needs access appropriate care while also protecting those tasked with caring for them. 
“It has been really challenging to navigate accountability in the court system with patients that have been deemed to lack the capacity to stand trial,” said Couto, who spoke with VTDigger in her capacity as the director of the Vermont Emergency Nurse Association, “but also protect the individuals that are expected to be there and care for them, as well as every other patient in that setting.”
“There needs to be some sort of balance between healthcare and the judicial system to support both ends of these really challenging situations,” she added. 
There are frustratingly few options to genuinely address the underlying needs of those who commit these acts of violence against healthcare workers, according to Aliena Gerhard, the Lamoille County state’s attorney who prosecuted the case against Hubbell. If a judge finds a person incompetent to stand trial, as one might due to mental illness, the state cannot prosecute the case.  
“A lot of states have laws that permit some sort of resolution that protects the victim while acknowledging that the defendant might be incompetent or going through a mental health crisis,” Gerhard said, pointing to the mental health courts that other states have. There, a multidisciplinary team of attorneys, case managers, mental health representatives and others meet to devise a plan that balances treatment, community support and accountability.
 “But here we have nothing,” she added.
Instead, Vermont primarily uses orders of non-hospitalization, court orders that put the defendant in the custody of the state Department of Mental Health and guide a treatment plan for them. But a patient has to willingly engage in their care, and in the cases where a patient does not follow the order’s guidelines, there is little the state can do to enforce compliance.
“(Orders of non-hospitalization) do literally nothing to protect our victims,” Gerhard said. “We need to do better for the defendants. We need to do better for the families. We need to do better for our communities.”
“It’s not always doing someone a service to have them in a non-secure facility,” she continued. “Should they be in jail? No, absolutely not. They shouldn’t be in jail, but they need to be in a safe place, and Vermont is not providing that.”
Resources such as better housing facilities, mental health specialists embedded in police departments and more collaboration between defense attorneys and prosecutors could help law enforcement identify what a person is struggling with and how to better connect them to the services they need, Gerhard said.
Samuel Demers, a staff nurse in the UVMMC’s emergency department, argued that investing in social services that assist someone before they land in the ED is essential to helping patients and also protecting healthcare workers from this kind of violence.
Long wait times, unmet behavioral health needs, intoxication and prolonged warehousing while awaiting psychiatric placement all feed the likelihood of violence, he said.  
“There can be an over-reliance on the ED as a last resort safety net when community systems do not meet the needs of the population,” he told VTDigger. “We will always provide compassionate care to everyone who comes to us for emergency care, but our capacity is limited.”
Rep. Anne Donahue, I-Northfield, has long been a staunch advocate for better mental health care and for the rights of people struggling with their mental health. She thinks that much of the violence in emergency departments could be stemmed by expanding access to alternative settings. 
Mental health urgent care clinics, for instance, can be a much more appropriate place for a person in crisis to be seen by a clinician or talk with a peer support volunteer, she said.

READ MORE

“I think it’s a serious problem that we don’t have enough availability of alternative resources, and I think that’s one of the struggles,” she said. 
She also suggested training hospital staff in trauma-informed care, allowing clinicians to feel better equipped to navigate situations that might unknowingly trigger a patient.
It’s particularly difficult when a patient arrives in the emergency room with a court order for an emergency psychiatric evaluation and requires treatment at a high-level psychiatric facility, explained Kristen Schieman, the emergency department nurse manager for Central Vermont Medical Center. There are only four hospitals in Vermont with this type of high-level psychiatric unit — and CVMC is not one of them.
High-need psychiatric patients can spend days in the emergency department, Schieman said, waiting for a bed to open up or for transportation to a high-level psych unit. The week she spoke with VTDigger, she said, two patients at CVMC needed to wait four to five days for placement.
Couto sees some glimmers of hope in recent legislation that creates a treatment facility for those who have been found not competent to stand trial or not guilty by reason of insanity when charged with extreme criminal offenses. The law seeks to stand up the program, called a forensic facility, in one of Vermont’s prisons.
Though this year’s legislation carves out eligibility for a small subset of individuals charged with extreme offenses, Couto said she thinks it sets an important foundation for helping people in psychological distress get care while also protecting hospital workers from the ongoing threats of violence.
“In the past, it’s really felt like the judicial system works in their own silo, and the healthcare system works in their own silo, and the legislature is trying to figure out what to do to blend all of that,” she said. 
The forensic facility legislation is just one part in a series of recent laws that have sought to address the intersection of violence against clinicians and people in mental health crises.  
In 2023, lawmakers increased the penalties for threatening healthcare workers and made it easier for law enforcement to arrest people who assault healthcare workers.
Last summer a new law went into effect requiring the state’s hospitals to develop a reporting system to track workplace violence, including data on the number of incidents reported to law enforcement. It also requires that hospitals use that data to create security plans aimed at reducing violence. 
Already, some hospitals have seen decreases in workplace violence. At UVM Medical Center in Burlington, violence in the emergency department has fallen 64% between 2022 and 2026, according to Demers. The department now has around-the-clock security staff, metal detectors, and screening policies for patients and visitors.
Still, it’s a decrease in a much larger, national increase: the last 15 years have yielded unprecedented heights of violence in healthcare settings.
To Couto, having healthcare workers involved in the legislative and judicial processes has been essential in producing these modest wins. 
“When we see how the system as a whole can work to be successful to support reduction of workplace violence in healthcare, as well as patients’ needs,” she said, “it’s validating.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump Team’s Use of Arcane Budget Rule Threatens Medicaid Coverage
description: About 200,000 low-income Arkansans could see major changes to their health coverage next year after the Trump administration recently informed state officials it will not renew a key Medicaid agreement with the federal government. The decision by federal officials, citing authority granted under President Donald Trump’s signature tax-and-spending law, sugges[...]
text:
A panel of Arkansas lawmakers on Wednesday approved proposed changes to state gun laws that will expand some areas where carrying firearms is allowed.
(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)About 200,000 low-income Arkansans could see major changes to their health coverage next year after the Trump administration recently informed state officials it will not renew a key Medicaid agreement with the federal government.
The decision by federal officials, citing authority granted under President Donald Trump’s signature tax-and-spending law, suggests the GOP-led state’s predicament could foretell other repercussions in how states are allowed to run the program under federal waivers.
Nearly every state has at least one waiver to run its Medicaid program differently than required by federal law, such as allowing the use of private managed-care plans or expanding eligibility for mental health or long-term care services. Some Medicaid waivers have stretched decades, renewed by presidential administrations of both parties, effectively making the demonstration programs they created permanent.
Arkansas is one of a dozen states with a waiver expiring Dec. 31 that face the additional restrictions the Trump administration has placed on new or renewed waivers.
Though it has yet to finalize its decision, the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said Arkansas’ 13-year-old waiver does not comply with new “budget neutrality” rules that take effect in January, said Gavin Lesnick, a spokesperson for the Arkansas Department of Human Services. The rules tighten a policy forbidding Medicaid waivers from increasing federal spending on the program beyond what it would have increased without the waiver.
Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion

The state is now seeking a two-year extension after hearing from CMS that its request for a five-year renewal would not be granted. If its Medicaid expansion waiver is not renewed, Arkansas officials have said they will continue offering expanded eligibility through existing Medicaid law, a change that could leave enrollees with access to fewer doctors and other health providers.
Rather than place more people in its traditional Medicaid program serving largely children, pregnant women, and disabled people, Arkansas obtained a waiver to buy Affordable Care Act marketplace policies from private insurers for adults covered by the Medicaid expansion. This “private option” gave enrollees greater choice of doctors and other health providers, because some doctors are more willing to see patients with private coverage, which generally pays more than regular Medicaid.
The move helped cut the state’s uninsured rate by nearly half, but it also ended up costing more than if beneficiaries were covered under Medicaid’s traditional, fee-for-service program.
Critics characterize the new waiver rules as part of a Trump administration effort to dramatically shrink Medicaid, the government program for those who are low-income or disabled, which grew rapidly under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden.
“What we have here is a sneaky way to cut Medicaid expansion and the Medicaid program,” said Nicole Huberfeld, a professor of health law at Boston University.
Medicaid enrollees won’t know whom to blame if they lose coverage because the administration is using arcane regulatory processes to make the changes, Huberfeld said.

At issue are waivers granted by the government that allow states flexibility from existing Medicaid law in how they cover low-income residents, as long as the changes will not increase what Medicaid costs the federal government.
Pivoting from the long-standing practice of checking only retroactively whether states were keeping their budget promises, the Trump administration said in June that it would not renew or approve any waivers unless CMS first certified that they would not increase costs to the federal government.
In its new guidance, the agency said the new waiver rules are expected to reduce federal spending.
“Characterizing enforcement of a statutory budget neutrality requirement as a cut misrepresents both the law and this guidance,” CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster said in an email to KFF Health News. The federal waivers are intended “to test innovative approaches to delivering care, not provide an open-ended mechanism for increasing federal spending.”
Other states with waivers expiring at the end of December include Georgia, which has added about 18,000 low-income people to Medicaid under its waiver, and California, which has used its waiver to expand coverage of social services including food and housing.
California and Georgia Medicaid officials told KFF Health News that they are still working with CMS in hopes of renewing their waivers. The loss of federal waiver approval could cause states to curtail benefits or eligibility expansions.
In Arkansas, it would mean redesigning the state’s Medicaid expansion program.
Arkansas’ initial waiver was granted in 2013, when its Democratic governor at the time worked with a Republican-controlled legislature to adopt a pioneering style of Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act.
It was one of the first Southern states to expand Medicaid, granting coverage to many low-income residents. Forty states and Washington, D.C., have also fully expanded Medicaid to cover more low-income adults under the law also known as Obamacare.
The state’s Medicaid expansion enrollees were already facing a confusing time. Starting in January, they will need to prove they work or meet an exemption to be eligible for coverage under Trump’s law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. And one of the state program’s two private health insurers — Centene — announced in July that it was pulling out at the end of the year.
Sam Dubke, a spokesperson for Republican Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, told KFF Health News that the Sanders administration is trying to negotiate a temporary extension of its waiver “to ensure impacted Arkansans maintain access to quality, affordable healthcare during this transition period.”
“Looking ahead to the next legislative session, CMS has provided the state with an opportunity for bold, conservative healthcare reform, and the governor will work with her partners in the legislature to build a sustainable model that maintains the same high quality of care and saves taxpayer dollars,” Dubke said.



Let us know what you think...


 


The Trump administration’s new restrictions on waivers, implemented under the same law that imposes work requirements as a condition of eligibility and reduces Medicaid spending by about $900 billion over a decade, could affect millions of enrollees and billions in spending. About a third of the almost $600 billion in federal spending on Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program in 2024 supported programs created by waivers, according to CMS.
In a 2014 report, the Government Accountability Office found that the three-year spending limit the federal government approved for Arkansas’ Medicaid waiver was nearly $800 million more than what the state would have spent through its traditional Medicaid program.
Arkansas is one of several states that expanded Medicaid under the ACA using a waiver, with others including Indiana, Michigan, New Hampshire, and Iowa.
States will have to clear several more bureaucratic hurdles to retain waivers under the new CMS guidance, said Alice Lam, a managing director with consulting and legal firm Manatt. That could lead to fewer benefits or reduce the number of people eligible for Medicaid, she said.
Robert Nelb, director of policy at America’s Essential Hospitals, which represents safety net hospitals, said he and most experts believed when it passed that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was merely codifying CMS policy on budget neutrality.
But the Trump administration has interpreted the law to restrict states’ use of waivers, he said.
Nelb said many long-standing waivers that have been renewed multiple times are now at risk and that the loss of state waivers could threaten money hospitals rely on to cover uninsured patients and improve care in their communities.
“There is a real concern that this will put added burdens on states up front and slow down new innovations in Medicaid,” Nelb said.
In 2025, the Trump administration told states it would no longer renew Medicaid waivers to help enrollees with job training or to allow continuous eligibility for adults and children for specific time periods without verifying their income eligibility.
