name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom seeks to do the near impossible – defeat an incumbent Mississippi senator
description: Scott Colom, Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat, speaks to the media after giving a speech at the Neshoba County Fair on Wednesday, June 24, 2026, near Philadelphia.
text:
Democrat Scott Colom is trying to do what has not been done since 1942 – defeat an incumbent United States senator from Mississippi.
Colom, the district attorney for the Columbus area in parts of northeast and east central Mississippi, is considered a longshot to defeat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for a number of reasons.
First of all, Mississippi is considered a solid Republican state that has not elected a Democratic governor since 1999 and has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1982.
And to make matters worse for Colom, former Democrat Ty Pinkins is running as an independent in the November general election and could siphon more votes from him than from Hyde-Smith in a contest where the challenger needs every vote he can get.
And finally, Mississippians do not vote incumbent senators out of office. There is no better definition of job security than holding one of Mississippi’s two U.S. Senate seats.
For those reasons and others, it really is not surprising that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee opted not to allocate any of the $40 million pledged on electing Democratic senators this November to Colom in Mississippi. Based on polling data, the Democrats have a realistic chance to garner control of the Senate and the powers that be chose not to spend their finite resources in a state where the odds of winning appear long.
U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith speaks to supporters during her reelection campaign launch at the Mississippi Agriculture Museum in Jackson, Miss., on Thursday, Aug. 28, 2025.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Still, Colom and Democrats can cite reasons for a glimmer of hope. In high-profile statewide elections the past few years – Senate races between Hyde-Smith and former U.S. Rep. Mike Espy and recent gubernatorial elections – Democrats have been relatively close to victory.
So, Colom continues the campaign grind, hoping to do what has not been done since 1942 – defeat an incumbent Mississippi senator.
But the specifics of the 1942 campaign also do not provide Colom much reason for hope. It was an unusual turn of events that led to James O. Eastland defeating incumbent Wall Doxey in 1942. After that fateful 1942 election, Eastland, a Democrat, went on to serve until he retired in 1978 and was replaced by Republican Thad Cochran.
Eastland was originally appointed in 1941 by Gov. Paul Johnson to fill a Senate seat vacated when Pat Harrison died in office. But in accepting the appointment, Eastland promised not to run in the upcoming special election later that year. He did not. Doxey won the special election, but a short one year later lost the regularly scheduled election for the full six-year term to  Eastland, who had sat out the special election to fulfill his promise.
Actually at the start of the process where senators were elected by the people instead of the state legislatures, it was not that uncommon for an incumbent Mississippi senator to lose. The 17th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1913, provided for the election of senators by the people.
In 1912, Mississippi opted to hold the first popular vote to elect a U.S. senator, jumping ahead of the ratification of the 17th Amendment in 1913. In that election, Delta planter LeRoy Percy, who originally was elected by the Legislature, lost to notorious racist James K. Vardaman. Then Vardaman, who was one of six senators to vote against America entering World War I, was defeated in 1918 by Harrison. In 1934 incumbent Hubert Stephens of Union County was upended by another notable racist – Theodore Bilbo. And then there was the 1942 election.
Those are the examples where incumbent Mississippi senators have been defeated in popular elections or by a vote of the people – Percy, Vardaman, Stephens and Doxey.
Scott Colom is hoping to add Hyde-Smith’s name to the list of defeated U.S. senators from Mississippi.
Perhaps, in reality the odds are in his favor. It is bound to happen eventually.

name: VTDigger
title: Nonprofits are more than charities in the Northeast Kingdom
description:
Rural organizations wear many hats and stretch every dollar. Coordinating them is a necessity, not a luxury.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Nonprofits are more than charities in the Northeast Kingdom.
text:
This commentary is by Abby Long, the executive director of the Northeast Kingdom Collaborative.
I love the Northeast Kingdom.
Not just because we’re surrounded by stunning working landscapes, world-class outdoor recreation, vibrant arts and some of the best local food and drink. I love it because it’s home. It’s the community my family chose, and like so many, I want it to thrive.
The very qualities that make the Northeast Kingdom, the NEK, such a remarkable place are due in part to the region’s rural nature. Yet that rural character brings unique economic and social challenges. Our region is geographically isolated, and we continue to experience population decline and deep poverty. So much so that the federal government has designated the NEK a Rural Economic Area Partnership zone, one of only five in the nation, to stimulate citizen-led rural revitalization and secure additional, priority federal funds for economic and community development. As the nonprofit holding the REAP zone agreement with U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development, the Northeast Kingdom Collaborative serves as the region’s neutral convener, ensuring that investments reflect regionally defined priorities. But our role extends far beyond that agreement.
Every day, we bring together community members, leaders, municipalities, businesses, nonprofits, educators, providers, state agencies and economic development organizations to better understand what our region needs most. The Northeast Kingdom Collaborative’s role is not to replace the incredible work already happening across the region, but to connect it, celebrate it and strengthen it. We help organizations find common ground, align around shared priorities and invest limited resources strategically rather than twice over. That work is especially important in a rural region like ours, where organizations often wear many hats and stretch every dollar. Collaboration isn’t just a nice idea; it’s how we make progress. 
Over the past year, we’ve seen collaboration in action. Through the annual NEK Together Conference, regional leaders come together to identify shared priorities and begin building coordinated action plans around the issues that matter most. We’re looking forward to hosting this year’s convening at Essex County’s Island Pond on Nov. 4; registration is now open. These priorities are communicated to USDA Rural Development and taken to Montpelier for NEK Day at the Statehouse, where leaders engage directly with policymakers. We also launched sector convenings, such as the Housing Hubbub, that bring together everyone with a hand in housing to tackle one of our greatest barriers to growth. Housing is too complex for any single organization to solve.
That approach paid off when the Northeast Kingdom Collaborative joined forces with the Vermont State Housing Authority, in partnership with the state of Vermont, to bring awareness to the Mobile Home Infill Program, address housing affordability and development challenges exacerbated by recent flooding and build up to 40 new homes in the NEK. Through this program, participating mobile home park owners and manufactured home communities are improving lots and fast-tracking the placement of new affordable homes. We hosted an NEK housing tour to view homes and learn about eligibility, the homebuying process, down payment assistance, reduced mortgage rates and closing cost discounts.
Behind the scenes, the NEK collaborative works to ensure the region’s priorities are reflected in regional and statewide planning efforts. For example, we helped shape northern Vermont’s comprehensive economic development strategy for the U.S. Economic Development Administration, necessary for further federal resources, and advocated successfully alongside USDA Rural Development and Vermont’s congressional delegation for the release of delayed REAP zone funding, which brings more than $1 million in federal funds into the region annually.

READ MORE

Aug. 17 is National Nonprofit Day, an opportunity to recognize that nonprofits are far more than charitable organizations. They are community builders, problem solvers, employers, advocates, educators and trusted partners. They respond to immediate needs while also planning for the future. 
Here in the Northeast Kingdom, nonprofits are not only supporting collaboration but strengthening our working lands; encouraging entrepreneurs; creating housing opportunities; expanding access to healthcare; uplifting our arts, culture and recreation; and responding when disasters strike. Time and again, they are among the first to step forward and the last to leave.
As we celebrate National Nonprofit Day, I hope we recognize not only the organizations serving our communities, but also the staff, volunteers, board members, partners and neighbors whose dedication makes this work possible. The challenges facing rural Vermont are too great for any one organization or person to solve alone. But together we are building a more resilient and vibrant Northeast Kingdom.

name: Delaware
title: Banana Ball Pairs Entertainment with Baseball in Front of Sold Out Frawley Stadium
description: The Texas Tailgaters and Loco Beach Coconuts of the Banana Ball Championship League played the first ever Banana Ball game in Delaware in front of a sold out crowd Thursday, August 13.   WILMINGTON, DE — “You’re going to see the most entertainment during a baseball game with tricks and being fans first [both] players and staff.” That’s how Texas ... Read Mor[...]
text:
Fans enter the stadium from the plaza to witness the first Banana Ball game ever played in Delaware. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Texas Tailgaters and Loco Beach Coconuts of the Banana Ball Championship League played the first ever Banana Ball game in Delaware in front of a sold out crowd Thursday, August 13.
 
WILMINGTON, DE — “You’re going to see the most entertainment during a baseball game with tricks and being fans first [both] players and staff.” 
That’s how Texas Tailgater Zach Watson said he’d sum up Banana Ball in a sentence to a new fan. 
Watson got to meet with many new fans as Banana Ball took over Frawley Stadium, Thursday night, in the first ever Banana Ball game in Wilmington, Delaware. The game featured Watson’s team — the Texas Tailgaters — in a matchup against one of Banana Ball’s newest teams, the Loco Beach Coconuts.
Banana Ball isn’t a traditional baseball setting. For starters, the Coconuts were the home team but in this format they’re deemed the “headliners”. That’s because Banana Ball is geared to constantly entertain its fans with more than just the product on the field.
“I don’t think there’s ever a quiet moment,” Watson said.
Pregame
Fans lined up outside the front parking lot of Frawley Stadium around 3:00 p.m. waiting to enter the plaza area for the “rope drop” at 3:30. The plaza was themed in accordance with the weekend’s headliners. Beach themed signs, palm trees and surf boards transformed the parking lot into “Loco Beach”. The Coconuts’ players and staff greeted the fans under the Loco Beach Coconut themed archway and welcomed them into the plaza over three hours before the game was set to officially start. 
The minute fans enter the plaza their Banana Ball experience begins.
Fans could check out the merchandise available for both teams at merchandise tents or grab free refresher samples at the Dunkin truck. Tropical Smoothie Cafe served smoothies out of a small tiki hut and a couple of food trucks were available for hungry patrons.
The real excitement of the plaza experience wasn’t any of that though. It was the players and cast members themselves.
The players spent over an hour outside meeting with fans, taking pictures and signing autographs. Each interaction was genuine. Players not only signed but had a conversation with each family or fan that approached. Cast members like the Hulagans and Loco Beach lifeguards did the same, creating an environment completely in line with the Banana Ball motto of “Fans First. Entertain Always.”
“Just going out there and making sure a fan has the best time of their life,” Watson said. “Even if it’s trying to influence one fan, hoping they’re having fun and introduce yourself and talk to them, so yeah, fans first.”  
The players eventually left the plaza area, but some fans didn’t even notice, because a pregame party was erupting on the stage to the right of the stadium. The official band of the Coconuts — Sitting on Saturn — ushered in the start of the Loco Beach Live Show — a portion of the pregame festivities.
The Band
Sitting on Saturn is a band from California that found their way to Banana Ball through a direct message from Banana Ball creator Jesse Cole.
“I guess he saw like one of our TikToks and listened to like our album and was like ‘I’m starting up a team called the Coconuts and I would love if you guys would be like, you know, play some music for us’ and I’m like, ‘dude I’m so down’,” said lead singer Hoyt Yeatman.
The three person band includes guitar players and singers Yeatman and Kyle Hart as well as drummer Trevor Smith.
Yeatman and Hart said the band was thrown right into the action performing their first show with the Coconuts at Petco Park — the home of the San Diego Padres — in March of this year, becoming the official band of the Coconuts. The band travels with the team, plays pregame and postgame shows and are a part of the action during the game whether that be playing a song on the field or in the stands.
“We can’t like see what the players are doing behind us so we’re just playing our, what we normally do, and yeah, they’re dancing and stuff and we normally [don’t] see it until we watch the video after,” Hart said.
“We’ll be playing a song or something and then they have like a dance that they’re doing with us and it’s like you got the whole team, like it’s just like when two worlds collide kind of. I don’t think it’s ever really been done honestly. It’s cool,” Yeatman said.
Yeatman and Hart said their experience in Banana Ball and playing live music in coordination with a live baseball game is still a little strange, but it’s an experience they’re thankful to be a part of.
“Honestly, it’s cool. We have like our own baseball card, Banana Ball card, and I’m like, I would never in a million years think that our band would have like a baseball trading card, but like here it is,” Yeatman said. “It’s so cool we’re very blessed, very fortunate.”  
Game Time
The Loco Beach Live Show continued up until the gates to the field opened at 5:30 p.m. entertaining fans with the band’s music and interactive games coordinated by each team’s Banana Ball Host.
The entertainment didn’t stop once the fans entered the stadium. 
Even as fans were finding their seats or grabbing concessions for the game there was a member of the Banana Ball cast interacting with a fan, hosting an activity or setting up for the next activity.
As fans entered the stadium, the excitement to see the actual on field product was palpable. First time viewers speculated on what they were about to witness while some fans that had seen clips or portions of Banana Ball before, speculated on what trick plays they’d get to see. 
Once the clock hit 7:00 p.m. anticipation and speculation became reality.
Banana Ball is a fast-paced game that never lacks in action. Banana Ball rules like no mound visits, no bunting and no stepping out of the batter’s box keep the game moving to fit within the two hour time limit. The players on the field are always participating in something whether that be the game itself, cheering from outside the dugout or interacting with the audience from the field. 
“I say to anybody that’s joining, it’s Crossfit baseball,” Watson said. “You got two hours of nonstop movement. You don’t sit down ever.”
Some normal baseball rules still apply. There are nine defenders, one batter in the box and the pitcher still initiates the play with a pitch. The bases are the standard distance and when a runner crosses home it still counts as a run scored, though that doesn’t mean the team is up one to nothing.
In Banana Ball, the goal is to get the most points. Points are earned by winning an inning. The team that scores the most runs in an inning earns the point, making each frame its own mini game. The final inning is more traditional where every run that crosses the plate counts as a point. 
On Thursday, the Tailgaters won the game 6-3, earning a point with wins in the second, sixth and seventh innings. The Tailgaters also won the equalizer point awarded to the team with the most trick plays going into the final inning. The Tailgaters pulled off 14 trick play outs sending hitters back to the dugout with tag team catches and grabs with a cowboy hat. 
The trick plays are an exciting feature to what is still a competitive baseball game at its core. 
There is still plenty of entertainment to the product on the field. Players have creative walk-up dances, skits and antics during play. For example, after a hit by pitch the Coconuts recreated the scene of Jack and Rose from “Titanic” and during one at-bat Coconut player, Kaden Bowler, took an at-bat while riding a hoverboard designed to look like a surfboard. Those creative entertainment features add spectacle to what is a high level baseball game played by high level athletes. 
“It’s a completely different game than what you see on TikTok,” Watson said. “You just see the dances and everything mostly on TikTok so when you actually come to a game you’re like dang these boys are actually, we’re actually playing baseball. You don’t expect that.”  
Postgame
After the game is over there is still more to experience.
Players from both teams returned to the plaza to sign autographs and talk with fans. Sitting on Saturn played more music and the entertainment continued until about 9:30 p.m. when the venue closed. The postgame plaza party ends a Banana Ball experience that begins over three hours before a pitch is even thrown.
“I’m excited for these fans, if they have never been, to experience Banana Ball in a different way,” Watson told Delaware Live before the game.
The Tailgaters and Coconuts wrapped up their three game series in Delaware, Saturday night, with a 4-3 win from the Tailgaters giving them the 2-1 series win. The Tailgaters have already secured their spot in the Banana Ball Championship League postseason, but the Coconuts are still fighting to claim one of the three remaining spots. 
Fans that want to keep track of the rest of the 2026 Banana Ball World Tour can check the Banana Ball website for upcoming events and ways to watch the games.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota families, childcare providers frustrated by growing waitlist for assistance
description: Nearly 1,900 North Dakota families are on a waitlist for state childcare assistance. A bill draft to be considered for North Dakota’s upcoming special legislative session would add $9 million in state funding to get some of the neediest families off of the growing waitlist. “This is about low-income families who want to work,” said […]
text:
Omelia Henderson of Legacy Childcare in Fargo, North Dakota, talks with children she supervises on Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) Nearly 1,900 North Dakota families are on a waitlist for state childcare assistance.
A bill draft to be considered for North Dakota’s upcoming special legislative session would add $9 million in state funding to get some of the neediest families off of the growing waitlist.
“This is about low-income families who want to work,” said Senate Minority Leader Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, the primary sponsor of the bill draft to be presented to legislative leaders on Monday.
State lawmakers of both parties say it’s time to rethink America’s fragile childcare system

Lawmakers learned in December that the Child Care Assistance Program had a projected $35.5 million shortfall, prompting the Department of Health and Human Services to implement a waitlist and reduce the amount of assistance for working families. 
State officials said at the time they underestimated the demand for childcare subsidies, which had been touted as a way to reduce the state’s worker shortage. The average annual cost of childcare in North Dakota exceeds the annual tuition and fees at a North Dakota public university, according to data presented to lawmakers last year.
As of Aug. 9, the state had 1,892 families on a waitlist for childcare assistance, according to Rebecca Askins, interim director of the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services’ Economic Assistance Section.
In June, the state provided childcare assistance for 6,263 children, a decrease of more than 1,300 children compared to June 2025, according to figures provided by Askins.
Krissy Wold, who owns Legacy Childcare in Fargo, said the state hasn’t done enough to communicate with the public about the waitlist. 
“When the waitlist came to be, we had no fair warning,” she said.
She said she knows of several families who expected to qualify for assistance and were blindsided by the news they were waitlisted.
Data centers, vapes, childcare aid emerge for North Dakota special session consideration

Legacy Childcare recently opened two new rooms for infants, Wold said. 
Several families with newborns signed up for the space, but could no longer afford daycare when they were unexpectedly waitlisted for assistance, Wold said.
One of the new rooms is now at half capacity and the other is still empty, Wold said. She said she expects to fill both rooms this fall. 
Wold said she’s working hard to rebuild her business in spite of the waitlist’s impact.
“There’s a lot of financial loss that you can’t even count,” she said.
The waitlist is also affecting Legacy Childcare’s ability to qualify for other funding sources that keep it afloat, Wold said.
For example, she said Legacy Childcare receives funding from the federal Child and Adult Care Food Program, which helps it serve healthy food. The subsidy is tied in part to the percentage of enrolled families receiving child care assistance, she said. 
If Legacy Childcare’s percentage of families in the program dips any lower due to a lack of available funding, the daycare may lose its food program benefits, too, said Wold.
The program changes have also impacted daycares’ ability to recruit staff, she said.
Childcare workers in North Dakota are eligible for childcare assistance under the Child Care Workforce Benefit program, which was implemented in summer 2024.
The benefit has helped daycares attract high-quality teachers, Wold said. But now some of those teachers are ending up on the waitlist, she said.
Though Legacy Childcare is fully staffed for the time being, Wold said she previously lost two strong teachers because they were waitlisted.
Budget shortfall will reduce North Dakota child care assistance for some families

Daycares and families are still struggling to understand the changes to the program, said Wold.
“The unknowing is awful,” she said.
Lisa Lehmann, who owns Growing Graces Childcare & Learning Center in Hankinson, said she’s sent several emails to state leaders this year urging more transparency about the waitlist.
“I know there’s been daycares in the state that have closed down because of it,” she said. 
Legislative leaders will decide Monday whether to consider childcare assistance during a special legislative session, which starts Sept. 2 and is expected to last three days, primarily focused on regulating kratom.
Lehmann said she’s interested in testifying on the effects of the program change during the special session. She has urged legislators to fully fund childcare assistance and eliminate the waitlist. 
“North Dakota’s childcare system is not ‘strained,’” she wrote in one email sent to state leaders in May. “It is not ‘challenged.’ It is breaking. And when childcare breaks, the workforce breaks with it.”
The bill draft by Hogan, which has bipartisan support, would not fully fund childcare assistance, but would add more state funding this budget cycle to get low-income families off the waitlist. 
“It’s a Band-Aid for the poorest of the poor families,” Hogan said.
Co-sponsor Rep. Alisa Mitskog, D-Wahpeton, said lawmakers made significant investments in childcare because they recognized it as essential to the state’s workforce and economy.
“But now we are at risk of going backwards,” Mitskog said. “We need a sustainable solution that keeps parents in the workforce and supports childcare providers.” 
North Dakota Monitor editor Amy Dalrymple contributed to this report.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Farm Bill impasse tests Arkansas Sen. John Boozman’s low-key approach
description: Ten years ago, Republican U.S. Sen. John Boozman faced a challenge from a Democratic rival who portrayed the lawmaker as out of touch with Arkansas and too aligned with Donald Trump. His challenger, Conner Eldridge, brought in then-Sen. Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota to campaign for him. Heitkamp, a Democrat who sat on the Agriculture […]
text:
(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Ten years ago, Republican U.S. Sen. John Boozman faced a challenge from a Democratic rival who portrayed the lawmaker as out of touch with Arkansas and too aligned with Donald Trump.
His challenger, Conner Eldridge, brought in then-Sen. Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota to campaign for him. Heitkamp, a Democrat who sat on the Agriculture Committee with Boozman, talked up Eldridge’s candidacy.
Then reporters asked her what she thought of Boozman.
“I love John Boozman. He’s a great guy,” she said.
It was the kind of exchange that made Democrats in Arkansas cringe: a surrogate professing her admiration of the incumbent they were hoping to defeat. 
But it was also an example of one of Boozman’s strengths. An unassuming figure who speaks in a near-whisper, Boozman is known more for congeniality than combativeness. That has earned him the respect of Democratic lawmakers, no small feat in an increasingly polarized Washington.
Boozman’s reputation as someone who’s built up relationships is being put to the test. The third-term lawmaker who chairs the Senate Agriculture Committee faces an uphill battle to advance the Farm Bill that’s in jeopardy over a fight about cuts to the nation’s food stamp program. 
The massive legislation crafted by Boozman stalled before the Agriculture Committee over a dispute about when states will shoulder a share of costs from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
Boozman, who recessed the committee, said he remains optimistic that the bill will move forward and can win the 60 votes needed in the Senate. But he admits to frustration over the dispute.
“I’m a guy that’s pretty low key and pretty good at working with people to get things done,” Boozman said. “And we’ve worked really hard to get this done. Farmers desperately need it.”
Fewer states need it more than Arkansas, which led the nation in farm bankruptcies last year and where farmers have been bearing the brunt of Trump’s trade wars.



Let us know what you think...


 


But concerns about farmers’ plight are also running up against worries about the additional costs states will face for SNAP under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Trump signed last year.
Beginning in October 2027, states will have to pay for part of SNAP if their payment error rates are in excess of 6%. Democrats and advocacy groups have warned of the harms the cost shift will have on low-income Americans and most states.
They had urged a two-year delay in the cost shift. Boozman amended the bill to instead extend the deadline for a year, but that wasn’t enough to get the bill out of committee.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the top Democrat on the committee, noted that the bill as written would advantage high-error states over ones with mid-level error rates. A two-year-delay would give states equal footing to work out their error rates. 
Boozman said time is running out but he’s hopeful that the recess will give Democratic senators a chance to see support for the measure. 
“I hope that after people are home visiting with their constituents, visiting with their farmers, visiting with their states…that the Democrats will vote for the bill,” he said.
Looming federal cuts prompt concerns about food aid in Arkansas

His office has pointed to support that groups in Boozman’s home state like the Arkansas Hunger Relief Alliance has offered for the compromise.
Another hopeful sign for Boozman is how Democratic Senate hopefuls in conservative states have split with their own party on the legislation. They include state Rep. Joshua Turek, the party’s nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa.
In Arkansas, Senate Democratic nominee Hallie Shoffner said she would have voted the bill out of committee if she had been on the panel.
“To be clear, this Farm Bill is insufficient. But it is something,” Shoffner, who is running against Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, said in a statement after the vote. 
But none of that may be enough to ensure the bill will eventually get the Democratic votes it needs to pass. Democrats have valid concerns about the impact of the SNAP changes and have reasonable worries that a one-year extension isn’t enough. But it’s hard to see a compromise on the issue that wouldn’t risk losing some Republican support.
The Farm Bill used to be a bipartisan undertaking that would unite various causes, but that has fractured like so many other aspects of Washington politics. Finding a way out of the stalemate may be more than anyone can expect in the Trump era, but Boozman’s style may be the best suited to give it a try.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s first state-funded methadone vans expand access to treatment
description: The mobile units aim to reach clients in CT's rural corners and destigmatize the use of methadone to fight opioid use disorder.
text:
Mobile methadone units did not exist in Connecticut when Frankie DeJesus started his recovery in 2012. He wishes they did.
DeJesus, a recovery support specialist for Community Health Resources, has spent nearly all his life in Enfield, right by Connecticut’s northern border. After a Percocet prescription for knee pain developed into a dependence on heroin and other opioids, DeJesus began traveling to Hartford’s Root Center to receive methadone, widely considered the most effective treatment for opioid use disorder. 
The Root Center, though 20 miles away from Enfield, was the closest methadone clinic to DeJesus’s home. Every day for a year and a half, he would make the 30-minute drive to receive his dose of methadone before driving back to work. Dosing windows were short and often coincided with rush hours. Sometimes, he’d take the HOV lane to ensure he arrived at the clinic in time. Other times, reluctant to break the law, he’d miss the morning window and would have to leave work early to get his dose before the clinic closed.
“It was a huge barrier to my recovery,” DeJesus said. 
Beginning this summer, clients struggling to access methadone treatment may be able to receive care more easily. Large mobile units — often referred to as “vans,” though they are closer to RVs — have begun traveling to parts of northeastern and southeastern Connecticut that experience high opioid overdose rates. They are the first state-funded mobile methadone units in Connecticut’s history. 
The state has invested more than $4 million, drawn from opioid settlement funds, into the development of the vans. The APT Foundation launched two units in July, serving communities along Greater New Haven and the southeastern shoreline, and CHR’s van will begin traveling across northeastern Connecticut on Aug. 18. Providers and researchers say the vans will expand access to life-saving treatment and reduce the stigma of receiving care for opioid use disorder. 
“There’s a lot of people we’re not getting to,” said Kevin Laymon, a recovery support specialist at CHR and the driver of the van. “We’re going to bring it to people instead of having them come to us and struggle.”

Recovery specialist Kevin Laymon, left, and clinician Selena Perez-Suarez talk about how they will work with patients during a tour of Community Health Resources’ mobile methadone unit at the company’s Pathways Putnam location on Friday, July 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Traveling to treatment in the Quiet Corner
CHR’s van will serve Connecticut’s northeastern region, also known as the Quiet Corner. Data from the Department of Public Health shows that, in 2024, Windham reported 62.9 unintentional drug overdose deaths per 100,000 people — the seventh-highest in the state and four times the national average. 
Most towns in the northeastern region, which is mostly forest and farmland, have a population of fewer than 10,000. There are only three clinics that offer methadone treatment in the region: two in Windham and another in Putnam.
“I understand the thought process of more people, more resources,” said Selena Perez-Suarez, a CHR clinician serving the van. “But then we have this community that’s overlooked. I think that’s why addiction is so high in this area.”
Methadone, along with buprenorphine and naltrexone, is one of only three FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorder. It reduces craving and blunts pain from withdrawal. As a Schedule II substance, it’s also the most tightly regulated out of the three medications: unlike the two other drugs, physicians cannot prescribe it for pick-up at a pharmacy to treat opioid use disorder.
Instead, clients must travel in-person to clinics certified by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to dispense methadone. Often, this means waking up early to receive a dose in time for work, and many clients in early stages of treatment must make trips every day to mitigate the most severe withdrawal symptoms. 
But for many, committing to this form of treatment is easier said than done. In 2024, researchers at Yale University and Virginia Tech University found that some Connecticut residents, such as those living in parts of Middlesex and Litchfield counties, would have to drive at least 45 minutes to the nearest methadone clinic. 
The burden is even greater for people who rely on public transit: some, particularly in eastern Connecticut, may spend up to three hours on a bus or train for a one-way trip to the nearest clinic. And this assumes they have access to public transport at all.
There are no trains and only two taxi services covering three towns in the northeastern region, according to Perez-Suarez. Almost all buses serving the Northeastern Connecticut Transit District start running after 8 a.m. and stop by 5 p.m., outside the windows of time when clients typically travel to get their doses. 
The state offers non-emergency medical transportation on request but only to those who have insurance to cover those services. Cameron Breen — a street outreach case manager at Liberation Programs, which runs several methadone clinics — also notes that some people who need treatment are homeless or do not have a stable address where they can be picked up. 
“Those individuals lacking an address, in a lot of circumstances, are also usually lacking a phone and the ability for [the operator] to contact them to say, ‘Hey, we’re on our way,’” Breen said. 
Starting Aug. 18, the van will try to meet those who cannot make it to a brick-and-mortar any other way. CHR workers will first restock the van with methadone at CHR’s office in Putnam. They’ll drive 40 minutes to treat clients near CHR’s clinic in Willimantic, which does not offer methadone treatment, before making stops in other towns. Though they will only determine a final route after assessing need during the first few months of operation, they anticipate making rounds through Plainfield and parts of Killingly. 
“The main thing we carry to the Quiet Corner of the state is transportation,” Laymon said. “People can’t get around because of the transit system.”

Nurse Julie Wardell checks her security cameras during a tour of Community Health Resources’ mobile methadone unit at the company’s Pathways Putnam location on Friday, July 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

A solution on the road
Mobile methadone units have existed as early as 1979, when a municipal bus program in Amsterdam dispensed methadone to pockets of the city with high drug use. In 1988, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration approved the nation’s first methadone “clinic on wheels” in Brockton, Mass., as a response to the AIDS epidemic. Brockton residents fiercely opposed the construction of brick-and-mortar clinics, but, as the New York Times reported, “The mobile clinic has been largely accepted because it treats the problem, then goes away.”
The DEA continued to approve units on an ad hoc basis until 2007, when concerns about diversion prevented the administration from issuing new licenses. Eventually, the advent of synthetic opioids and historically high overdose rates during the coronavirus pandemic prompted bipartisan efforts to increase access to treatment. SAMHSA updated its regulations to make COVID-era emergency measures such as telehealth screening and unsupervised take-home doses permanent, while a final rule issued by the DEA in 2021 lifted the ban on mobile methadone units.
At least 17 states have launched mobile programs since then, and Connecticut — armed with $185 million in opioid settlement funds, 22% of which are dedicated to increasing access to treatment — is following suit. 
“We’ve had to build these carve-outs,” said Benjamin Howell, assistant professor of public health at the Yale School of Medicine and one of the researchers who conducted the travel time study. “This legacy of regulation has been on the books for years — we’re just stuck in the status quo.”
CHR’s van — 33 feet long and 12 feet high, with a front painted lime green — is hard to miss. From Mondays through Fridays, 7 a.m. to 11 a.m., clients will enter from the van’s back entrance. They’ll register at a front desk and receive their dose of methadone, bitter pink liquid in a cup. If they need to, they’ll do case management in a room outfitted with a medical examination table or counseling in a private room near the front of the vehicle before leaving through a side door. 
The van’s setup allows every stage of the process to remain private and clients to receive one-on-one care tailored to their needs. By contrast, DeJesus’s treatment process would be quick: walk in, get his dose, drive away. He sought counseling, but counselors at methadone clinics typically have a caseload of 60 to 80 clients each.
“My counselor was rarely ever there,” he said. “I didn’t know what else was available besides methadone.”
DeJesus eventually stopped receiving methadone treatment in favor of trying to white-knuckle sobriety. Periods of relapses and eventual hospitalization for suicidal ideation pushed him to try seeking support again. It would take six years before “life got different,” he said, then better. He attributes this shift to counseling and communities such as his church and long-term recovery support groups and hopes clients can find similar forms of support through the vans.
“Without connection to said communities, I don’t know where I’d be,” he said.
The van’s visibility among those in need may also reduce the stigma surrounding methadone. In 2024, a vocal group of Guilford residents strongly opposed the construction of a methadone clinic run by the APT Foundation, citing concerns about the site’s proximity to schools. The clinic opened with the support of Guilford’s first selectman and without the disruptions to safety that some residents feared. 
Amy Di Mauro, senior vice president for adult behavioral health services at CHR, said the organization hasn’t encountered anyone who opposed the van’s operations. Instead, most people she’s spoken to have been supportive.
“There’s opportunity for dispelling myths that lead to the stigma and discrimination of substance use disorder,” she said. “It’s not a moral failing — it’s a medical condition.”

Recovery Specialist Kevin Laymon walks down the stairs during a tour of Community Health Resources’ mobile methadone unit at the company’s Pathways Putnam location on Friday, July 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Growing connections
Even as the two vans begin making their way across Connecticut, the issue of access remains contested in Congress. Two bills introduced over the past 10 months may pull access to methadone in opposite directions. The first, introduced last September by U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin, R-Ind., calls for the reversal of the updated SAMHSA guidelines that expanded access to methadone treatment across the country. 
“I’m not concerned about that,” Di Mauro said. “It doesn’t have enough support.”
On the other hand, bipartisan legislation spearheaded by Sens. Ed Markey, D-Mass., and Rand Paul, R-Ky., in June would allow some doctors to prescribe methadone to patients for direct pickup at a pharmacy. Howell believes the bill would further “normalize” methadone as a form of treatment, as the two other FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorder can be prescribed for pick-up. 
Di Mauro is more hesitant, wondering if further deregulation would dissuade people from seeking “clinical services, recovery services and full person care, not just the medication.”
In the meantime, CHR’s team looks forward to the launch of their van on Tuesday. They anticipate a small client pool in the first few months of operation but expect this number to grow as word of mouth encourages more clients to register with the van.
“It’s really just going to take a village,” Laymon said. “That’s the only way to attack the problem: keep initiating new things like this, fresh ideas, because that’s going to make the process easier for people.”
Long-term funding remains up in the air. The cost of running the van is similar to the cost of running a brick-and-mortar clinic, with the added expense of mileage, according to Di Mauro. But she added that CHR has made space for the van in their budget, even after the organization receives its last parcel of opioid settlement funds in 2027. 
Perez-Suarez is hopeful that CHR’s strong relationships with communities in the northeastern region will encourage more hesitant individuals to register for the van’s services. Her clients often tell her about their reluctance to get lab tests or go to the hospital, where they say they feel treated as addicts rather than patients.
“So I think something like this is really going to help further get rid of that stigma,” she said, referring to the van. “I think the reason the death rate is so high is because they don’t feel connected to anyone.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: A storm punctuates a summer of epic anxiety — and pelts hapless mortals with ancient truth
description: The hail storm that struck a couple of weeks ago was violent. On Constitution Street, the quarter-sized hail drummed on the roof, ricocheted off our windows and dimpled the hood of the Jeep as if it had been peened with an icy hammer. The barrage came at 10:58 p.m. on Wednesday, Aug. 5, and it […]
text:
Dark clouds swarm a late summer sky, possibly signifying storms ahead. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)The hail storm that struck a couple of weeks ago was violent.
On Constitution Street, the quarter-sized hail drummed on the roof, ricocheted off our windows and dimpled the hood of the Jeep as if it had been peened with an icy hammer. The barrage came at 10:58 p.m. on Wednesday, Aug. 5, and it hit Emporia with such precision that you might have thought there was a target painted on the street.
I’m not typically afraid of storms, even though I’ve seen more than my share of death and destruction at Greensburg and Joplin, but this one put a lump in my throat. I didn’t hear the NOAA weather radio warning because I had my headphones on listening to the James Horner score for “Legends of the Fall” while attempting to write that week’s column. I knew it had been thundering, and the wind grew fierce, but the hail got my attention. It was the kind of loud that you feel.
I removed the cans and left the writing desk and went to the front door to peer at the white pellets pinballing across the porch. Kim had heard the radio alert and appeared out of the darkness behind me. I sputtered something about the windows and the cars and the roof, which we’d had repaired after a previous storm.
“It’s just hail,” she said.
We’ve had unusual weather here in Kansas this summer, and it seems to match a collective sense of cultural unease. It’s been too wet or too hot and much too windy. There were too few days that felt normal, not enough meals cooked on the grill, not enough time spent casting a lure or chasing a ball. Now summer was all but gone. My reaction to the hail could not have been sharper had it scattered flaming on the ground, as it does in the 1956 Cecil B. DeMille movie, “The Ten Commandments.”
At least the Cottonwood River hasn’t yet turned to blood.
Kim was not indulging my invocation of the Bible and Hollywood technical effects. The cars will still run, even with hail damage. If the roof leaks or we have broken windows, we’d deal with it the next day. Go write your column, she said.
The hail storm wasn’t even a big event, at least not historically.
The hail that pelted Emporia was, at its largest, the size of a quarter, just about one inch in diameter. The heaviest hailstone in Kansas history fell Sept. 3, 1970, at Coffeyville, according to the National Weather Service. The “hideous hailstone,” as the weather service dubbed it, measured 17.5 inches in circumference, was 5.7 inches in diameter, and weighed a whopping 1.67 pounds. It held the record for the heaviest in the United States until 2010, when a hailstone weighing nearly 2 pounds landed in South Dakota.
The recent Emporia hail storm set no records, but I’ve been thinking of that storm often. While there’s no correlation between politics and the weather — none, that is, if you don’t count how federal policy is contributing to global warming — the barrage was the end of a summer of unease and the beginning of an autumn of uncertainty.
In Greek mythology,j Zeus is the god of storms, hurling thunderbolts at hapless mortals. He’s the supreme deity of the pantheon, the sky father who has rules about how you treat strangers. If you’ve seen Christoper Nolan’s “The Odyssey” then you know mortals break the rule of hospitality at their own peril. If you haven’t seen the film, get a good pair of earplugs before you go, because it is loud. Like all pieces of art, the movie isn’t about the ancient past but is a lesson about now, with Matt Damon as the hapless hero who’s been 20 years away from home because of his own hubris. He must pay, among other debts, for his transgression in using the Trojan Horse — an ostensible gift — to topple Troy.
After Odysseus has his crew tie him to the mast so he can hear the singing of the sirens, something no mortal has listened to and lived, he’s asked what the song was like.
“All the things you wanted to be and then all the things you wished you never wished for,” Nolan’s Odysseus answers. “It was a delicious itch you want to scratch but you find it under the skin and can’t reach it. It told you what you most want is what you most can’t have and that the most you can’t have is what you already had and lost. It was a song of all the promises I failed to keep.”
While Nolan’s film impressed many, Emily Wilson — whose translation of “The Odyssey” was published in 2018 — was having none of it. In the London Review of Books, she declares that she would have been “ashamed” to have written any part of the script.
“Nolan’s spectacle threatens to drown out his story just as the towering waves of the wine-dark sea — more grey than purple — threaten to overwhelm his hero’s ship,” Wilson writes.
The film doesn’t show that war or killing are wrong, she observes, only that good men sometimes feel bad about it. There is no perspective from the victims of Odysseus’s violence, and we know nothing of the Trojans because they are unnamed and hidden by masks.
The dialogue between Nolan and Wilson has defined the summer of 2026.
It is a dialogue of two powerful and informed perspectives, addressed not to one other but to their respective audiences. In Wilson’s case, the missiles are sometimes barbed with wit. This isn’t an argument, but more of an exploration of what it means to make art now. There is a sense of disappointment in Wilson’s piece, a longing for what could have been had Nolan taken one of Western literature’s oldest stories as seriously as he did Dunkirk or the race to build the atomic bomb in “Oppenheimer.”
This is not to say there is no art in “The Odyssey.”
But it’s difficult to hear it.
Fitting, because this has been the summer of loudness and hope and desperation. The volume at which events were flung at us increased as the weeks burned away, and foremost among these was an ever-widening war in Iran. That war has claimed the lives of 18 service members and left nearly 500 wounded. More than 7,000 have been killed in Iran, according to reporting by the BBC. These thousands of nameless and faceless dead should haunt the conscience of every American.
The economic costs of the war are felt every time we buy groceries or put gas in the car. Prices are up by 3.4% over last year, according to reporting by the New York Times, while the nationwide average for a gallon of gasoline was $4.06. Gas is somewhat lower in Kansas, according to the American Automobile Association, averaging $3.78 on Aug. 12.
The day before the Emporia hail storm was the August primary in Kansas, another source of anxiety. But voters soundly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that would have resulted in the popular election of state supreme court justices, so there was some hope.
The right to abortion and equity in school funding was nowhere in the text of the amendment, but those were the reasons the GOP majority in the Kansas Legislature put the question on the ballot. Had voters approved the change, it would have opened up the Kansas Supreme Court to the big money and regressive politics that hold sway in the statehouse. It was a replay of a 2022 ballot question, in which voters were asked to approve a provision to the state constitution denying the right to an abortion. Both the 2022 and 2026 questions failed by margins close to 60-40.
Collectively, Kansans are not as regressive as the legislative majority.
This is a gubernatorial election year in the state, and those races were set by the August primary results. There are also contests for U.S. Senate and all four Kansas House seats, but there’s no need here to describe any of these races. They’ve been amply covered elsewhere and you’ll be deluged by campaign ads soon enough. What is worth noting is that for every general election of the last 10 years, it has seemed like democracy itself has been on the ballot.
But there is even more gravity to this November’s midterm.
The federal government is broken. The imperial presidency of Donald Trump has wreaked havoc on the mechanisms of government built to preserve the health and welfare of Americans of all ages. Health insurance has been denied to millions, thousands of food safety inspectors, scientists, and other federal workers have been fired, and the government has clawed back billions in federal funding to local health departments. At the same time the administration has been busy gutting protections for average Americans, it has rewarded tech oligarchs with unprecedented wealth and influence.
The administration has also waged a campaign of retribution against nonconforming “others” — those of a different political or cultural persuasion, those who choose to define themselves differently in sexual or social relationships, those who insist on a factual and sometimes uncomfortable narrative of America’s past. Above all, the administration has sought to punish immigrants, and it has empowered a virtual army of federal agents and built a chain of concentration camps to do so. It also plans to give ICE officers shock gloves, a bit of stolen lightning to help “remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses,” according to the Associated Press.
This last would invite the wrath of Zeus for violating his sacred law of hospitality. The Greek word is “xenia” and it means food and shelter must be freely offered to weary travelers, even though they be strangers.
“Those who traveled to an unfamiliar land used the norms and expectations of xenia to form bonds with people who might otherwise have treated them as too ragged and dirty to deserve a welcome,” writes Wilson in the introduction to her translation, “or as too dangerous to accept into their home.”
It is a complicated concept, Wilson notes, because it can be used not only to encourage hospitality but also to punish those who are reluctant to welcome possible pirates or bandits. It is the ethical dilemma of the most ancient of times — and of now.
Simplified, it’s the Golden Rule.
Given time, it evolves into western liberal democracy.
Just as our democracy was inspired by the Athenian model, so too have the classic Greeks shaped our ways of thinking about politics, power, and justice. It’s why we turn one of the oldest stories in Western literature into a summer blockbuster and debate its merits in forums ranging from the London Review of Books to your local newspaper. It’s why it rankles that Trump attempted to evade a “credible threat” while leaving Turkey in July, according to the Washington Post, by hiding in a catering truck that secretly carried him away from an older version of Air Force One to a waiting military jet. What kind of hospitality are you showing the journalists and Cabinet officials who travel with you when you let them think you’re on the same plane, when they’re just sitting decoys?
Back in May, Chinese president Xi Jinping alluded to the Thucydides Trap in his meeting with Trump in Beijing. The trap, named for the ancient Greek historian of the Peloponnesian War, refers to the threat of war when a rising power displaces an older one. Two and a half millennia ago, the rise of Athens resulted in a 10-year war with Sparta.
Today, the administration has plunged the United States into sharp decline, both domestically and internationally. While Xi declared the U.S. and China could avoid the trap and establish a new power paradigm, he was also implying that a weakened America had left a power vacuum the Chinese were eager to fill.
Since then, the war with Iran has only exacerbated that weakness.
As we squander our missiles in a war with no identifiable realistic objective, our foreign policy has been dictated by chaos and disorder. Our leader hides in a catering truck from the threat of assassination while the world stumbles closer to catastrophe.
Whatever the weeks and months were like before the Second World War, it must have felt something like this — hoping for the future while steeling oneself for what nightmares may come. A feeling that you were a hapless mortal tossed on the wine-dark sea of history, a target for the vengeful gods and fodder for the foolish kings without empathy.
That’s why I had such a powerful reaction to the Emporia hail storm. It just took me a little while to figure it out. And, as usual, I’ve been in my own head, thinking of Odysseus and Agamemnon and the toppled towers of Troy.
Kim, meanwhile, sees no signs and wonders in hail storms or Hollywood blockbusters. Tomorrow, she says. There will be time to assess the damage then. Get some sleep. She is Emily Wilson to my Christopher Nolan. Later, Kim hands me a copy of Wilson’s translation, whose first line is: “Tell me about a complicated man.”
Sometimes we’re home and just don’t know it.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The high-speed railroad never built — 120 years ago
description: Alexander Miller knew the importance of straight-running tracks to achieve and hold high speeds, a lesson we in Connecticut wish they’d learned.
text:
What happens when a great transportation idea gets ahead of itself?  Consider the story of the greatest American railroad that never got built.
We are all familiar with The Twentieth Century Limited and The Broadway Limited, the crack trains of the New York Central and Pennsylvania Railroads that ran for decades between New York and Chicago.



Those daily trains defined deluxe, pampering passengers with plush Pullman cars, fine dining and even an on-train barber shop.  But they each took up to 20 hours to make the run because they took different, circuitous routes.  The New York Central followed the “water level route” north to Albany, then across upstate New York and down the coast of Lake Erie.  The Pennsylvania Railroad’s “Broadway Limited” (which would start in 1912) journeyed south to Philadelphia, then west to Pittsburgh and beyond.
But way back in 1905, inventor Alexander Miller had a better idea:  build a brand new, flat and straight interurban railroad that would run directly between the two cities, The Chicago – New York Electric Air Line Railroad.
Even over 120 years ago Miller knew the importance of straight-running tracks to achieve and hold high speeds, a lesson we in Connecticut wish they’d learned before building the New Haven Railroad along our winding coastline.

Credit: The Black Cat / Public Domain,

Miller’s train would be “faster than the limited” and make the run between New York City and Chicago in just 10 hours for $10 a ticket (worth about $380 today).  Powered by the new marvel of electricity, the train could operate at a third the cost of steam engines.  And by running in a straight line the 743 mile route would be 168 to 237 miles shorter than its competitors.  In principal, it was brilliant.  And the timing was perfect.
Mind you, this railroad’s interurban cars (think trolley cars on steroids) might not be as plush, but they would average 70+ mph thanks to the almost flat grade of one percent and no pesky grade crossings.  There would also be few stops as the route would bypass all major cities.  And this train would be fast… 100 mph on the straight-aways!
Two million dollars worth of stock was issued with shareholders promised first priority for thousands of potential jobs.  Railroads were the dot-coms of the era, and people rushed to invest.  With no bonded debt, the company’s prospectus promised stock dividends of 14% on top of the shares’ appreciation. You just couldn’t lose!
Construction began from west to east, as the railroad would open in stages to help pay for itself and further building toward New York.  A mighty four track railroad, akin to Metro-North, was envisioned and it was hoped that the project would be completed in just ten years.  Spur lines would be constructed to serve the cities by-passed by the “air line”.
Then, reality set in with the depression of 1907 – 1908.  Construction got as far as Chesterton IN, about 50 miles east of Chicago, when the money started to run out.  The engineering of this mighty railroad was just too expensive.
Shareholders revolted when news came that the railroad’s officers were getting fat paychecks as the coffers were drained.  A hoped-for bailout by British banks never happened.  Those shareholders lost everything.  And the impending arrival of automobiles might have doomed the line anyway.  Even The Twentieth Century and Broadway Ltd eventually succumbed to the competition of true “air lines”.
But for a brief moment, a century ago, a dream almost became a reality in the greatest railroad that never was.

title: Secretary of state candidate Ryan Peterman calls for election changes
description: Democratic secretary of state candidate Ryan Peterman said Saturday he believes recent changes to Iowa election law dealing with early voting and voter identification do not make Iowa elections more secure — but do make elections less accessible. Peterman, who is challenging incumbent Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate in the 2026 election, gave a […]
text:
Ryan Peterman, the Democrat running for Iowa Secretary of State in the midterm election, spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic secretary of state candidate Ryan Peterman said Saturday he believes recent changes to Iowa election law dealing with early voting and voter identification do not make Iowa elections more secure — but do make elections less accessible.
Peterman, who is challenging incumbent Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate in the 2026 election, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair, where he called for Iowans to elect a secretary of state who “knows who they work for.”
The Democratic candidate, a former naval officer, criticized his opponent for sharing voter registration data, including personally identifiable information like driver’s license and Social Security numbers, with the U.S. Department of Justice. Pate had announced in May that Iowa complied with the DOJ request after consulting with the secretary of state’s legal team and the Iowa Attorney General’s Office, which found that the U.S. attorney general had the power to demand this information.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement, Pate said, “we do not take the obligation to turn this information over lightly. The Department of Justice has assured us that the data will be protected appropriately under federal law, and we expect them to uphold that promise.”

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood

Peterman told fairgoers that Pate was not required to take this action, because secretaries of state and attorneys general in other states had refused the DOJ demand for voter information. The DOJ has challenged in court the decision of 30 states to not share voter, and so far 20 of the cases have been dismissed, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. In July, the Democratic candidate filed four public records requests to obtain more information about what data Iowa provided to the DOJ.
He called for Iowans to choose a secretary of state in the 2026 general election who ensures “every eligible voter has an opportunity to cast a ballot, has an opportunity to make their voice heard, has a say in choosing the leaders who shape the future of our state and the future of our country.”
Peterman also criticized measures passed by the GOP-controlled Iowa Legislature in recent years to shorten the state’s early voting window to 20 days, saying he does not believe the shorter early voting window improved Iowa’s election system.
“The same amount of work has to be done, we have shorter amount of time to do it,” Peterman said. “Ballots need to be ready further in advance anyway, so we can apply the federal voting rules for overseas troops — so I don’t see who benefits. I don’t think it improves security, it just hinders accessibility. And I think we have to make sure that we’re focused on doing both.”
He said he was “not so naive as to believe that I can unilaterally change that on my own, but I will advocate to the Legislature to make (the early voting window) as long as we can” if elected to the office.
He also criticized a 2026 law removing the ability for a voter to confirm their identity through a fellow voter’s attestation, and would advocate for bringing back this way to confirm a person’s identity. He said there was “no evidence of fraud being committed because of attestation.”

description: Rick Stewart, a Libertarian running for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, said Saturday that he wants to end income taxes, overhaul the nation’s immigration policy and replace government assistance programs with a universal basic income.  Stewart also called for a universal carbon tax and to “eliminate” all nuclear weapons.  Stewart is running against Repub[...]
text:
Rick Stewart, a Libertarian candidate running in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District spoke Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Rick Stewart, a Libertarian running for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, said Saturday that he wants to end income taxes, overhaul the nation’s immigration policy and replace government assistance programs with a universal basic income. 
Stewart also called for a universal carbon tax and to “eliminate” all nuclear weapons. 
Stewart is running against Republican Joe Mitchell, Democrat Lindsay James and independent candidate Dave Bushaw, who spoke earlier in the day. It is an open race as current U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson pursues a bid for the U.S. Senate. 
Stewart, who lives in Cedar Rapids, has run for office several times, as a Libertarian candidate for governor in 2022, for U.S. Senate in 2020 and in 2018 for Iowa secretary of agriculture.
“The one thing you should not do is you should not vote for a Republican or a Democrat,” Stewart said. 
When asked what sets him apart from Bushaw, who is also running against the major party candidates, Stewart said “45 years of experience.” 
Five policies that ‘won’t cost a nickel’ 
Stewart explained five policy priorities, which he said would not cost more than existing programs already cost. 
First, he called for an elimination of nuclear weapons, because he said they are an “existential threat” to the nation and “nobody needs them.” 
Next, he said he would do away with all income tax, which he said has complex regulations that end up being “just a place where politicians can pass laws.” 
Instead of income tax, Stewart suggested a land tax, which would be levied on top of property tax, based on the value of the land. 
“So income taxes are the worst conceivable idea,” Stewart said. “A land tax is the most fair tax of all.” 
The land tax, he argued, would be easier to understand, and pay, compared to the current income tax program. 
Stewart’s third policy point was an overhaul the current immigration policy that he said “costs a lot of money and makes a lot of people angry.” 
Instead, Stewart suggested a system that allows vetted immigrants to bid for lifetime green cards in an auction system to enter the country. He said refugee and humanitarian cases for immigration should be decided by U.S. citizens, rather than the government. 


Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood


Stewart, who said he spends part of his year in Guatemala, said his immigration reform would also allow “anyone who’s not an actual criminal” to purchase a visa to visit the U.S. 
“That’s what we need to do here in America, is an immigration system that’s fair, honest, and makes money,” Stewart said. 
He also said a universal tax on carbon would help to reduce carbon emissions, which contribute to global warming. The money collected by the carbon tax, Stewart said, would then be passed along to everyone living in a participating country. The carbon tax rebates, as he called them, would be spread on a per capita basis. The citizen demand to receive the rebates, he argued, would push countries to participate in the carbon tax program. 
“This will work because it gives people the incentive to do the right thing,” Stewart said.
Stewart said that current programs, especially Social Security and Medicare, represent “income transfers” between people who are “relatively poor and working to people who are relatively wealthy and not working.” 
By redirecting payroll taxes from Social Security and Medicare and funding from other government assistance programs, Stewart argued the nation could supply a “universal basic income” to all citizens. 
“So this system is, practically, 100% funded already, and it will guarantee that the only thing that happens is relatively wealthy people will give money to relatively poor people,” Stewart said. 
He explained the universal basic income would be distributed monthly to every citizen 18 years and older, regardless of total income or work status. 
With the universal basic income, he said the nation needs to “eliminate every single welfare program in the entire country” including school lunch vouchers, or farm subsidies for example.  
“I happen to be very passionate about government,” Stewart said in closing. “The one we have is not the one we want. Vote for me because if you vote for a Democrat or a Republican, all you’re doing is you’re voting to perpetuate the current system.”

text:
Michael Bridgford, an independent candidate running in Iowa's 1st Congressional District spoke Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Michael Bridgford said Saturday at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox that a couple of independent candidates, like him, in the U.S. House would be able to “push” for votes on issues like term limits, campaign finance reform, and chamber leadership. 
Bridgford is running as an independent candidate in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District against Republican incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democratic candidate Christina Bohannan. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bridgford said he is a candidate for 1st District voters who are “frustrated” with Congress. 
“People feel as though they’re not being represented, they’re not being heard, and we’re going to change that this year,” Bridgford said. 
According to a Gallup poll from January, 45% of U.S. voters identified as independent in 2025. Bridgford said there is a “national movement” currently to support independent candidates. 
Michael Bridgford, an independent candidate running in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, spoke Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Iowa’s 1st Congressional District is one of the less than 20 “toss-up” districts for the House. 
The major-party candidates, Miller-Meeks and Bohannan, faced off in 2024, when Bohannan lost to the incumbent by about 800 votes.
“When Iowa 1 sends an independent to Congress, it’ll be the most important district in this country,” Bridgford said. 
Affordability, agriculture and healthcare 
Bridgford, who is a small business owner from the Quad-Cities region, said affordability, agriculture and healthcare policies are some of his top priorities. 
He said the affordability crisis is driven largely by increases to the country’s money supply and a lack of consistency in trade policies. 

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:

Bridgford also said he would push for proposals like price transparency and pharmacy benefit managers reform to help address the high healthcare costs. 
When asked if he would have voted for Republican’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made significant reforms to various programs, including Medicaid, Bridgford said he would have tried to “leverage” his position to “make it better for the average person versus just people at the very top.”
Bridgford said he grew up during the farm crisis of the 1980s, when his family lost their hog farm. 
“Unfortunately, our farmers now are approaching a similar type of crisis to the 1980s, and the politicians are playing political football with ag policy,” Bridgford said and referenced the stalled progress on a new farm bill. 
Bridgford said farmers need a new farm bill with year-round, nationwide E15 and more support for family farmers. 
Speaking with reporters after the Soapbox, Bridgford said he was not supportive of certain Republican policies, like the Save Our Bacon Act, which would block states from stipulating how livestock are raised. 
Bridgford said he is his campaign’s biggest donor and that he is in the race for the “right reason.” 
“The parties, they just want to fight,” Bridgford said. “They’re not interested in actually solving the problem.”

text:
Dave Bushaw, an Independent candidate running in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District, spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Independent congressional candidate Dave Bushaw asked for Iowans’ support Saturday at the Iowa State Fair as he works to build an “independent movement” past the 2026 election season throughout the state.
Bushaw is running as an independent candidate in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, but has a history in Democratic politics, having worked as an organizer for U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign during the 2020 Democratic presidential nominating cycle. But during his speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox, he criticized both the Democratic and Republican parties as “two wings of the same bird that feed corporate greed,” which he said do not represent working class Americans.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The hard truth, folks, is that this freedom isn’t going to be won within the corrupt two-party establishment,” Bushaw said. “I became the first no-party candidate to secure ballot access in northeast Iowa in modern history because working-class voters wanted it to be that way.”
Bushaw will appear on the ballot with Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James and Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state lawmaker. The 2nd District is an open race, as current U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson is on the ballot as the GOP nominee for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat.
While the seat is expected to be less competitive than the congressional races for Iowa’s 1st and 3rd Districts, according to political forecasters, Democrats still hope the seat could be a potential pick-up in the midterms.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood

Bushaw said his campaign did not have party infrastructure in the 2nd District, which covers much of northeast Iowa, or the financial support his major-party opponents have, but said his campaign came to the race with a small amount of money and “folks that were ready to fight.” Bushaw reported raising $12,555 in the most recent Federal Election Commission reporting period, falling below James, who raised $755,587 and Mitchell, who raised $377,769.
“While the media often fixates on enormous amounts of money raised and spent by these candidates in the Democratic and Republican Party — which I find more disgusting than impressive — we’re showing that working-class poor folks can build infrastructure and run a strong campaign without money backing them,” he said. “That’s called fiscal responsibility, and it’s a foreign concept to most politicians.”
While he called for voters in the 2nd District to support his campaign for Congress, he also said he plans to build a greater independent “movement” in future election cycles.
“This doesn’t stop in 2026,” Bushaw said. “I’ve been organizing for 15 years. … I intend on starting here in the 2nd District, but we are going to build an independent movement here in Iowa in all districts and across this country — 2028, 2030, and 2032. That’s a promise.”
If elected in 2026, the first measure he would introduce would be to allow for national ballot initiatives that would allow U.S. voters to directly weigh in on certain measures at the federal level, like the legalization of cannabis and campaign finance reform.
“There’s 435 members in Congress right now, and almost all of them are completely bought out by the corrupt two-party duo. I believe that representative democracy, in some facets, has outlived its usefulness. These aren’t the days of horse and buggy, when you had to send a ballot box on a you know, all the way across from Oregon to Washington (D.C.) — we all have cell phones, we all have computers. We’re hyper connected. I believe and I trust the American people to make decisions ourselves. … I trust the American people to make the right decisions on these things, so I want to give more direct democracy power to the American working people.”
