name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Controlling wild pigs can work if it’s a group effort
authors: Chris Boyer, The Conversation, Aaron Smith, The Conversation, Eunchun Park, The Conversation
description: The federal government is injecting millions of dollars into efforts to combat feral hogs – and it’s considering spending even more in the coming years. The problem has grown for decades, but our research has found that a recently revived federal effort offers the potential for bringing the hogs under control. Feral swine roam in […]
text:
Feral Hog in south FloridaThe federal government is injecting millions of dollars into efforts to combat feral hogs – and it’s considering spending even more in the coming years. The problem has grown for decades, but our research has found that a recently revived federal effort offers the potential for bringing the hogs under control.
Feral swine roam in 35 states, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The most recent population figures, from 2016, estimated that 7 million feral pigs were loose in the nation then. That number may be much higher today: Feral hogs breed year-round and each year can produce up to two litters of four to 12 piglets per litter. Feral hog populations have been estimated to be able to double in just four months.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that wild pigs do between US$2.5 billion and $3.4 billion in property damage each year. At least $800 million of that is destruction of crops.

Beyond crops, feral hogs spread disease to livestock, damage farm infrastructure such as fences and roads needed for agricultural production, destroy recreational parks and cause extensive environmental damage to wildlife habitats, water quality and plant ecosystems.
They’re hard to control because feral hogs roam across large areas of privately owned land. If neighboring landowners don’t work together, the hogs just move rather than being killed or contained. Basic economic theory says landowners would wait for others to spend the time, money and energy to control hogs – which means nobody does, and the problems grow.



Let us know what you think...


 


An initial test

	In the 2018 Farm Bill, a major piece of legislation covering wide areas of agricultural policy, Congress agreed to spend $75 million to encourage private landowners to step up together to kill feral hogs.
That program was active in selected counties in 10 hog-plagued states: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Texas. Starting in 2020, the U.S. Department of Agriculture funded private landowners’ purchases of trapping equipment, on-farm trapping efforts and restoration of land the hogs had damaged.
Originally slated to end in 2023, the program was given $105 million more to spend through 2029 in the major budget and immigration package Congress passed in July 2025. Through Sept. 21, 2026, the government is accepting grant applications for the first $35 million allocation from that money.
The Farm Bill that has passed the House and is awaiting debate in the Senate would increase that funding by $150 million and extend the effort through 2031.
A useful question, before spending all that money, is how effective the first test of the program was.
Reducing hogs’ damage to cornfields

	Our research team of agricultural economists at the University of Tennessee and the University of Arkansas set out to examine the program’s performance.
We used federal data on crop insurance claims to compare crop damage in counties where the program was active against counties where it was not, both before and after the federal trial began.
Not all the counties reported crop damage from wildlife. Among those that did, counties where the program wasn’t operating had crop insurance claims for wildlife damage to corn that averaged 70 acres (17.5 hectares) per policy.
In counties where hog eradication efforts were coordinated, however, the average claim for cornfield acres damaged from wildlife declined to 10 acres per policy. That is a statistically significant result – and given the scale of corn production across the study region, it represents a meaningful reduction in losses.
When comparing crop insurance claims for soybeans, wheat, cotton and peanuts, however, we found no difference between counties with active hog control efforts and those without.
A way forward

	Corn is reportedly the crop most commonly damaged by feral swine. That could help explain why we found cornfields to have the only statistically significant reduction in damage.
More generally, the program’s effectiveness may have been more limited because it launched during the COVID-19 pandemic, which restricted the community meetings and public outreach that could have boosted landowner participation. Also, the fact that it was a pilot effort may have made people reluctant to commit, fearing the program might disappear in a few years.
It is likely our study underestimates the benefits of the program. Some farmers have crop damage that is not severe enough to warrant an insurance claim, so those numbers are excluded from our analysis. And our study did not evaluate any potential changes in noncrop damage from feral hogs, such as to property, livestock, recreational parks and the environment in general.
Our research indicates the hog control program can be effective and offers several ideas for improving it, both over time and with more funding. For instance, if the efforts focused specifically on corn-producing counties, it might yield more success per dollar invested. And expanding participation through additional outreach efforts could mean more hogs are caught or killed across a wider area, amplifying the return further.
Feral hogs will be nearly impossible to eradicate completely, and the damage they cause isn’t going away either. The data suggests that with the right design and sustained investment, the federal government has a program that can make a real difference for America’s farmers.

name: Maryland Matters
title: BGE PSC Pinsky
description: Most investors would be thrilled to earn a 10.4% return on investment, but that's the "bare minimum" Baltimore Gas and Electric says it needs to survive in it latest rate filing. It's nothing but a money grab, writes Paul Pinsky, and it's past time for the PSC to say no.
text:
The site of a news \natural-gas fired power plant proposed by Constellation Energy in Perryman, which has angered local residents. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Baltimore Gas and Electric’s  recently proposed rate hike “is the bare minimum to keep the lights on,” claimed the company.  This is the company’s justification for requesting a guaranteed 10.4% profit next year.  No area ratepayers who are lucky enough to have investments, are guaranteed to make a 10.4% return.  In fact, it’s pretty unlikely that Baltimore residents have any money left for even the smallest investments after paying their rising BGE bill.
BGE has a regional monopoly to provide gas and electricity and is a “regulated” utility.  Any costs it incurs to “keep the lights on” are also guaranteed. Profit or “return-on-investment” is the money left after expenses and has no relation to “keeping the lights on.” The utility’s profit, taken from your pocket,  goes to the investors.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




This unreasonable profit that executives and investors squeeze from employees and consumers amounts to nothing short of corporate greed.
Whether you think that the growing income inequality between the ultra rich and everybody else requires simple tinkering to improve our capitalist system or whether it calls for a real democratic socialist makeover, BGE’s request for a 10.4% profit is unconscionable and should be rejected by Maryland’s Public Service Commission (PSC), the body that sets rates.
Over the last 10 years,  BGE has been guaranteed a 9.3%-9.7%  yearly return by the PSC.  If you held investments, your financial adviser would probably tell you that a 5% return over a five to 10 year span would be great, even with the ups and downs of the stock market. BGE has been receiving almost double that and it’s been made on the backs of Baltimore area residents. The company doesn’t even have to be concerned about the uncertainty that small investors face when investing. For BGE, the profit is guaranteed.
Why has the PSC approved these large profit margins? Two reasons: because they ‘always have’ and because neighboring states provide similar profit rates.  Neither make convincing arguments.
Maybe BGE’s 10.4% ask is simply a negotiating ploy to make sure that a 9.4% rate appears more reasonable.
Whatever the case, it’s time to say no to this company owned by corporate giant Exelon. BG&E has a monopoly making them the only gas and electric company allowed to operate in the Baltimore region.
Currently, ratepayers shoulder this large financial burden and pay extra each month only to fill the company’s balance sheet.
The Public Service Commission, however, ultimately holds the cards, not BGE.  It’s way past time to say no to these large profits and it’s high time to bring down the utility bills of the area’s hard-working residents.

name: Maryland Matters
title: When data centers come knocking, Maryland counties should have a ‘wish list,’ officials say
description: If one thing was clear after the second panel on data centers at the Maryland Association of Counties conference, it's that data centers are not going anywhere any time soon. So counties should start drawing up a wish list of demands for when they come calling.
text:
Ian Ullman, deputy director for Gov. Wes Moore's (D) energy office, said at the Maryland Association of Counties conference Friday that Maryland counties should consider the financial investments data center companies are willing to make to improve their counties, such as road or school improvements. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) energy office has a message for all of the Maryland counties with temporary data center moratoriums: Make your wish list.
“Use the time that you have bought yourselves with your local moratorium, talk to other communities that have figured this out,” said Ian Ullman, deputy director of the Maryland Energy Administration. “And make your wish list. This is the time.”
If one thing was clear after the second major panel focused on the issue at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference, it was that data centers are not going anywhere — at least not any time soon. So counties should start preparing.
“Counties willing to negotiate can extract meaningful investment in their community’s futures while mitigating impact to their communities and residents,” Ullman said. “New schools, road upgrades, community centers, long-term support packages for local initiatives — it’s all on the table.”
Jason Stanek, executive director of governmental affairs at PJM, the multistate electric grid operator, speaks about data centers and struggles with siting new transmission infrastructure Friday ad the MACo conference. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Constellation Energy, represented on the panel by senior vice president of government affairs Mason Emnett, agrees.
“Engage, roll up your sleeves, identify what matters to you, what matters to your community, and in our experience, you’ll find partners who come forward and want to be in the solution space and get to yes,” Emnett told the audience in Ocean City.
Just over a week ago, Constellation learned that data center developer Amazon Web Services was pulling out from its planned project at the company’s Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Southern Maryland. It came after voters unseated three members of the county council amid data center backlash. Now, the county is considering a moratorium of its own.
Though the response of many Maryland counties — representing the majority of Maryland residents — has been to enact time-limited bans amid fierce pushback from voters to data center proposals, the demand for AI among consumers seems persistent. Data centers “aren’t going away,” said Jason Stanek, executive director of governmental services at PJM Interconnection, the electric grid serving Maryland and about a dozen other neighboring states.
“We need all levels of government: county government, state government, to address this situation because we see this train coming and it’s coming fast,” Stanek said.
And Maryland, which does not have a large volume of high voltage transmission lines, is in a precarious position as data centers outside the state continue to place pressure on the PJM grid. The Eastern Shore does not have any high voltage transmission, only one such line crosses the Western panhandle, and only a few lines exist near the Interstate 95 corridor.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“We have 14 states, and Maryland is one of the most concerning,” Stanek said. “We see challenges on the horizon in the near term. Next year, we expect possible disruptions of the grid in the state of Maryland.”
But efforts to add new lines can be fraught, said Stanek, who formerly led the Maryland Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities and power equipment in the state. For instance, PJM commissioned the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, a new high-voltage line for rural Central Maryland, and it’s been the subject of significant pushback from hundreds of landowners practically ever since. It currently sits before the PSC.
“It doesn’t take very long to build a data center: 18, 24 months,” Stanek said. “Try building a new power plant. Five years? Maybe, if you’re lucky. A transmission line? When I chaired the PSC, I approved every line that came across my desk. Not one got built because we couldn’t get it across other state lines.”
Now, PJM is challenging its member states to approve power plants in one year, and transmission lines in one to two years, Stanek said.
On Thursday, PJM filed a proposal that would allow new data centers to connect to the grid — but if they do not bring their own power generation, they would be first in line to be shut off in a power emergency, forcing them to rely on back-up generators. The proposal would have to be approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
Attendees of the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference watch a panel about data centers Friday. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“When electricity supply on the grid approaches dangerously low levels, a new emergency procedure would notify utilities to reduce or transfer the electricity demand from new Large Load customers ahead of any action that would serve to shut off traditional consumers, including residential consumers,” reads a news release from PJM.
Still, the demand growth projections — fueled largely by possible data centers — remain immense, said Maryland People’s Counsel David Lapp, who represents residential utility ratepayers in the state.
“By 2046, PJM forecasts adding about seven states of Maryland to the region. This is not normal growth in electric demand,” Lapp said. “It’s almost entirely due to data centers projected to arrive in record time and in concentrated locations.”
Most of this data center demand growth isn’t coming from Maryland. In fact, 93% of it is coming from Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Illinois, Lapp said during his presentation.
His office has been working to shield Maryland customers from paying for the energy buildout that data centers are requiring, because, currently, the costs of expanding and maintaining the system are shared by all ratepayers. But processes are underway at PJM, at FERC and at the state level to change the paradigm, Lapp said. That’s why slowing down on data centers — even slightly — has a lot of value, he said.
“These efforts should — if they’re done right — should provide good, solid protections for residential customers,” Lapp said. “But they take time.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Financing, permit challenges stand in the way of building new housing, officials say
description: State and local housing and planning officials say there is an urgent need to build more housing to bring down Maryland’s skyrocketing housing costs, but thee are two major hurdles: cumbersome permitting and securing financing for affordable housing.
text:
Housing Secretary Jake Day, along with housing directors Terry Hickey of Baltimore County and Scott Bruton of Montgomery County and, from left, were among state and local officials focused on building new housing units at a panel Friday. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)State and local housing and planning officials say there is an urgent need to build more housing supply to start bringing down Maryland’s skyrocketing housing costs as soon as possible.
But there are two major hurdles for getting those projects started: financing new affordable housing projects and navigating through gummed-up permitting processes, according to two different housing-related forums at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference Friday.
State officials on both panels said that counties should consider ways to boost financing options or speed up the permitting process if Maryland is to start chipping away at the estimated 100,000 housing unit shortage.
In a panel focused on speeding up county-level permitting for new development, Planning Secretary Rebecca Flora said department officials learned other states improved their permitting timelines by simply making the process more transparent while creating a report released this year.
Planning Secretary Rebecca Flora (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
“Transparency solved a huge part of the problem,” Flora said, “because once you have a transparent system of tracking a project that others can see and everybody knows what’s going on, they had some pretty significant gains.”
She added that the process can get gummed up because local agencies and developers may have different interpretations of the same building regulations, delaying the approval of a development until they come to a mutual understanding.
But for Pete Gutwald, director of permits approvals and inspections for Baltimore County, counties should simplify permitting processes to reduce delays in approval due to user error.
“The large projects have sophisticated teams that know how to work the system,” he said. “It’s actually the nonprofits, the smaller projects, the folks that are just getting started that are having the most challenges. And we really need to find ways to simplify, at all levels, because otherwise, that small business, those small projects … are the ones that are going to continue to have hurdles.”
Following the panel on permitting, Housing Secretary Jake Day focused on financing challenges facing affordable housing projects.
He said that affordable housing specifically is challenging to get off the ground compared to houses priced by the market. The lower rent that comes in from affordable housing development will not fully cover the cost it took to build new units.
“The development costs are the same-ish,” Day said, referring to both houses on the market and affordable housing options. “But there is a big financing gap that exists and … makes affordable housing more difficult to finance.”
Housing Secretary Jake Day (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
The state Department of Housing and Community Development has several programs to help fill in that financing gap, but Day said state housing officials are looking to counties that have successful affordable housing financing programs to see what policies could be expanded to a statewide capacity.
“We have to make up the difference between what it costs in the market and what the revenue that’s produced from reduced rents from affordable housing,” Scott Bruton, director for the Department of Housing and Community Affairs in Montgomery County.
Financing new units and speeding up permitting for those builds may boost supply and, in theory, slow the rising costs of housing a few years down the line – but those policies do not address the housing need of today.
Matt Losak, executive director for the Montgomery County Renters Alliance, raised that very issue with the panel, particularly for the rising number of Marylanders who are stuck renting because home ownership is financially out of reach.
“We’re just very concerned about that population that’s not going to buy a house any time soon,” he said.
Day agreed that the cost of rent is also soaring, and that the conversation around building new housing can include conversations on protecting renters too.
“We can’t build our way out of the problem, but I think we also have to say that we must build our way out of the problem,” Day said. “That is a part of the picture … There also needs to be rental protections. There also needs to be subsidies provided. There also needs to be regulations that protect our vulnerable populations.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: How American society shields perpetrators of child sexual abuse
description: Widespread denial accompanied the public exposure of Jeffrey Epstein’s decades-long sexual abuse and trafficking of girls and women. After the U.S. Justice Department released millions of case documents on Epstein in January 2026, billionaires, politicians, heads of state and academics proclaimed their ignorance of Epstein’s global network of sexual exploita[...]
text:
An array of pictures provided by the Department of Justice on Jan. 30, 2026, were part of the Jeffrey Epstein files. (Photo by Martin Bureau/AFP via Getty Images)Widespread denial accompanied the public exposure of Jeffrey Epstein’s decades-long sexual abuse and trafficking of girls and women.
After the U.S. Justice Department released millions of case documents on Epstein in January 2026, billionaires, politicians, heads of state and academics proclaimed their ignorance of Epstein’s global network of sexual exploitation.
Why would so many intelligent and powerful people repeatedly trumpet their lack of awareness, especially after Epstein’s 2008 plea agreement to underage prostitution charges?
And what about all of Epstein’s staffers and business associates who kept quiet about the suspicious behavior they observed?
As a human rights researcher who has conducted genocide research on four continents, I think denials of human rights atrocities can help people understand the denial of crimes like child sexual abuse and trafficking.
Avoiding accountability for atrocities requires two types of denial: by the perpetrator and by the community. It’s easy to understand why mass murderers and child rapists deny their horrific actions. More perplexing is why bystanders, law enforcement, colleagues, family and institutions claim ignorance.
Society understands that staying quiet after witnessing impermissible crimes is a form of complicity. Bystanders are likely to deny an atrocity when acknowledging it requires action, both morally and legally.
As sociologist Eviatar Zerubavel has noted: “Like silence, denial involves active avoidance. Rather than simply failing to notice something, it entails a deliberate effort to refrain from noticing it.”
 
US and international law
A network of international and domestic laws considers certain crimes so horrific that there are no extenuating circumstances for committing them. Other laws stipulate that everyday observers of certain crimes have a legal responsibility to report them and to protect victims if possible.
The 1987 United Nations convention against torture emphasizes: “No exceptional circumstances whatsoever, whether a state of war or a threat of war … may be invoked as a justification of torture.” And the 1948 U.N. genocide convention holds all signatory nations responsible for their inaction against genocide.
In the United States, the 1974 Federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act mandates that states have provisions requiring certain people – doctors, teachers, clergy and law enforcement – to report known or suspected cases of child abuse.
About a quarter of states go further and stipulate that “all persons who have cause to suspect that any juvenile is abused, neglected, or dependent or has died as the result of maltreatment shall report” to the authorities.
 
Perpetrator denial
In the context of government human rights abuses, sociologist Stanley Cohen in 2001 classified denial into three strategies: literal, interpretive and implicatory.
With literal denial, Cohen wrote, the perpetrator simply claims the event never happened. If successful, this form of denial makes the problem disappear.
During the U.S. war on terror after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, human rights groups accused the George W. Bush government of torturing detainees in Iraq and Guantanamo Bay.
Applying Cohen’s typology illuminates how the Bush administration cycled through strategies of denial, beginning with literal denial. Responding to evidence of U.S. torture of detainees in Iraq in 2006, Bush denied the accusations: “This country doesn’t torture; we’re not going to torture.”
After the failure of literal denial, the Justice Department employed interpretive denial, which admits to something having taken place, just not something that rises to the level of a crime. The DOJ redefined torture and referred to acts such as waterboarding – legally classified as torture – as “enhanced interrogation methods.”
Following his guilty plea to soliciting prostitution from a 14-year-old, Epstein used interpretive denial by comparing the severity of his crime to shoplifting: “I’m not a sexual predator,” he said. “I’m an ‘offender.’ It’s the difference between a murderer and a person who steals a bagel.”
When interpretive denial fails, perpetrators turn to what Cohen calls implicatory denial. It accepts the facts – torture of detainees, forced expulsions, mass killings – but denies the psychological or moral ramifications that follow.
In his memoirs, Bush did not deny the use of torture; he denied the immorality of the torture. “The choice between security and values was real,” he wrote.
 
Community denial

Research that I’m currently conducting revises Cohen’s typology to understand why bystanders to crimes like Epstein’s don a veil of ignorance.
Denial of child sexual abuse occurs within a community – a citizenry, a family, a congregation. The community establishes the parameters of morality, the relative power of each member, and which actions constitute crimes.
In cases where accepting the truth has a high communal cost – a reordering of the power structure, more egalitarian institutions, eradication of prejudice or social disgrace – many people calculate that the cost of justice is not worth reordering the structure of privilege from which they benefit.
In the case of institutional abuse, powerful groups, such as the Catholic Church, prioritized the reputation of the institution over the victims.
Much like perpetrators, a community adheres to its preferred version of reality by denying abuse at the literal, interpretive and implicatory levels.
With literal denial, bystanders negate the experience of one particular child. This is so prevalent among mothers of incest victims that the legal community is exploring criminally charging the mothers who fail to protect their children.
Community interpretive denial tells the victim they did not experience what they thought they experienced. This occurred repeatedly for many victims of Larry Nassar, a former physician who sexually assaulted hundreds of gymnasts in the guise of medical treatment.
Gymnast Larissa Boyce described what happened when the then-16-year-old reported Nassar’s abuse to her coach. “She just couldn’t believe that was happening. She said I must be misunderstanding what was going on.”
Community implicatory denial negates the moral implications of the atrocity by blaming the victim for the perpetrator’s actions.
During the Catholic Church sexual abuse scandal that erupted in the late 1980s, Milwaukee Archbishop Rembert Weakland admitted that sexual activity had taken place between some of his priests and their young parishioners, but he dismissed the notion that the priests were entirely to blame.
“Sometimes not all adolescent victims are so ‘innocent,’” he told The Catholic Herald in 1988. “Some can be sexually very active and aggressive and often quite streetwise.”
Communities blinded by the perpetrator’s stethoscope, billion dollars, clerical collar or Ivy League degree often refuse to acknowledge the stereotypes that protect privileged predators.
And that willful ignorance of child sexual abuse equals complicity. Through denial, members thus absolve themselves for inaction in the face of atrocity.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Van Hollen reports the ‘good news’, but mostly ‘bad news’ coming out of Washington
description: In his second town hall appearance before the Maryland Association of Counties as the state's senior senator, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md) rattled off a list of good news coming out of Washington, but a much longer list of bad news for the state.
text:
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen hosts his second town hall as the state's senior senator at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference on Friday. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md) returned for his second year to lead a town hall-styled forum at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference, an annual tradition where local and state officials, lobbyists and other interested parties ask Maryland’s senior U.S. senator about operations at the federal level.
This year, Van Hollen said upfront that he had some good news to report — but had a much longer list of “bad news” under the Trump administration.
“I think it’s no secret to any of you that there’s a lot of chaos coming out of Washington, D.C. these days,” he said.
“The good news – I wish that list was longer … we have been able to put together a fiscal year 2026 budget. That is a low bar, but in these divided times, it was important,” he said. “As a result, many Maryland priorities have received full funding.”
Those projects receiving funding include conservation efforts for the Chesapeake Bay, support for the National Institutes of Health, anti-erosion efforts for Ocean City and preserving full funding for the replacement of the Francis Scott Key bridge.
Another “good news story” is the $320 million in congressional direct spending included in the budget, which will support local projects around the state. Congress also passed legislation to tackle the nationwide housing affordability crisis, he said.
Van Hollen tells podcast he is ‘kicking the tires’ on potential run for president

But the “bad news” took up a majority of the 35-minutes Van Hollen spoke before taking audience questions.
Many of those challenges come from the budget resolution bill the Republican-lead Congress passed in 2025 called H.R. 1, also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”
That legislation aims to reduce federal spending for Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program by implementing stronger work requirements to qualify for those federal assistance programs.
He also noted that healthcare costs are going up for many families that buy their health insurance from the state’s insurance marketplace under the Affordable Care Act, as Congress did not act to renew popular federal tax credits that kept those costs down.
Van Hollen said that federal agencies are also still feeling impacts from the mass layoff and program funding cancellations under the so-called Department of Government Efficiency run by Elon Musk, or DOGE, which ended operations in July.
Also on his list of “bad news” were ongoing issues with federal immigration enforcement officers, costs rising due to tariffs and the war in Iran, and energy demand due to data centers.
“The bad news list just keeps going,” he said.
And it did. When the forum opened up for audience questions, local officials, advocates and local business leaders brought new concerns to the table – limited internet access in rural counties, rising costs of housing and rent, and a lack of accountability when the federal government oversteps its authority.
“At the end of the day, that has to happen,” Van Hollen said to the question about accountability. “We have a system of laws, we need to enforce them.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington state lawmaker hit with $15K fine in ethics case
description: Washington state Rep. Tarra Simmons was fined $15,000 on Friday by a state ethics panel for improperly using her position to steer public funds to a nonprofit where she worked, and trying to retaliate against the person who initiated the investigation against her. A unanimous Legislative Ethics Board concluded the Bremerton Democrat committed three violation[...]
text:
Washington state Rep. Tarra Simmons, D-Bremerton, listens to testimony during a hearing on allegations she violated state ethics laws on June 8, 2026. Simmons denies the charges. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)Washington state Rep. Tarra Simmons was fined $15,000 on Friday by a state ethics panel for improperly using her position to steer public funds to a nonprofit where she worked, and trying to retaliate against the person who initiated the investigation against her.
A unanimous Legislative Ethics Board concluded the Bremerton Democrat committed three violations of conflict of interest and special privilege laws, and levied the maximum $5,000 penalty for each. She also must pay the costs of state attorneys.
The board dismissed three other allegations stemming from efforts to help a friend get a job, donating unspent campaign funds to the nonprofit to pay for the friend’s position and working for an organization that received state funding.
The nine-member board issued its 15-page decision Friday afternoon, roughly six weeks after conducting a trial-like proceeding into allegations against Simmons. 
Simmons, who adamantly denies wrongdoing, said in a statement that the fine was unfair and excessive given that she had to pursue a hearing to prove three allegations were untrue. She also said she was better off compared to earlier in the case when she had a chance to settle.
“People shouldn’t be excessively punished when they actually prevail,” she said.
Simmons said she is planning to appeal in Thurston County Superior Court, where she can “finally be heard by a non-political entity lacking any personal interest in the outcome of her case, and where the repeated violations of her due process rights will finally be heard.”
The ruling arrives days after the primary election in which Simmons bested a fellow Democrat, Daria Ilgen, by a margin of 57.3% to 39%. The two will face off again in November.
Simmons is seeking a fourth term representing the 23rd Legislative District in Kitsap County that includes the communities of Hansville, Kingston, Poulsbo, Bremerton and Bainbridge Island. 
She serves as deputy speaker pro tem, a highly visible role that requires frequently presiding over floor sessions. She’s also garnered national attention as the first formerly incarcerated person to serve in the Legislature. 
A complaint filed in February 2025 triggered an investigation that led to Friday’s ruling, which hinged on whether Simmons violated the Ethics in Public Service Act. 
Simmons has said she rejected settlement offers in order to defend herself against charges she felt were motivated by personal animus and politics. 
The hearing took place in June. During three hours of hearing testimony, she insisted she’s been hypervigilant about complying with the rules since arriving in the Legislature in 2021. She said she was warned that, as the first formerly incarcerated person elected to state office, political foes would look for ways to derail her career.
Questions of improper influence
This case revolved around Simmons’ interactions with two nonprofit organizations: the American Equity and Justice Group and the Equity in Education Coalition.
Two violations are related to a $1 million grant Simmons helped secure in 2024 to support an expansion of a public dashboard of criminal justice data created by the American Equity and Justice Group.
The group was required to subcontract $500,000 of work with a nonprofit organization “that advocates for equity in technology and education to provide the public with data on social determinants that impact education outcomes.”
The only qualifying subcontractor was the Equity in Education Coalition, which focuses on improving education outcomes in disadvantaged communities. Simmons was employed as the coalition’s part-time director of strategy from December 2023 through Jan. 10, 2025, then an additional three months as an independent contractor.
In the June hearing, Assistant Attorney General Julia Eisentrout argued Simmons’ interest in securing the money through a budget proviso, even if it wasn’t financial, conflicted with her official duties as a legislator.
The ethics board agreed, concluding Simmons “personally benefited” because the grant funds supported continued operations of the coalition “and its ability to fund her $120,000 annual salary.”
The second violation stemmed from what the board deemed Simmons improper intervention in a dispute between the two nonprofits, the outcome of which preserved funding for the coalition.
American Equity and Justice Group sought help from the Administrative Office of the Courts because the coalition was not completing tasks required by terms of the grant.
Christopher Stanley, chief financial and management officer of the state agency, spoke with Simmons, then met with the groups and the contract terms were revised. While Stanley testified in the hearing that he did not feel Simmons pressured him, the board still concluded she overstepped.
The board “may infer, and does infer, that Christopher Stanley was improperly influenced by his conversation” with Simmons to ensure that the Equity in Education Coalition continued to receive funding.
In the hearing, Simmons denied influencing Stanley’s decision to direct the parties to amend their agreement but the board concluded she was “not credible.”
Lastly, the board ruled Simmons violated the ethics law by asking Anthony Powers, a friend and the leader of the American Equity and Justice Group, to rein in Kim Gordon, an employee and board member with the nonprofit who filed the complaint against the lawmaker.
Two weeks after Gordon filed her complaint, Simmons engaged Powers in a lengthy late-night text exchange in which she expressed frustration and threatened to withhold support for Powers’ organization.
Simmons “attempted to influence the outcome of the Board’s investigation through her attempted retaliation against the complainant in this matter,” the decision reads.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Landry says he won’t talk to New Orleans mayor until after Murrill indictment investigation
description: Gov. Jeff Landry said he won’t personally talk to New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno until after an investigation determines who was behind the July indictment of Attorney General Liz Murrill.
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry said he won’t personally talk to New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno until after an investigation determines who was behind the July indictment of Attorney General Liz Murrill. Gov. Jeff Landry said he won’t personally talk to New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno until after an investigation determines who was behind the July indictment of Attorney General Liz Murrill.  

“She’s always free to have a discussion with my staff,” Landry said about Moreno in a live interview WRKF-FM aired Friday. 

“I’m not going to be speaking to them personally until this investigation is done,” the governor said, “until I know who did what, what happened and why it happened and the way that it transpired,”

Moreno, a Democrat, took over as the elected leader of Louisiana’s most consequential city in January. But New Orleans’ relationship with Republican state leaders has deteriorated over the past few months. 

The situation hit rock bottom July 2 when a New Orleans grand jury indicted Murrill over allegations she had threatened and attempted to intimidate New Orleans elected officials. 

Charges against the attorney general have since been dropped, but Landry launched a Louisiana State Police investigation into the origins of the indictment. The governor and attorney general both have alleged the criminal proceedings were politically motivated by the city’s elected Democrats. 

“No one believes that this grand jury just, you know, on its own took up this matter,” Landry told  Talk Louisiana host Jim Engster. “I’m interested to get to the bottom of it.”
Moreno has said she was not involved in orchestrating the indictment. 
In May, Murrill sent letters to several New Orleans officials, including Moreno, warning them that Landry, as governor, could remove them from office if they continued to pursue a special election for the newly combined New Orleans clerk of court job. 
A couple of weeks before the letters, the Republican-led legislature and Landry approved a law to merge the civil and criminal clerks of court offices in New Orleans. Every other court district in the state, along with their corresponding clerks’ offices, handles both types of cases. New Orleans has had separate offices for nearly 150 years.

The new statute blocked Calvin Duncan, a formerly incarcerated person who has been exonerated, from taking over as criminal court clerk after he won the November election for the job.
Murrill and Landry opposed Duncan’s candidacy during his campaign. They also pushed state lawmakers to vote to abolish the office after Duncan won his election but before he took office in early May.
The letters Murrill sent to New Orleans officials warning them not to hold a special election for the combined clerk’s role was the basis for the attorney general’s indictment.

On the radio Friday, Landry repeatedly implied that New Orleans officials were behind the indictment, though he offered no specifics about those allegations. 

“We’re not going to allow people to weaponize our criminal justice system. I mean, that creates a banana republic state,” he said. 

Landry also didn’t rule out holding a special legislative session to change laws surrounding the New Orleans court system, which remains bifurcated even with just one clerk. 
“The governor always gets an opportunity to keep a special session card in his desk drawer,” Landry said. “I’ve heard from a number of legislators who have been eager to maybe go back to determine ways that we can further correct some discrepancies in Orleans Parish.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: After Alaska’s ‘final four’ primary, a silent primary may decide who’s on the ballot in November
description: Alaska’s two leading Democratic candidates for governor have quietly been discussing whether one of them should quit the race if both are among the top four vote-getters in Tuesday’s primary election.  Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich each said by phone on Thursday that they’ve been discussing different scenarios about what could happen when the final[...]
text:
From left to right, Click Bishop, Dave Bronson and Adam Crum, three of the 10 candidates at the Capital City Republican governor candidate forum, are seen on Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026, at the Baranof Hotel in Juneau. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)Alaska’s two leading Democratic candidates for governor have quietly been discussing whether one of them should quit the race if both are among the top four vote-getters in Tuesday’s primary election. 
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich each said by phone on Thursday that they’ve been discussing different scenarios about what could happen when the final votes are counted.
Republicans have been talking about similar maneuvers for months, with one prominent Republican group going so far as to run ads urging lower-finishing candidates to withdraw in order to consolidate the vote in November.
“Both sides are trying to figure out: What does the top four look like? And how are we best positioned for success?” said Bernadette Wilson, one of the leading Republican candidates for governor in Alaska’s 17-person race.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Under Alaska’s election system, the top four vote-getters — regardless of political party — advance to the November general election. That may mean multiple Republicans or Democrats on the same ballot, competing for the same votes.
In November, voters in the general election will be asked to rank those four candidates in order of preference. 
After all the votes are in, the candidate with the fewest number of first-choice preferences is eliminated. Any voters who ranked that candidate first will have their votes go to their second choice.
The process repeats until only two candidates are left. 
In theory, that means no vote splitting. Anyone whose favorite candidate is eliminated can instead vote for someone else.
In practice, some Alaska voters ranked only one or two candidates in the 2022 and 2024 statewide elections, leading to an unusual number of “exhausted” ballots whose votes went to neither of the final two candidates. 
Two years ago, that led to large amounts of post-primary maneuvering as lower-finishing candidates withdrew from races in order to force unfavorable matchups for one top finisher or another.
In the U.S. House race, two top Republican finishers withdrew after the primary, which put imprisoned Democratic U.S. House candidate Eric Hafner into the final four.
That November, Hafner was eliminated first, and fewer than half his votes transferred to the other Democrat, then-incumbent Rep. Mary Peltola. 
That was less than Peltola’s margin of defeat — Peltola was defeated by current Rep. Nick Begich III, R-Alaska — but in a closer race, it could have been decisive.
Now, as Peltola runs for U.S. Senate against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, a similar strategy is playing out. 
National groups have spent more than $2 million in an attempt to boost lesser-known candidates into the final four and potentially split the field. 
Dan J. Sullivan, unrelated to the incumbent senator, is on the ballot but told the Chicago Tribune that he’s uncertain whether he will remain in the race if he makes the top four. 
In the 17-person race to replace Gov. Mike Dunleavy — who is term-limited and unable to run this year — candidates have been talking for over a year about whether or not they will be willing to bow out after the primary.
Wilson entered the race in May 2025 and promptly pledged to withdraw after the primary if she finished behind another Republican. It’s a pledge she’s renewed since then.
“I don’t think that it’s smart to carry on. … I don’t think that we need any more division as we head into November. I don’t think that it’s smart to split up the voting base, the volunteers that help, I don’t think it’s smart to split up the finances,” she said.
Wilson also said that having multiple candidates from the same party risks denying the eventual winner a mandate — a margin of victory so large that it gives the winner political backing to implement their platform.
“I think it’s important that a governor win by a strong strongest margin as possible, because I think that it’s important for the stability and the unity of the state past November,” she said.
Wilson has also been campaigning hard to repeal Alaska’s current elections system with Ballot Measure 2, which will come in front of voters in November.
Post-primary juggling is evidence that ranked choice voting doesn’t work, she said.
Supporters of the state’s elections system and some detractors have said that it dilutes the influence of the Republican and Democratic parties. Wilson doesn’t see it that way. 
“I think it’s just made it worse,” Wilson said. “I think it’s handed more power to backroom conversations, and I just don’t think the public’s gonna like it.”
Jenny-Marie Stryker, executive director of the Alaska Democratic Party, was traveling on Friday and unavailable for an interview, a spokesman said. Carmela Warfield, chair of the Alaska Republican Party, did not respond to an email.
The Valley Republican Women, an influential group based in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, has an ongoing ad campaign that urges Republicans to “vote the primary, consolidate the vote” and “don’t split the field.” 
Julia Anastos, campaign manager for the group opposing Ballot Measure 2, said by email that gamesmanship isn’t new in Alaska.
“Parties and political insiders will always strategize about who should run and who should drop out. These kinds of maneuvers happen under a partisan primary as well, like in the 2014 and 2018 gubernatorial races, when would-be spoiler candidates dropped out to clear the lane for a stronger candidate,” she said. “Under our system now, ranked choice voting addresses that spoiler effect and ensures the winning candidate has earned majority support.”
The issue of what to do after the primary was a key issue at a forum earlier this month in Soldotna, when five candidates were directly asked about the issue.
“I would stay in,” nonpartisan candidate Meda DeWitt told forum attendees. 
As a nonpartisan, she sees herself able to attract second-choice votes from both Republicans and Democrats.
“I actually appreciate ranked choice voting because your vote is not lost if your top pick doesn’t get in,” she said.
Adam Crum, a Republican candidate and former Dunleavy cabinet official, said he thinks there’s an advantage to having multiple Republicans in the general election.
“It actually does make more sense for more conservatives to stay in it, because you actually work together,” he said. 
In the 2022 special election to replace Rep. Don Young, R-Alaska, Republican candidates Sarah Palin and Nick Begich III frequently fought each other on the campaign trail. That turned off Republican voters, Crum noted. 
During the current primary election campaign, he said, “We have actually done a very good job … of actually working together and pushing forward ideas.”
A cordial campaign keeps voters involved and going to the polls, he said.
“You actually increase the ceiling, and the math actually works out. I’m a numbers guy. Over time, it does work,” Crum said.
Matt Heilala, a podiatrist and Republican who has put more than $1.5 million of his own money into a campaign for governor, said that last year, “I had the thought that I would immediately withdraw because we saw what happened with Sarah and Nick.”
Now, he’s not as sure. What if there’s “an indictment, an October surprise, some kind of a shenanigan that the opposing party is going to play on the person that is 10 votes ahead of me, and they’re just waiting for me to leave?” he asked. 
In that case, having another Republican would be helpful, he suggested.
Dave Bronson, the former Anchorage mayor and Republican candidate for governor, said he intends to reserve his options until he sees what happens in the primary.
“The notion that I would stand up and say at this point in time I’ll absolutely get out if I’m No. 2 on the Republican side — that’s foolishness,” he said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sarah Trone Garriott says 3rd District opponent not truly ‘tough on China’
description: Democratic congressional candidate Sarah Trone Garriott said her opponent, U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, was not truly “tough on China” as she spoke to a crowd at the Iowa State Fair Friday. Trone Garriott opened her speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox introducing her background as a pastor and as “one of the rare […]
text:
Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, the Democrat running for Iowa's 3rd Congressional District, spoke to the crowd at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic congressional candidate Sarah Trone Garriott said her opponent, U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, was not truly “tough on China” as she spoke to a crowd at the Iowa State Fair Friday.
Trone Garriott opened her speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox introducing her background as a pastor and as “one of the rare Iowa Democrats that represents a Republican district in the state Senate.” She won her seat in 2022 by defeating then-Senate President Jake Chapman. She is again challenging a Republican incumbent in 2026 as she aims to unseat Nunn in the 3rd Congressional District.
She said since Nunn took office in 2023, he has voted for measures that are “hurting” Iowans and raising costs, pointing to his support for the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill Act” making cuts to Medicaid funding and his votes allowing the continuation of President Donald Trump’s tariff policies.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trone Garriott said to explain Nunn’s votes, “all you need to do is look at his campaign fundraising reports, and you’ll see the answer. His reelection campaign is entirely supported by corporate PACs, by big pharma, by pesticide companies.”
She said Nunn’s campaign has also received support from Chinese companies, and said his voting record in the U.S. House has shown this.
“Zach Nunn talks a tough game about China,” Trone Garriott said. “He is actually on the committee that’s supposed to hold China accountable, but he has not been able to show up to half of the committee meetings, to be part of that process. He couldn’t be bothered to show up. Why? Because he’s taken thousands from Chinese companies, and then he’s voted to sell out Iowa farmers and Iowa businesses. He voted for a tax cut for those Chinese corporations, and he voted to allow them to buy Iowa farmlands.”
Trone Garriott was referring to Nunn’s work on the U.S. House Select Committee on Communist China, a committee he was appointed to serve on in 2025. Her comments also follow Nunn speaking critically about China at a America First Policy Institute forum Wednesday, where the congressman said, “Republicans and Democrats in the past have always talked a big game about China. Very few have actually had the wherewithal to hold China accountable,” Radio Iowa reported.
A Nunn campaign spokesperson said Trone Garriott’s comments are contradicted by Nunn’s work in Congress.
“Sarah Trone Garriott’s lies can’t erase Zach Nunn’s record: 27 bills signed into law under Presidents Trump and Biden,” a Nunn campaign spokesperson said in a statement. “As an Air Force Colonel, counterintelligence officer, and Congressman, Zach has spent his career confronting the CCP — delivering bipartisan protections for Iowa farmland, food security, and national defense. She attacks Zach’s results because she has no record, or plan, of her own.”
Nunn has regularly criticized China in his role as a congressman, introducing and supporting several measures to combat certain Chinese trade practices, and target Chinese fentanyl producers. He also introduced legislation that would require the State Department to “analyze and mitigate legal and financial risks before accepting investment or lending from China or other foreign adversaries,” as well as a bill requiring the Secretary of State and other federal entities submit a report assessing the impact of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) on global infrastructure.
He has also been supportive of Taiwan maintaining self-governance from China, leading a trade delegation to Taiwan in April as chair of the Republican Study Committee’s National Security Task Force. Nunn said his support for Taiwan reflected the trade agenda advanced by the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress, saying, “I believe strongly in a free trade relationship, particularly for the countries that align with the United States — even as we look to decouple from countries who continue to cheat in tariffs, manipulate on tariffs.”
Trone Garriott told reporters Nunn’s actions in Congress did not reflect a true “tough on China” approach.
“Being tough on China would look like showing up and doing your duty, taking that responsibility very seriously, you know, being on the committee and actually being in all the meetings — not taking money from Chinese corporations, and making sure that Iowa farmland stays in the hands of the people of the United States,” Trone Garriott said.
While Trone Garriott criticized Nunn on his China position — as well as for not holding public town halls — Republicans have rallied against Trone Garriott as a “radical” candidate. U.S. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise linked Trone Garriott to democratic socialism at a Wednesday event in Iowa supporting Nunn, although Trone Garriott has not identified as a “socialist” and is not affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America organization. Nunn has also challenged her position on legislation related to transgender women being allowed to use women’s locker rooms or participate in women’s sports.
Trone Garriott said these claims are false, and that some of her votes in the state Senate have been “twisted out of shape by folks who will try to attack you” in campaign ads and statements.
“What they’re saying is just not true, and they don’t have anything good to talk about, so they’re going to attack me,” she said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Republican candidate for governor appears to massively violate a donation limit
description: Former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor, a Republican candidate for governor, violated state campaign finance laws by donating more than 60 times the maximum amount of money to his own campaign, according to disclosure documents filed this week. Those documents show his lieutenant governor candidate, Candice English, also violating the same limit.  Under[...]
text:
Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor speaks at a news conference on Thursday, Dec. 15, 2022, at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor, a Republican candidate for governor, violated state campaign finance laws by donating more than 60 times the maximum amount of money to his own campaign, according to disclosure documents filed this week.
Those documents show his lieutenant governor candidate, Candice English, also violating the same limit. 
Under state law, primary election candidates cannot give or loan their campaigns more than $5,000 after July 17. 
In a campaign finance disclosure report due Tuesday, Taylor says he donated $260,000 to his campaign on Aug. 3. He also reported buying plane tickets worth more than $3,400 with his own money. 
English and her husband, Stanley, reported donating $100,000 to the campaign on July 28, according to the same report.
Evan Lee, Taylor’s campaign manager, did not return emails on Thursday or Friday asking if the report was accurate and whether Taylor intended to return the contribution. Lee also did not return a text message or a call to his cellphone on Friday.
A separate disclosure report showed Taylor donated another $40,000 to his own campaign on Monday, for a total of $300,000 in cash contributions past the deadline in state law. 
Heather Hebdon is the executive director of the Alaska Public Offices Commission, which regulates campaign financial disclosures. She said on Friday that she was unaware of any complaints against the Taylor-English campaign and had not reviewed their filing herself.
In an article published Thursday by the Anchorage Daily News, Lee said Taylor views the donation limit as unconstitutional.
Neither state nor federal court records show any lawsuit by Taylor challenging the law in question. 
In 2021, a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals overturned Alaska’s limits on donations by non-candidates to candidates, but that decision did not touch the limit on donations by candidates to their own campaigns.
This week’s report by Taylor shows he has raised more than $1.58 million during his campaign to become one of the four finalists in the race to replace incumbent Gov. Mike Dunleavy. 
Dunleavy is term-limited and cannot run again this year.
Among the 17 candidates vying to replace Dunleavy, Taylor’s campaign is one of the best-funded. Among Republicans, only Matt Heilala has raised more — $1.59 million, according to this week’s filings. Most of Heilala’s campaign has been self-funded.
Among Democrats, former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has raised almost $2.3 million and former state Sen. Tom Begich has raised more than $1.2 million. 
Under Alaska’s current elections system, the top four vote-getters for a particular office — regardless of political party — advance from the primary to the general election.
Alaska’s primary election is Aug. 18, and final results are expected Aug. 28. The deadline for any of the top finishers to withdraw is Aug. 31.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lahn criticizes ‘personal attacks’ on residency, family in Iowa governor race
description: Zach Lahn told Iowa State fairgoers that “truth is on the ballot” in the 2026 gubernatorial election as he runs against Iowa Auditor Rob Sand. Lahn, a farmer, businessman and the GOP nominee for Iowa governor, delivered remarks Friday at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. He said there’s been a “big difference” between the […]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn spoke in the rain to a crowd gathered at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Zach Lahn told Iowa State fairgoers that “truth is on the ballot” in the 2026 gubernatorial election as he runs against Iowa Auditor Rob Sand.
Lahn, a farmer, businessman and the GOP nominee for Iowa governor, delivered remarks Friday at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. He said there’s been a “big difference” between the primary election where he won in an upset victory against U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, the 4th District representative endorsed by President Donald Trump, and the general election where he faces Sand.
“In the primary, people cared about my ideas,” he told the crowd. “That’s what the campaign was about, it was about how do we make life better for the people of Iowa for the next generation. As soon as I entered the general election, the ‘unity candidate’ on the other side decided to make this campaign about personal attacks on me and my family.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lahn has faced significant scrutiny over his state residency since becoming the official Republican nominee. The Kansas Reflector reported he registered to vote in 2024 and met the state’s two-year residency requirement to run for governor in 2026, but  previously lived in and was a registered voter in Kansas, where he launched a private pre-K through 12th-grade school named Wonder. In April, the Des Moines Register reported he frequently flew his personal airplane between Iowa and Kansas because he has a blended family with some children based out of Wichita, Kansas.
Opponents to GOP gubernatorial nomineee Zach Lahn held up signs calling the candidate a “part-time Iowan” as he spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
As he spoke at the fair, opponents to his campaign held up signs stating “Zach Lahn, part-time Iowan,” paid for by the Iowa Democratic Party. Lahn commented on the signs, saying it was “ironic” Democrats and Sand were criticizing him about his residency.
“Here’s the most ironic part about these signs: what Rob Sand actually says is that a sixth-generation Iowan is less Iowan than an illegal immigrant,” Lahn said. “He said they’re just as Iowan as you are. It’s wrong. It’s distasteful. And every time you talk about this — you’re actually bringing my family into it — and I will reject it and debate it every time. And you will lose because we have truth on our side.”
Lahn said the “truth” his campaign is focused on are the same issues that won him the GOP gubernatorial primary — “talking about the big agricultural conglomerates that are extorting our farmers, talking about clean water and how we need to lower our cancer rates,” he said.
He criticized Sand as a candidate “who’s been coronated because of how much money they have, and the donors they have, and the over-$10 million being given by their family,” referencing campaign contributions from his wife and wife’s family.

Maddie Moher, press secretary for Rob Sand for Iowa, said in a statement that Sand “has spent his career working with Republicans, Democrats, and independents to hold government accountable, uncover misspent taxpayer dollars, and deliver results for Iowans,” and will “do the same as Governor.”

“Zach Lahn is a career political operative, and his latest attacks are a distraction from his own record and frequent flights to Kansas,” Moher said. “While Rob Sand is offering Iowans a new path, Lahn only offers Iowans more of the same one-party rule that has left our economy struggling, public schools under attack, and with a skyrocketing cancer rate. Iowans know Rob will bring people together across party lines to solve the problems that actually matter — not play the same political games that have failed our state.”
Lahn, alongside Iowa GOP Chair Jeff Kaufmann, held a news conference earlier Friday where they criticized Sand for portraying himself as a moderate candidate. While Sand has positioned himself as a moderate and criticized the two-party system, Kaufmann said his position as a Democrat is proven by his support from others in the Democratic Party like Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker, California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
“This whole idea of, ‘well, the two political parties, they kind of get in our way,’ and you’re just walking away from the Democratic Party — I would too if I had that crew that that he has from coast to coast, but you, again, can’t have it both ways,” Kaufmann said.
Though Republicans have held the governor’s seat for more than a decade, political forecasters rate the race as a “toss-up,” and some recent polls have shown Sand leading in the race.
Lahn said though some polls show him behind, he believes “the trend is that we’re closing the gap, and I think we’re only going to continue doing that.”

title: Data centers, vapes, childcare aid emerge for North Dakota special session consideration
authors: Michael Achterling, Jack Dura, Jeff Beach
description: North Dakota lawmakers have four proposals for restricting kratom and more than a dozen on other topics for a special session beginning next month, according to draft legislation made public on Friday. A top legislative panel meets Monday to decide which bill drafts from 20 proposals to advance to the special session, which begins Sept. […]
text:
Senate lawmakers meet May 1, 2025. A panel of legislative leaders meets Monday to decide which topics will be considered during a special session in September. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers have four proposals for restricting kratom and more than a dozen on other topics for a special session beginning next month, according to draft legislation made public on Friday.
A top legislative panel meets Monday to decide which bill drafts from 20 proposals to advance to the special session, which begins Sept. 2. The proposals include kratom restrictions, a funding fix for the stalled Military Gallery project, data center restrictions and other topics.
Line of credit, more oversight proposed for stalled North Dakota Military Gallery project

The panel will weigh whether topics must be addressed immediately or can wait until next year, said Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot, who chairs Legislative Management. 
“If the matter can wait and benefit from a more thorough review by the regular legislative process, it should wait,” he said.
Lawmakers have a goal to wrap up the special session in three days.
Here’s a look at some of the proposals:
Kratom
State officials have expressed concerns about the substance kratom and two related components called mitragynine and 7-OH. Gov. Kelly Armstrong has linked overdoses and deaths to kratom-related products, and called the special session for passing restrictions, regulations and criminal penalties. He also banned kratom products statewide for 30 days.
A five-member, all-Republican working group of lawmakers was tasked with advancing kratom legislation.
Kratom comes from a tropical tree in Southeast Asia. People use kratom to relieve pain, boost energy and cope with withdrawals from certain drugs.
Proposals from the working group’s leaders include one to classify mitragynine synthetic products as a controlled substance on the same level as heroin and LSD, and to set criminal penalties, including higher penalties based on repeated offenses of possession, all the way up to a class C felony punishable up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
Another would set would set an age restriction of 21 for kratom with related penalties, 
including an infraction – penalized up to a $1,000 fine – for selling kratom to someone underage, and differing low-level penalties for underage people who buy, possess or use kratom.
The bill draft also would add kratom licensing requirements, labeling standards, attorney general enforcement authority and a $20,000 public health campaign. 
Two lawmakers who are not part of the working group also submitted kratom proposals.
Data centers
North Dakota lawmaker eyes data center transparency, temporary moratorium for special session

Legislators from both parties authored bill drafts related to data centers. 
One filed by Sen. Desiree van Oosting, R-Judson, would mandate that data centers file a quarterly report with three different state agencies and a committee of legislative leaders. The data centers would be required to report electricity use, water use and other information. 
The bill also calls for the data center operator to pay for any costs related to shutting down the facility. 
Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, filed two bills drafts to address data centers. One would put a temporary ban on new data center permits while the other would prevent public officials and agencies from agreeing not to share information about data center development plans. 
Mathern also introduced a resolution encouraging legislative leaders to consider bills to ensure transparency regarding data centers. 
Clemency resolution
North Dakota lawmaker wants clemency for men who killed 2 federal agents

Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, plans to propose a draft resolution that would urge President Donald Trump to grant clemency to Scott Faul and Yorie Kahl, two men convicted of the 1983 killings of two federal marshals and sentenced to life sentences in federal prison.
While he is “very sympathetic” to the families of the victims, Magrum said he believes justice has not been served in this case.
North Dakota Attorney General Drew Wrigley, who twice served as U.S. attorney for North Dakota, called Friday for Magrum to withdraw his resolution, which he said “ignores the brutality of their vicious crimes.”
“Someone has seriously misguided Senator Magrum on this matter, and it is not too late for him to withdraw his resolution,” Wrigley said via text message. 
Childcare assistance
Senate Minority Leader Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, is sponsoring a bill draft to add $9 million to the Child Care Assistance Program, which lawmakers learned last December has a severe budget shortfall. Hogan’s proposal aims to get some of the lowest income families off of a waitlist. 
Budget shortfall will reduce North Dakota child care assistance for some families

The program is serving fewer families compared to a year ago and had 1,892 families on a waitlist as of Aug. 9, according to Rebecca Askins, interim director of the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services’ Economic Assistance Section.
Prediction markets
Rep. Colette Brown, D-Warwick, sponsored a bill draft to study prediction markets, which have become controversial because of their similarity to sports betting and looser regulations outside of federal and state gaming laws.
“This will prepare us for the 2027 legislative session,” Brown said.
Regulating vape products
A bill draft from Rep. Eric Murphy, R-Grand Forks, would ban the sale of vape products that are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. The FDA has approved 45 vape products, including only menthol and tobacco-flavored products.
The bill includes fines for retailers ranging from $25,000 to $100,000 and the potential loss of their tobacco license for repeat violations. 
“That will get people’s attention,” said Murphy, whose term ends before the next regular legislative session. “I view law as a deterrence.”
English language driver’s test
Rep. SuAnn Olson, R-Baldwin, sponsored a bill draft that would require the driver’s license test in North Dakota to be offered only in English. 
Olson said the draft is aligned with an executive order signed by President Donald Trump and guidance released by the U.S. Department of Transportation in 2025 that requires truck drivers to adhere to English proficiency requirements. 
“If we are concerned about the safety of our citizens, it would seem that the same rules apply across the board because, Lord knows, there’s millions of more miles being traveled by the public in cars and pickups,” Olson said. “Driving is a privilege. It’s not necessarily a right.”
Right to repair
Sen. Chuck Walen, R-New Town, is proposing a bill draft requiring equipment manufacturers to make replacement parts and diagnostic and repair documentation available to the equipment owners and independent repair operators at the same cost as an authorized repair provider.
The manufacturer may not void the equipment warranty due to repairs made by the owner or independent repair operator, according to the bill draft. Manufacturers who violate the law would be guilty of a civil penalty and fine of up to $500 for each violation.
Monday’s meeting is set for 10 a.m. in the Roughrider Room of the Capitol and will be livestreamed. Typically public testimony would not be accepted until the special session.

title: Most rejected Lindstrom signatures came in Lancaster County, where only 25% were approved
description: LINCOLN — The vast majority of the 2,407 petition signatures rejected for former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom’s nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor came in Lancaster County, where just 24.6% of signatures were valid. Lindstrom submitted 2,210 signatures total for review in Lancaster County. Just 543 were valid. This is not the first petition campaign to face[...]
text:
The backroom of the Lancaster County Election Commission on April 24, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The vast majority of the 2,407 petition signatures rejected for former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom’s nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor came in Lancaster County, where just 24.6% of signatures were valid.
Lindstrom submitted 2,210 signatures total for review in Lancaster County. Just 543 were valid.
This is not the first petition campaign to face allegations of fraudulent signatures this year or in Lancaster County. The county is home to Nebraska’s capital city of Lincoln and the heart of state government. It’s there that five petition circulators for three related Lincoln-only ballot measures now face two felony charges each for allegedly gathering fraudulent signatures this summer.
Lindstrom fails to qualify nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor; many signatures flagged for fraud

Three of those circulators also helped Lindstrom’s campaign, the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Friday. Lindstrom blamed those individuals for keeping him from the ballot and said he was unaware of the suspected fraudulent activity.
“We are pursuing every legal avenue available to us and intend to hold those responsible accountable,” Lindstrom said Friday in a statement.
County officials check names, addresses and dates of birth on file before turning to signatures. Fraudulent signatures include those where a suspected signer is not believed to be the voter on file.
Allegations of wrongdoing on Lindstrom’s petitions have been forwarded to Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office. He served with Lindstrom for six years in the Legislature.
Lindstrom turned in 5,765 signatures for review. He needed at least 4,000 valid signatures to qualify for the ballot as the fourth candidate for Nebraska governor this year. His total also needed to include at least 750 signatures per congressional district. 
According to a county-by-county breakdown from the Secretary of State’s Office, Lindstrom collected signatures from 63 of Nebraska’s 93 counties statewide. In 56 of those counties, Lindstrom had at least one valid signature.
The seven counties where Lindstrom collected one or two signatures but they were all rejected were: Box Butte County (two signatures) and Arthur, Cedar, Dixon, Garden, Garfield and Kimball counties (one signature each).


About 58.2% of Lindstrom’s signatures statewide were valid. He needed a validity rate higher than 70%.
After Lancaster County, the next most rejections came in Douglas and Sarpy counties, the first and third most populous counties. However, Lindstrom had a much higher signature validity rate, more than 82%, in both of those counties.
The most valid signatures per capita came in Burt County (1.34% of 4,847 registered voters as of Aug. 1). 
Of all valid signatures, about 39% of them came from Lindstrom’s home county, Douglas, and 16.7% came from neighboring Sarpy. Lancaster County accounted for an additional 16%. About 7% of valid signatures came from Hall County, and 5% came from Adams County, both in central Nebraska.
Lindstrom’s signature gathering largely excluded the Panhandle and Sandhills, with the exception of Scotts Bluff County, where he had four valid signatures.
The general election is Nov. 3.
