name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas panel revises proposal restricting access to ‘sexually explicit’ library materials
description: The Arkansas State Library Board on Friday revised its proposed rule limiting access to “sexually explicit” materials over concerns its original proposal could unfairly punish libraries that accidentally place restricted books on shelves. Arkansans will have until Sept. 13 to give the state Department of Education feedback on the new version of the proposal,[...]
text:
Executive directors Clare Graham of the Mid-Ark Regional Library System and Allie Gosselink of the Calhoun County Library give feedback on proposed library funding rules to the Arkansas State Library Board on Aug. 14, 2026. Education Department attorney Daniel Shults (right) worked with the board on drafting and revising the rules. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas State Library Board on Friday revised its proposed rule limiting access to “sexually explicit” materials over concerns its original proposal could unfairly punish libraries that accidentally place restricted books on shelves.
Arkansans will have until Sept. 13 to give the state Department of Education feedback on the new version of the proposal, which would hinge libraries’ funding on preventing patrons age 16 or younger from checking out materials that depict or describe sexual contact and behavior. 
Dozens of Arkansans told the department earlier this year that they opposed the effort to limit access to books. The restrictions come as librarians have raised questions about how to enforce a 2023 law that would impose criminal penalties for providing “harmful” materials to minors. 
Dozens object to rule requiring Arkansas libraries to restrict ‘sexually explicit’ materials

The previous version of the rules required libraries to “ensure the appropriate placement of sexually explicit materials.” The version updated by the Arkansas State Library Board at its Friday meeting replaces “ensure” with “take all reasonable steps,” a suggestion from Education Department attorney Daniel Shults.
Board Chairman Clay Goff said the term “ensure” was too harsh in case a book is improperly shelved by mistake. He referenced the portion of Act 372 of 2023 that gives local governments the final say on the placement of a library book a community member seeks to relocate.
The provision was among those blocked in federal court until July 30, and the law does not require local officials to read a challenged book before deciding where to place it. Goff said it’s “crazy” not to require this.
“I can’t hold y’all to a higher standard than that,” he said, addressing the library directors present at Friday’s meeting.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals removed the injunction on the two blocked portions of Act 372, but the formal order allowing the decision to take effect hasn’t been issued yet. The law would allow anyone who “furnishes, presents, provides, [or] makes available” an item that is “harmful to minors” to be charged with a Class A misdemeanor, punishable by a maximum prison sentence of one year.
Library directors have said they have several unanswered questions about Act 372, including whether a book is “made available” simply by being on a library shelf.

Arkansas librarians grapple with enforcing book restriction law after court ruling

 

Adam Webb, a library director from Garland County, told the State Library Board that the law’s classification of images of human genitalia as sexually explicit would require him to remove an encyclopedia with an image of Michelangelo’s David statue from his library’s children’s section. 
Goff suggested adding clarifying language to the rules to make sure they don’t impede children’s access to encyclopedias.
The rules include an exception for children 11 and older to access “age-appropriate information designed to prepare minors for the sociology of puberty” with parental consent.
One of the seven branches of the Arkansas River Valley Regional Library System has a partnership with the state Department of Health to display an educational module on breastfeeding, regional director Misty Hawkins said. 
She asked the board if this display would be considered sexually explicit and said the “mental bandwidth” it takes to keep up with proposed regulations affecting library funding is exhausting.
The proposed rules would also drastically increase the amount of required documents for libraries to submit to the state in order to receive funds, said Jenn Wann, the State Library’s consulting and development services director.
“I want to keep the administrative burden for those librarians as low as possible so they’re not [just] administrators, but so that they are librarians in their communities,” Wann said.
Library directors agreed that some of the paperwork requirements would be too burdensome.
“I don’t think that the problem is sending it as much as it is gathering it [and] keeping up with it,” said Calhoun County Library director Allie Gosselink, who also said state aid makes up less than 20% of her budget.

“So I have to really consider: is that 20% worth it if it’s taking 20% of my time?” she said.
The board agreed to require libraries to submit documents to the state by April 30, a change from the initial proposal of Jan. 31.
After the public comment period closes, the board will vote on whether to approve the rules and send them to the Arkansas Legislative Council, the Legislature’s governing body when it’s not in session. The council must approve the rules for them to go into effect.
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders appointed all six board members last year in compliance with a law to remove and replace the previous lineup.
The board’s primary responsibility is to disburse state funds quarterly to public libraries, which the board did Friday with no debate or dissent.
Board member Sydney McKenzie, wife of Rogers GOP Rep. Brit McKenzie, said she hopes the panel discusses the enforcement of Act 372 at its next meeting on Nov. 13.

title: Nebraska’s July tax receipts come close to economic forecasts as impact of tax refunds wanes
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s tax receipts for July fell less than 1% below economic forecasts, according to the state Department of Revenue, as data shows a steadily lessening impact of higher-than-expected tax refunds. The Department of Revenue’s report on July’s tax receipts showed a net loss of 0.1% compared to what Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board[...]
text:
The Nebraska State Capitol. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s tax receipts for July fell less than 1% below economic forecasts, according to the state Department of Revenue, as data shows a steadily lessening impact of higher-than-expected tax refunds.
The Department of Revenue’s report on July’s tax receipts showed a net loss of 0.1% compared to what Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board had predicted in late February. That difference equates to about $402,000 less revenue headed to the state’s coffers.
Nebraska’s tax receipts have consistently fallen below forecasts for most of 2026 so far. The last time revenue came in above forecasts was January.
While July’s tax report was the closest the state has come to seeing tax revenues rise above forecasts since then, the $402,000 difference will still add to the state’s projected budget deficit, currently set at $208 million.
July’s report also lists that state tax refunds for the month were 7.3% (or $7.7 million) above economic forecasts. Tax refunds have consistently come in above forecasts since March, with April being the peak at 98.3% ($162 million) above forecasts.
Since April, the impact of issued tax refunds has steadily waned. May’s tax refunds were 32.5% ($45.5 million) above forecasts, and June’s was 12.5% ($15 million) above forecasts.
Gov. Jim Pillen in April pointed to the higher-than-expected tax refunds as the reason why individual income tax revenues were low during those months. Pillen argued that this was a good thing.
“Nebraskans are keeping more of their pay instead of giving it to government,” Pillen said in an April press release. “That’s the objective we want to achieve for hard-working Nebraskans. At the same time, we need to relentlessly cut spending to ensure that the state is living within its means.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Neil Sullivan, the state budget director, said the forecasting board’s projections for tax refunds were far lower than what was actually allocated. He said the board projected about $802 million in refunds for all of fiscal year 2026, but the year instead brought about $1.1 billion in refunds.
For FY 2027, which began in July, Sullivan said, the board projected refunds at $842 million. He said he is more confident this forecast will be more accurate.
Lawmakers spent the 2026 session working to fill a fluctuating shortfall that peaked at roughly $646 million. If receipts continue on this trend, the 2027 session could be the third in a row that lawmakers have had to grapple with a projected deficit.
During the 90-day session that begins in January, state senators will form the budget for the next biennium, July 1, 2027, to June 30, 2029. They may have to fill two separate deficits. An $846 million deficit is projected for the 2027-2029 budget.
As the impact of tax refunds wanes, it’s possible that future revenue reports will balance out or possibly rise above forecasts. Sullivan, however, said he doesn’t expect to see a “surge” in receipts and instead is hoping they remain flat to forecasts in the coming months.
“The message of this month’s receipts is that it’s on track, and that’s a great start for fiscal year (2027),” Sullivan said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: New rule allows dogs on Alaska’s Pribilof Islands for anti-rat duties
description: For decades, dogs have been verboten on the Pribilof Islands under a rule imposed by the federal government to protect the world’s largest concentration of northern fur seals. Now, dogs are welcome — with important caveats. Under a new interim rule enacted by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, dogs may be brought to the […]
text:
The community of St. Paul is seen from the island's beach. The Pribilof Island community has managed to fend off rat infestations. Residents are now allowed to enlist rat-hunting dogs to help with the efforts. Dogs have long been banned from the islands, but a new rule makes an exception for rat-prevention purposes. (Photo by Jamie Musbach/National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration)For decades, dogs have been verboten on the Pribilof Islands under a rule imposed by the federal government to protect the world’s largest concentration of northern fur seals.
Now, dogs are welcome — with important caveats.
Under a new interim rule enacted by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, dogs may be brought to the islands, but only for the specific purpose of hunting for rats. Dogs allowed on St. Paul Island or any other part of the five-island archipelago must be trained and certified as rat-detectors and catchers, and their stays are limited to 180 days. The general ban on dogs, in place since the 1980s, remains intact, but the new rule creates an exception for dogs enlisted in the anti-rat work.
The Pribilofs have managed to stay rat-free even as other Alaska islands and coastal areas have become infested with the non-native rodents.
 

Murres congregate on a cliff on St. Paul Island in the Pribilofs in 2008. The isolated volcanic islands are used by millions of seabirds, including common and thick-billed murres. Invasive rats on other Alaska islands have ravaged bird populations there. (Photo by Dean Kildaw/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	Rat-sniffing dogs would help keep things that way, according to the residents of St. Paul Island, site of the main community in the archipelago.
“We work very, very hard to keep this a rat-free island. And we also recognize that shipping lanes are opening up right in the Arctic and there’s just potentially, if not already, going to be more vessel traffic in this part of the world,” said Chelsea Campbell, marine mammal programs manager for the Aleut Community of St. Paul Island, the local tribal government.
Allowing dogs to help is a bit of “forward thinking,” she said. The idea is that “maybe we should have some ability to get a rat sniffing dog out here, just in case,” she said.
Rats are not native to any part of Alaska. But, introduced by ships, they have infested several coastal regions and become one of the most destructive invasive species in the state.
Once established, they can devastate natural ecosystems, especially on islands where bird populations have evolved without exposure to or defenses against any land-based predators. It is a longstanding problem for islands around the world. Invasive rats are even believed to be partly to blame for the extinction of the Dodo.
On St. Paul, there have been a few isolated cases of rats escaping ships, but almost all of those were caught immediately in traps set up at the harbor. One rat escaped that gauntlet in 2018; it was found dead 10 months later.
A reported but unconfirmed rat sighting in 2024 was the main impetus for the new rule, said Mike Williams, NOAA’s Pribilof Islands program manager. No rat was ever found, so if there had been one that escaped from a ship, it apparently died, he said.
Another impetus, Campbell said, was a visit in recent years by a cruise ship that underreported its rat-infestation problem.
 

Rat tracks are seen on a beach on Kiska Island. in the Aleutians (Photo by Lora Haller/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	Compared to other vulnerable Alaska islands, the Pribilofs have some advantages in their fight against rats.
Community members have been vigilant in the anti-rat program, in coordination with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game and other entities and organizations.
Additionally, ship traffic through the Pribilofs is not quite as heavy as that through the Aleutians, Wiliams said. And a “saving grace” for the archipelago, he said, is the native population of Arctic foxes.
The Pribilof foxes make up a genetically distinct population known for the blue tint that shows up in the animals’ fur. Williams said they do not bother the fur seals.
They have a varied diet that includes birds, eggs, marine resources and berries. And they are on hand to hunt and eat rats, Williams said.
One of the first rats ever seen on St. Paul, an event in the 1990s, was actually in the mouth of a passing fox, he said.
The new rule went into effect on Aug. 6. For now, Williams and Campbell said, there is no particular dog or dog trainer yet identified as a candidate for Pribilof work.  
Williams said that if a rat-catching dog is sent to St. Paul, it might make the most sense to have it there in the winter, when any rats on the island would be concentrated in town rather than across a wider area where they may not be able to find food.
“You want a small, focused area to search rather than the whole entire island,” he said.
On the other hand, having a rat-sniffing dog on duty during the summer might be useful to ensure that ships that come to the island are safe, Campbell said.
Rat eradication
Although it is difficult to eject rats once they are established, it is not impossible.
Rat eradication has been successful at some islands, and possibly most famously at an Alaska site formerly called Rat Island. It got the name because it was the first place in Alaska to be invaded by rats; it is believed that the rodents swam ashore from a wrecked Japanese sailing ship in the late 1700s.
A cooperative effort between the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and two nonprofits, Island Conservation and the Nature Conservancy.
By 2012, the bird populations there had recovered, and the island was officially bestowed with its Unangan name: Hawadax.
The Fish and Wildlife Service is now planning for similar rat eradications on four other Aleutian islands: Kiska, Attu, Amchitka and Great Sitkin. Like Hawadax, all four islands are part of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Different types of rat poison are being considered, along with genetic biocontrol technology, which is a process that uses genetic engineering to limit reproduction.
 

Dead auklets found in a rat cache on Kiska Island are displayed. (Photo provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	Kiska and Attu were occupied by the Japanese during World War II, and a brutal battle occurred on Attu in 1943. The rats there are war legacies. The threat is particularly ominous in Kiska because that rugged volcanic island is home to what is considered a “superflock” of seabirds, particularly auklets, but also an ever-expanding population of rats using the same rocky crevices to kill and stash their prey. Since Kiska is much bigger than the island now called Hawadax, rat eradication there would be more challenging, the Fish and Wildlife Service notes.
The rat eradication proposals for the four Aleutian sites are moving forward, though gradually.
Scoping, the initial phase that leads to an environmental impact statement, was conducted in 2024. A draft environmental impact statement is expected to be released later this year. A draft environmental impact statement is expected this fall, to be followed by a final EIS and a decision on action next year, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service.

name: VTDigger
title: ICE recently arrested at least 9 people in Vermont as the agency appears to ramp up immigration enforcement across the state
description:
Arrests have been reported in Londonderry, the Upper Valley and Cornwall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ICE recently arrested at least 9 people in Vermont as the agency appears to ramp up immigration enforcement across the state.
text:
A federal agent wears a badge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement while standing outside an immigration courtroom in New York in June 2025. File photo by Yuki Iwamura/AP

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested at least nine people across Vermont last weekend in three separate operations — including arrests of workers heading to or from job sites — a pattern that advocates say points to more federal agents than usual operating in the state.
“The Trump Administration is utilizing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised. Anyone who has been deported received full due process,” the agency’s field office spokesperson wrote in a statement to VTDigger. 
The weekend’s arrests stand out not only for their total number but for their form: workplace and commuting arrests of groups, which immigration attorneys describe as rare in Vermont and a possible marker of racial profiling. They come amid months of heightened enforcement in the state — most visibly the March 11 Dorset Street raid in South Burlington — and against a backdrop that advocates say obscures the full scope of activity, because Vermont has no centralized system to track ICE arrests and detentions.
On Aug. 7, five construction workers were arrested in Londonderry and one person in White River Junction. A raid in Cornwall on Aug. 8 led to additional arrests of two roof repairmen, according to Will Lambek of the immigrant advocacy group Migrant Justice. 
An ICE spokesperson did not confirm the specific operations or how many people were arrested, stating that ICE Boston “routinely” conducts raids across New England, including in Vermont.
Lambek also provided details on at least one additional arrest in the Upper Valley in Vermont, but did not have full information on the location or identity. Three people allegedly were detained by ICE in West Lebanon, New Hampshire, according to Upper Valley Immigration Solidarity, a local volunteer group.
ICE operations have drawn heightened scrutiny in recent months. 
Recently, the American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont filed federal claims, a required precursor to lawsuits, against ICE stemming from the March 11 operation, alleging constitutional violations against the people detained when their home was raided.
“Though less visible than the high-profile raids ICE conducted earlier in the year, the fact is that ICE and Border Patrol have continued to target our neighbors and tear apart our communities with almost no meaningful oversight or accountability,” Vermont ACLU Executive Director James Duff Lyall wrote in a statement to VTDigger.
Some observers, however, don’t agree that operations have increased. Based on intakes of people who have contacted the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project for legal help with ICE detentions, Executive Director Jill Martin Diaz said the arrests over the weekend were not an especially strong indication of an increased ICE presence in the state. 
“What we don’t see so often are workplace arrests where there are groups of people arrested at once,” she said. “That’s a little bit of an anomaly.”
Diaz called the ICE arrests, particularly the ones that occurred in the workplace, “opportunistic,” saying detentions tend to ensue when racial profiling is involved.  
“Structurally there’s lots of requests for help for detentions that come our way that don’t get publicized,” she added. 
Recent ICE arrests 
The White River Junction arrest was allegedly of a Haitian man who had previously entered into a national parole program in Manchester, before he was relocated to the town in 2025, the executive director of the organization Grace Initiative Global, Yvonne Lodico, told VTDigger in an email. 
Lt. William Furnari of the Hartford Police Department said he was unaware of any ICE arrests in White River Junction. 
ICE agents came to the Haitian man’s door at 7 a.m., according to Lodico, who said the man has employment authorization and an asylum application under review. He was moved several times while in detention before landing in New Hampshire on Friday, Lodico said.  
His wife, who requested anonymity for safety reasons, told VTDigger in an interview that she had driven to where her husband was taken, but when she asked ICE agents where they were taking him, one of them pulled his gun out and pointed it at her while she was in her car. 
The ICE action was one of at least two in Vermont that day. Agents also arrested five people in a Londonderry operation. 
Windham County Sheriff Mark Anderson told VTDigger on Aug. 7 that none of his officers were in Londonderry at the time of the ICE raid. 
“People who know my agency know what our feelings are towards how we deal with civil immigration enforcement, which is we don’t,” he said. 
Anderson said the Windham County Sheriff’s Department adheres to the state’s mandated Fair and Impartial Policing Policy, which limits how local and state police can assist in federal immigration enforcement. 
“When we are dealing with the civil immigration enforcement side of things, it destroys trust, and so then we are actually hurting public safety just as a matter of consequence of civil immigration,” he added.
The Addison County Sheriff’s Department did not immediately respond to a message left Friday morning asking for comment on the ICE arrests that occurred Aug. 8.
Diaz, of the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project, said Vermont’s lack of an intake system to track ICE arrests and detentions has caused many to go unnoticed since immigration enforcement efforts have intensified under the Trump administration. 
“There isn’t a centralized intake system. There isn’t reliable data,” she said. “In the public discourse, we only ever have access to half the story of what’s going on with ICE enforcement in Vermont, and it cuts both ways.”

title: Republican Joe Mitchell supports constitutional fix for campaign cash
description: Republican Joe Mitchell said Friday voters could trust his pledge to combat “corruption” in Congress because his campaign is not accepting corporate political action committee money — a position that he said makes him distinct from other GOP candidates. Mitchell, the Republican candidate for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, told the crowd gathered at the D[...]
text:
Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state lawmaker who is running for Iowa's 2nd Congressional District, spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Republican Joe Mitchell said Friday voters could trust his pledge to combat “corruption” in Congress because his campaign is not accepting corporate political action committee money — a position that he said makes him distinct from other GOP candidates.
Mitchell, the Republican candidate for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, told the crowd gathered at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair that when he launched his campaign in September 2025, one of his first commitments was to not take corporate PAC money.
“We said number one, we’re not taking any corporate PAC money,” Mitchell said. “Right — so no money from BlackRock, no money from Pfizer, no money from Goldman Sachs, no money from any of these huge, gigantic institutions and corporations that have screwed us over for years. I’ll be the only Republican in Congress not taking corporate PAC money, by the way. So we’re going to start that trend.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mitchell, a former state lawmaker and the founder of Run Gen Z, a young conservative organization, said he had other plans to reform Washington, D.C., and rein in corporate influence in politics. He highlighted goals to implement term limits, ban insider trading and “stop the lawmaker-to-lobbyist pipeline,” he said.
Three of these four proposals could be tackled through legislation, Mitchell told reporters. But he said preventing politicians from taking corporate PAC money is “a little more difficult,” as it would require a constitutional amendment to overturn the 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, a ruling that struck down limits on how much money a corporation can directly spend on political campaigns.
Mitchell said he was willing to work with Democrats and others to overturn Citizens United, as well as advance other policies he supports.
“Being the only person not taking corporate PAC money and criticizing the Citizens United court decision in 2010 makes us unique in that part, and we’ll work with Democrats,” Mitchell said. “This is a bipartisan issue. Everything we talk about is pretty much bipartisan issue on the anti-corruption platform that we have, and so we’re willing to work with Democrats in Congress to get those things done. And we think it’s important for the American people, and shouldn’t be a partisan issue.”
Though Mitchell said his campaign does not take corporate PAC money, his campaign has taken $17,500 in funding from political action committees associated with home builders and mortgage industries, Iowa Starting Line, a left-leaning outlet reported. He said these groups are not corporate PACs — “I mean, there’s plenty of Democrats that say, ‘no corporate PAC money,’ that take trade association money,” Mitchell said.
His comments about opposing lawmakers becoming lobbyists has also been a point of scrutiny, as Mitchell was a founder of the Iowa Real Estate Developers Association. Mitchell told reporters he has never been a registered lobbyist at the Iowa State Capitol, and said, “I couldn’t lobby legally because there’s a moratorium for two years, and I’d left the organization before that two years was up for the lobbying period.”
However, he said his experience at the association, as well as working as a regional administrator for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in the Trump administration, position him well to take on these issues.
“I actually think that it makes me a better advocate to make sure that we don’t have, you know, former legislators going in there — because I never intended to be a lobbyist, which is why I wasn’t a lobbyist and went back into public service to work for the Trump administration last year,” he said. “And so, I’ve seen firsthand people that have went from being legislators or being Congresspeople to lobbying in D.C., which is a much worse problem.”
Mitchell also said he stood by an earlier statement he made against his general election opponent, state Rep. Lindsay James, a Democratic state lawmaker and ordained Presbyterian minister and chaplain. He called her a “PINO,” or “Pastor In Name Only.” James said in a video response she was “disappointed” by Mitchell’s comments, adding, “it’s not just disappointing to me, it’s disappointing to all pastors and Christians across the state of Iowa.”
The Republican candidate said he believed James’ beliefs on LGBTQ+ issues, particularly acceptance of transgender youth, disqualify her as a pastor.
“I think that, if you’re a pastor and you think that 6-year-olds can change their gender? I don’t think you’re much of a pastor,” Mitchell said. “And a lot of people agree with me on that.”
Friday was first day for The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox, which continues during the 11 days of the fair. See the schedule here.

name: VTDigger
title: Post office photography exhibit removed for ‘political content’
description:
The exhibit in the Morristown post office lobby featured photographs of protesters at the four-way village intersection, some of whom have been gathering there nearly every Friday since the death of George Floyd in 2020.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Post office photography exhibit removed for ‘political content’.
text:
River Arts executive director Jonah Rabinowitz takes in an exhibit that was relocated from the Morrisville Post Office gallery, where some of the photographs were deemed to contain “political content.” Photo by Gordon Miller/News&Citizen

This story by Patrick Bilow was first published in the News & Citizen on Aug. 13, 2026.Morrisville arts organization River Arts removed an exhibit from the town post office’s walls after complaints that the artwork was too political.
River Arts has for years supported local artists by helping curate art installations in heavily trafficked public buildings throughout Morristown. The latest exhibit, displayed in the post office lobby, featured photographs of protesters at the four-way village intersection, some of whom have been gathering there nearly every Friday since the death of George Floyd in 2020.
Earlier this summer, the post office requested that the exhibit be removed just weeks after it was hung due to several customer complaints about its political content, said River Arts Executive Director Jonah Rabinowitz.
Olea Smith-Caland, a Morristown resident, took the photographs earlier this year. At the time, she was enrolled in an iPhone photography class taught by Lamoille Neighbors, a group that seeks to enhance the well-being of older adults in the area. Photographs produced by the class have been displayed throughout town for years, Rabinowitz said.
“We don’t take any curatorial process with that,” he said. “We just assume it’s seniors. They’re learning how to use their iPhones to take great photos, but also how to manipulate them in the apps. What a great program, right?”
While the photographs often stick to landscapes, flowers or shots of loved ones, Smith-Caland chose to focus on the frustration that the Friday protesters express.
“To me there was absolutely nothing about the artwork that was offensive or controversial. Quite frankly, it depicts things that all you have to do to witness on any given Friday is stick your head out the door and look up the street,” Rabinowitz said. “But while one person may not think it’s political, as long as another person thinks it is, that’s all that’s required.”
Morristown’s postmaster did not respond to a request for comment before press deadline.
Rabinowitz said River Arts, like the post office, considers itself an objective institution, but that the post office achieves that metric through exclusion of artwork, while his arts organization does so through inclusion of many different political beliefs. However, he said he’s sympathetic to the post office because it has its own policies to navigate.
“When I say we don’t have a political bent, I mean that everybody who’s an individual here has their own viewpoint,” Rabinowitz said. “But as an organization, we choose to show things or to invite people based upon a variety of criteria, and quite frankly, most of the times it has nothing to do with politics.”
Not this time, however.
According to Rabinowitz, the post office specifically requested that River Arts remove parts of the exhibit that featured political messaging, but Rabinowitz said all the components in Smith-Caland’s exhibit deserve to stay together. It’s “all or nothing,” he said.
The exhibit was transferred to the nonprofit’s headquarters on Portland Street and a new, less-political exhibit by local artist Peggy Smith was installed at the post office.
“We are still providing a space for it to be viewed by the public,” Rabinowitz said of Smith-Caland’s exhibit. “If they want to come see it they can. I mean it’s literally a 30-second walk from the post office.”
Some individuals were not so happy with the settlement, according to Rabinowitz. Members of Lamoille Neighbors, for example, expressed concern that removing the artwork may have violated the artist’s First Amendment right to free speech.
Rabinowitz takes that claim seriously, but he’s not convinced of the First Amendment violation.
“I am personally not getting the pitchfork and going up and down the street protesting this,” Rabinowitz said. “I don’t think it has risen to that level, but there are a lot of people in the community who did, and who do, and they have to deal with that.”
While the post office exhibit was the rare political test for River Arts, Rabinowitz said his role in the process was to judge neither the viewer’s sensibilities nor the content of the artwork.
“It’s not my job to judge,” Rabinowitz said. “It’s to facilitate. My position was to get the art displayed and make sure everyone was feeling OK.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Line of credit, more oversight proposed for stalled North Dakota Military Gallery project
description: Top North Dakota Republican lawmakers are proposing tens of millions of dollars in a line of credit for restarting construction of the Military Gallery that has been paused for more than a month due to a fundraising shortfall.  Their proposal also gives final decision-making authority and approval of donor naming rights to boards that lawmakers […]
text:
Construction is paused July 3, 2026, on the Military Gallery addition to the North Dakota Heritage Center due to insufficient fundraising. (Photo by Amy Dalrymple/North Dakota Monitor)Top North Dakota Republican lawmakers are proposing tens of millions of dollars in a line of credit for restarting construction of the Military Gallery that has been paused for more than a month due to a fundraising shortfall. 
Their proposal also gives final decision-making authority and approval of donor naming rights to boards that lawmakers lead or sit on. 
The bill draft made public Friday is for a $35 million line of credit through the state-owned Bank of North Dakota, to be repaid by the State Historical Society via donations.
If donations garnered through March 2029 aren’t enough, taxpayers would be on the hook through a deficiency appropriation. The goal is still for half of the $78 million project to be funded by donations.
The bill draft is among 20 proposals lawmakers are pitching for a special session Gov. Kelly Armstrong called for restricting kratom and related products. A top legislative panel on Monday will pick what bills go forth into the special session, which begins Sept. 2.
Gov. Armstrong announces special session, emergency actions to ban kratom in North Dakota

A fix for the Military Gallery is not officially part of the special session, though the governor has said he hopes lawmakers find a solution. Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot, sponsored the bill, joined by House Majority Leader Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, and the Republican chairs of the House and Senate budget writing committees.
Their proposal also gives oversight and final decision-making authority over the project to the Capitol Grounds Planning Commission, a nine-member panel that includes four lawmakers, all of whom Hogue said have good construction administration experience. The project has primarily been managed by a museum advisory committee, which does not include lawmakers.
The State Historical Society would have to update a 47-member board of legislative leaders and budget writers every quarter on the project during the 2027-28 interim between sessions. Those updates would include construction status; use of lines of credit; donations projected, pledged and received; and the expected completion date.
The legislation also would require approvals from the Budget Section, as well as the governor-led Emergency Commission for authorizing donor naming rights for any part of the museum.
Naming rights are “of significant value” and should be evaluated by elected representatives, Hogue said.
He declined to comment on the overall handling of the project.
“I try to solve problems, and I’m not going to go down the path of second-guessing what was done in the past,” Hogue said.
The 70,000-square-foot project on the Capitol Grounds is a joint effort among the State Historical Society, the North Dakota National Guard and their foundations. The gallery must clinch one-third of its fundraising goal in pledges – about $12.8 million – before it can use $15 million the 2025 Legislature approved for the project.
Additionally, the Legislature previously approved a $20 million line of credit – already spent – and $4.2 million for repaying another line of credit for planning and design, for a total of more than $39 million in state funding already approved.
Construction of the Military Gallery began in July 2025 and has been paused since July 3 due to the fundraising shortfall. It’s unclear exactly how much cash on hand the project has.
Fundraisers have received at least $800,000 in pledge payments and have secured nearly $4.2 million in pledges, said Shannon Schweigert, managing partner at PACE Fundraising, a Fargo-based consultant the North Dakota National Guard Foundation hired. Most pledges are to be paid over the course of five years, Schweigert said.
ND lawmakers react to halted Capitol grounds construction project that ran out of money

Fundraisers have approached businesses and veteran service organizations and considered charitable gambling proceeds and other sources, said Jackie Huber, president of the North Dakota National Guard Foundation. Potential benefactors are sometimes reluctant to donate “until they know ‘What am I donating for?’ and ‘What’s my piece of the pie going to look like?’” she said.
The committee overseeing the project has not met since June. State Historical Society Director Bill Peterson said, “There’s not much to discuss.” The project had no path forward at the time of the pause, he said.
“This is a fantastic project, and we’re still pretty surprised that we’ve had any kind of trouble raising money for this,” Peterson said. PACE fundraisers are “still confident that this a very winnable and doable campaign,” he said.
Under Hogue’s bill, the museum committee would still have reporting requirements to lawmakers, but no decisionmaking authority. 
Another proposal, by Sen. Sean Cleary, R-Bismarck, would require future projects to secure 75% of nonstate funds as cash, contracts or grants before breaking ground. His proposal would not apply to college and university projects. Cleary said he felt there should be safeguards for the state going forward. 
“Really, to me, it just didn’t make any sense that they broke ground with such little fundraising momentum,” Cleary said of the Military Gallery project.

title: Iowa cancer researchers focus on white blood cell maturation, resiliency
description: Researchers at Iowa’s public and private universities are focusing their efforts on white blood cells as they explore potential new cancer treatments. Iowa State University and Des Moines University faculty have published research on the growth and internal operations of white blood cells, which handle the body’s immune response to infections and diseases li[...]
text:
Iowa State University and Des Moines University faculty are conducting research into cells tasked with combating cancer. (Stock photo courtesy of NIH)Researchers at Iowa’s public and private universities are focusing their efforts on white blood cells as they explore potential new cancer treatments.
Iowa State University and Des Moines University faculty have published research on the growth and internal operations of white blood cells, which handle the body’s immune response to infections and diseases like cancers.
Raquel Espin Palazon, ISU associate professor of genetics, development and cell biology, has studied what causes leukemia cells to halt their maturation into white blood cells, leading them to remain functionless and spread without dying, which makes people sick. At DMU, biochemistry and nutrition professor Elitsa Ananieva is studying certain white blood cells’ internal functions to better sustain them in the fight against cancer cells.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both researchers cited their fascination with the immune system and its intricacies as drivers of their work, and said they hope their reports can serve as a base for further study and eventual new treatments for those dealing with cancer. Maintaining balance in the immune system to ensure it can protect the body but not become overactive and end up hurting healthy tissue is “one of the most important aspects of staying healthy,” Ananieva said.
“The first step is to understand how nature works, how our bodies work, right?” Espin Palazon said. “And then, once we understand, we can cure disease.”
Helping blood cells mature
Espin Palazon said she’s dedicated her research career to inflammatory signals in blood cell creation. Her most current work has drilled in on a protein called progranulin, which she said is a highly expressed gene in a type of white blood cells called macrophages.
The team studied these cells and the protein in zebrafish, she said. Their embryonic development is as quick as 48 hours and they have two kinds of progranulin — one only found in immune cells. They found that progranulin is “critical to generate these mature white blood cells,” but when examining human leukemia cells to see if they would also mature with the protein, it didn’t work.
This could mean two things, she said, one being that the protein doesn’t have the same function in humans and zebrafish, or that they were missing a piece of the puzzle. After going back to further study the fish, Espin Palazon said they found that a signaling pathway must also activate in order for the cells to mature.
The signaling pathway collects information from outside the cell through chemical signals and brings it into the cell’s DNA.
“We were able to now activate those two components, progranulin and the other signaling pathway, and then we were able to see that the leukemia cells started to differentiate and to express the markers of the mature white blood cells,” Espin Palazon said.
By overcoming the blockage that stops leukemia clones from leaving their progenitor state and maturing, Espin Palazon said they are then short-lived and die, stopping them from accumulating in the bone marrow and disrupting blood production.
Leukemia is the most common cancer among children, Espin Palazon said, and she hopes that one day this treatment can contribute to increasing survival rates.
“It would be amazing to know that many kids can be saved because of that basic knowledge that we have gained thanks to the zebrafish, thanks to this model organism,” Espin Palazon said.
Creating T cell resiliency 
Ananieva’s research focused on the internal health of T cells — a white blood cell that can recognize and fight infections and tumors. She explored how to ensure the cells’ resiliency in a tumor environment that can sap their ability to function.
“T cells can recognize and destroy cancer cells, but the tumor microenvironment places them under significant metabolic stress, leading to a dysfunctional state known as exhaustion,” Ananieva said in an email. “Although these T cells can still detect the tumor, they often lose their ability to eliminate it effectively. Our research focuses on identifying metabolic interventions that can restore T-cell function and enhance anti-tumor immunity.”
Rather than zebrafish, Ananieva worked with mice genetically modified to her specifications in order to create the correct conditions for her team’s research. Certain metabolic genes were taken out of the different mouse groups’ T cells to see how they would fare against lymphoma, and the team found that tumor growth was reduced by as much as 75%.
By identifying the genes that can aid in T cell resiliency when reprogrammed, Ananieva said they can then target those areas with pharmaceutical interventions and elevate the efficacy of other cancer treatments. One such treatment is CAR T-cell therapy, where a patient’s blood is taken and their T cells engineered to attack their specific cancer before going back into the body.
Ananieva’s hope is that one day medical professionals have expansive access to the drug cocktails and treatments they need for patients based on their specific profile, what she called “personalized medicine.” This would be something all scientists could contribute to.
Some of those contributors could be the students she works with today, she said.
“One of the most rewarding things for me is seeing medical students become excited about scientific discovery. I am passionate about engaging future physicians in research because it allows them to connect basic science with patient care,” Ananieva said in an email. “It is truly gratifying to watch students become inspired by the investigative process and gain insights that they can carry forward into their medical careers, whether they are caring for patients, evaluating new therapies, or contributing to clinical research themselves.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: Debate questions no one asked for
description: For Nebraskans trying to make sense of the “Working,” “America,” “First,” “Family,” “People” political party word salad, this week should offer some relief. That’s when a Lancaster District Court judge is scheduled to rule on whether to certify a couple of political newbies to state politics and the November ballot. If you’re thinking her decision […]
text:
A Nebraska State Fair banner at the State Fair on Aug 29, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)For Nebraskans trying to make sense of the “Working,” “America,” “First,” “Family,” “People” political party word salad, this week should offer some relief. That’s when a Lancaster District Court judge is scheduled to rule on whether to certify a couple of political newbies to state politics and the November ballot.
If you’re thinking her decision will clear things up, don’t hold your breath. If this election cycle has proven anything, it’s that the voting booth and the courtroom are becoming inextricably linked. While the courts are critical to ferreting out the phony and fictitious, I worry that winning with better ideas has become archaic. 
Meanwhile, some good news has arrived. The state’s U.S. Senate candidates, GOP incumbent Pete Ricketts and nonpartisan challenger Dan Osborn, will debate on Sept. 1 at the Nebraska State Fair in Grand Island. More on their tête-à-tête below.
They will be in a good spot. As one of two panelists during a nationally televised Senate debate between Bob Kerrey and Deb Fischer in 2012, I can assure you that the State Fair is among Nebraska’s most appropriate debate venues.
Political debates have their limits, from canned answers to punchless platitudes to timed responses to delays in fact checking to the onset of shouting  … between candidates or from a candidate to a moderator.
Still, debates can provide voters with a side-by-side comparison of a candidate’s ability to think on his or her feet. Seeing how someone who would write laws, make policy and affect my life reacts to tough but fair questions can be enlightening, too. I’m also always curious about whether their answers are based on data, evidence and science rather than politics.
Joining Sen. Ricketts and Osborn with debates this campaign cycle are GOP Rep. Mike Flood and challenger Democrat Chris Backemeyer in District 1. In the Blue Dot Special (District 2), Democrat Denise Powell and GOP nominee Brinker Harding have three debates planned before Election Day. 
As was the case four years ago, incumbent Gov. Jim Pillen will not be debating. His campaign at that time called such events “political theater.” We remain unsure of what they meant by political theater, but if showing differences between candidates and providing details into their character evokes a little drama, so what? Healthy democracies can handle that. Buy us some tickets.
 Nor are regular interactions with voters the same thing as a debate. What separates political debates from more controlled gatherings — “regularly connect(ing) with constituents,” as 3rd District Rep. Adrian Smith’s office put it — is that too many of those confabs comprise only grips, grins and softball questions. They are not to be confused with town hall meetings, which can be raucous, rambunctious assemblies. See Flood videos for details.
Which brings us back to the main event, the State Fair face-off between Ricketts and Osborn, who, to date, seem to have very little in common according to their endless TV spots with charges and countercharges of fakery and financial missteps. 
Nobody asked, but here’s hoping the debate lasts long enough for moderators to get answers about the cost of everything, Iran, tariffs, the Farm Bill, ICE (Shock gloves? Seriously?) and Epstein but save enough time to ask something along these lines:

Yes or No. Did Joe Biden legitimately win the 2020 presidential election?
Was the recent debacle at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool the result of vandals? If yes, what’s your evidence? If no, what was the cause?
Are vaccines in the U.S. safe and effective? Please explain.
A congressional committee recently voted to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he evoked his Fifth Amendment right when testifying before the committee. Do you agree with that decision and if so, are you saying Fifth Amendment rights should be negated when someone testifies before Congress? (Hint: They’re not.)
Do you believe in the birthright citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment and, if not, how would you determine citizenship?
In the last 10 years in Nebraska, out of the estimated 64% of high school students who participate in sports, a number in the several hundreds of thousands, how many transgender students have petitioned to play school sports? (Hint: It’s 8.) So why the inordinate focus on it?
What’s your primary source of information and news?
Is the detailed study of slavery and its consequences in the U.S. imperative to understanding American history? Why or why not?
Recent research concluded that we are reading fewer books than ever. The first week in October is Banned Books Week. What banned books have you read? What book — banned or not — are you currently reading?

Time to open the doors of this season’s political theater.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Southeast Tech and Thune honor late US senator with $18 million manufacturing building
description: SIOUX FALLS — Southeast Technical College’s newest building will train welders and machinists — and carry the name of a South Dakota politician who spent his career championing rural workforce development. Local, state and federal officials gathered Friday for the groundbreaking of the $18 million James Abdnor Center for Advanced Manufacturing in northwester[...]
text:
A rendering of the future James Abdnor Center for Advanced Manufacturing in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. (Courtesy of Southeast Technical College)SIOUX FALLS — Southeast Technical College’s newest building will train welders and machinists — and carry the name of a South Dakota politician who spent his career championing rural workforce development.
Local, state and federal officials gathered Friday for the groundbreaking of the $18 million James Abdnor Center for Advanced Manufacturing in northwestern Sioux Falls.
The building is set to open in fall 2028, funded by $6 million from the state, $6.5 million in federal Housing and Urban Development funds and millions more in private contributions.
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, helped secure the federal funding. Thune and Abdnor met after one of Thune’s high school basketball games in the 1970s. Abdnor later hired him to work in his U.S. Senate office, became a mentor and was his “biggest advocate” when Thune ran for public office, Thune said.
“I wouldn’t be where I am without Jim Abdnor,” Thune said. “There’s no question about that.”

U.S. Rep. James Abdnor, R-South Dakota, left, poses for a picture in front of the U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., with 18-year-old John Thune in 1979. (Photo courtesy of Sen. John Thune’s Office)

Abdnor was raised in Kennebec, served in World War II and was elected to state and federal offices including the U.S. Senate. He lost that seat in 1986 to Tom Daschle, a Democrat who went on to become majority leader. Thune ousted Daschle in 2004 and became Senate majority leader in 2025. Abdnor died in 2012.
Southeast Technical College President Cory Clasemann said the building was named for Abdnor because of Thune’s role in securing funding and Abdnor’s lifelong support for “the next generation of leaders” in South Dakota.
The college’s construction, HVAC, mechanical engineering, plumbing and welding programs are all at capacity. Clasemann said the new building and expanded lab space will triple manufacturing program capacity and double the number of welding booths. Last year, Clasemann estimated the new building and a planned expansion will bring the total cost of the project to $24 million.
Advanced manufacturing, Clasemann said, accounts for one in 10 jobs in South Dakota and is expected to grow its workforce by 6% through 2032.
“Manufacturing is not a huge program right now, but we know it’s one that needs to be bigger, and it’s only been limited by capacity at this point,” Clasemann said.
Southeast Tech requested $8 million from the state before this year’s legislative session. Gov. Larry Rhoden said the state cut the contribution to $6 million due to budget constraints. Rhoden, who has owned a custom welding business for decades, praised the project.
“I’ve always believed that there’s dignity in working with your hands and in making something from start to finish,” Rhoden said. “There’s something special about being able to step back at the end of the day and see what your hands have built, what you fix or what you made better.”
Rhoden said the new building and other trade school investments fill industry workforce needs while giving students “practical hands-on education.”
Clasemann said the college is still fundraising to fill a $2 million gap left by the state. Several private entities have contributed, including $1 million from Sioux Falls-based Marmon Energy and $775,000 from the Forward Sioux Falls campaign, a joint venture of the Greater Sioux Falls Chamber of Commerce and the Sioux Falls Area Development Foundation.
