The 2025 Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act charged a committee made up of behavioral health experts and state leaders to review proposals from 13 regions across the state — modeled after the state’s 13 judicial districts — to rebuild behavioral health services after former Republican Gov. Susana Martinez’s fraud accusations led to an exodus of providers.
As of Friday, the committee overseeing the effort had signed off on seven such plans. Nick Boukas, the executive committee chair and director of the state Health Care Authority’s Behavioral Health Services Division, told Source NM after the meeting that he hopes to sign off on the remaining six by the end of the year.
Lawmakers and rural officials overseeing individual regional plans have frequently expressed frustration at interim legislative committee hearings this year over the plan’s slow rollout, “nebulous” goals and varying local politics.
New Mexico lawmakers express frustration with long process to rebuild behavioral health system

The five plans approved Friday covered the regions surrounding Roswell, Socorro, Farmington, Silver City and Clovis and identified funding priorities such as school-based behavioral health resources, crisis services and workforce development. 
Regional plans can identify up to five such priority areas that local governments will address through the funding. Committee member Alanna Dancis, the state Health Care Authority’s acting Medicaid director, told her fellow committee members that she was concerned that many regional plans seemed to be “missing half the population.”
“I didn’t want to in any way slow down the approvals of the plans, but I did not really see pregnancy or family housing mentioned very much,” she said. That is “something I’m really looking at and continue to be very concerned that it doesn’t seem to be a priority of the regions.”
A dispute over funding for Pueblos, tribes, nations
After the committee approved the five plans, committee member Violette Cloud introduced several proposals aimed at changing how the committee awards money to Pueblos, tribes and nations.
She said the funding formula the committee had long relied on had flaws in its underlying data and argued that the current structure could unfairly award some Pueblos, tribes or nations more money than others.
Nick Boukas, the executive committee chair and director of the state Health Care Authority’s Behavioral Health Services Division, pictured on Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
Boukas, the committee chair, told Cloud he appreciated her concern but believed that voting on it Friday would be premature. He said he thought any need for course-correcting likely rests with the Legislature and added that it would be more appropriate after formal tribal consultation.
“I just feel like every time that we’re meeting and we’re trying to change, I think it’s very difficult for the accountable entities to try to keep up with what has changed,” Boukas said.
While the committee didn’t take a vote on several of Cloud’s proposals, it did approve her motion to set aside 9.5% of the committee’s budget exclusively for Pueblos, tribes and nations.
Under the prior funding formula, leaders from New Mexico’s Pueblos, tribes and nations did not always have clarity of whether they were applying for their own pot of money or whether they were included by default in their corresponding region’s plan, Cloud said.
After the meeting, Boukas told Source NM that the approved change was aimed at “making sure that the tribal partners know how much they have to spend.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Gender-affirming care, Russia sanctions and Kalshi: CT politics news
description: Plus: A ruling on HUD funding, Connecticut's CEO-worker pay gap, 'Sales-Tax-Free' Week and a storm forces a Ryan Fazio event to relocate.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more news about the 2026 legislative session, campaigns, elections and more, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Gender-affirming care for kids
Connecticut Children’s reached an agreement earlier this month with the U.S. Department of Justice to resolve an ongoing investigation into the hospital’s gender-affirming care services for children. According to a DOJ release, the hospital has agreed to stop providing gender-affirming care to minors, including hormones and puberty blockers, and to dedicate $500,000 in medical care to people “living with the harmful consequences of ‘gender affirming care’.”
A spokesperson for the hospital confirmed a resolution had been reached and that the hospital was able to resolve the matter without disclosing any protected patient information to the U.S. government. 
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
Blumenthal on Russia sanctions bill
Speaking in front of a Ukrainian Catholic Church in Hartford, U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal celebrated the Senate’s recent passage of his bipartisan bill to ramp up economic pressure on Russia and its oil and natural gas exports.
The focus now shifts to the House, which introduced the bill earlier this week. Blumenthal, who said he’d make a return trip to Ukraine soon, said there’s “powerful momentum going forward because of the overwhelming bipartisan support.”
Timing is uncertain, and Congress doesn’t return until September. But Blumenthal said he’s “very hopeful that it will be imminent,” noting support from GOP leadership and the White House. 
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
HUD funding
A Rhode Island judge ruled Monday that the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development must continue to fund programs that provide housing for formerly homeless people.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong was part of a multistate lawsuit that challenged an order from HUD saying more funding had to go toward other housing programs, rather than the permanent, supportive housing it has historically supported.
This funding shift could have left thousands without a way to pay rent. The ruling follows a previous attempt to cap money spent on permanent housing that a court struck down earlier this summer. 
— Ginny Monk, Investigative Reporter
CT’s sports betting rules for Kalshi
Kalshi was dealt a blow this week after a federal judge denied the platform’s request for a preliminary injunction in Connecticut, ruling that its sports betting markets can be regulated by the state.
Kalshi sued the state Department of Consumer Protection in December after the agency sent a cease and desist letter to several companies operating sports betting through their online prediction markets, including Kalshi, Robinhood and Crypto.com.
The prediction markets say they should only be regulated by the federal government. States counter that the markets should be subject to state regulations. Earlier this month, Connecticut Comptroller Sean Scanlon included a report warning of the markets’ “dark side” in his agency’s monthly economic update. 
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CSCU may expand in-state tuition to MA, RI
The governing body for Connecticut State Colleges and Universities is considering allowing more New England students to receive in-state tuition throughout the system, a move some members say could help the schools stay competitive as colleges across the country work to reverse enrollment declines.
On Wednesday, the Board of Regents’ Finance and Infrastructure Committee discussed a proposal to expand discounted tuition to students from Massachusetts and Rhode Island. The change would be implemented in the 2027-28 academic year.
During the meeting, some speakers said the change would benefit some schools in the system far more than others. Still, the proposal was advanced. The full Board of Regents is expected to discuss the matter at an upcoming meeting.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CEO-worker pay gap in CT
While the gap between CEO and worker pay is widening in many states, Connecticut is something of an exception, according to a new report.
In its annual Executive Paywatch report, the AFL-CIO found that nationally, the gap between average CEO and median worker pay at S&P 500 companies increased from a 285:1 ratio in 2024 to a 312:1 ratio in 2025.
In Connecticut, however, the gap narrowed slightly, falling from a 334:1 ratio in 2024 to a 300:1 ratio last year. The reduction is due to two factors: a decrease in the average S&P 500 CEO pay (from $19.5 million to $17.9 million) and an increase in median workers’ annual pay (from $58,400 to $59,690).
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT launches Sales-Tax-Free Week
Connecticut will sponsor its 27th annual Sales-Tax-Free Week starting Sunday and running through Saturday, Aug. 21.
This year’s promotion, which waives sales tax on all clothing and footwear items costing $300 or less, also is complemented by a new, ongoing sales tax exemption on non-electronic school supplies, such as pens, markers and notebooks — regardless of price.
The week-long tax holiday is expected to save shoppers $6 million, according to Department of Revenue Services Commissioner Mark Boughton, who added that the ongoing exemption for school supplies — which began July 1 — likely will save consumers another $6 million over the fiscal year.
With new federal tariffs and higher fuel prices creating a chaotic year, the sales tax promotion also is crucial for businesses, said Timothy Phelan, president of the Connecticut Retail Merchants Association.
Further information about the sales tax holiday and the school supplies exemption can be found on the department’s website.
— Keith Phaneuf, State Budget Reporter
Storm changes Fazio’s plans
Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio was forced to move a planned campaign event Thursday evening after the original venue, the carousel pavilion in New Haven’s Lighthouse Point Park, was heavily damaged in a storm.
The overnight storm produced wind gusts recorded at 103 mph at Lighthouse Point, according to NBC Connecticut Chief Meteorologist Ryan Hanrahan. The damage to the pavilion forced the city to close the park “indefinitely.”
Fazio, who was unopposed in Tuesday’s GOP primary, had been scheduled to host an event focused on “Connecticut’s Future” at the pavilion Thursday evening. Instead, he posted on social media that the event would be held at the Silver Sands Beach Club in East Haven.
“It was just horrendous,” Fazio said. “I’m really hoping the building and the carousel can be repaired.” 
— John Moritz, Energy and Environment Reporter

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise.
description: New analysis of more than 300 bear encounters suggests our canine companions often increase odds of conflict and rarely serve as early warning systems many recreationists assume.
text:
A brown bear wades through river water in Katmai National Park and Preserve on Aug. 12, 2023. (Photo by F. Jimenez/National Park Service)
Earlier this summer, I was jogging on a local trail with my 7-year-old black lab mutt, Camas, when she suddenly froze. The fur along her spine bristled. Then she let out a single, sharp bark — a timbre I’d never before heard.
I caught the unmistakable musk of an animal and my hand shot to the bear spray on my chest. Halfway up a tree less than 20 yards away, a beautiful, small cinnamon black bear stared back at us.
The bear scampered off as Camas growled, standing her ground in front of me on the trail. “Good girl,” I told her, my heart rate slowing to a normal pace. My dog, I assumed, warned me early of a potential threat. I was proud.
In bear country, common wisdom holds that dogs serve as early bear alarms, or even deterrents. That belief, however, has long rested mostly on anecdote. Until recently, almost no one had tested whether it was actually true.


Credit: Journal of Wildlife Management




 

A new study in the Journal of Wildlife Management analyzed bear-dog conflicts involving black, polar and brown bears from Alaska to Florida. The results challenge the idea that dogs make people safer in bear country and they have me rethinking my relationship with Camas in the woods.
“If you think a house pet is likely going to be your bear, not only detector but deterrent, you might want to think twice about that,” lead author of the paper Tom Smith told me over Zoom, one of his dogs begging for attention in the background while mine snoozed next to me.
Smith, a research wildlife biologist at Brigham Young University in Utah, analyzed 326 bear-dog encounters spanning more than a century, drawing from newspaper articles, federal and state government reports, books, records compiled by other bear specialists, and internet searches.
Smith began working with bears more than 30 years ago in Alaska’s Katmai National Park. He’s published influential research on bear spray and guns as bear deterrents, and has become one of the world’s leading experts on human-bear interaction. “As soon as you become the bear guy, then everybody comes running to you for advice on how to be safe,” he said. “So I thought, ‘I’m going to have to get to the heart of this.”
Smith has long been interested in the way dogs impact humans’ odds of an encounter in bear country. But the issue became urgent and tangible to him following a 2023 attack that left two people and their dog dead in a tent in Canada’s Banff National Park. The issue hasn’t gone away. This summer alone, a jogger and his dog were mauled near Island Park, Idaho, while recordings of separate encounters involving dogs in Banff and Alberta went viral online.
 The findings

The data show people are largely unprepared for bear encounters and naive to their possible consequences. Dogs ran away, fought with bears, provoked confrontations, drew owners in to fight off bears barehanded, and even boomeranged bears back to people.
The first surprise in the data was how few people carried any deterrent at all. That might be because people thought, erroneously, Smith says, that dogs would be sufficient to keep bears away. Recreators wielded bear spray in only about a tenth of cases and a firearm in roughly a third. All told, five people and 56 dogs died in the encounters Smith analyzed.
Contrary to some common wisdom, dogs also weren’t effective warning systems for bears. In fact, they alerted their owners early of a bear in only 1 in 11 of the encounters the study analyzed. Dogs provoked the bear, instigating the encounter, in more than half the cases. After the bear conflict began, things didn’t look much better: Dogs tangled with bears about 40 percent of the time, ran away in 20 percent of encounters, and didn’t engage at all in about 17 percent of cases. So much for dogs being excellent protectors.

Credit: Journal of Wildlife Management

Other findings were less surprising. Leashes were a major decider in the severity of the interaction. Unleashed dogs were involved in six times as many incidents as leashed pets. Smith said dogs without a leash can dart ahead of owners or crash through brush and spook a bear. Canines can also act as bear boomerangs. In 27 of the encounters, dogs brought a bear back to their owners. In 70 percent of these instances, the dog owner was injured. Worse yet, many owners in the data came to rescue their pet when it got in a scuffle with a bear, often with no deterrent. The result: 85 percent of the time, those owners were injured.
Additionally, the data reinforced something bear experts have known for years: the larger the group of people, the less likely the encounter. However, the presence of a dog dramatically shifts that risk. Dogs roughly doubled the odds of a conflict compared to the same-sized groups with no canine companions.
Taken as a whole, the data paint a portrait in which bears and domestic dogs don’t get along. Smith suspects it’s part of the long evolutionary relationship between bears and wolves. For thousands of years, wolves competed with bears for food, killed cubs and even kicked bruins off carcasses. Some of this behavior is on public display in places like Yellowstone National Park, where populations of both species flourish. Modern dogs may still trigger those ancient instincts.
Smith recognizes limitations and nuance in his data, too. For one, it’s important to note that the dogs in the analysis were domestic companions, not highly-trained guardian dogs meant to fend off predators — which data show can reduce bear presence at ranches and farms. Also, data on human-bear conflict inherently shows a bias, depicting only the encounters that went majorly wrong rather than the majority of experiences when people venture into the places bruins live and the species coexist without incident. “For the most part, people and their dogs pass through bear country without incident,” Smith wrote in the paper.
 Should your pup join the hike?

“The takeaway isn’t to keep dogs out of bear country,” Smith said. “The takeaway is there are things you can do that greatly improve your odds.”
Best practices, backed by Smith’s data, say to travel in groups, eliminate smells if you’re camping and make noise. Bear bells, he says, don’t work. Above almost all else? “You have no business being in bear country without a deterrent,” Smith said.
Dogs just don’t cut it on that front. According to Smith, bear spray has the highest likelihood of fending off an aggressive bear for the vast majority of recreationists in bear country. But firearms can work too for experienced users. Carry your spray (or gun) where you can reach it in a split second. No matter what deterrent you choose, practice with it. Bear encounters can happen in seconds.

The author’s companion, Camas, in bear country.(Photo by Nick Mott)

If you do take your dog, consider a leash. “It’s not just dogs and bears,” Smith said. “It’s also dogs and everything else.” Smith’s own dog had been sprayed by a skunk twice in the last month. Mine finds few greater joys in life than chasing ground squirrels, marmots and grouse. So, we’re both faced with navigating how to behave in wild places with these family members that, if they see a deer or elk or bear, may not be able to hold themselves back.
Since talking with Smith, I’ve thought about the role Camas plays in bear country in a more nuanced way. She’s warned me about bears — even since that encounter on my jog. But she’s also ignored bears less than 30 yards away, chased wildlife she shouldn’t and, even in her younger days, treed a black bear.
The lesson isn’t that dogs don’t belong in bear country writ large. It’s that they’re dogs. If recreating in bear country is an odds game, they’re not doing you any favors. As much as we love and trust them, they’re unpredictable. And they can make things worse as often as they make things better.
“It’s a personal thing, it really is,” Smith said. “We work in statistics with a pool of instances. But you are not a pool of instances. You’re you.”
This story was originally published by Mountain Journal at mountainjournal.org.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Five judges so far file to run for SC Supreme Court seat
description: Five have filed to run for SC’s highest court, including the ex-wife of a late state representative and two sitting Appeals Court judges.
text:
The South Carolina Supreme Court in Columbia. (Photo by Mary Ann Chastain / Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Five judges, so far, have filed to run for a seat on South Carolina’s highest court, including the ex-wife of a late Republican state representative and two sitting Appeals Court judges.
Hopefuls still have until Aug. 24 to turn in an application, according to the panel that screens judicial applicants in the state. To date, the five candidates seeking a 10-year term on the state Supreme Court are:

Administrative Law Court Judge Ralph “Tripp” Anderson
S.C. Appeals Court Judge John Geathers
Judge Eugene “Bubba” Griffith, Jr., a Circuit Court judge from Newberry
S.C. Appeals Court Judge Blake Hewitt
Judge Maite Murphy, a Circuit Court judge from Summerville

South Carolina Supreme Court justices, and most other judges, are elected by the legislature. The Supreme Court opening comes after former Justice John Few dropped his bid for re-election in March, a day before the Legislature was scheduled to vote.
Last year, Few became the first sitting justice in more than 20 years to face a challenge to keep his seat. His three opponents included the former leader of the state House.
SC Supreme Court election canceled after sitting justice drops out of race

Few dropped out of the running when it became clear he would not win and that Jay Lucas, the former House speaker, had sealed up the vote.
Lucas was criticized as a political insider with no judicial experience, though that did not appear to deter his supporters. However, Few’s resignation ultimately forced the election’s cancellation and reopening of the application process.
So far, Lucas is not among the applicants.
Of those on the list, Murphy is the latest to file.
The now 57-year-old also ran in 2022 for the seat vacated by former Justice Kaye Hearn, who was retiring.
Murphy dropped out almost two months before screenings began amid questions about whether her then-husband, former state Rep. Chris Murphy, then chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, would lead to too much influence. Hearn, who Murphy sought to replace, had ascended to the Supreme Court while her husband, state Rep. George Hearn, R-Conway, was in office and a member of the same committee.
Kaye Hearn served on the high court from 2009 until early 2023.  Her final opinion, written for a 3-2 majority, struck down the state’s first so-called “fetal heartbeat” law as violating the state constitution’s protection from unreasonable invasions of privacy.
In considering her replacement, legislators and lawyers questioned whether Hearn, one of only two women ever to serve on the Supreme Court, should be replaced by a man or a woman. They ultimately elected Court of Appeals Judge David “Gary” Hill.
The Legislature then passed a new version of the law that bans abortions after six weeks of pregnancy, which the all-male court then upheld.
Murphy started her career as a magistrate in 2009 and rose to the circuit court bench in 2013. If legislators were to elect her, Murphy would join sitting Justice Letitia Verdin as a second woman on the state Supreme Court.
Legislators elect 3rd female SC Supreme Court justice in state history

Murphy’s application comes less than a month after the death of her ex-husband in his home in Dorchester County. The two divorced in May, court records show. Chris Murphy resigned from the House in 2025.
Of the other candidates, Anderson and Geathers have the most experience. Both started their judicial careers in 1995 on the Administrative Law Court.
Anderson has been on that court ever since and became the court’s chief judge in 2009. The 66-year-old Columbia judge has made numerous unsuccessful runs for the Supreme Court.
The General Assembly elected Geathers to the Court of Appeals in 2008. He was last re-elected in 2024.
Before becoming a judge, he was senior counsel to the Office of Senate Research for the state Senate.
If elected, the 65-year-old from Blythewood would be the third Black justice on the state Supreme Court since Reconstruction.
A recent law change also would mean Geathers could serve all but seven months of the 10-year term. The law, signed Thursday by Gov. Henry McMaster, raised the mandatory retirement age for South Carolina judges from 72 to 74. Geathers could stay on the bench through the end of 2035.
Geathers’ Appeals Court colleague, Hewitt, is making his third consecutive run for the Supreme Court.
The Conway native has made two unsuccessful bids. The first was in 2024 for the vacancy caused by the retirement of former Chief Justice Don Beatty and ascension of now Chief Justice John Kittredge to that role. The second was last year as a challenger to Few. Hewitt, 48, was first elected to the bench in 2019 after years as an appellate lawyer.
Griffith has been a Circuit Court judge since 2009. Before that, the 62-year-old was in private practice, reopening the office formerly operated by his father and grandfather.
His grandfather, the late Judge Steve C. Griffith, was also a judge, serving 22 years in the 8th Circuit.
Hearings begin Nov. 16 to screen all applicants. An election is tentatively scheduled for March 3, 2027.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico officials say they’re still at an ‘impasse’ with feds over spreading chromium plume
description: New Mexico Environment Department officials said this week that the Los Alamos National Laboratory has not complied with its February demands aimed at quickly and safely stopping the spread of a massive underground chromium plume that recently reached the boundaries of a nearby Pueblo.
text:
A depiction of the Los Alamos National Laboratory chromium plume as of 2021. State environmental officials said Aug. 13, 2026, at an interim legislative meeting that they are still at an “impasse” with federal Energy Department and Los Alamos Laboratory officials about the best way to remediate the plume.(Photo courtesy New Mexico Environment Department)New Mexico Environment Department officials said this week that the Los Alamos National Laboratory has not complied with its February demands aimed at quickly and safely stopping the spread of a massive underground chromium plume that recently reached the boundaries of a nearby Pueblo. 
The NMED in February issued a $6 million fine against LANL, asserting the federal laboratory had failed to comply with state water standards and the terms of a discharge permit related to its handling of the decades-old plume of chromium. The toxic chemical can increase risk of certain cancers after long-term ingestion. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lab workers historically used chromium as a way to prevent pipes from rusting in a power plant’s cooling towers and then periodically flushed chromium-contaminated water down Sandia Canyon between 1956 and 1972. The plume was discovered in the groundwater supply in 2005. 
Since then, how to mitigate the plume has been the subject of ongoing and sometimes contentious debate between state and federal officials, namely the Environment Department and the U.S. Department of Energy. 
In the meantime, the plume has continued to spread. State officials announced in November that the chemical spill had spread beyond LANL property to San de Ildefonso Pueblo land. 
Federal and state officials have stressed that the plume’s spread does not pose imminent threats to drinking water in the Pueblo or in Los Alamos County because it is not near any known private or public wells.
Santiago Rodriguez, deputy director of NMED’s Resource Protection Division, told lawmakers on the interim Radioactive and Hazardous Materials Committee on Thursday that NMED and LANL are still at an “impasse.” The state and federal governments still differ on the best way to treat the contaminated water once it’s been pumped from the aquifer, among other disagreements, he said.
NMED officials contend the treated water should not be reinjected into its original aquifer, saying doing so actually propels the plume forward. They are urging the federal agency and laboratory to come up with alternative measures. 
LANL officials stopped attending regular workshops between the Pueblo, state agencies and Los Alamos County shortly after the February lawsuit, Rodriguez said. The workshops were aimed at placing “key decision makers and impacted parties together in one room to discuss and develop plans for a path forward,” he said. 
Stephanie Gallagher, a DOE spokesperson, told Source NM on Friday that the department was working on a response to Source NM’s questions regarding the Thursday meeting. 
Lawmakers request feds and state officials find third party in chromium plume fight

However, the department has held its own public meetings in recent months and also continued to pressure NMED to allow it to resume reinjecting treated water back into the aquifer. In late June, the DOE issued a statement arguing that injecting the treated water should begin as soon as possible. 
“Groundwater well sampling data shows that the [reinjection] has a positive effect,” the June 25 statement reads. “Injection establishes a hydraulic barrier in the area of injection, which helps to control and reduce the plume, while also preserving aquifer water, a precious natural resource.”
The DOE also cites recommendations from an independent research team’s 980-page report, released December 2024, that says its “single most important recommendation” is to restart injections while other studies and investigations move forward. 
Still, NMED officials have pushed the DOE to find alternative uses for the water once the chromium is removed, while also ordering them to pump a minimum of 170,000 gallons per day of contaminated water. 
One possible alternative the NMED has pointed to is to “land apply” the treated water, which would mean allowing the treated water to more gently reabsorb into the aquifer by spraying or sprinkling it onto the surface. The NMED’s lawsuit does not identify a preferred alternative to injection but instead seeks to spur federal officials to come up with a plan as soon as possible. 
“We are using the tools that we have to hold them accountable,” Justin Ball, chief of the NMED’s Ground Water Quality Bureau, told lawmakers Thursday. “To me, it’s shocking that a world-renowned research institution can’t think of alternative options for disposing of this water, and that they, frankly, won’t even seem to consider alternative options.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Bureau of Elections waives fees, admits error led to Doug Lloyd’s late AG campaign filing
description: The Michigan Bureau of Elections admitted their own error caused an issue underlying a campaign finance complaint against Doug Lloyd, the Michigan Republican Party nominee for Michigan attorney general, which alleged that his pre-convention finance report was knowingly both late and inaccurate. “Because our office mistakenly provided inaccurate information,[...]
text:
Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd (left) and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini (right) at the Michigan Republican Party Endorsement Convention. March 28, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceThe Michigan Bureau of Elections admitted their own error caused an issue underlying a campaign finance complaint against Doug Lloyd, the Michigan Republican Party nominee for Michigan attorney general, which alleged that his pre-convention finance report was knowingly both late and inaccurate.
“Because our office mistakenly provided inaccurate information, we will waive fees associated with the late filing and void the Failure to File notice,” said a letter sent to the Lloyd campaign on Friday from the Michigan Department of State.
A spokesperson for the department confirmed to Michigan Advance that the full complaint had not been resolved, only the portion pertaining to the failure to file.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Michigan Democratic Party initially filed the complaint against Lloyd on Thursday. 
Lloyd’s campaign had told the Advance on Thursday that the Michigan Department of State’s Bureau of Elections provided the campaign with an incorrect deadline to file its pre-election finance filing, causing the discrepancy.
Under the Michigan Campaign Finance Act, pre-election reports — including those in the lead-up to each party’s nominating convention, which will take place for the Republicans on Aug. 22 — are due 11 days prior to the event, making Lloyd’s filing due on Aug. 11. The complaint filed by the state’s Democratic Party asserts, in line with online records in Michigan’s campaign finance database, that Lloyd filed his report a day late, on Aug. 12.
However, according to an email provided by Keith Schipper, a spokesperson for the Lloyd campaign, a staff member at the Bureau of Elections told the treasurer of Lloyd’s campaign that the pre-convention report was due on Aug. 16 and the close of books for the report was Aug. 11.
“We always seek to assist campaigns in understanding campaign finance requirements, and we regret that we provided accurate information in response to your question,” the Friday letter from the Department of State said. “Accordingly, we are taking the action described above. However, in the future the campaign should also review our website, materials, applicable laws, and notifications from our office to confirm compliance with filing due dates.”
The letter also notes that “candidate committees supporting candidates seeking nomination at a convention were provided notice of the correct due date” in early August, though Schipper said that the Lloyd campaign never received that notice.
The complaint also argued that the listed campaign contributions and expenditures, which show that its latest reported contribution is on Feb. 28, 2026, and its last reported expenditure is on Jan. 17, 2026, are “entirely implausible” for a report spanning from Jan. 1 to Aug. 6, 2026.
The letter from the Michigan Department of State did not address that portion of the complaint.
In a statement to the Advance, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said, “the fact that the report was filed late, because the Lloyd campaign is apparently unable to subtract 11 days from the date of the convention on their own, is the least concerning aspect of all of this.”
“By the Lloyd campaign’s own account, once the campaign learned that they had blown the deadline, they made the intentional decision to file a false and illegal campaign finance report,” Hertel said. “Their report certifies that its ‘contents are true, accurate and complete,’ but entirely omits more than five months of campaign-finance activity they were required to report.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Justice family to share ownership of The Greenbrier
description: A New York-based investment firm will now have controlling ownership in The Greenbrier, one of West Virginia’s top tourist attractions, company officials announced Friday.
text:
The family of U.S. Sen. Jim Justice and Kennedy Lewis Investment Management announced on Friday that the two had agreed to a joint venture for The Greenbrier resort, located in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia. (Photo by Chris Jackson /West Virginia Watch)A New York-based investment firm will now have controlling ownership in The Greenbrier, one of West Virginia’s top tourist attractions, company officials announced Friday. 
The family of U.S. Sen. Jim Justice and Kennedy Lewis Investment Management announced that the two had agreed to a joint venture for the facility. 
West Virginia MetroNews reporter Brad McElhinny, who has closely followed the resort’s financial strife, reported the amount was $500 million. 
The transaction “provides The Greenbrier with a robust financial foundation and underpins long-term investment in the resort, its facilities and the guest experience,” the companies said in the news release. 
“The Greenbrier is a truly unique American institution, with a remarkable history, dedicated employees and a special connection to West Virginia and its guests,” David Chene, Kennedy Lewis’s managing partner, said in a statement Friday. “By combining Kennedy Lewis’s financial, strategic and operational resources, Lloyd Nathan’s thoughtful and proven oversight as Chairman and the Justice Family’s deep local roots, we have built a powerful platform to invest in the property’s long-term future, and reinforce its standing among the premier destination resorts in the world.”
“Today marks an exciting new chapter for The Greenbrier and an important moment for everyone who loves this resort,” Jill Justice, daughter of Sen. Jim Justice, said in the news release. “This property is so much more than a resort. It is part of the history of West Virginia, an economic anchor for this community and a place where generations of families have celebrated the most important moments of their lives. Our collaboration provides the financial strength, expertise and long-term investment needed to protect everything that makes The Greenbrier special.”
Kennedy Lewis appointed Lloyd Nathan to chair The Greenbrier’s board.
“The Greenbrier is one of the truly irreplaceable destination resorts in the United States,” Nathan said in the news release. “Very few properties can match its history, natural beauty, scale, amenities and emotional connection with generations of guests. Our intent is not to change what makes The Greenbrier special but to invest in its future, enhance what makes it exceptional and ensure America’s Resort continues to thrive for generations to come.
The Greenbrier has also been authorized to continue operating its casino while the West Virginia Lottery Commission reviews the transaction, the news release says. Earlier this week, the Justices indicated they may close the casino and lay off 90 employees rather than wait for the Lottery commission to sign off on the deal, MetroNews reported.
The resort will remain open and fully operational throughout the transition, the news release says. Existing reservations, meetings, conferences, weddings and other scheduled events will continue as planned.
The Justice family has owned The Greenbrier since 2009, when now Sen. Jim Justice bought it out of bankruptcy. Over the last several years, financial challenges related to the property have mounted for the Justices, who have owed millions in loan repayments as well as taxes on The Greenbrier and several other nearby properties.
Earlier this year, the Justices alleged in a lawsuit that Texas-based TRT Holdings, parent company of Omni Hotels, conspired with Carter Bank to stop the Justices from making payments on their loans. Carter Bank & Trust was a major lender for the Justices when they bought The Greenbrier. In recent years, the relationship between the family and the bank has become fraught, as the bank claims that numerous loan and interest payments have gone unpaid. 
The hotel, facing foreclosure due to the Justices’ unpaid debt, came close to being auctioned at the Greenbrier County Courthouse in 2024. 
Along with the transaction, the Justice family and TRT agreed to settle the civil lawsuit, according to court documents. 
The resort employs 1,500 to 2,000 workers, depending on the season.
In a statement Friday, Gov. Patrick Morrisey said he welcomed the investment firm to West Virginia. 
“With Kennedy Lewis now officially controlling the resort, I welcome them to West Virginia,” he said. “I also want everyone to know — especially those in Greenbrier County — that I will do everything in my power to protect this historic West Virginia jewel and its employees.
“I have asked the Lottery Commission to take all necessary steps to prevent the loss of Greenbrier employees during this transition of ownership. I’m hopeful that Kennedy Lewis and the entire Greenbrier team will help restore the beauty of the resort to its former glory.”

title: Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte joins Ex-Guard for Kalispell ribbon-cutting
description: For many Montanans, colliding with animals on the roadway is not a when, it’s an if, and it’s only fitting that a company that specializes in high-end grille guards for semi-trucks and pickups would manufacture them in Montana.  On Thursday, Iowa-based Ex-Guard held a ribbon-cutting ceremony with Gov. Greg Gianforte for its new manufacturing and logistics fa[...]
text:
Ex-Guard manager Ryan Holt and Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte cutting the ribbon for the Ex-Guard manufacturing facility in Kalispell. (Courtesy photo)For many Montanans, colliding with animals on the roadway is not a when, it’s an if, and it’s only fitting that a company that specializes in high-end grille guards for semi-trucks and pickups would manufacture them in Montana. 
On Thursday, Iowa-based Ex-Guard held a ribbon-cutting ceremony with Gov. Greg Gianforte for its new manufacturing and logistics facility in Kalispell.
“We needed access to the West Coast and Canadian markets, and Montana was a very attractive place to move part of our company to expand the business,” Ex-Guard manager Ryan Holt told the Daily Montanan. 
Holt said the reception from the local government, as well as Montana’s overarching focus on reducing governmental barriers in business and continual reductions in income taxes, made the state an appealing place to set up shop. 
The Ex-Guard facility is located at the Glacier Rail Park, a 44-acre property that has been a decade-long focus of Kalispell’s core area redevelopment project. The company purchased its lot in 2025, and Holt said they bought an adjacent lot this spring for future expansion. 
Ex-Guard’s high-tensile steel grille guards are “built to take the hit, keep trucks moving, and reduce downtime,” according to the company. Ex-Guard’s website is rife with testimonials from truck drivers that hit animals on the highway, but came away with vehicles intact. 
Montana is one of the leading states when it comes to wildlife collisions on the roadways, according to the state Department of Transportation. More than 6,000 carcasses are collected by maintenance crews from the state’s roadways annually, and the Highway Patrol responds to more than 3,200 wildlife-related collisions each year. 
The event was the latest in a series of high-profile business openings Gianforte has attended in recent months. 
“This investment means more investment in our communities and opportunities for Montanans across the state, especially right here in the Flathead,” Gianforte said in prepared remarks. “I often say Montana is open for business, and my job with the government … is to stay out of your way so that you can do your business and prosper.”
Gianforte was a businessman before he became a politician and often refers to himself as Montana’s CEO. A priority of his tenure in office has been bolstering the state’s business-friendly environment. 
“If you want jobs, you need employers, and government doesn’t create jobs,” Gianforte told the Daily Montanan. “We have employees, and they do very important work, but they don’t grow the economy. We need private sector businesses like Ex-Guard in our communities to provide livelihoods.”
Gianforte pointed out that the new facility — which will have around 40 employees at full capacity — also created jobs in construction and landscaping, which are key parts of a growing economy. 
The Governor’s Office in recent weeks has announced Montana is among the top five states with the fastest-growing economies, and that the state ranks second in annual hourly wage growth.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, from 2024 to 2025, the average hourly wage in Montana increased 4.7%, to $29.27.
“Because of our policies, basically letting people keep more of what they earn, getting rid of excessive regulations, we’re one of only two states where wage growth has actually exceeded inflation over the last five years,” Gianforte said.
The increase in wages isn’t enough to make up for high housing prices in Montana, especially in areas like the Flathead Valley and Bozeman, but Gianforte said he’s working on bringing down the cost of housing too.
He said his administration has cut regulations on new buildings, which account for a high portion of the cost of housing.
“You want wages to go up faster than inflation, but I don’t want to minimize at all the affordability issues,” Gianforte said.

description: After days of deadly storms, historic flooding and widespread power outages, Indiana Gov. text:
Flood damage in Cambridge City, Indiana, on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo courtesy Indiana Governor Flickr)After days of deadly storms, historic flooding and widespread power outages, Indiana Gov. Mike Braun on Friday requested a presidential emergency declaration to bring federal assistance into the state.
The request, submitted through the Federal Emergency Management Agency, seeks federal support for emergency response costs. That could include expenses associated with water rescues, restoring electricity and other immediate work in affected communities, according to the governor’s office.
The severe weather began Aug. 11 and has included tornadoes, extensive flooding and a derecho.
The emergency has caused deaths and injuries, destroyed homes, businesses and infrastructure, displaced families and disrupted emergency services and communications, state officials said. The governor’s office did not provide numbers for the deaths, injuries or damaged properties in its announcement.
Power outages peaked at more than 300,000, while flooding reached 100-year marks in some areas and damaged or closed roads, according to the governor’s office.
Story continues below.



“I will do everything in my power to protect Hoosier lives and livelihoods as we respond to this historic severe weather,” Braun said. “I have mobilized state and local resources, declared a Statewide Disaster Emergency and deployed the Indiana National Guard. Now, I am requesting immediate federal assistance to strengthen those efforts and provide direct assistance to impacted communities.”
Braun’s federal request follows his statewide disaster emergency declaration issued Thursday. That order directed the Indiana Department of Homeland Security to coordinate assistance among local, state and federal agencies.
The governor also mobilized the Indiana National Guard to provide personnel and resources in Gary, Munster and Hobart. State agencies have provided communities with boats and water-rescue personnel, debris-removal equipment, emergency generators, fuel, oxygen support and evacuation assistance.
Hoosier officials said the National Guard and state agencies remain mobilized as communities begin recovery efforts.
Indiana 211 was accepting property-damage reports Friday from Dearborn, Franklin, Henry, Lake, LaPorte, Madison, Newton, Pike, Porter, Pulaski and Wayne counties. Residents can call 211 or 866-211-9966.
Officials directed residents to 511in.org for road conditions and on.in.gov/travel-status for county travel advisories. People facing an emergency should call 911.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: As summer heat waves intensify, North Carolina advocates push for farmworker protection
description: When the heat index tops 105°F, as it has this week in central North Carolina, the National Weather Service issues a heat advisory. Meteorologists warn people to limit their time in the sun and advise that hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat-related illness. But for many workers, taking a break from summer’s extreme […]
text:
Farmworkers tend to young seedlings during a sweltering summer day. (Photo: Getty Images) When the heat index tops 105°F, as it has this week in central North Carolina, the National Weather Service issues a heat advisory. Meteorologists warn people to limit their time in the sun and advise that hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat-related illness.
But for many workers, taking a break from summer’s extreme conditions is not an option.
Andressia Ramirez, an advocacy and civic engagement manager at Casa Azul de Wilson, said farmworkers in North Carolina are expected to work long hours even in triple-digit conditions.
Ramirez was joined by a group of Latine agricultural workers at the state capitol Thursday to highlight the contributions of immigrant farmworkers and the workplace dangers they face.
Ramirez, who grew up in rural Wilson County, said she was recently visiting a farmworker camp when she noticed a young man sitting alone on a bucket underneath a tree.
The man told Ramirez he had a fever. He should have been resting inside the mobile home, but the coolest place he could find on the 95-degree day was outdoors underneath a tree.
In North Carolina, farmworker housing is still not required to have air conditioning.
“This isn’t just about one young man. It is about the conditions we have allowed to become normal,” said Ramirez.
Esmeralda Juarez, Xitlali Gomez, and Andressia Ramirez highlight the need for better workplace conditions for workers in agriculture and construction. (Photo: Alanna Joyner/Progress NC)
The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration offers guidelines for prevention of heat illness, but it has not yet implemented any specific heat standards for workers apart from its general duty clause.
Seven states have enacted their own specific occupational heat safety standards designed to protect workers when temperatures become hazardous. North Carolina is not among those states. State lawmakers have said requiring farmers to follow heat safety rules would hurt them economically.
The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), which is under the CDC, recommends limiting worker heat stress, enforcing work-rest cycles, rotating tasks, and encouraging hydration during moderate work, but those are not legal requirements.
Esmeralda Juarez was never offered those protections.
Juarez, who works for the Kinston nonprofit NC Field, told reporters Thursday that she began working in the tobacco fields at age 13.
“My head would hurt, my stomach ached, and I would feel so nauseated that I’d want to throw up,” Juarez said.
Juarez said many farmworker families endure pain and unbearable heat without complaint out of need.
“Many people would tell me, if you don’t feel well, don’t go,” said Juarez. “But poverty does not give families that kind of choice.”
Juarez said agriculture is one of the most dangerous industries in the U.S. and North Carolina lawmakers must do more to protect farmworkers and child laborers from extreme conditions.
Farmworkers sue over Trump’s low wages for foreign guest workers

“Water alone is not enough. Workers need shade. We need training that we can actually understand, and time to adjust to extreme heat,” said Juarez.
Immigrant workers make up 12% of North Carolina’s workforce, and by conservative estimates contribute $60 billion annually to the state’s economy, according to the left-leaning N.C. Budget and Tax Center.
Ramirez said she often hears lawmakers talk about struggles that farmers are facing, with higher input costs, tariffs, and this summer’s punishing drought.
“I agree, our farmers deserve support, but why must one lose for the other to gain?” Ramirez said. “We can support our farmers without sacrificing the people who work in their fields.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas firefighters union advocating for staffing increase alleges government violated free speech
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas firefighters union and county government are “at loggerheads with each other,” a federal judge said Wednesday, complaining they threw the case at him to solve after months of conflict. The Kansas City, Kansas Professional Firefighters Association’s lawsuit against the Unified Government of Wyandotte County was filed against the backdrop of[...]
text:
The International Association of Fire Fighters Local 64 is suing the Unified Government of Wyandotte County over alleged free speech violations rooted in understaffing issues at the Kansas City, Kansas, Fire Department. Attorneys for the union and the government appeared on Aug. 12, 2026, at a Kansas federal courthouse, which appears here in April 2025 in Topeka. (Photo by Grace Hills/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas firefighters union and county government are “at loggerheads with each other,” a federal judge said Wednesday, complaining they threw the case at him to solve after months of conflict.
The Kansas City, Kansas Professional Firefighters Association’s lawsuit against the Unified Government of Wyandotte County was filed against the backdrop of a December fire that left four firefighters with second- and third-degree burns. A federal agency investigated the incident, finding that one of the factors that contributed to the injuries was understaffing. 
The union said its members had been trying to speak about inadequate staffing levels with the Unified Government’s board of commissioners, which was also named in the Aug. 4 lawsuit, and public safety committee, but the Unified Government “repeatedly quashed these requests, falsely claiming that state law forbids the union from speaking to elected officials about issues affecting the KCKFD,” the lawsuit said.
The Unified Government forbade union representatives from speaking at monthly public safety committee meetings, which the union said violated its members’ First and 14th Amendment rights.
The Unified Government argued the union was subverting its shared collective bargaining agreement, which includes a minimum staffing requirement.
In August 2024, the Unified Government’s board of commissioners approved a revenue-neutral budget for 2025 that reduced staffing on ladder trucks and other equipment from four to three. The National Fire Protection Association’s standard is a minimum of four firefighters. 
About 3:45 a.m. on December 29, 2025, the Kansas City, Kansas, Fire Department responded to a fire at an abandoned house. The house’s first floor collapsed, and four firefighters fell through, into the basement, where the fire had likely been burning for “an extended time,” according to a federal investigation. One firefighter was trapped from the waist down and screamed for help, according to the federal report. The first to fall in tried to radio “mayday” but wasn’t readable, according to the federal report. 
The four were rescued and hospitalized, and they survived with second- and third-degree burns and minor injuries.
The investigation from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health found that eight factors contributed to the career firefighters’ injuries.
“Responding units faced two of the most dangerous types of structure fires. A below grade fire combined with an abandoned structure significantly raises the life safety risk to firefighters,” a report published in April said.
Among the factors were communication errors, risks associated with fires in abandoned structures and inadequate staffing.
The firefighters union homed in on the inadequate staffing factor in its efforts to persuade the Unified Government to modify its budget and increase fire department staffing levels. The union asked to appear on the public safety committee’s agenda instead of speaking during the designated, time-limited public comment period, which the Unified Government denied. The government’s attorney said union representatives can’t communicate directly with elected officials about topics subject to bargaining. 
Attorneys for the union want a federal judge to grant them a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, which could force the Unified Government to allow union representatives to speak at public meetings before the Unified Government finalizes its budget in September. 
Jake Miller with Kansas City-based firm Grissom and Miller and Tamara Imam with a Washington, D.C.-based labor law firm are representing the union, and the Unified Government is represented by Ryan Denk. 
U.S. District Court Judge Toby Crouse criticized the union’s attorneys at a hearing Wednesday for failing to notify the Unified Government’s attorney that they were filing a request for a temporary restraining and preliminary injunction, noting that lawyers typically “have the courtesy to pick up the phone and have a conversation.”
Denk said Wednesday the Unified Government would try to get the case dismissed. 
He said in a Tuesday court filing that before the lawsuit, union represented didn’t respond to a written offer to coordinate a private meeting with a designated Unified Government official.
Counsel wrote in a May 12 letter to the union: “If you would like to schedule a formal meet and confer session, please let us know and we will proceed with scheduling the same.”
“The Unified Government never received a response to this letter and the plaintiff never requested to meet and confer relating to the subject of staffing,” the court filing said. “Rather, the plaintiff waited three months and then filed a lawsuit along with a request for an emergency TRO due to the timing of the last Public Works and Safety Subcommittee meeting.”
The timing, Denk said, was driven by the union’s failure to meet and confer with the Unified Government in private.
Crouse said the parties were “throwing” the case at him after they’ve been in conflict for months. 
“I’ve got to deal with it,” he said, and, he added, “I don’t know half of what you know.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Rep. Mandy Lindsay defends caucus payments during ethics hearing
description: Colorado Rep. Mandy Lindsay told lawmakers on Friday that she did not fully understand the level of financial responsibility involved when she became co-chair of the House Democratic Caucus, and that there was an unset expectation around the accounting and organization of caucus funds. “I did not interpret that role this way. I ran for […]
text:
The Colorado House of Representatives is pictured on the final day of the 2026 legislative session on May 13, 2026, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Rep. Mandy Lindsay told lawmakers on Friday that she did not fully understand the level of financial responsibility involved when she became co-chair of the House Democratic Caucus, and that there was an unset expectation around the accounting and organization of caucus funds.
“I did not interpret that role this way. I ran for this role to feed people, to connect us, to host fun events, to plan fun retreats,” she said. “Looking back now, obviously, I did not know what I was undertaking and did not understand the level of responsibility I was undertaking.”
Lindsay, an Aurora Democrat, made the comments during the final day of an evidentiary hearing for an ethics complaint she is facing over alleged mismanagement of caucus funds. She was the last witness to speak with the bipartisan House Ethics Committee. As caucus co-char, Lindsay is in charge of collecting member dues, leading meetings, supplying meals occasionally, and other morale boosters such as birthday cards and flower deliveries.
“We made sure everyone had breakfast and lunch all the time, and sometimes we were being really scrappy to figure out how to do it. To me, that was the end product that mattered,” she said. “I want to nurture and make everyone in the caucus feel that they are a part of something, that we have fun, that we care about each other, and that this workplace can be full of people who have meaningful relationships.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The complaint is based on a series of reimbursements Lindsay made to herself from the caucus bank account. Some of those checks were initially written in error, she said, but the reimbursements were ultimately for thousands of dollars she spent in personal funds for caucus activities over the years.
Colorado ethics panel begins hearing over Rep. Mandy Lindsay’s handling of caucus bank account

“I’m not a bookkeeper,” she said. “But I wasn’t just willy-nilly spending and not knowing how much we had or not knowing how much (dues money) people owed.”
She said it is “abundantly clear” she did not know enough about general accounting practices. Witnesses throughout the two-day hearing said Lindsay’s actions were akin to disorganized bookkeeping, not intentional negligence.
Both Lindsay and co-chair Rep. Junie Joseph, a Boulder Democrat, described a dysfunctional relationship in their partnership. Joseph said it took months for her to access the caucus’s bank account and when she did, she noticed the seemingly suspect transactions. She said she then asked Rep. Bob Marshall, a Democrat from Highlands Ranch, to look over the bank account because of his finance experience.
“I needed a second set of eyes on it,” she said. “Rep. Lindsay and I were not having a lot of conversations, and I didn’t want it to just be me going to her. I wanted to make sure someone else looked at this.”
Marshall ended up filing the complaint against Lindsay early this year.
“I already had big issues with the caucus fund in terms of putting money in and not knowing what the hell it’s doing. I realized it was a big stinking pile of mess, but it wasn’t my mess. But Junie brought this, put it right in front of me,” he said.
Lindsay addressed the largest reimbursement check on Friday, a payment for about $6,000. She said she originally wrote the check when she thought a hotel charge for a caucus retreat in November 2024 would hit her personal card on file. She realized a few weeks later, following what she described as a tumultuous time in her personal life, that the caucus card was the one actually charged.
“I realized that I had foolishly, and crazily, misunderstood what (an email from the hotel) said,” she said. “I was horrified.”
But Lindsay kept the check as a partial reimbursement to herself for accrued costs as co-chair. She hadn’t done the hard math of totaling exactly what she was owed, she said, but she knew it was more than the cost of that hotel charge.
“Once I realized that the charge had not been made to my personal account, I was like ‘OK, well I wrote this check, what should I do?’” she said. “I believe I should have done something different about it, process-wise, but I was also owed about seven grand. And so I’m beginning this process now.”
The committee will make a final determination on the complaint during a meeting on Sept. 4. Members could dismiss it entirely or make a range of recommendations to House leadership about consequences.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. House candidate Bohannan commits to spend more on cancer research
description: IOWA CITY – Morgan Newman was a 24-year-old dental assistant when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer, a disease that is more common in women ages 35-64.  “I had a metastatic recurrence to my lungs,” Newman, of Norwalk, said as she sat by her mom, Kendra, at an event Friday at Sidekick Coffee & Books […]
text:
Christina Bohannan, Iowa City Democrat running for U.S. House in Iowa’s 1st District, talks with American Cancer Society volunteers and staff at Sidekick Coffee & Books on Aug. 14, 2026 in Iowa City. (Photo by Erin Jordan for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
IOWA CITY – Morgan Newman was a 24-year-old dental assistant when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer, a disease that is more common in women ages 35-64. 
“I had a metastatic recurrence to my lungs,” Newman, of Norwalk, said as she sat by her mom, Kendra, at an event Friday at Sidekick Coffee & Books in Iowa City. “She sat by my side and watched me go through everything I did.” 
Ten years later, Newman is cancer free. But her battle led her to the American Cancer Society, where she now is the Iowa grassroots manager. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Newman and six others talked Friday with Christina Bohannan, an Iowa City Democrat running for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District. The ACS’s Cancer Action Network is asking Iowa candidates for Congress and governor to state their commitment to fighting cancer, a disease that an estimated 2 million Americans will be diagnosed with this year. 
Iowa has the fastest-rising cancer rate in the nation and the state is second, behind Kentucky, in the number of incidences of cancer. The Iowa Cancer Registry expects 21,700 new invasive cancers will be diagnosed this year and 6,400 more Iowans will die from the disease. 
“One of the things that is really alarming to me is not only the number of people I talk with who have cancer, but the number of young people,” Bohannan said. “The age that people are starting to get diagnosed is younger in a way we didn’t hear about in the past.” 
People under 50 are increasingly being diagnosed with some cancers, including colorectal, breast, prostate, uterine and pancreatic cancer, the American Cancer Society reported in 2025. The chances of young people dying from cancer have declined, but the anxiety and expense of fighting the disease take a toll on millions of American families. 
Bohannan, 55, felt some of that anxiety after a recent health screening, she told the group.  
“Recently, I had an abnormal mammogram and it was very, very scary to me,” she said.  
Cancer funding
Bogdan Buzdugan, 23, a cancer researcher at the University of Iowa, said he chose his career path after a friend was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a type of cancerous brain tumor. He wanted to know if Bohannan would support annual increases for cancer research funding to the National Institutes of Health. 
“That is absolutely something we need to support and increase,” Bohannan said. 
Bohannan criticized her opponent, incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican from Ottumwa, for voting last year for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which slashed spending on healthcare and is predicted to result in 15 million more people not having health insurance coverage by 2034, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. 
The biggest change under the bill is a requirement that most Medicaid recipients spend at least 80 hours a month working, volunteering or going to school in order to keep their coverage.
Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist, recently supported reauthorizing early breast cancer screening. ACS-CAN said it is “in discussions” with Miller-Meeks’ campaign about scheduling her for a similar forum.
Bohannan, whose father died from emphysema after many years of smoking, said she would support continued funding for smoking-cessation programs and oppose efforts to reduce government regulation of tobacco. 
Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer deaths in Iowa. 
“Many people start (using tobacco products) young before they really know the risks and then they get addicted,” Bohannan said. “That’s something I really want to work on.”
Loss of rural health care options
In her travels across Iowa’s 1st District, which covers the southeastern quadrant of the state, Bohannan said she’s heard about Iowans having to drive an hour or more for doctor appointments because some rural hospitals have closed. 
MercyOne closed its health care center in Ottumwa in January and the Southeast Iowa Regional Medical Center in Fort Madison ended birthing and delivery services last December. 
Rural residents also are underrepresented in cancer research trials, Bohannan said. 
“I want to make sure our rural residents are included in some of those studies because there are some issues that affect rural areas sometimes more than other areas,” she said. 
Agricultural risks
Because cancer risk is a mix of genetics, lifestyle and environmental factors, it’s hard to pinpoint exactly why rates are rising in Iowa. But agricultural chemicals have been under increased scrutiny, especially as cities struggle to remove nitrate from public drinking water.
Bohannan said she would like to make more federal money available to incentivize farmers to implement conservation practices, like growing cover crops, that reduce fertilizer runoff. She does not want to tie federal crop insurance to farming practices. 
“We need to keep crop insurance for what it was intended for, which is to make sure that there’s a little bit of a fallback there if things go wrong,” she said.

title: Mississippi faith leaders denounce Ag Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Muslims, Sharia
description: Rev. Andy Andrews, of St. Christopher's Church, speaks during a press conference concerning Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Islam and Sharia law at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in Jackson on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026.
text:
Mississippi faith leaders on Friday denounced recent comments about Muslims made by state Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, a gubernatorial candidate in next year’s elections.
“This reckless and dangerous rhetoric by an elected official and a candidate for governor has no place in our public discourse,” said Rhoda Yoder of Open Door Mennonite Church, on behalf of Working Together Jackson and Working Together Mississippi, two groups that organized the event. 
The groups invited Gipson to meet with them for “an open and honest dialogue.”
The recent appointment of attorney Assma Ali as municipal judge by the small Mississippi Delta town of Benoit drew social media backlash from internet trolls and a few Mississippi politicians, and even reportedly some threats, because she is Muslim. Her appointment prompted Republican Gipson, a former longtime state lawmaker, to renew his vows to ban “Sharia law and the influence of Islam” if he’s elected governor, even though use of Sharia law in Mississippi courts was already banned by the Legislature in 2015 when Gipson was a lawmaker. 
Leaders from several faith communities gathered at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in downtown Jackson on Friday in response to a social media post Gipson made about the museum and invited Gipson to meet with them.
Gipson has made several social media posts about Islam and Sharia law in recent days, including: “If you are among those who think Sharia law is ‘not an issue in Mississippi,’ you’d better think again. You see what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan. But did you know that in our own capital city, in Mississippi, there is a center for Muslim Culture at the Planetarium in Jackson?”
The organizations said that one commenter on Gipson’s post called for the museum to be burned down. They said they have historically felt safe in Mississippi but that this has prompted them to take extra security precautions.
Many people and groups have criticized comments by Gipson and others and have come out in support of Ali, saying the U.S. native is a qualified and upstanding member of Mississippi’s legal community. Ali has vowed to uphold the U.S. Constitution and Mississippi law in her role as a city judge, mainly handling traffic violations, misdemeanors and other minor legal issues.
This week, Benoit officials defended Ali and their decision to appoint her as city judge.
“Religion is not listed as a qualification for service as a Municipal Court Judge in the State of Mississippi. Being Muslim is not a lawful basis for denying or terminating the appointment,” the mayor and board wrote, “We are pleased to have her.”
The groups that held the Friday event are nonpartisan civic engagement organizations made of nonprofits, churches and other religious institutions from across Jackson and the state. 
Members of Working Together Jackson and Working Together Mississippi join in prayer during a press conference concerning Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Islam and Sharia law at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in Jackson on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In a social media post, Gipson said that on day one if he’s elected governor he would ban Sharia law and Islam’s influence in Mississippi. But the Mississippi Legislature already banned Sharia law in 2015, when Gipson was a member of the state House. He voted in favor of the law that outlaws enforcement of any “foreign law” in Mississippi, which at the time was billed as being an anti-Sharia law measure.
“Sharia law, it’s like the law of Moses. Like the Ten Commandments. It’s just about the laws that govern a just, upright community of people,” said Okolo Rashid, one of the museum’s founders.
In a post, Gipson also included a photo of the museum, which says that it is America’s first Muslim museum, that featured Rashid at an exhibit on the shared heritage of Muslims, Christians and Jews. The museum opened in 2001 and is dedicated to educating the American public on Islamic history, art, and culture.
Members of Working Together Jackson and Working Together Mississippi gather for a press conference concerning Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Islam and Sharia law at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in Jackson on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I want to invite Commissoner Gipson to come sit down with us so we can share with him what the museum has to offer,” Rashid said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Supreme Court shuts door on appeal to use police misconduct findings in murder defense
description:
“The decision to send an ill-equipped, untrained officer into an ongoing chase was a decision that cost her life,” a defense attorney said of law enforcement actions in a deadly pursuit. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Supreme Court shuts door on appeal to use police misconduct findings in murder defense.
text:
The Vermont Supreme Court in Montpelier on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Vermont Supreme Court has dealt a legal setback to the defense team of the driver charged with murder in a police chase that killed a Rutland City officer more than three years ago.
The state’s highest court in a ruling this week denied a bid by attorneys for 23-year-old Tate Rheaume to challenge a Rutland judge’s decision blocking the introduction at trial of a damning internal affairs report that found officer misconduct in the pursuit.
Rheaume’s lawyers had asked to appeal that decision by Rutland Superior Court Judge Cortland Corsones. The judge denied the request, and Rheaume’s attorneys then asked the Supreme Court for permission to appeal. 
The high court, in a unanimous decision, stated it would not grant the appeal request, meaning Corsones’ decision will stand.
The lower court, the ruling stated, “acted within its discretion in denying permission to appeal.”
The Vermont Supreme Court decision is a blow for Rheaume’s defense. He faces several charges, including aggravated murder, in the July 2023 pursuit that led to the death of 19-year-old Jessica Ebbighausen, a Rutland City police trainee.
A great deal of legal wrangling in the case has focused on an internal affairs report, which became public last year. 

READ MORE

That report strongly criticized officers’ actions leading up to and during the chase, finding that officers had committed several policy violations. Those policy violations, according to the report, included conducting a pursuit for something other than a violent felony and not seeking authorization to continue a pursuit.
Then-Rutland City Police Commander Sam Delpha, the author of the internal affairs report, wrote in his conclusion, “The death of Officer Ebbighausen WAS preventable.” Delpha has since retired from the department.
Rheaume, according to charging documents, was allegedly fleeing from authorities after reports that he was inside the home of a former partner in Rutland on July 7, 2023.
Rheaume’s lawyers had sought to introduce testimony regarding the internal affairs report at trial, contending that it was important for jurors to consider officers’ conduct.
However, Corsones rejected that attempt.
“Under these circumstances,” Corsones wrote in the ruling, “any violations by the involved officers of the internal departmental pursuit policy could not be found to be an efficient, intervening cause breaking the chain of causation of the defendant’s actions, in the criminal context.”
David Sleigh, an attorney for Rheaume, said Friday he was disappointed with the Vermont Supreme Court’s decision.
“It seemed to us that the decision to send an ill-equipped, untrained officer into an ongoing chase was a decision that cost her life,” Sleigh said.
“It’s our view that the jury should be able to consider that argument,” he added, “but apparently the view of the Vermont court is that they can’t. That is disappointing to say the least.” 
Rutland County State’s Attorney Ian Sullivan declined to comment Friday.
No trial date has been set. The next hearing in the case is set for Oct. 5.
