title: PUCN denies public session on NV Energy’s data center-driven resource plan, advocates call foul
description: The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada denied an application for a PUCN-led consumer session last week, an unprecedented move advocates say follows a pattern of cutting public input in recent months. Advocates say the denial is another example of utility regulators thwarting public comment on contentious utility issues.  In June, the PUCN delayed and resc[...]
text:
Alexander Simpson speaks during a press conference at the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada's offices in Las Vegas on June 15, 2026. (Photo by Bryan Steffy/Getty Images for People's Action)The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada denied an application for a PUCN-led consumer session last week, an unprecedented move advocates say follows a pattern of cutting public input in recent months.
Advocates say the denial is another example of utility regulators thwarting public comment on contentious utility issues. 
In June, the PUCN delayed and rescheduled key consumer sessions after facing intense public backlash when dozens of attendees were forced to wait outside in triple-digit Las Vegas heat during contentious utility rate hearings.
The PUCN lead consumer session denied last week was requested by the Bureau of Consumer Protection (BCP), which is under the state Attorney General’s office, in order to provide public input on NV Energy’s 2027 Integrated Resource Plan, a proposal outlining the utilities strategy to meet Nevada’s future energy needs. 
The PUCN, which regulates utility companies like NV Energy and Southwest Gas, is not required by law to hold consumer sessions to discuss utility filings, which can be approved or denied on a case-by-case basis. 
However, requests for those consumer sessions for major dockets with the potential to impact ratepayers are common and rarely if ever denied. 
Several advocacy groups signed on in support of the BCP’s consumer session request, arguing it would allow the public to provide input on NV Energy’s 2027 Integrated Resource Plan once it was officially filed with regulators in its final form. 
In its request, the Bureau of Consumer Protection said the session would provide the public an opportunity to discuss the unprecedented load growth driven by proposed data centers described in NV Energy’s  plan. The BOC noted that a joint application by NV Energy documents requests for up to 22 gigawatts of energy from data center developers. 
Making the PUCN’s denial of the session even more unusual, representatives for NV Energy indicated they did not object to the consumer session.
Olivia Tanager, the director of the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter, said the organization had also filed a request for a consumer session on NV Energy’s resource plan, with full expectation it would be approved, and was surprised by the commission’s departure from established practice. 
“Two other consumer sessions were canceled and postponed with very limited notice from the Public Utilities Commission. Now this consumer session is being denied outright, despite the Bureau of Consumer Protection requesting it,” Tananger said. “This seems like a concerted effort to lock the public out of the Public Utilities Commission spaces.”
In denying a public session, the PUCN said consumer-session comments are not evidentiary and that statute does not require a consumer session in every docket.
Regulators at PUCN said it would not be “in the public interest for the Commission to preside over a consumer session” as it “would not create a meaningful opportunity for consumers to effectively participate.” 
“To the extent that the BCP’s motion requests a Commission-conducted consumer session, the motion is denied,” reads the PUCN’s order, adding that the PUCN “strongly encourages the BCP to hold a BCP-sponsored consumer session to hear directly from those consumers whom the BCP represents.”
Peter Kostes, a spokesperson for the PUCN, pushed back on the characterization that the commission denied the inclusion of a consumer session and public participation, saying the BCP was authorized to hold a consumer session of its own.
Kostes said the commission’s order on the motion “facilitates the scheduling of a consumer session where consumers’ input can actually be incorporated into the decision-making process,” by requesting the state’s consumer advocate conduct their own consumer session.”
Tananger, the director of the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter, argued the responsibility to hold consumer sessions related to utility regulation should remain with the PUCN, adding that the BCP is already overworked. 
Angel DeFazio, a regular attendee of PUCN meetings, said commissioners have regularly bristled at the manner in which members of the public participate in commission public comment sessions, adding that the process is already opaque and difficult to navigate. 
As public interest in the PUCN’s activities have heightened, more barriers have been put in place, said DeFazio, including the PUCN’s decision to only hold afternoon sessions, rather than evening sessions when more people are able to attend.
DeFazio also attended the meeting in June that did not provide an overflow room for the large crowd, resulting in people succumbing to heat-illness while waiting outside in triple-digit heat during a general consumer session. 
“The commission does not want to deal with ratepayers, so they denied it,” said DeFazio. “They don’t want to hear from the ratepayers, and that’s the problem. So yeah, this is to be expected.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Stowe Center explores independence in Black abolitionists’ stories
description: Thousands of formerly enslaved Black Americans made individual declarations independence. Hartford's Stowe Center is sharing their stories.
text:
There is the Declaration of Independence Americans learn about in school, the one signed in Philadelphia in 1776 and celebrated every July 4. 
Then there are thousands of more personal, individual declarations of independence that came afterward — from people who had been enslaved and used their stories, writing and activism to demand freedom and recognition of their humanity.
The Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford is putting those stories at the center of its new exhibition, “6,000+ Declarations of Independence.” 
Through original comic art by Connecticut artist Joe Young, the exhibit features the stories of Black freedom seekers and abolitionists including Frederick Douglass, Harriet Jacobs, Sojourner Truth, Josiah Henson and Phillis Wheatley. It asks visitors to look beyond the familiar story of America’s founding and consider what July 4 meant to the millions of people who remained enslaved, and what independence meant to those who had to fight for it.

Lisenn Rielland, from left, her aunt Elisette Hunter and uncle Marc Hunter, all visiting from France, talk  about the 6000+ Declarations of Independence exhibit featuring original comic art by artist Joe Young at the Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford on Friday, August 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

For Erika Slocumb, the Stowe Center’s director of interpretation and visitor experience, the exhibit reflects a broader effort to change how American history is told. 
“We’ve inherited our freedom because of the work that they put in,” Slocumb said.
The idea for the exhibit began in the Stowe Center’s archives, when Director of Collections Kat White discovered an unpublished narrative written by the Rev. William Phillips after the Civil War. In it, Phillips described a Fourth of July gathering where he stood before his community and delivered a speech declaring his freedom. 
White began wondering whether stories like Phillips’ could be understood as their own declarations of independence.
That idea became the foundation for the exhibit’s title, which refers to more than 6,000 freedom narratives identified by historians. Some were written by people who experienced enslavement, others were dictated, and some were preserved through oral traditions. The Stowe Center intentionally uses the term “freedom narratives” rather than “slave narratives” to emphasize the voices and agency of the people telling their stories.

Reproductions of “The North Star” are seen in the Harriet Beecher Stowe House during an “inheriting freedom” tour at the Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford on Friday, August 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

For Slocumb, those stories are also about helping people see themselves in American history. She said she grew up loving Black history but rarely saw those stories reflected in what she learned in school. 
“I hated history growing up because I never saw my story,” she said. 
Now she wants children who visit the Stowe Center to see Black history as part of the broader American story, rather than as something separate. “I want to tell Black history in a way that is relatable, that doesn’t feel separate,” she said.
Young approached that same goal through comic art. The Hartford artist said comics helped him when he struggled in school. He used to call himself “the fisherman,” he said, because his grades were “below sea level.” 
Young said he believes visual storytelling can help young people connect with history in ways traditional presentations sometimes cannot. “Comic art is just so inviting, and it’s fun,” he said.
Young also deliberately centered Black figures, he said, because “they were left out.” He wants the exhibit to highlight both well-known and lesser-known Black individuals whose voices and actions helped shape the country. 

Anna Boers, visitor experience and collections associate, answers questions in the Gallery for Hope & Freedom during an “inheriting freedom” tour at the Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford on Friday, August 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The exhibit comes as America is commemorating 250 years since the Declaration of Independence, but Slocumb said the Stowe Center’s work is about more than marking an anniversary. Over the past two and a half years, the center has reshaped how it presents history, placing greater emphasis on Black freedom seekers and the narratives that helped inspire change. 
Slocumb said she hopes broader understanding can help people recognize the connections between America’s past and present. If everyone understood that history, she said, “I think we would have a less divisive country.”
Young said he hopes young visitors leave with more than knowledge of figures such as Douglass, Truth, Henson and Wheatley. He wants them to recognize their personal connections to the nation’s history. 
“Black folks, we’re part of the whole American story,” he said.
The “+” in the exhibition’s title leaves room for the stories still being discovered in archives, family collections and oral traditions — as well as the declarations that have yet to be written, its curators said.
“Come out and learn about history and be inspired to tell the next story where Black folks are included,” Young said.
The exhibition is on view through December.

name: Nevada Current
title: Buck hitches wagon to defense contractor who schemed to defraud taxpayers
description: When Nevada State Senator and Republican congressional candidate Carrie Buck paraded around Boulder City on the Fourth of July, it was on a truck belonging to a Nevada-based defense contractor who admits he colluded to defraud the U.S. government.   John Buscema, the owner of S.A.F.E. Structure, a Nevada company, and USA Manufacturing, a Florida corporation,[...]
text:
A S.A.F.E. vehicle advertises congressional candidate Carrie Buck's campaign at a 4th of July parade in Boulder City. (Photo courtesy of a parade attendee)When Nevada State Senator and Republican congressional candidate Carrie Buck paraded around Boulder City on the Fourth of July, it was on a truck belonging to a Nevada-based defense contractor who admits he colluded to defraud the U.S. government.  
John Buscema, the owner of S.A.F.E. Structure, a Nevada company, and USA Manufacturing, a Florida corporation, admitted in 2024 that his companies plotted from 2014 through 2023 with another defense contractor to rig bids for military contracts. Buscema agreed last year to pay a $1 million settlement to resolve the government’s False Claims Act suit.. 
Buscema contributed $7,000, the maximum allowed for an individual, to Buck’s campaign for Congress. She’s challenging Rep. Dina Titus, a Democrat, in Nevada’s Congressional District 1. 
Buscema also chipped in an additional $3,000 to GOP Winning Women, a Super PAC that has contributed $28,439 to Buck. 
S.A.F.E. Structure designs and manufactures support equipment and logistics for the U.S. Armed Forces. In addition to the military, it lists Boeing, Airbus, Cessna, and Learject among its clients. 
On his personal website, Buscema “attributes all his success to his Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ…” 
Buscema admitted to assisting in bid rigging by using his companies to make more than 100 bids for contracts he had no intention of winning, according to the settlement agreement. His companies coordinated with NOBLE, a Boston-based defense contractor that provided details to colluders that allowed another vendor to submit a lower bid, though higher than one resulting from a legitimate process.   
Buscema also paid other vendors to submit some 60 false bids so that his companies would win the contracts. 
“As evidenced in this settlement agreement, these contractors gamed the system to line their own pockets. They manipulated and undermined the fair and open bidding process designed to save our military – and taxpayers – money,” U.S. Attorney Joshua S. Levy of Massachusetts said in a news release last year. “Contractors should be scrupulous in dealing with the government, not coordinating with each other to pad their bottom line. When defense contractors collude, rather than compete, they violate the law and the public’s trust.”
Cheating the Dept. of Defense not only wastes taxpayer money, but also compromises the security of troops by supplying the government with inferior or defective weapons. It also deprives the military of revenue that could be used to support the troops. 
Buck has a personal interest in the well-being of U.S. troops. She is the mother of an Army Green Beret and combat medic. 
It’s unknown if she was aware of Buschema’s fraudulent acts when she accepted his contributions. The candidate and her campaign did not respond to requests for comment. 
“This is the height of hypocrisy,” Titus’ campaign spokesman Dick Cooper said in a statement. “She should return the money, just like John Buscema had to pay $1 million to settle the charges against him by the Department of Justice.”
Buscema also did not respond to the Current’s inquiries.

name: Nevada Current
title: Majority of Nevadans support tobacco tax hike, survey says
description: Nearly two-thirds of Nevada voters would support raising the state’s tobacco tax, according to a new survey commissioned by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network. The survey, conducted by Lake Research Partners and The Tarrance Group, comes as ACS CAN and other public health groups push state lawmakers to consider backing a tobacco tax […]
text:
Public health advocates are pushing Nevada lawmakers to raise and revise Nevada's taxes on tobacco products. (Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)Nearly two-thirds of Nevada voters would support raising the state’s tobacco tax, according to a new survey commissioned by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network.
The survey, conducted by Lake Research Partners and The Tarrance Group, comes as ACS CAN and other public health groups push state lawmakers to consider backing a tobacco tax hike. Nevada’s per-pack cigarette tax rate hasn’t been raised since 2015. Advocates argue raising the tax would increase revenue for the state while decreasing the number of smokers, particularly in young and low-income communities.
According to ACS CAN, 63% of likely voters in Nevada indicated they would support a tobacco tax increase whose revenue would be dedicated to programs that prevent tobacco use. 
The survey also found that 59% of likely voters in Nevada are either very (33%) or somewhat (26%) concerned about young people in the community using tobacco products.
ACS CAN Nevada Government Relations Director Jennifer Atlas said in a statement that the survey shows voters “want their lawmakers to pass a meaningful tobacco tax so future generations are protected from the health effects of using tobacco and those who are addicted to tobacco products can quit.”
Advocates made their tobacco tax hike pitch to an interim legislative committee focused on revenue last month. They are pushing to double the cigarette tax and raise the “other tobacco products” tax to keep taxes equitable. That committee is expected to select what bills it will back when it meets later this month.
Recent surveys in other states also found broad support for raising tobacco taxes.
The ACS CAN survey also found 85% of likely voters in Nevada believe it is extremely (53%) or very (33%) important that all Americans, no matter what health insurance they have, should have access to cancer screening and treatment that is close to home and affordable.
It also found that a vast majority — 91% — agreed with the sentiment that “families across the country are feeling squeezed by rising healthcare and insurance costs” and “leaders should focus on making care more affordable and protecting access to health services people depend on.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Jay DeBoyer could help John James avoid a nasty GOP convention fight
description: Lansing legislative experience, support from the grassroots wing of the Michigan Republican Party and a path to a smooth convention vote later this month were all reasons for GOP insiders to be excited about state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) as Republican gubernatorial candidate John James’s running mate in the November general election. James, a congressman [[...]
text:
Michigan House Oversight Committee Chair Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township) talks to reporters on continuing allegations of ethics violation by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel. Dec. 16, 2025 | Screenshot Lansing legislative experience, support from the grassroots wing of the Michigan Republican Party and a path to a smooth convention vote later this month were all reasons for GOP insiders to be excited about state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) as Republican gubernatorial candidate John James’s running mate in the November general election.
James, a congressman from Shelby Township, announced Thursday that he had selected DeBoyer, the current chair of the House Oversight Committee.
Several Republican consultants who spoke to Michigan Advance for this story said that was likely a wise choice following James’ tough primary fight against businessman Perry Johnson — who had launched a grassroots opposition campaign against James in the August election, and drove a wedge between him and James with GOP voters across the state.
Jason Roe, who previously served as executive director of the Michigan Republican Party, said DeBoyer has focused his work as chairman of the oversight committee “to highlight  excesses of Democratic leadership, the lack of transparency, and some of the waste, fraud, and abuse within government.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That would make DeBoyer “a very good wingman for John James in terms of reminding people of the failures of Democratic leadership over the last eight years of Gretchen Whitmer.”
Roe said that he believed Lansing legislative experience — which James does not have — was an absolute top priority for a running mate choice. DeBoyer is in his second term in the Michigan House and likely could have an upward leadership trajectory if he chose to remain in the House. As a candidate for reelection this year, DeBoyer was set to defend his 63rd House District seat against Democrat Jamie Sonnenberger.
Gongwer News Service, a Lansing-based statewide political news outlet, noted that DeBoyer would give up his seat if officially nominated at the Michigan Republican Party’s Aug. 22 convention.
Andrea Bitely of Bitely Communications, and the previous spokesperson for Mike Duggan’s suspended 2026 independent gubernatorial campaign, also highlighted DeBoyer’s legislative knowledge, as well as his good reputation in the gun rights and pro-life communities, calling him a “help no hurt” candidate.
Michigan State Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) speaks at a Second Amendment March event outside the Michigan Capitol Building on Sept. 19, 2024. | Photo: Anna Liz Nichols
“He’s not somebody that has, as far as I know, a lot of baggage that he brings to the campaign,” Bitely said. “So he’s going to be theoretically helpful, but he’s not going to create drama for the James team, in any way, shape, or form.”
James came out on the top of a divisive primary against Johnson — as well as former attorney general Mike Cox and Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt, who both suspended their campaigns prior to the Aug. 4 primaries. 
While James enjoyed the backing of much of the party establishment, including President Donald Trump, who endorsed him in June, Johnson rallied significant grassroots support, especially after Nesbitt and Cox dropped out of the race.
“They are working very hard to bring everybody back to the table, and a Jay DeBoyer pick is that,” Bitely said, adding that James might be hoping this will bring Johnson voters back onto his side. “It is uniting, not dividing.”
DeBoyer is also a strategic pick because of his role heading the House Oversight Committee, a role which he has used to investigate and question top Democratic officials, including Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor. 
Both Bitely and Roe said that they expect DeBoyer to act as an “attack dog” for the campaign, with Roe noting, “he probably knows her vulnerabilities as well as anybody in Lansing, and so I think that’s going to be a huge benefit.”



Quotation







There’s always the potential of some mischief at convention and ratifying the lieutenant governor pick. ... I think Jay really puts all that conversation to bed.


– Jason Roe, a Republican political consultant


On the other hand, Dennis Lennox, a Republican public affairs consultant, was more skeptical of DeBoyer as the choice for running mate, noting in a statement, “I would have named a woman because I believe that parties need to balance the ticket, but it wasn’t my selection to make.”
He added that James “chose a governing partner, not a geographic or demographic box-checker” in DeBoyer.
DeBoyer joins James on the all-male statewide Republican ticket, along with former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers as the U.S. Senate candidate, Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd as the attorney general candidate and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini as the secretary of state candidate.
But concerns about the gender makeup of the Republican ticket were not shared by Roe or Bitely.
“I don’t think it’s going to make a difference at all, and I say that as someone who would prefer to have a woman on the ticket,” Bitely said. “I think it matters more on the Democratic side than it does on the Republican side at this point.”
Roe noted that, although it is the first time that Republicans have not had a female candidate on the top of their ticket in decades, he believes that voters are more focused on “competence and a commitment to reforming government.”
Lennox also said that DeBoyer was seen as a potential future leader in the legislature for the Republican Party, but must now give up his House seat to run for the position of lieutenant governor.
DeBoyer ran unopposed in the Republican primary for re-election to his seat in House District 63 this year –- a district which he won twice with over 60% of the vote in the 2024 and 2026 general elections. Republican officials in Macomb and St. Clair counties, which DeBoyer’s district covers parts of, will have to choose a replacement for him on the ballot.
Michigan’s U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township (center right), a Republican candidate for governor, speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump (center) at General Motors Proving Grounds in Milford, Mich. James was invited on stage by Trump, along with former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake (center left), the GOP candidate for the U.S. Senate, US. Rep. Tim Walberg of Tipton (left) and U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain of Bruce Township. July 27, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
All three consultants emphasized the importance of a smooth nominating convention, to be held in Mt. Pleasant later this month, to officially name their candidates in the general election.
“There’s always the potential of some mischief at convention and ratifying the lieutenant governor pick, and there were certainly some smoke signals being sent that there might be mischief at our convention,” Roe said. “I think Jay really puts all that conversation to bed. I think he’s got such broad support within the activist base that he should get approved without any challenge.”
Bitely agreed that James needs an easy convention, and Lennox similarly said there would be “no chance” that DeBoyer’s selection would be derailed at the convention because “malcontents would have to defeat the rules just to put forth an alternative candidate.”
Roe — who is also working with Republican campaigns for U.S. House and Michigan House seats — said that having DeBoyer stumping for incumbent Republicans in down-ballot races, especially his state House colleagues, is very helpful because he can speak about those candidates with authority.
“I also think because of his focus on waste, fraud, and abuse, and transparency, that he brings a very strong messaging resume to the ticket that I think all the candidates in the party, whether they’re at the state or federal level, will be talking about,” Roe said. 
That confidence is a contrast to the type of concerns raised by Lennox both before and after the primary: That James’ nomination as governor might hurt down-ballot candidates, as he had significantly less cash on hand at the end of the primary than Johnson, who almost entirely self-funded his campaign to the tune of around $30 million.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Most of this Utah county’s license plate camera data is searched by out-of-state law enforcement
description: License plate cameras are under scrutiny as questions on misuse and surveillance emerge throughout the country. In Utah, a political action committee is sounding the alarm, after having found that the vast majority of the camera records searches in one county originated outside the state. The records of 10 license plate cameras from the Flock […]
text:
A Flock Automated License Plate Reader on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)License plate cameras are under scrutiny as questions on misuse and surveillance emerge throughout the country. In Utah, a political action committee is sounding the alarm, after having found that the vast majority of the camera records searches in one county originated outside the state.
The records of 10 license plate cameras from the Flock Safety network installed in Weber County streets were searched 5.1 million times between February 2022 and July 2026. Almost 97% of those searches came from law enforcement agencies outside of Utah, an investigation from the Utah Civic Compact found. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The No. 1 searcher of Weber County camera records was the Houston Police Department, which accounted for over a third of all activity.
“When the Flock cameras were proposed, it was pitched to the public as a mechanism by which public safety can be protected, and how technology can make us safer,” Clark Dice, communications director of the Utah Civic Compact said on Thursday. “The more that we dive into this issue, the more we’re learning that these cameras and this technology and the data is being utilized to surveil people who either live, work, or visit Utah.”
It’s not clear how many license plate reader cameras there are in Utah, but the website lprmaps.com has logged 944 in the state, ranking it No. 28 in the nation for total cameras.
The Flock network uses license plate recognition technologies and vehicle data to help law enforcement investigate crimes. According to its website, the company says its platform is currently used to solve about 2,000 crimes per day.
The Utah report comes at the same time as Flock Safety’s announcement of changes to its platform to address privacy concerns and “documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement,” according to a report from the Associated Press.



Let us know what you think...


 


Among the updates set to be implemented next year, all law enforcement customers must establish an audit tool to flag abnormal search behavior. Retention of the data the cameras capture will also be reduced from 30 days to seven, unless it is evidence tied to a case, and law enforcement will need a case number to do a search.
The Utah Civic Compact isn’t alleging any unlawful activity, Dice said. It is possible they have an automatic procedure to use the data available in the network. But that’s unclear so far. The Houston Police Department didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment on Thursday.
However, members of the compact worry about the disproportionate number of out-of-state searches, and wonder what laws those agencies have to adhere to before getting access to Utah data.
Utah law limits searches to active criminal investigations, outstanding warrants, or to search for a missing or endangered person or a stolen vehicle, the Utah Civic Compact said in a release. 
“Save for conducting individual audits of 3,343 agencies (that have searched for Weber County data) there is no mechanism to even know if searches by non-Utah agencies are adhering to Utah’s ALPR search restrictions,” the group said in a release.
The Utah Civic Compact is asking for a legislative audit of the license plate cameras operating in the state, as well as other actions to close the “jurisdictional gap” that happens when out-of-state agencies search for Utah data.
“We want it codified into Utah state law that if you’re going to surveil this very sensitive data, there must be an established process by which you can do it,” Dice said. “Right now, it is our understanding that there’s a bit of a loophole that’s being utilized and we want that to stop as soon as possible.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Defunding of student loan repayment program another hit to teachers amid state’s staffing shortage
description: Rose Wright works on the decorations in her classroom at Bailey APAC Middle School during the school district's Beautification Day in Jackson, Miss., on Friday, July 18, 2025.
text:
The email this summer came as a shock to Alanna Lawrence. 
For the past two years, Lawrence and her husband, Jeremy, had received $9,000 each toward their student loans, thanks to a state-funded program that helps teachers pay off their debt. They teach in the Vicksburg-Warren School District, which the State Board of Education has designated an area critically short of teachers. 
They were expecting $6,000 more each this year. But, they learned from the email, for the first time since the state Legislature created the Winter-Reed Teacher Loan Repayment Program in 2021, educators such as Lawrence will receive no assistance — even as Mississippi continues to grapple with a teacher shortage. 
Lawrence said defunding the program sends a confusing message to the state’s educators. 
“They say how much they appreciate us,” she said. “But the actions aren’t matching up.”
The Winter-Reed program provides up to three annual loan payments toward participating teachers’ student debt. Teachers who work in critical geographic shortage areas can receive $6,000 in the third year. Teachers who work in noncritical shortage areas can receive a third-year award of $3,500.
Earlier this year, the Mississippi Office of Student Financial Aid requested $6.5 million from the Legislature for Fostering Access and Inspiring Hope, or FAITH, scholarships and the Winter-Reed Teacher Loan Repayment Program. Lawmakers appropriated $3 million for both. 
State representatives vote on a teacher pay raise bill in the Mississippi House chamber on Friday, March 6, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The state’s Postsecondary Education Financial Assistance Board voted in May to award all $3 million to FAITH applicants, leaving no money for Winter-Reed. 
The state financial aid office notified roughly 236 Winter-Reed applicants in June that it could not provide awards this year because of the funding shortage.
The shortfall comes as thousands of teaching jobs across the state are unfilled. According to a report released by the Mississippi Department of Education in December, the vacancies are up hundreds from previous years. 
Teachers say their low pay is driving the staffing shortages. This past session, lawmakers gave teachers a raise, but it was far smaller than they originally promised, leaving many educators disappointed. 
Sen. David Blount, a Democrat from Jackson who was instrumental in creating the program, said he was disappointed the Legislature underfunded the request this year, blaming it on state leaders’ decision last year to phase out the income tax.
Blount said he proposed the “inexpensive and targeted” program in 2021 with the teacher shortage in mind.
“It’s an extra incentive that makes the difference in someone choosing the profession,” said Blount, who is also vice chairman of the Senate Education Committee. “We shouldn’t put programs on the books if we’re not serious about meeting that commitment.”
While he plans to advocate for the program’s funding next session, Blount said the decision to eliminate the income tax will continue to impact what the state can pay for.
Senate Appropriations Chairman Briggs Hopson, a Republican from Vicksburg, did not respond to a request for comment. 
Winter-Reed isn’t the only state financial aid program facing a funding shortfall. The state’s financial aid office still faces a $7.3 million funding gap that could reduce aid for nearly 27,000 students such as those receiving the Mississippi Tuition Assistance Grant (MTAG), Mississippi Eminent Scholars Grant (MESG) and the Higher Education Legislative Plan (HELP). 
Last week, the Woodward Hines Education Foundation pledged $800,000 toward FAITH scholarships for the year, and college and university foundations also pledged support. 
Chatham Hodges, a teacher in Lowndes County schools, relied on the Winter-Reed program to pay off her student loan debt. The loans, on top of a low salary, can make it hard for teachers to make ends meet or work toward other financial goals, she said. 
Sen. David Blount asks questions during a TANF hearing at the State Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, December 15, 2022.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Without programs like this, I don’t think I would have had the same opportunity to move forward financially as a young teacher,” said Hodges, who has taught kindergarten for five years. “It made a huge difference in my life.”
Hodges said she was frustrated when she learned the program wasn’t being funded this year. 
“Teachers are already being asked to do so much, and programs that help recruit and retain teachers are incredibly important, especially when Mississippi is facing a teacher shortage,” she said. “When programs like this disappear, I worry that it makes it harder to recruit new teachers and retain the teachers who are already here.”
Darien Spann, president of Mississippi Association of Educators, said he hopes legislators can find funding to restore the Winter-Reed program. 
“Everybody should have the opportunities to obtain the necessary credentials that they need to remain teachers in the state,” Spann said.
Lawrence and her husband follow education policy, so they knew lawmakers were making cuts this year. But because the program is billed as a three-year commitment, she didn’t expect they would receive rejection emails after receiving the money for two years. 
The money is applied directly to the loans, which makes a huge impact and cuts straight into the debt, Lawrence said. Now, her family is figuring out how to deal with larger-than-expected monthly student loan payments. 
“We’re going to have to be really tight on our budget,” she said. “My husband coaches and we have a daughter, so second jobs aren’t an option for us.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Cancer research needs sustainable funding from New Jersey, advocates say
description: Advocates say New Jersey needs dedicated annual state funding of $10 million for support cancer research given federal funding instability.
text:
Advocates in New Jersey want the state to dedicate $10 million annually to cancer research, funding they say is especially needed now that federal funding for scientific research has been cut drastically by the National Institutes of Health. (Photo courtesy of National Institutes of Health)As federal funding for scientific studies continues to decline, New Jersey-based scholars, doctors, and health advocates want the state to step up – and sustain – its own investment to cancer research within the Garden State.  
Advocates are urging lawmakers to adopt legislation to allocate $10 million annually from the state’s tobacco tax revenue to the New Jersey Commission on Cancer Research, which funds competitive grants to researchers studying cancer issues at facilities around the state. The state collected more than $58 million through taxes on cigarettes, cigars, and vape products last year.  
The commission, created in 1983, will get $4 million this year as part of the $60.7 billion budget Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed in late June. But their allocation has varied widely over the years and was zeroed out entirely during former Gov. Chris Christie’s two terms, according to the advocates, who say stable funding is urgently needed. 
“I see this as an opportunity for a state that holds ourselves up as a beacon of innovation, science, and research. We should know that cancer research cannot operate effectively on year-to-year uncertainty,” said Quinton Law, government relations director for the American Cancer Society’s political advocacy arm, which is helping build support for the legislation.   
Existing state dollars allowed the commission to fund about a quarter of the grant requests it received in the latest funding cycle, Law told the New Jersey Monitor, supporting work at public and private universities, hospital systems, and research institutes. The $4.8 million the commission awarded between 2012 and 2015 also attracted $98 million in federal dollars, he said. 
“What are we leaving on the table, just because we don’t have the money?” he asked.  
Dr. Kenneth Adler, a blood cancer specialist and the commission chairman, said stable state funding is especially needed now that the National Institutes of Health, which has traditionally provided critical dollars for biomedical research, drastically cut funding for scientific research under the Trump administration. NIH grant funding dropped from $1.3 billion on average annually to $604 million in 2026, according to the Association of American Universities 
Dr. Yibin Kang, a molecular biologist at Princeton University who received more than $500,000 from the New Jersey commission starting in 2005, said the instability in federal funding is “deeply concerning” to researchers. Studies require long-term planning and labs make commitments to researchers that extend years, he said.  
“When researchers cannot predict whether federal funding will remain available, they naturally become more cautious about starting ambitious and creative projects, hiring young scientists, or pursuing innovative ideas that carry greater scientific risk,” Kang told the New Jersey Monitor.  
This research itself has direct benefits on New Jersey’s economy, Kang said, and can prompt discoveries that eventually advance patient care. The state funding helped him build a lab that has made critical discoveries around how breast cancer spreads, work that contributed to the development of multiple treatments and prompted him to co-found three biotechnology companies, he said.
While state funding can’t replace NIH support, Kang said, the cancer commission’s work plays an important role in supporting the scientific ecosystem.  
“Even relatively modest awards can allow investigators to kickstart a new laboratory and research program, test a new idea, generate preliminary data, support a talented young scientist, or bridge a temporary funding gap. Those investments can subsequently leverage much larger amounts of federal, foundation, and private funding,” Kang said.  
The New Jersey commission funds students at various academic levels working on cancer studies related to prevention, detection, treatment, survivorship, and more, Adler said. Last year it received 100 requests for research funding, of which 25 were approved, and it got 160 project proposals this year, Adler said, an increase he attributed to insecurity around federal funding.  
More than 50,000 people are diagnosed with cancer each year in New Jersey, according to Screen NJ, a public-private partnership that offers prevention and screening programs, and some 15,000 die, making it the second leading cause of death after heart disease. Roughly one-half of men and one-third of women will develop some form of cancer, with the most common forms being colorectal, lung, and prostate for men or breast cancer among women. 
New Jersey’s current budget invests millions in cancer treatment, with more than $41 million for the Cancer Institute of New Jersey, a nationally designated program operated by RWJ Barnabas Health, and at least $27 million for the South Jersey Cancer Program, run by Cooper University Health Care. Millions more is allocated for education, early detection, and screening programs, some run by Screen NJ.  
Sen. Robert Singer (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Sen. Robert Singer (R-Ocean), the lead sponsor of the research funding bill, said lawmakers routinely find money for their personal priorities, including tens of millions Democratic leaders set aside for the World Cup. Singer lost his mother to cancer when he was 7 and often hears from constituents struggling with the disease, he said, making cancer prevention and treatment a priority for him.  
“Something that is this important and that affects thousands and thousands of families that live and have grown up in New Jersey, and you can’t put at least $10 million toward it?” he said.  
The bipartisan bill, which has nearly two dozen sponsors in both the Senate and Assembly, passed the Senate health committee in May but has yet to be heard by an Assembly committee. Lawmakers are on break for the summer, and it is unclear when they will return to work in Trenton, given the political focus on federal elections this fall. 
Adler thanked lawmakers for the support they have provided over the years, including money to rebuild after the Christie era. But he said the solution is in the legislation, which would create a dedicated fund and allocate $5 million to general cancer research and $5 million to pediatric cancer studies.
Without a secure fund, support is “up to the whim of the governor in charge,” Adler said.
Law said the legislation also aligns with Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s goals to support research and job creation. Funding the work also helps researchers here secure some funding from the National Institutes of Health, even if less federal money is available overall, he said.  
“And if these people can’t get their projects funded here, where are they going to go? They’re going to go to other states. They’re going to go to other places, other countries perhaps. These are dollars that are leaving New Jersey,” Law said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: As Kansas City Council rushes towards a Royals stadium vote, key questions go unanswered
description: Kansas City officials are looking to cut a ballpark deal within weeks that will define the city for decades. Publicly, at least, the details remain sparse. City officials are scrambling to finalize plans to help finance the Royals’ proposed $1.9 billion ballpark at Crown Center before the end of the month. If things had gone […]
text:
Kansas City and Royals officials are aiming to have a new ballpark in Crown Center ready to open by the time the team's lease at Kauffman Stadium expires in 2031 (Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon).Kansas City officials are looking to cut a ballpark deal within weeks that will define the city for decades.
Publicly, at least, the details remain sparse.
City officials are scrambling to finalize plans to help finance the Royals’ proposed $1.9 billion ballpark at Crown Center before the end of the month.
If things had gone according to plan, the Kansas City Council could have been voting on the deal to provide $600 million for the project on the afternoon of Aug. 13 — less than three days after paperwork was distributed to City Council members on Monday night.
Instead, the city’s Finance, Governance and Public Safety committee held the ordinance on Tuesday, delaying the vote for at least a week.
But the public still has precious little information about where the money will come from, whether the deal will impact other taxing jurisdictions or whether Hallmark and the Royals intend to deliver any of the community benefits the City Council previously promised to negotiate.
And the clock is ticking.
According to one council member, the city’s legal department told the council that Kansas City could be forced to let voters have a say on the deal if the agreements are not signed by Aug. 31.
That, Mayor Quinton Lucas said, would delay the deal by more than six months.
The alternative path — the one the council appears to be taking — means that a $600 million deal with 30-year contracts and debt obligations could move forward with limited public input or oversight.
 Let’s make a deal

The new Royals ballpark is proposed for the current Hallmark Cards headquarters site at Crown Center.
The stadium would cost a total of $1.9 billion, making it the fourth-most expensive major league ballpark of all time, after adjusting for inflation. The broader ballpark district plan calls for an additional $1 billion in nearby development.
Out of that $1.9 billion for the ballpark, Kansas City intends to finance $600 million. The local contribution is required to unlock an additional $200 million to $300 million that would be financed by Missouri taxpayers.
Including extra money for debt service, upward of $1.5 billion in state and local subsidies would go toward financing the stadium over the next 30 years.
Technically, Kansas City’s portion will be covered by a tax-increment financing deal. Under that plan, the city will draw a “tax redirection” area surrounding Crown Center. The boundaries of that area have not been disclosed.
The city expects tax revenues to increase in that area, in part due to the Royals stadium. The increase in revenue from that area will be used to pay down the $600 million in debt until it’s paid off in 30 years.
Under a traditional TIF deal, half of the increase in tax revenue would be used for the ballpark development. In theory, at least, the rest would go toward financing public services.
The reasoning goes that the increase in tax revenue would not happen without the stadium. So in that sense, some argue, the stadium is paying for itself.
(You can read more about the mechanics of a tax-increment financing deal, or TIF, in this previous article.)
Renderings presented by the Royals at the April 22 announcement. (Courtesy of the Kansas City Royals)
But in practice, Kansas City taxpayers would be on the hook for tens of millions of dollars per year for the next 30 years.
That’s because the city is expected to guarantee repayment of the $600 million debt, instead of the Royals or Hallmark.
If the project doesn’t generate enough tax revenue to cover its own debt, that money would come from the city’s general fund at the expense of services including police, fire, public transit and neighborhoods.
The city financed the Power & Light District under a similar structure. As of 2023, the city had paid a total of $167 million over 16 years to cover debt payments.
To prevent that from happening with the Royals ballpark, the city plans to draw the boundaries of that tax-redirection area so large that it can collect enough money to pay off the debt.
In the process, the city is making the assumption that increased economic activity in that area over the next 30 years is a result of the stadium.
In addition to the TIF deal, the city may create a community improvement district in the area around the stadium to help subsidize the stadium. Council member Johnathan Duncan suggested on Tuesday that this is included in the documents that were distributed to the City Council on Monday night that have not yet been made available to the public.
 What’s the rush?

Looming over the City Council’s deliberations this month are nearly 4,000 petition signatures that were certified in June.
That petition, organized by Missouri Workers Power, calls for a city ordinance that would require a public vote before the city can give a subsidy for a “stadium, arena or similar venue” with more than 2,500 seats, such as the Royals ballpark.
The City Council has until Aug. 31, 60 days from when the petition signatures were certified, to either approve that ordinance or schedule an election for voters to weigh in.
If that ordinance is approved, the petition organizers argue, the city would then need to call a second election to ask voters for permission to subsidize the Royals ballpark.
But when the signatures were turned in, Lucas said it was too late.
“I think the deal is likely to get done before we even have some of these discussions,” Lucas said in June, “if we ever get to the point of a public vote.”
Mayor Quinton Lucas’s term will expire in 2027, and he will not be eligible to run for reelection. (Zach Bauman/The Beacon)
Now, two months later, the city is scheduling last-minute votes and potentially even special council sessions to get the development and funding agreements signed.
City staff worked overtime last weekend to prepare the agreements in time to present them to the Finance, Governance and Public Safety committee on Aug. 11.
Those documents include:

The team’s proposed lease
Nonrelocation agreement for the Royals
Development agreement
Community impact partnership agreement (also known as a community benefits agreement)
Funding agreement

Those documents were distributed to the City Council less than 12 hours before Tuesday’s committee meeting. If the plan had moved forward, the public could have had just two days to review them before the council finalized the 30-year deal.
Lucas said the committee vote was delayed so that the council and the public could have more time to review the agreements.
So The Beacon submitted an open-records request to review those documents.
Kansas City rejected The Beacon’s request because “records pertaining to ongoing negotiations for agreements not yet executed are closed pursuant to RSMo. Sec. 610.021(12).”
Reporting by The Kansas City Star suggests that Lucas may have been misrepresenting the reason for the delay. Duncan told The Star that he’d heard the delay was because the Royals had backpedaled on a verbal commitment.
 Political math

If you ask Lucas, the citizens’ petition and the Aug. 31 deadline to put it on the ballot have nothing to do with the city’s rush to reach a deal.
“The city does not have a deadline or a timeline” to approve the Royals deal, he told reporters on Tuesday, “at least as to how it would act on any ordinances either before us or in the future relating to the baseball stadium that are triggered by any outside petition efforts.”
Council member Duncan, however, disagrees.
After reporters spoke with Lucas, Duncan said the entire City Council had received an email briefing that the city would be in the best legal position if it approved the agreements before Aug. 31.
“Maybe the mayor should go back and check his email about the briefings we received,” Duncan told reporters. “The whole point of rushing these agreements is to ensure that these agreements are finalized and signed prior to a vote of the people, to circumvent the will of the people and to prevent this from going to a public vote.”
The Royals presented renderings of the proposed stadium at the April 22 announcement. The ballpark will sit on the site of the current Hallmark headquarters in Crown Center. (Courtesy of the Kansas City Royals)
Duncan said the council’s rush to approve a $600 million subsidy for the Royals is coming at the expense of taxpayers.
He has been advocating for a provision in the Royals agreement that would give Kansas City a share of the revenues — ideally 30%, which is the portion of stadium costs that the city is shouldering.
But because the deal is moving so quickly, Duncan said it’s limiting the city’s ability to get more concessions from the team and Hallmark.
“The Royals cannot move forward with this development without the city’s equity,” he said. “We deserve an equity position and a return on investment that includes a portion of the profits. Is it 30 percent? I think it should be, but I’m happy to negotiate. Right now, it’s zero percent.”
In addition, Duncan said that the taxing jurisdictions like the school district and the library have not had a seat at the table for any negotiations.
The last time the Royals pitched a downtown ballpark in 2024 — tied to renewal of a Jackson County sales tax, which voters overwhelmingly rejected — the team had promised to make payments to the school district with annual increases to make up for the property taxes the team wouldn’t have to pay. It’s unclear whether this is the case in the latest proposal the council is considering.
Sam Mellinger, a spokesman for the Royals, declined to comment on the city’s process. He added that under the proposed agreements, the school districts will not see a drop in property tax revenue.
The City Council has not yet announced when it will take up the Royals agreements again. The committee held the ordinance until the next committee meeting.
Lucas suggested on Tuesday that he may call a special meeting as soon as next week.
The City Council would otherwise be taking the week off.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Same knee surgery, twice the price: Hospital monopolies push up healthcare costs
description: This article first appeared on KFF Health News. More than a million times a year, a U.S. surgeon slices open a knee, strips out worn cartilage, caps the leg bones with metal, and drops in a plastic spacer to allow the new joint to glide. While knee replacement procedures have become standard, however, the prices […]
text:
Marcelle Crago, a nurse and lactation consultant in Asheville, North Carolina, needed knee surgery after she tore her meniscus last year. She shopped around and arranged to have the procedure done at an outpatient center, where it cost her less than a third of the price Mission Health listed. (Katie Linsky Shaw for KFF Health News)This article first appeared on KFF Health News.
More than a million times a year, a U.S. surgeon slices open a knee, strips out worn cartilage, caps the leg bones with metal, and drops in a plastic spacer to allow the new joint to glide.
While knee replacement procedures have become standard, however, the prices charged have not.
At Catawba Valley Medical Center in Hickory, North Carolina, for example, the cost of the procedure under a Blue Cross Blue Shield health plan this year was about $16,000, according to data from Serif Health, a San Francisco startup that collects recently released data from hospitals and insurers. Little more than an hour’s drive west, however, at Mission Hospital in Asheville, the cost of the procedure under the same health plan was around $40,000, or more than double, the data showed.
Formed by the merger of the two largest hospitals in the region, Mission has little competition and more power to demand the higher price.
This comparison between these two hospitals illuminates how large hospital systems created by a wave of U.S. mergers in recent decades can dominate the competition and push up healthcare costs.
While many factors affect the price of a medical procedure, hospitals with few competitors can charge more, health economists say.
The hospital price hikes mean patients and their insurers must pay more for an episode of healthcare. But there is an important side effect, too, even for people who don’t require medical care. When insurers face higher hospital prices, they pass the costs on and raise the prices they charge for everyone’s health insurance.
Using Serif Health’s pricing data, it is possible to see how mergers like the one that created Mission Hospital influence costs. For years, it was difficult to determine how much hospital monopolies boosted charges. But since 2021, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has required hospitals to disclose prices, making it possible to gather comprehensive data such as Serif Health’s.
The connection between market power and prices exists across the country. In Melbourne, Florida, Holmes Regional Medical Center is part of a health system, Health First, that dominates surrounding Brevard County. The center has charged Cigna two times what a hospital two hours north did for a knee replacement this year, the Serif Health data shows.
Banner North Colorado Medical Center, which ranks as the leading healthcare provider in Weld County, Colorado, charged a UnitedHealthcare patient $20,000 more for the surgery in Greeley than a health system an hour’s drive south in Denver, according to Serif’s figures.
The American Hospital Association has argued that hospital mergers can improve quality and reduce healthcare costs by creating “a fiscally sustainable environment.” A Mission Hospital spokesperson said comparing hospitals’ prices was unfair or misleading because their practices and constraints vary so much.
For years, economists suspected that the run of mergers beginning in the late 1990s was a main driver of the rising costs of U.S. healthcare. From 2002 to 2020 alone, more than 1,000 hospital mergers unfolded in the United States.
But until the recent federal disclosure rule, the effect of healthcare monopolies on pricing was often overlooked or harder to detect. Hospitals do not advertise their prices, and even when they are revealed on a bill, patients scarcely notice the bottom line because they don’t pay most of it — their insurers do.
“What the data shows pretty clearly is that when hospitals have bargaining leverage, they tend to have higher prices,” said Zack Cooper, an associate professor of public health and economics at Yale University who has spent more than a decade studying hospital monopolies.
Over the last quarter century, Cooper said, hospital prices have risen faster than those for any other economic sector, and “hospital consolidation is one of the primary drivers.”
Federal and state officials have wavered over when to intervene when hospitals are proposing to merge. Last summer, President Donald Trump revoked former President Joe Biden’s 2021 directive that urged federal agencies to challenge mergers that could harm consumers, reversing course from Biden’s more aggressive enforcement of antitrust law. In a March memo, however, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson called for a task force on healthcare mergers that are leading to “higher prices” and “decreased quality” of care.
Several states have sought to curb healthcare monopolies. In 2023, Minnesota passed a law banning anticompetitive healthcare mergers and bolstering state oversight. In 2022, California passed a law requiring healthcare businesses to give the state a 90-day notice of large mergers and created an agency to investigate their effects on competition. And Oregon passed a law in 2021 enabling the state health department to block acquisitions and mergers of hospitals.
Nothing has stopped the overall trend, however, as hospitals seek to grow and gain leverage over insurers and competitors. Last year alone, hospital and health systems announced 46 mergers and acquisitions, according to Kaufman Hall, a healthcare business consulting firm. Five ranked as “mega-mergers,” meaning they were valued at more than $1 billion. One merged 28 hospitals across Connecticut and New York into a powerful interstate health system. Another linked Sanford Health and Marshfield Clinic Health System, a deal that created a 56-hospital system across the Midwest — including Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Wyoming — with combined revenue of about $10 billion.
Other mergers have been proposed in California, Hawai‘i, and Minnesota.
Asheville’s dominant hospital
Few places in the United States better exemplify how hospital mergers reshape healthcare than Asheville.
In 1998, the state authorized a deal that joined the city’s two acute-care hospitals, St. Joseph’s Hospital and Memorial Mission Medical Center, to create Mission Hospital. Ever since, its effects have been studied and its prices fiercely contested.
Mission Hospital, in Asheville, North Carolina, was created when the state authorized a merger that joined the city’s two acute care hospitals. More than 1,000 hospital mergers unfolded in the U.S. from 2002 to 2020. (Katie Linsky Shaw for KFF Health News)
Marcelle Crago, a nurse and lactation consultant, is one of many patients who have accused Mission Health, which operates Mission Hospital, of gouging consumers. Last year, she tweaked her knee while cross-country skiing.
“My knee went ‘pop, pop, pop,’” she recalled. She had torn her meniscus, the rubbery cartilage around the knee that acts as a shock absorber. A doctor advised her to have a portion of it removed.
Two days before the surgery, Mission Health told her the total charge would be over $9,000, according to paperwork on her case filed with the state’s Consumer Protection Division.
“I was shocked at the number,” she said.
Crago’s insurance policy from UnitedHealth Group had a high deductible, so she would have had to pay most of the cost. She decided to postpone the surgery and shop around, eventually arranging to have it done at an outpatient center not affiliated with Mission. There, the bill came to less than a third of the price Mission Health charged, according to paperwork she kept.
“The way Mission Health handled the whole thing felt predatory,” Crago recalled, noting that when she balked at the $9,000 figure, the hospital offered a 20% discount if she paid up-front. “It makes you wonder how much they are playing with prices.”
In responding to Crago’s complaint with the state, an attorney for Mission and HCA Healthcare, which owns the hospital, wrote that hospital charges “represent the cost for supporting the entire episode of care” and must cover the hospital’s investments in advanced technology, training, staff, and other critical needs.
“Patients are certainly entitled to ‘shop around’ for surgical procedures,” wrote the attorney, Phillip Jackson.
It is not just patients who bear the burden of rising hospital prices.
Marcelle Crago was cross-country skiing when she hurt her knee. She needed a portion of it removed in surgery and says she “was shocked” at the estimated $9,000 cost from Mission Health. (Katie Linsky Shaw for KFF Health News)
Over time, anyone who pays for health insurance pays a price for hospital monopolies, as insurers boost premiums as medical costs rise. The full cost for an employer to pay for an average family health insurance plan rose to more than $27,000 in 2025, up from $21,000 just six years ago, according to figures from KFF.
Around Asheville, employers and employees complain that their insurance premiums are higher because Mission’s prices are so high.
As the chef and co-founder of Cúrate restaurant in Asheville, a business with about 100 employees, Katie Button provides employee health coverage and believes she has been paying for Mission Hospital’s excessive prices, according to a pending class-action lawsuit she filed in 2021 with five residents who say the monopoly has harmed them.
Any insurance plan in Asheville must include Mission Hospital, she said, because it is the only one around. This makes the burden of its prices unavoidable.
“We are where we are because we don’t have a choice of hospitals,” Button said. “There is no other option.”
The steady creep of healthcare costs is top of mind not just in Asheville but for most U.S. voters, according to an April KFF poll. Nearly two-thirds of U.S. adults were worried about being able to afford healthcare, the poll found.
Yet while federal law allows regulators to step in and block mergers deemed to create monopolies, the FTC intervened in only about 1% of such cases from 2002 to 2020 to stop a hospital merger, according to a Yale University study. The FTC has since announced challenges to five other hospital mergers.
Birth of a monopoly
When Mission Health was formed by a merger in 1998, state officials recognized that Asheville’s new dominant hospital system would have the power to raise prices and required Mission to sign an agreement to limit spending and profit margins.
Even with these restrictions, the hospital substantially hiked prices, according to economic research cited by the FTC. But Mission’s prices were about to go up even more. In 2015, Mission Health lobbied the state legislature to drop the state restrictions, abandoning the profit limits.
“After 20 years of the hospital behaving itself, the state decided to terminate its oversight,” said Mark Hall, a professor emeritus at Wake Forest University who has written an account of the hospital’s merger history. Then, three years later, HCA, the largest hospital corporation in the country, bought Mission Health. (The Dogwood Health Trust, a nonprofit established as part of HCA’s purchase of Mission Health, helps fund KFF Health News’ coverage.)
“This put a prepackaged monopoly into the hands of the world’s largest for-profit hospital corporation,” Hall said.
Across a range of services, Mission Hospital charges more than other North Carolina hospitals, according to figures from Serif Health.
Consider the prices that Mission negotiated with UnitedHealthcare compared with those the insurer pays at Catawba Valley Medical Center. For a breast biopsy, UnitedHealth pays $7,500 at Mission and $1,700 at Catawba, according to Serif. For a hernia repair, it pays $17,700 at Mission and $9,600 at Catawba.
“The prices hospitals charge are one of the leading drivers of rising healthcare costs,” according to a UnitedHealthcare statement sent by spokesperson Cole Manbeck.
Mission spokesperson Katie Czerwinski, in a statement, said that it can be misleading to compare one hospital with another.
Mission Hospital is almost three times as large as Catawba Valley Health and is a Level 1 trauma center serving a different population, Czerwinski said. She also said that pulling individual rates for comparison paints an incomplete picture.
But other figures indicate that prices at Mission Hospital are relatively high, even when viewed collectively.
A team at the think tank Rand, led by Christopher Whaley, now a Brown University health economist, uses commercial insurance records to compare average hospital prices across the U.S. relative to those paid by Medicare. According to the Rand figures, Mission Hospital in 2024 charged prices that were 334% of prices set by Medicare. Catawba Valley Medical Center charged 237%. The state benchmark for prices is 280% of Medicare, Rand figures showed.
“The prices we pay for healthcare vary tremendously and are uncorrelated to the value we receive,” according to the Rand website.
For many in Asheville, the primary complaints about Mission Hospital focus on the quality of patient care. This is consistent with academic studies showing that the quality of care declines when hospitals have little competition.
Amid rising complaints about hospital services, North Carolina state Sen. Julie Mayfield, a Democrat, helped launch a nonprofit organization two years ago called Reclaim Healthcare WNC to hold Mission “accountable for its harmful practices.”
“Within a year of the HCA sale, I started hearing stories from physicians and other friends about all the terrible things that were happening there,” Mayfield said, most of them caused by severe staff cuts and physicians leaving.
Three times since 2024, state health inspectors working on behalf of CMS have issued “immediate jeopardy” findings to Mission Hospital, indicating problems so severe that they posed an imminent risk of serious injury or death to patients.
In the most recent CMS report, an 88-year-old woman recovering from a fall and hip surgery at Mission Hospital died after going a night without receiving a blood transfusion.
Czerwinski, the Mission Hospital spokesperson, said a proposed plan of correction “allows Mission to address the findings from the survey and complete a comprehensive review of operations.”
As more hospitals across the United States plan to merge, Mayfield said, the experience in Asheville represents a cautionary tale.
“Unregulated monopolies have never gone well for the public.”
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Washington State Standard
title: With PNW electricity demand surging, planners map out major grid upgrades
description: The Pacific Northwest will need a massive buildout of new energy infrastructure over the next six years to meet rising electricity demand, according to a draft regional power plan released Thursday.  Implementing the plan will cost the Pacific Northwest approximately $2.3 billion. And the rate of building will need to quicken to make it happen […]
text:
(Photo by Clinton Carpenter/Bonneville Power Administration)The Pacific Northwest will need a massive buildout of new energy infrastructure over the next six years to meet rising electricity demand, according to a draft regional power plan released Thursday. 
Implementing the plan will cost the Pacific Northwest approximately $2.3 billion. And the rate of building will need to quicken to make it happen by 2032. 
Last year, the Northwest Power and Conservation Council forecast regional electricity demand to increase anywhere from 50% to 100% over the next 20 years. That’s largely due to data centers, the electrification of vehicles and buildings, and population growth.
On Thursday, the council released a draft of its Ninth Power Plan. Deemed by one councilmember as the “roughest of drafts,” it will serve as a guide on the region’s path to meeting future electricity demand. Public comment for the draft is open until Oct. 16. 
The plan calls on Washington, Oregon, Idaho and western Montana to add 11,000 megawatts to the region’s grid. That’s about a third of the electricity the Northwest uses at peak demand, such as during a heat wave.
Getting there won’t be easy, and the plan doesn’t rely solely on renewable energy. 
“No single resource on its own will be able to meet our growing need for energy in the future,” said Jennifer Light, director of power planning. “Rather, a regional portfolio of cost-effective resources will achieve the right balance of economics, efficiency, reliability, and adequacy.”
Across the four-state region, the plan includes 9,000 megawatts of renewables and 2,100 megawatts of natural gas. 
In Washington, the plan calls for adding between 500 MW and 1,250 MW of natural gas to the grid by 2032. That is in accordance with the state’s clean energy policies, said Peter Jensen, a spokesperson for the council. 
While the plan directs the largest power wholesaler in the region, the Bonneville Power Administration, on which resources it should acquire, it also influences the decisions of other electricity providers in the region. The BPA operates under the U.S. Department of Energy and owns approximately 75% of the Pacific Northwest’s grid.
Throughout the two-year planning process, the BPA has “consistently expressed concerns” over the costs and complexity of the council’s energy conservation recommendations. 
This part of the plan focuses on how technology like efficient appliances, as well as building code changes, can reduce electricity demand. The region has spent billions on these types of upgrades over the last decade, according to the plan.
The BPA also questions whether the council’s proposed strategy would be less favorable for utility customers in Idaho and Montana, compared to Oregon and Washington, when it comes to providing access to energy efficiency assistance programs. 
The plan was created amid a great deal of uncertainty. Council staff pointed out that it was a challenge to predict how much electricity will be needed to supply data centers. Also unknown is how fast the region can upgrade and expand transmission line capacity and how extreme weather events could strain the grid. 
The council has published regional power plans about every five years since 1983, to lay out how the region will maintain an affordable and adequate power supply. The latest plan is expected to be finalized either by the end of this year or the beginning of 2027. 
The Northwest Power and Conservation Council was formed in 1981 following the passage of the federal Northwest Power Act. That act directed the four states to work together on regional energy planning and to stop the decline of native Columbia Basin fish species, which is primarily due to the development of hydroelectric dams in the region.
